178.quote: When a female prairie vole begins to express attraction to a male vole, she experiences a 50% increase of dopamine activity in parts of this reward system. An increase of dopamine in the brain is also associated with mate attraction in female sheep. Hence, this neural mechanism for attraction must have evolved in many species of birds and mammals - to enable individuals to prefer and focus on specific mating partners, thereby conserving valuable courtship time and energy.
178.content: Cross-species evidence: when a female prairie vole begins to express attraction to a male vole, she experiences a 50% increase of dopamine activity in parts of the reward system. An increase of dopamine in the brain is also associated with mate attraction in female sheep. This neural mechanism for attraction must have evolved in many species of birds and mammals - to enable individuals to prefer and focus on specific mating partners, thereby conserving valuable courtship time and energy.
178.where: Chapter 2 'The Drive to Love... a Natural Addiction' p. 36

179.quote: Tennov measured the duration of romantic love from the moment infatuation hit to when a 'feeling of neutrality' for one's love object began. She concluded, 'The most frequent interval, as well as the average, is between approximately 18 months and three years.' But data vary. A study that indicates serotonin activity in the blood suggests that this intoxication lasts twelve to eighteen months. And in our 2012 national Match.com survey of singles, 29% of over 5,000 men and women of every age group, background, and sexual persuasion reported that this passion lasted for two to five years; 8% remained intensely in love for six to ten years, and 18% reported that they remained madly in love for over ten years.
179.content: The duration of intense romantic love varies but is bounded. Tennov concluded that 'the most frequent interval, as well as the average, is between approximately 18 months and three years.' A study of serotonin activity in blood suggests 12 to 18 months. In the Match.com survey of over 5,000 men and women, 29% reported the passion lasting for two to five years; 8% for six to ten years; and 18% for over ten years. Either the nerve pathways for dopamine and related neurochemicals become habituated to these natural stimulants, or the production and distribution of dopamine decline.

180.quote: in another of our brain scanning experiments, led this time by psychologist Bianca Acevedo, we put seventeen long-married women and men into the fMRI scanner, ten women and seven men. Their average length of marriage was twenty-one years; most had grown children; and all had told us that they were still in love with their spouse. The results were astonishing: the VTA and other basic brain regions associated with early-stage intense romantic love were just as active among these long-term lovers as among our newly-in-love younger men and women. With one exception: Our newly-in-love participants showed activity in a specific brain region associated with anxiety, whereas in our long-term lovers this angst was replaced by new activity in brain regions linked with calm and pain suppression.
180.content: In Acevedo et al.'s fMRI brain scanning experiment, seventeen long-married women and men were scanned while viewing photos of their spouse. Average length of marriage was twenty-one years; most had grown children; all said they were still in love with their spouse. The results were astonishing: the VTA and other basic brain regions associated with early-stage intense romantic love were just as active among these long-term lovers as among newly-in-love younger men and women. One exception: newly-in-love participants showed activity in a brain region associated with anxiety, whereas in long-term lovers this angst was replaced by new activity in brain regions linked with calm and pain suppression.
180.where: Chapter 2 'The Trajectory of Love' pp. 38-39, Acevedo, Aron, Fisher, Brown long-term marriage fMRI study

181.quote: Please recall the prairie vole. These individuals form lifelong pair-bonds soon after puberty and raise several litters as a team. And this pairing has been directly correlated with neurochemical activities in the brain. When prairie voles first engage in sex, copulation triggers activity in oxytocin receptors (in the nucleus accumbens) among females and vasopressin receptors (in the ventral pallidum) among males. This stimulates dopamine release in several brain regions - producing feelings of wanting, seeking, focus, energy, pleasure, and motivation - driving these furry little creatures to prefer a particular mate, initiate a pair-bond, and express enduring attachment behaviors. But specific variations in a particular gene in the vasopressin system contribute to variability in the strength of a male prairie vole's pair-bond, including the degree to which a male expresses sexual fidelity to his partner.
181.content: When prairie voles first engage in sex, copulation triggers activity in oxytocin receptors (in the nucleus accumbens) among females and vasopressin receptors (in the ventral pallidum) among males. This stimulates dopamine release in several brain regions - producing feelings of wanting, seeking, focus, energy, pleasure, and motivation - driving these furry little creatures to prefer a particular mate, initiate a pair-bond, and express enduring attachment behaviors. Specific variations in a particular gene in the vasopressin system contribute to variability in the strength of a male prairie vole's pair-bond, including the degree to which a male expresses sexual fidelity to his partner.
181.where: Chapter 4 'Why Adultery?' Biology of Adultery section, pp. 92-93

182.quote: Men who inherited this gene scored significantly lower on the Partner Bonding Scale, a questionnaire that measures one's degree of attachment to a mate. Moreover, scores were dose-dependent. Men carrying two copies of this gene showed the lowest scores on the Partner Bonding Scale; those carrying one copy expressed more feelings of attachment; and men who had no copies of this gene were the most attached to their partner. Men carrying this vasopressin gene had also experienced more marital crises during the previous year, including threats of divorce. Once again, these results were dose-dependent. Last, the spouses of men with one or two copies of this gene scored significantly lower on questionnaires measuring marital satisfaction.
182.content: A Swedish study of 552 men, all either married or living with a partner for at least five years, investigated whether a vasopressin-receptor gene affects pair-bonding behavior. Men who inherited this gene scored significantly lower on the Partner Bonding Scale. Scores were dose-dependent: men carrying two copies of this gene showed the lowest scores; those carrying one copy expressed more feelings of attachment; and men who had no copies of this gene were the most attached to their partner. Men carrying this vasopressin gene had also experienced more marital crises during the previous year, including threats of divorce. Spouses of men with one or two copies of this gene scored significantly lower on questionnaires measuring marital satisfaction.
182.where: Chapter 4 'Why Adultery?' pp. 93-94, Walum et al. 2008 AVPR1A finding

183.quote: when neuroscientist Larry Young and colleagues modified a harmless virus to carry the genetic code for vasopressin receptors and injected the virus into males of another species, meadow voles (creatures that do not form pair-bonds), these animals also began to make solid attachments to their current sexual partners. And most important to this book: men with related genes for vasopressin transmission also tend to make more stable partnerships.
183.content: Larry Young and colleagues modified a harmless virus to carry the genetic code for vasopressin receptors and injected the virus into males of meadow voles - creatures that do not normally form pair-bonds. These animals then began to make solid attachments to their current sexual partners. This direct genetic manipulation from non-monogamous to monogamous behavior at the single-gene level is one of the strongest demonstrations that the vasopressin system is causally involved in mammalian pair-bonding.
183.where: Chapter 7 'Satisfaction Hormones' pp. 178-179, citing Larry Young prairie vole → meadow vole vector experiment

184.quote: In the now classic 'sweaty T-shirt' experiment, women sniffed the T-shirts of several anonymous men and selected the T-shirts of those they felt were the sexiest. Interestingly, they selected the T-shirts of men with genes that were different from their own in a specific region of the immune system, the major histocompatibility complex. Perhaps these women were unconsciously attracted to men with different genes because similarity between partners in this part of the immune system can lead to complications of fertility and pregnancy. Tellingly, in a subsequent investigation, women married to men who shared similar genes in this part of the immune system were also more adulterous. And the more of these genes a woman shared with her spouse, the more extra partners she engaged.
184.content: In the 'sweaty T-shirt' experiment, women sniffed the T-shirts of anonymous men and selected the T-shirts of those they felt were the sexiest. They selected the T-shirts of men with genes that were different from their own in a specific region of the immune system - the major histocompatibility complex (MHC). These women were unconsciously attracted to men with different MHC genes because similarity between partners in this part of the immune system can lead to complications of fertility and pregnancy. In a subsequent investigation, women married to men who shared similar genes in this part of the immune system were also more adulterous. The more of these genes a woman shared with her spouse, the more extra partners she engaged.
184.where: Chapter 4 'Why Adultery?' The Sweaty T-Shirt Experiment, pp. 94-95, citing Wedekind et al. 1995 and follow-up

185.quote: We are a pair-bonding species. Some 85% of cultures permit a man to have several wives, but few men actually build a harem. A man has to have a lot of goats, cows, land, money, or other impressive resources to get several women to share his wedding bed. Even then, having more than one wife can be a toothache. Co-wives fight; sometimes they even poison one another's children. We are built to rear our babies as a team of two - with a lot of helpers near the nest.
185.content: Fisher's cross-cultural / cross-species framing of human reproductive architecture. The pair-bonding species claim is grounded in two distinct empirical observations from different parts of the book: (a) the cross-cultural pattern - 85% of cultures permit polygyny but most men have only one wife at a time (Fisher prologue, source lines 100-106); and (b) the cross-species rarity - only 3% of mammals form pair-bonds to rear their young, while ~90% of avian species do (Fisher Chapter 3 on adultery in other species, source line 1710). The two findings jointly establish pair-bonding as part of human architecture while showing it is a robust but distinctive mammalian pattern.
185.where: Prologue and Chapter 3 'Is Monogamy Natural?' pp. 1 and 39-40

186.quote: The Taita of Kenya say that love comes in two forms: an irresistible longing, a 'kind of sickness'; and a deep, enduring affection for another. Brazilians say, 'Love is born in a glance and matures in a smile.' For the Koreans, sarang is a word close to the Western concept of romantic love, while chong is more like feelings of long-term attachment.
186.content: Love is distinguished by men and women around the world. The Taita of Kenya say that love comes in two forms: an irresistible longing, a 'kind of sickness'; and a deep, enduring affection for another. Brazilians say, 'Love is born in a glance and matures in a smile.' For the Koreans, sarang is a word close to the Western concept of romantic love, while chong is more like feelings of long-term attachment. Nisa, the !Kung woman of the Kalahari Desert, explained the arc of love: 'When two people are first together, their hearts are on fire and their passion is very great. After a while, the fire cools and that's how it stays. They continue to love each other, but it's in a different way - warm and dependable.'

187.quote: The contemporary psychological investigation of human attachment began with a British psychiatrist, John Bowlby, and an American psychologist, Mary Ainsworth, who proposed that, to promote the survival of their young, primates have evolved an innate attachment system designed to motivate infants to seek comfort and safety from their primary caregiver, generally mother. Since then extensive research has been done on the behaviors, feelings, and biological mechanisms associated with this attachment system in human adults and other creatures. Moreover, researchers have proposed that these attachment circuits remain active throughout the life course - serving as a foundation for emotional commitment between pair-bonded partners for the purpose of raising offspring.
187.content: The contemporary psychological investigation of human attachment began with Bowlby and Ainsworth, who proposed that, to promote the survival of their young, primates have evolved an innate attachment system designed to motivate infants to seek comfort and safety from their primary caregiver. Extensive research has shown that these attachment circuits remain active throughout the life course - serving as a foundation for emotional commitment between pair-bonded partners for the purpose of raising offspring. The adult pair-bond attachment system is an extension of, not a replacement for, the infant-caregiver attachment system.

188.quote: Like vasopressin, oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus. Unlike vasopressin, oxytocin is released in all female mammals (including women) during the birthing process. It initiates contractions of the uterus and stimulates the mammary glands to produce milk. But oxytocin also stimulates bonding between a mother and her infant. And more and more data now indicate that oxytocin can also produce feelings of attachment to a preferred mating partner. You have undoubtedly felt the power of these 'cuddle chemicals,' as vasopressin and oxytocin are sometimes called. At orgasm, the activities of oxytocin spike in men and women. These 'satisfaction hormones' undoubtedly contribute to your sense of fusion, closeness, and attachment after sweet sex with a beloved.
188.content: Like vasopressin, oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus. Unlike vasopressin, oxytocin is released in all female mammals (including women) during the birthing process. It initiates contractions of the uterus and stimulates the mammary glands to produce milk. But oxytocin also stimulates bonding between a mother and her infant. And more and more data now indicate that oxytocin can also produce feelings of attachment to a preferred mating partner. At orgasm, the activities of oxytocin spike in men and women. These satisfaction hormones undoubtedly contribute to your sense of fusion, closeness, and attachment after sweet sex with a beloved.

189.quote: From a Darwinian perspective, it is easy to explain why men are - by nature - interested in sexual variety. If an ancestral man bore children with one woman, he had, genetically speaking, 'reproduced' himself. But if he also engaged in dalliances with another woman and, by chance, sired another child, he doubled his contribution to the next generation. So those men who sought sexual variety throughout deep history also tended to have more children.
189.content: From a Darwinian perspective, it is easy to explain why men are interested in sexual variety. If an ancestral man bore children with one woman, he had, genetically speaking, reproduced himself. But if he also engaged in dalliances with another woman and sired another child, he doubled his contribution to the next generation. So those men who sought sexual variety throughout deep history also tended to have more children. Women's adultery has separate evolutionary logic: four hypotheses include (1) resource supplementation via gifts/food from lovers, (2) insurance policy against death or desertion of a primary mate, (3) 'upgrade' of genetic quality when the primary mate is deficient, and (4) genetic diversity of offspring against unpredictable environments.

190.quote: In spite of this common course of love, the three basic brain systems for mating that I have elsewhere proposed - lust, romantic love, and attachment - can actually ignite in any order. Some people have sex first, then fall in love. Some fall madly in love with someone they just met, then have sex several weeks down the road. Some even build a deep attachment to a friend at work or in their social circle, then later fall madly in love and have sex with him or her. Yet, generally, feelings of lust and passionate romantic love are triggered first, followed by feelings of deep attachment - what psychologist Theodor Reik called the warm 'afterglow.'
190.content: After a while the fire cools and that's how it stays. The three basic brain systems for mating generally transition: feelings of lust and passionate romantic love are triggered first, followed by feelings of deep attachment - what psychologist Theodor Reik called the warm 'afterglow.' But the three systems can also ignite in any order. Some people have sex first, then fall in love. Some fall madly in love with someone they just met, then have sex several weeks down the road. Some build a deep attachment to a friend at work or in their social circle, then later fall madly in love and have sex with him or her.

191.quote: Brain activations occurred in several regions of the reward system. Included were regions of the ventral tegmental area (VTA) associated with feelings of intense romantic love; the ventral pallidum, associated with feelings of deep attachment; the insular cortex and the anterior cingulate, associated with physical pain, anxiety, and the distress associated with physical pain; and the nucleus accumbens and orbitofrontal/prefrontal cortex, brain regions associated with assessing one's gains and losses - as well as craving and addiction. Most relevant to our story, activity in several of these brain regions has been correlated with the craving for cocaine and other drugs.
191.content: When my colleagues redid the brain scanning experiment to look at rejection, we found that feelings of romantic rejection lit up activity in several brain regions linked with profound attachment, deep addiction, and physical pain. When you are rejected in love, many brain systems go to work, and rejection is one of the most painful experiences a human being can endure.
191.where: Chapter 5 'Blueprint for Divorce' pp. 127-128, Fisher/Brown rejection fMRI study

192.quote: schizophrenia, Parkinson's disease, and other ailments alter dopamine pathways. In fact, in the last chapter of this book, 'Future Sex,' I will discuss my theory that several serotonin-enhancing antidepressants, such as Prozac, Zoloft, and the newer serotonin boosters, can suppress dopamine pathways, dull the emotions, and potentially kill romantic passion.
192.content: Several serotonin-enhancing antidepressants, such as Prozac, Zoloft, and the newer serotonin boosters, can suppress dopamine pathways, dull the emotions, and potentially kill romantic passion. The romantic-love component of M14 depends on the dopamine-norepinephrine-low-serotonin neurochemical profile; increasing serotonin chemically disrupts this profile and may interfere with the normal operation of the romantic-love system.
192.where: Chapter 2 'Love Blindness' pp. 36-37 and Chapter 16 'Future Sex'

193.quote: So I shall propose that these brain systems for lust, romantic love and attachment began to take their human forms soon after our forebears descended from the fast-disappearing trees of Africa to walk on two feet instead of four and form pair-bonds to rear their helpless young at least through infancy as a team. Lucy loved, some 3.2 million years ago. She felt sexual craving, passionate rapture, and deep feelings of attachment toward her mate - a symphony, sometimes even a cacophony of joyous, exciting, and calming sensations.
193.content: The three basic brain systems for lust, romantic love and attachment began to take their human forms soon after our forebears descended from the fast-disappearing trees of Africa to walk on two feet and form pair-bonds to rear their helpless young at least through infancy as a team. Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis) loved, some 3.2 million years ago. She felt sexual craving, passionate rapture, and deep feelings of attachment toward her mate - a symphony, sometimes a cacophony of joyous, exciting, and calming sensations.

194.quote: And men feel this passion just as powerfully as women. Tennov wrote of her 800+ informants that men and women experienced this intense passion 'in roughly equal proportions.' My colleagues and I have now confirmed this. In our fMRI study of young happy lovers, men showed just as much activity in the VTA and other neural pathways for romantic passion as women did.
194.content: In our fMRI studies of romantic love, men and women showed equivalent activation in the core romantic-love brain regions (VTA and related dopamine pathways). Tennov reported that men and women experience this passion in roughly equal proportions from her 800+ informants. In contrast to folk belief that men are less emotional or less capable of romantic love, the neural data show men and women feel this passion equivalently.

195.quote: Many things surprised me when I first walked into a Hadza camp mid-morning on a torrid, sunny day in 2013, but I remember being especially struck by how everyone was apparently doing nothing. Hadza camps consist of a few temporary grass huts that blend in with the surrounding bushes. I didn't realize I had walked into a camp until I found myself amid about fifteen Hadza men, women, and children who were sitting on the ground as shown in figure 2. The women and children were relaxing on one side, and the men on another. One fellow was straightening some arrows, and a few children were toddling about, but no one was engaged in any hard work. To be sure, the Hadza weren't lounging on sofas, watching TV, munching potato chips, and sipping soda, but they were doing what so many health experts warn us to avoid: sitting.
195.content: Lieberman's first-person observation of a Hadza hunter-gatherer camp in 2013 contradicts the standard Western assumption about hunter-gatherer activity levels. Upon arrival he found Hadza men, women, and children sitting on the ground, doing light chores, with no one engaged in hard work. This became the load-bearing empirical touchstone for M10's resolution-conditions framing: 'normal' human physical activity is embedded in daily life rather than set aside as 'exercise', and includes substantial rest and sitting.
195.where: Chapter 1 'Are We Born to Rest or Run?' pp. ~15-17

196.quote: Among the many studies of the Hadza, one asked forty-six Hadza adults to wear lightweight heart rate monitors for several days. According to these sensors, the average adult Hadza spends a grand total of three hours and forty minutes a day doing light activities and two hours and fourteen minutes a day doing moderate or vigorous activities. Although these few hours of hustling and bustling per day make them about twelve times more active than the average American or European, by no stretch of the imagination could one characterize their workloads as backbreaking. On average, the women walk five miles a day and dig for several hours, whereas the men walk between seven and ten miles a day. And when they aren't being very active, they typically rest or do light work.
196.content: Quantitative data from Hadza heart rate monitor study: average adult Hadza spends ~3h40m/day on light activities and ~2h14m/day on moderate-vigorous activities. Hadza men walk 7-10 miles/day, women walk 5 miles/day and dig for several hours. This is roughly 12x more active than the average American or European - but the absolute level is modest, not 'backbreaking'. The finding grounds M10's claim that hunter-gatherer physical activity is embedded rather than exercise-shaped, and is far less than Western intuitions assume.
196.where: Chapter 1 'Are We Born to Rest or Run?' pp. ~17

197.quote: Although there is much variation, PALs of hunter-gatherers average 1.9 for men and 1.8 for women, slightly below PAL scores for subsistence farmers, which average 2.1 for men and 1.9 for women. To put these values into context, hunter-gatherer PALs are about the same as those of factory workers and farmers in the developed world (1.8), and about 15 percent higher than PALs of people with desk jobs in developed countries (1.6). In other words, typical hunter-gatherers are about as physically active as Americans or Europeans who include about an hour of exercise in their daily routine. In case you are wondering, most mammals in the wild have PALs of 3.3 or more, nearly twice as high as hunter-gatherers. Thus, comparatively speaking, humans who must hunt and gather all the food they eat and make everything they own by hand are substantially less active than average free-ranging mammals.
197.content: Physical Activity Level (PAL) data across populations reveals the surprising result that typical hunter-gatherers are only about 15% more active than industrialized people with desk jobs - equivalent to adding one hour of walking per day to a sedentary Westerner's routine. Hunter-gatherer PALs average 1.9 (men) / 1.8 (women) vs 1.6 for desk workers. Wild mammals average PAL 3.3+, nearly twice hunter-gatherer levels. This is Lieberman's central empirical claim against 'we evolved to exercise' intuitions: humans are at the less-active end of the mammalian spectrum, and the Western sedentary gap is smaller than folk imagination assumes.
197.where: Chapter 1 'Are We Born to Rest or Run?' pp. ~19-20

198.quote: My opinion is that while many animals are driven by deep instincts to move, sometimes causing pleasure, exercise as we define it - discretionary, planned physical activity for the sake of physical improvement - is a uniquely human behavior. In fact, I think it is fair to make two generalizations about human exercise. First, while youngsters have always played and sports are a human universal, exercise outside the context of sports was extremely rare until relatively recently. Second, as recent technological and social developments have diminished industrialized people's need to be physically active, a growing chorus of experts has never ceased to raise the alarm that we aren't exercising enough.
198.content: Lieberman's theoretical framing of exercise as a uniquely modern human behavior rather than an evolved adaptation. He distinguishes play (common across mammals, driven by deep instincts) from exercise (discretionary, planned physical activity for physical improvement - rare outside sports until recently). This is load-bearing for M10's framing that 'normal' movement is embedded in life rather than set aside as exercise, and for DA4's reading of exercise as a proxy category that only emerged when daily physical activity was extracted by technological laborsaving.
198.where: Chapter 1 'Are We Born to Rest or Run?' pp. ~21-22

199.quote: We have also medicalized exercise. By this I mean we pathologize a lack of physical activity, and we prescribe particular doses and types of exercise to help prevent and treat disease. The U.S. government recommends I engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate or 75 minutes of vigorous exercise a week and weight train at least twice a week. Epidemiologists have calculated that this level of activity will reduce my risk of dying prematurely by 50 percent and lower my chances of getting heart disease, Alzheimer's, and certain cancers by roughly 30 to 50 percent. Insurance companies offer me incentives to exercise, and entire professions have sprung up to motivate me to exercise in the first place, help me work out, and fix me up once I get injured.
199.content: Lieberman's description of the medicalization, commercialization, and industrialization of exercise as modern substitutes for the daily physical activity that industrialization extracted. He frames this explicitly as pathologizing inactivity and prescribing dose-response exercise. This is a clean DA4 Proxy Hijacking case: the embedded daily-movement target has been replaced by a market proxy (gym membership, specialized clothing, activity trackers, prescribed minutes) that only partially captures the original function.
199.where: Chapter 1 'Are We Born to Rest or Run?' pp. ~24

200.quote: When Herman Pontzer and his colleagues measured daily energy expenditures in the Hadza, they were surprised to find that the highly active Hadza spend about the same total number of calories per day as sedentary industrialized people with the same lean body weight. In addition, when Pontzer and colleagues collected energetic data from adults in many countries including the United States, Ghana, Jamaica, and South Africa, they observed that more active people spent only slightly more calories per day than more sedentary people who weighed the same. In addition, individuals who were more physically active didn't have total energy budgets as high as their exertions would predict. How could someone who spent five hundred extra calories a day exercising not have a total energy budget that is five hundred calories higher? The proposed explanation is that people's total energy budgets are constrained: if I use five hundred extra calories walking, I'll spend less energy on my resting metabolism to help pay for my exertions.
200.content: The Pontzer constrained energy expenditure hypothesis: highly active Hadza spend about the same total daily energy as sedentary industrialized people with the same lean body weight. Across countries (US, Ghana, Jamaica, South Africa), more active people spend only slightly more calories per day than sedentary people of the same weight. The proposed mechanism is metabolic compensation - when one burns extra calories exercising, resting metabolism is reduced to keep total energy budget roughly constant. This is load-bearing for M13 Energy Regulation and for DA4 (exercise-as-weight-loss is a weak proxy for metabolic health).

201.quote: Among the many hyperbolic statements written about sitting, maybe the most extreme is that sitting is the new smoking. While cigarettes are novel, addictive, expensive, smelly, toxic, and the world's number one killer, sitting is as old as the hills and utterly natural. More truthfully, the problem isn't sitting itself, but hours upon hours of inactive sitting combined with little to no exercise. If our ancestors from generations ago behaved like today's hunter-gatherers and farmers, then they likely sat for five to ten hours a day, as much as some but not all contemporary Americans and Europeans. But they also got plenty of physical activity when not sitting, and when these chairless ancestors plunked themselves down, they didn't rest in supportive chairs with seat backs; instead, they squirmed as they squatted, kneeled, or sat on the ground, using about the same degree of muscle activity in their thighs, calves, and backs as when they stood. When the Hadza sit, squat, or kneel, they typically do so for only fifteen minutes at a time.
201.content: Lieberman explicitly debunks the 'sitting is the new smoking' meme as hyperbolic. The problem is not sitting itself - hunter-gatherers sit for 5-10 hours per day, as much as many Western office workers - but rather hours of inactive sitting without intervening physical activity. Hunter-gatherer sitting is typically shorter bouts (15 min at a time for Hadza), combined with light chores, child care, and frequent standing. The claim reframes M10 as a cascade about muscle-engagement distribution throughout the day rather than a blanket condemnation of rest.

202.content: The Danish 2-week sedentary-forced experiment: healthy young men paid to sit for a fortnight and take no more than 1500 steps per day (about a mile) gained 7% more organ (visceral) fat and began to exhibit classic signs of chronic inflammation including reduced ability to take up blood sugar after a meal. The mechanism is clear: inactivity + adequate calories → organ fat accumulation → inflammatory cytokines → metabolic dysregulation. This is load-bearing for the M10/M8/DC1 cascade - sedentarism drives the allostatic-load pathway through the organ-fat-inflammation channel.

203.quote: In order to elucidate the links between exercise and aging, I propose a corollary to the grandmother hypothesis, which I call the active grandparent hypothesis. According to this idea, human longevity was not only selected for but also made possible by having to work moderately during old age to help as many children, grandchildren, and other younger relatives as possible to survive and thrive. That is, while there might have been selection for genes (as yet unidentified) that help humans live past the age of fifty, there was also selection for genes that repair and maintain our bodies when we are physically active. As a result, many of the mechanisms that slow aging and extend life are turned on by physical activity, especially as we get older. Human health and longevity are thus extended both by and for physical activity.
203.content: Lieberman's own theoretical contribution - the active grandparent hypothesis - proposes that human longevity was not only selected for but also made possible by physical activity in older age. The core mechanism: humans evolved unique longevity BECAUSE grandparents who stayed physically active (walking, digging, carrying, provisioning grandchildren) increased their inclusive fitness through kin-selection effects, AND natural selection favored genes that repair and maintain the body in response to physical activity stress. Human longevity is thus extended BOTH by and FOR physical activity. This is the central evolutionary argument for M10's cascade - the repair/maintenance mechanisms that slow aging are turned on by movement, especially as we age, because natural selection never had a version of our species in which old people were inactive.

204.quote: One of the most venerable long-term studies on how exercise affects aging is the Cooper Center Longitudinal Study in Dallas, started in 1970 by the man who coined the term 'aerobics,' Dr. Kenneth Cooper. One of its analyses tracked more than ten thousand men and three thousand women older than thirty-five to test if physically fit exercisers lived longer and healthier lives. They generally did. After adjusting for age (because an older person is more likely to pass away in a given year than a younger person), Cooper found that the most physically fit men and women had mortality rates about one-third to one-fourth of those who were least fit. Further, a subsample of those who were initially out of shape but started to exercise and increased their fitness halved their age-adjusted mortality rate compared to those who remained inactive and unfit.
204.content: The Cooper Center Longitudinal Study (Kenneth Cooper, Dallas, 1970-) tracked 10,000+ men and 3,000+ women over age 35 to test the effect of cardiovascular fitness on mortality and chronic disease. Findings: the most physically fit had mortality rates about one-third to one-fourth of the least fit after age adjustment. A subsample initially out of shape who increased their fitness halved their age-adjusted mortality rate. Among 18,000+ middle-aged individuals tracked for chronic disease, the most fit were about half as likely to develop diabetes and Alzheimer's, and if they got sick, did so later. This is a primary empirical grounding for M10's cascade effects on health span.

205.quote: In a celebrated study, the Stanford medical professor James Fries showed that preventive medicine could help people stay healthier for longer through a compression of morbidity. Fries initially based his argument on a massive study that measured life span, disability, and three risk factors for disease (high body weight, smoking, and lack of exercise) among more than twenty-three hundred alumni from the University of Pennsylvania. Predictably, the alums with two or more risk factors died 3.6 to 3.9 years earlier than those with one or no risk factors; perhaps more impressively, they lengthened their period of disability prior to death by 5.8 to 8.3 years. Simply put, an unhealthy lifestyle affects morbidity twice as much as mortality.
205.content: Fries's compression-of-morbidity model: preventive behavior (exercise, not smoking, normal weight) shortens the period of disability before death. From a University of Pennsylvania cohort of 2,300+ alumni, people with two or more risk factors died 3.6-3.9 years earlier AND lengthened their disability period by 5.8-8.3 years. Unhealthy lifestyle affects morbidity roughly twice as much as mortality. This is load-bearing for the M10 health-span-vs-life-span distinction: physical activity's effects are primarily on compression of morbidity, not on raw life extension.

206.quote: One effort to do this is the Stanford Runners Study conducted by, once again, James Fries. In 1984, he and his students began studying more than five hundred members of amateur running clubs along with more than four hundred healthy but physically inactive controls. Back then, the subjects were over the age of fifty and healthy: few smoked, none drank heavily, and none were obese. Then, for the next twenty-one years, Fries and his colleagues patiently kept track of each subject's physical activity habits, administered a yearly disability questionnaire that measures functions like the ability to walk, dress, and do routine activities, and recorded the year and cause of every death that occurred.
206.content: The Stanford Runners Study (Fries 1984-2005, 21-year follow-up): 500+ amateur runners over age 50 vs 400+ healthy sedentary controls matched on smoking and obesity status. After 21 years, non-runners were ~3x more likely to die in a given year, ~2x more likely to die of heart disease and cancer, ~3x more likely to die of neurological disease, and >10x more likely to die of infections. Runners' disability scores were roughly half of non-runners' by study end - equivalent to being ~15 years younger by this measure. This isolates physical activity's effect on morbidity from the confounds of smoking and obesity, and is load-bearing for the M10/DC1 compression-of-morbidity cascade.

207.quote: My last book, The Story of the Human Body, made the case that many of the diseases that kill us slowly today are mismatch diseases caused by our bodies being imperfectly or inadequately adapted to modern environmental conditions like smoking, obesity, and physical inactivity. Although these diseases are commonly classified as diseases of aging because they tend to arise when we are middle-aged, they are not caused by age, nor should they be considered inevitable consequences of aging. Plenty of people live to old age without getting these diseases, which rarely if ever afflict elderly hunter-gatherers and many aged people who live in subsistence societies.
207.content: Lieberman's explicit mismatch framing of the epidemiological transition and 'diseases of aging'. Many chronic noninfectious diseases that kill us slowly today (heart disease, type 2 diabetes, Alzheimer's, chronic respiratory disease, osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, autoimmune diseases) are mismatch diseases caused by our bodies being inadequately adapted to modern environmental conditions like smoking, obesity, and physical inactivity. Although they are commonly classified as 'diseases of aging' because they tend to arise in middle age, they are not caused by aging per se and are rare among elderly hunter-gatherers. This grounds P3 (systematic mismatch) at the epidemiological scale and M10 specifically as one of the three primary mismatch axes.

208.quote: For thousands of generations, the health span and life span of a typical hunter-gatherer who did not die in infancy probably looked something like the top graph in figure 28. The graph is based on medical surveys of hunter-gatherers, who mostly die from respiratory and infectious diseases, violence, and accidents and have a relatively low incidence of long-term chronic noninfectious conditions. These and other data indicate that about two-thirds of older hunter-gatherers remain at high functional capacity with limited morbidity until just before death, which most often occurs in the seventh decade. Accordingly, their health span and life span are very similar.
208.content: Medical surveys of hunter-gatherers show ~2/3 of older hunter-gatherers remain at high functional capacity with limited morbidity until just before death, which most often occurs in the seventh decade. Their health span and life span are very similar - they die mostly from respiratory and infectious diseases, violence, and accidents rather than from chronic noninfectious diseases. This is the empirical contrast case for the industrial extension-of-morbidity pattern and is load-bearing for M10's cascade framing: sedentarism contributes to the gap between life span and health span that defines the industrialized mortality profile.

209.quote: In a famous 1986 study, Eric Ravussin and colleagues asked 177 people to spend twenty-four hours (one at a time) in an enclosed ten-by-twelve-foot chamber that measured precisely how many calories they spent. To the researchers' surprise, the individuals who fidgeted spent between one hundred and eight hundred calories more per day than those who sat inertly. Other studies have found that simply fidgeting while seated can expend as much as twenty calories an hour as well as promote beneficial levels of blood flow to restless arms and legs. One study even found a 30 percent lower rate of all-cause mortality among people who fidget after adjusting for other forms of physical activity, smoking, diet, and alcohol consumption.
209.content: The Ravussin 1986 chamber-calorimeter study: 177 people each spent 24 hours in a sealed chamber measuring precise caloric expenditure. Fidgeters spent between 100 and 800 calories MORE per day than those who sat inertly. Subsequent work: fidgeting can expend ~20 calories per hour while seated. One study found a 30% lower rate of all-cause mortality among fidgeters after adjusting for other physical activity, smoking, diet, and alcohol. This is a counterintuitive but load-bearing data point for M10's cascade framing - low-intensity involuntary movement throughout the day has measurable metabolic and mortality effects, reinforcing the embedded-movement reading of the mechanism.

210.quote: play fighting typically involves the use of behavior patterns from other, functional contexts, is the nape nuzzling of rats derived from serious fighting or from some other form of social behavior? In chapter 2, we will characterize the aggressive and the sexual and non-sexual amicable behavior of rats and place playful nape nuzzling in an appropriate context.
210.content: Pellis & Pellis's 1987 foundational finding: play-fighting in rats differs from serious fighting in both the TARGET of attack (the nape of the neck in play vs other body regions in serious fighting) and the TACTICS of fighting (role reversal between attacker and defender in play vs persistent asymmetry in serious fighting). This is the load-bearing behavioral-marker finding for identifying play as a real behavioral category distinct from aggression - not merely 'low-intensity fighting' but a qualitatively different behavior with its own rules and developmental trajectory.

211.quote: Ablation of the orbital frontal cortex (OFC) produces subordinate rats that fail to make this discrimination; these rats are most likely to use the partial rotation tactic, irrespective of the social status of their partner. What is more, OFC-damaged rats also fail to adjust their responses depending on the identity of their social partners in non-play social interactions. The OFC thus seems critical in modulating social responses in a way that is sensitive to the identity of the partner.
211.content: Pellis lab finding: ablation of the orbital frontal cortex (OFC) in rats produces animals that fail to discriminate social partners - they use the same defensive tactics regardless of whether their partner is a dominant or subordinate male, and they fail to adjust responses by partner identity in non-play social interactions too. This is the specific neuroanatomical evidence that the OFC is load-bearing for social-partner-sensitive behavioral calibration - the exact mechanism M4 Social Calibration/Play depends on.
211.where: Chapter 4 'So, What Does Playing Buy You?' pp. ~90

212.quote: We found that play fighting in juvenile rats alters the dendritic branching of the neurons of the prefrontal cortex, with the arborization of the basilar dendrites of the OFC cells increasing and that of the apical dendrites of the mPFC cells decreasing.
212.content: Pellis lab original finding: juvenile play fighting experience changes the dendritic branching (arborization) of neurons in the prefrontal cortex - specifically, basilar dendrites of OFC cells increase and apical dendrites of mPFC cells decrease in response to play fighting experience. Rats raised with more play partners (3 peers vs 1 peer vs adult female only) show a progressively incremental level of play experience and corresponding PFC anatomical changes. This is the clearest empirical evidence that play physically shapes the brain circuits underlying social calibration.
212.where: Chapter 4 'So, What Does Playing Buy You?' pp. ~91-92

213.quote: Play deprivation leads to a reduction in the ability of the animal to formulate and engage behavioral options dependent on the executive functions of the prefrontal cortex - the same kinds of problems that animals have when they are reared normally but are subjected to experimental damage of their prefrontal cortex. Complementary to these findings is our demonstration of play fighting experience changing the anatomy of neurons in this area of the cortex.
213.content: Play deprivation leads to a reduction in behavioral options that depend on prefrontal-cortex executive functions - the same kinds of deficits produced by experimental PFC damage in normally-reared rats. Play-deprived rats show cognitive, sexual, and social deficits. This directly parallels the PFC-damage phenotype, giving a functional bridge between play experience and PFC development: play shapes the circuits, and the circuits mediate social competence.
213.where: Chapter 4 'So, What Does Playing Buy You?' pp. ~92

214.quote: The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), another important subdivision of the prefrontal cortex (see figure 3.6), has also been implicated in regulating some features of juvenile play fighting - rats with damage to the mPFC initiate less play and seem to have problems in suppressing the use of defensive tactics that make reciprocity difficult to maintain. That is, these rats are less interested in playing, but once they do play, they play to win. Their lack of reciprocity leads to a greater likelihood of escalating to serious fighting with their intact partner.
214.content: Medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) damage produces rats that initiate less play AND fail at reciprocity once engaged - they 'play to win' rather than maintain the back-and-forth of normal play fighting, escalating to serious fighting. This complements the OFC finding (partner-discrimination failure) by showing that a different PFC subregion handles the reciprocity-maintenance function. The OFC/mPFC dissociation grounds M4 at a specific neuroanatomical level.
214.where: Chapter 4 'So, What Does Playing Buy You?' pp. ~91

215.quote: The prefrontal cortex, of which the OFC is a part, is what is known as the executive area of the brain; a part of the brain that guides one's choice in how to behave in different situations based on the prevailing context, on goals, past experiences, and available alternatives. It is an area of the brain that matures over the juvenile and early pubertal period, and appears to be, during this time, particularly sensitive to experiential feedback.
215.content: Pellis & Pellis's theoretical framing of the prefrontal cortex as the 'executive area' that matures during the juvenile and early-pubertal period, and is particularly sensitive to experiential feedback during that window. This framing establishes the juvenile period as a critical developmental window for M4 Social Calibration - play fighting is not just one of many juvenile behaviors but is the specific experience that tunes the maturing executive circuits.
215.where: Chapter 4 'So, What Does Playing Buy You?' pp. ~90-91

216.quote: emotional responses are dependent on the activation of the amygdala, and, as we discussed in chapter 3, the amygdala is likely crucial to ensuring playful reciprocity. The prefrontal cortex dampens the activity of the amygdala, which thus prevents emotional overreaction. Here is a potential mechanism by which experience with play fighting in the juvenile period refines the prefrontal circuits, and, in doing so, produces animals that are better able to regulate their subcortically generated emotions.
216.content: Pellis's causal-mechanism proposal: play fighting in the juvenile period refines prefrontal circuits that dampen amygdala activity, which in turn prevents emotional overreaction in adult social situations. The amygdala is load-bearing for emotional-response generation (including the emotional content of play reciprocity), and the PFC dampens the amygdala - so play-induced PFC refinement is how juveniles develop adult emotional regulation.
216.where: Chapter 4 'So, What Does Playing Buy You?' pp. ~93

217.quote: In rats, play fighting is not limited to the juvenile period - although it is most frequent at that age - and seems to be used to achieve both delayed and immediate benefits. By engaging in play fighting, both juveniles and adults can regulate their stress response. That is, by playing, the animals can calm themselves following a frightening, but not too frightening, experience. In addition, male adult rats use play fighting as a means of social assessment and manipulation in the context of dominance relationships. Thus, in at least two ways, play fighting provides the rats with immediate benefits.
217.content: Pellis's synthesis: play fighting has BOTH delayed benefits (social competence developing over the juvenile period) AND immediate benefits (stress regulation in both juveniles and adults). By engaging in play, animals can calm themselves following frightening but not too-frightening experiences. Adult male rats also use play fighting as social-assessment and manipulation in dominance relationships. This dual-timescale functionality challenges the common definition of play as 'behavior without immediate purpose' and is load-bearing for M4's cascade structure.

218.quote: From the standpoint of murid rodents, only rats seem to have moved play beyond its immediate involvement in the development of sexual skills. In rats, the organization of play fighting is more modified than we see in Syrian golden hamsters, and is crucially involved in the development of socially competent behavior that extends into many domains beyond the sexual. Thus, the juvenile version is modified so as to ensure the development of social competence more generally. Even more strikingly, play fighting itself is retained into adulthood as a tool for social assessment and manipulation.
218.content: Pellis's four-stage evolutionary model of play fighting: (1) precocious sexual behavior; (2) increased frequency of rudimentary juvenile play to facilitate sexual development; (3) modification of play organization for prolonged wrestling bouts (true play fighting); (4) complete emancipation from sexual function, with play serving broader social-competence development and being retained into adulthood (emancipated play fighting). Rats are the clearest case of stage 4 among murid rodents. This model is Pellis's own theoretical contribution and grounds the phylogenetic claims for M4 and DA8.

219.quote: Not all the deficits that arise from lack of play fighting experience in the juvenile period require the actual physical contact afforded by play fighting. When deprived of play fighting experience as juveniles, rats show a range of cognitive, sexual, and social deficits. As shown by Dorothy Einon and her colleagues, juveniles reared in social isolation grow into cognitively competent adults if they have but one hour per day of exposure to a peer, with whom the majority of the time is spent in play fighting. In the 1950s, the Forgays showed that if rats that had been reared in social isolation as juveniles were given the opportunity to watch normally raised juveniles engage in peer interactions, they would also grow into adults that were not cognitively challenged. Thus, for rats, merely observing other rats play fighting is enough to protect their developing brains from the ill effects of being raised in isolation. But watching other rats engage in normal interactions seems to be insufficient for these rats to develop normal sexual competency, or the ability to execute socially coordinated actions.
219.content: Critical methodological finding: not all the deficits from play deprivation can be explained by a single mechanism. Rats reared in social isolation but given an hour a day of peer exposure (with most of that time in play fighting) grow into cognitively competent adults. Rats that merely WATCH normally-raised juveniles also recover cognitive function. BUT watching is insufficient for normal sexual competency or socially coordinated action - those require actual play-fighting experience. Guinea pigs show a different pattern (watching sexual play is sufficient for sexual competency). This dissociation demonstrates that play fighting has multiple developmental functions operating through different mechanisms.
219.where: Chapter 4 'So, What Does Playing Buy You?' pp. ~89

220.quote: Measures of cortical thickness reveal that these more masculine rats have a greater volume of cortex and that the sex-typical asymmetry of their right hemisphere versus their left one is exaggerated relative to control males that were injected with an equal volume of oil. There is nothing particularly unexpected in this finding. However, when the untreated playmates of the testosterone-treated and oil-treated animals were compared, it was found that the partners of the more playful rats also tended to have greater cortical thickness. Just growing up with a more playful partner influences the development of the cortex!
220.content: Pellis lab finding: male rats injected with testosterone shortly after birth play more AND develop greater cortical thickness, with exaggerated right-vs-left hemisphere asymmetry. Critically, the UNTREATED playmates of testosterone-treated rats also tended to have greater cortical thickness. Just growing up with a more playful partner influences cortical development in the observer. This is strong evidence that play experience (including as a partner) physically shapes the brain - cortex is not just passively maturing during the juvenile period but is being actively shaped by social play interactions.
220.where: Chapter 4 'So, What Does Playing Buy You?' pp. ~93

221.quote: During the juvenile period, play fighting is organized in such a manner as to maximize the experience of losing and regaining control over one's own body and that of one's play partner. A lack of such experience leads to a reduction in social competence, as does brain damage to specific brain areas. Conversely, this juvenile experience alters the organization of those same areas of the brain. That is, experience in play fighting in the juvenile period
221.content: Pellis synthesis at chapter-summary level: social competence can be compromised by two distinct mechanisms - either by lack of play fighting experience during the juvenile period OR by brain damage to specific prefrontal and amygdala regions. These two mechanisms produce similar phenotypes (failure to discriminate social partners, failed reciprocity, escalation to serious fighting), confirming that play fighting is not incidentally correlated with social-competence development but is causally necessary for it.

222.quote: Our model is thus consistent with the general model developed by Gordon Burghardt to account for the multifaceted evolution of all kinds of play throughout the animal kingdom. Primary processes, such as piecemeal behavioral development, sufficient extra nutrition and freedom from predation, make play-like behavior possible, and then, secondary and tertiary processes can transform that play-like behavior into more complex and functionally diverse play.
222.content: Pellis frames their own rat-fighting model as consistent with Gordon Burghardt's broader evolutionary model of play across the animal kingdom. Burghardt's framework: primary processes (piecemeal behavioral development, sufficient extra nutrition, freedom from predation) make play-like behavior possible; secondary and tertiary processes can then transform that play-like behavior into more complex and functionally diverse play. This provides the phylogenetic scaffolding for why play evolved in some lineages and not others - it's not just a neurochemical affordance but requires specific ecological and developmental conditions.

223.quote: In neurological terms, this change can be readily affected by a minor alteration to the reward systems of the hypothalamus, nucleus accumbens and amygdala. With a minimal change in the regulation of these juvenile interactions, it becomes reasonable to label them as play, albeit of a rudimentary form
223.content: Pellis's identification of the neural substrates for play-motivated behavior: juvenile play interactions can be readily modified by alterations to the reward systems of the hypothalamus, nucleus accumbens, and amygdala. At the earlier evolutionary stages of play, these subcortical reward circuits are the primary regulators; at later stages (stage 4 emancipated play in rats), cortical mechanisms (PFC, motor cortex) add novel control layers on top. This grounds M4 at the subcortical-reward level and connects it to the DA8 phylogenetic-priority cascade (older circuits, newer cortical elaboration on top).

224.quote: If a rat is experimentally injected with infectious bacteria, it behaves a bit like I did after the dentist. It withdraws from social contact with other animals, it doesn't move so much, its sleeping and eating cycles are disturbed. In short, infection reliably causes a syndrome in animals - called sickness behaviour - that is roughly recognisable as akin to the human experience of depression. In fact, you don't even need to infect a rat to see this sickness behaviour. It is enough to inject the rat with cytokines, proving that it is not the germ itself that causes sickness behaviour but the immune response to infection. Inflammation directly causes depression-like behaviours in animals - that is beyond doubt.
224.content: Dantzer's foundational finding (Bullmore synthesizes): injecting a rat with infectious bacteria produces sickness behavior - social withdrawal, reduced movement, disturbed sleep-wake cycles, reduced eating. Injecting cytokines alone (without bacteria) reproduces the syndrome, demonstrating it is the IMMUNE RESPONSE that causes sickness behavior, not the pathogen itself. Inflammation directly causes depression-like behaviors in animals. This is load-bearing for M8's cascade - the immune system drives behavioral change via cytokine signaling regardless of pathogen presence.
224.where: Chapter 1 'Daring to Think Differently' pp. early chapters

225.quote: when healthy young people were injected with a vaccine against typhoid, their immune systems reacted like the immune system of a rat injected with bacteria, and cytokine levels spiked in their blood. The vaccinated volunteers also became mildly depressed and their post-vaccination depression was associated with greater activation of regions of the brain that we know are hard-wired for emotional expression.
225.content: Human bridge experiment: healthy young people injected with a typhoid vaccine had their cytokine levels spike (mirroring the rat-bacterial-injection response), became mildly depressed, and showed greater activation of brain regions hard-wired for emotional expression on fMRI. This provides the human-side causal chain: peripheral cytokine elevation → altered brain activity → mood change. The bridge between animal model and human experience that had been missing from the inflammation-depression hypothesis.

226.quote: In much the same way as an infected animal, a wounded or sick human, like me after root canal work, shows a characteristic pattern of behaviour. Ill or invalid human beings withdraw from social contact, reduce their physical activity, eat less, and are less hedonic. They are also quietly anxious and have disturbed sleep. This is a very engrained and consistent pattern of behaviour, written into our DNA by genes that must have evolved millions of years before H sapiens. As we have seen, this sickness behaviour is strongly driven by innate inflammatory mechanisms.
226.content: Bullmore's evolutionary framing of sickness behavior: in ancestral environments with high infant/adult mortality from infection, genes that made the innate inflammatory response more aggressive would be selected. Those same genes drive the characteristic sickness-behavior syndrome (social withdrawal, reduced activity, loss of appetite, disturbed sleep, anxiety) - not as a defect but as an evolved protective response. Sickness behavior is 'genetically programmed convalescence' that conserves metabolic resources for immune function.
226.where: Chapter 5 'Why?' - evolutionary framing of sickness behavior

227.content: Bullmore's key hypothesis on the function of sickness-behavior social withdrawal: it serves a tribe-level protective function in ancestral human groups. Extended-family tribes of few hundred genetically related individuals were vulnerable to contagious disease wiping out the whole gene pool. Isolation of the sick individual - quarantine - reduces the risk of uninfected tribal members becoming infected. The patient's inflamed behavior puts HIM at anxiety-provoking risk of predation at the margins, for the sake of the tribe as a whole. Sickness behavior was naturally selected as much for tribal-DNA survival as individual-DNA survival.

228.quote: You can imagine that gene mutations that made the macrophages slightly angrier, or that made cytokine signalling slightly stronger, could be advantageous if they strengthened the front-line defences of the innate immune system against the bacterial killers that attack babies and young children. Genes that have randomly mutated to deliver enhanced killing power against germs will be naturally selected because people who have inherited them will be more likely to survive childhood and reach the reproductively active stage of life at puberty. In an environment like the ancestral savannah, with a high infant mortality rate due to infection, there will be a strong natural-selection pressure on genes that boost innate inflammatory response.
228.content: Bullmore's argument that natural selection in the ancestral environment strongly favored genes that boost innate inflammatory response: gene mutations making macrophages 'slightly angrier' or strengthening cytokine signaling would be advantageous given the high ancestral infant mortality from infection. This selection pressure for enhanced inflammatory genes produces, as a side effect, the enhanced sickness-behavior syndrome - we inherit the aggressive inflammation that kept our ancestors alive, and the behavioral cost is built into the same genetic package.
228.where: Chapter 5 'Why?' - natural selection for inflammatory response

229.quote: In the 30 years following Prozac, the field has not flourished but fizzled out. There have been no major new advances in drug treatment, or psychological treatment come to that, for depression or any other mental health disorder, since about 1990. I'll say that again. When I started specialist training as a 29-year-old psychiatrist, at St George's Hospital and then the Bethlem Royal and Maudsley Hospital, in London in 1989, it was recommended we study a couple of standard textbooks that covered all the major theories and therapeutics that were then considered important for psychiatry. To this day, in 2018, I could still safely and acceptably treat most patients with mental health disorders based solely on what was written in those textbooks.
229.content: Bullmore's critique of the serotonin-hypothesis genesis: Eli Lilly scientists started from a theoretical target (serotonin), engineered a drug that hit it cleanly, and then reverse-inferred the disease from the drug effect. The first SSRI trial FAILED - patients were no less depressed than placebo controls. Scientists pushed forward anyway based on 'belief' in the mechanism. A subsequent trial worked and Prozac was licensed in 1987. The 30 years since Prozac have seen NO major new treatments for depression or any mental health disorder. Most psychiatrists' 2018 training is essentially unchanged from 1989 - a situation unthinkable in oncology, rheumatology, or neurology. This is Bullmore's indictment of the monoamine-paradigm psychiatric orthodoxy.
229.where: Chapter 4 'Farcical Serotonin' - critique of monoamine paradigm

230.quote: Even as Schildkraut unveiled his new theory of depression he pointed out that there was a hole in it. There was very little evidence in 1965 that patients with depression had abnormal levels of adrenaline or noradrenaline in their brains. The same was true of serotonin when the Lilly scientists started their hunt for the first SSRI about 1975. It was a drug target, fair enough, but not a well-validated one.
230.content: Bullmore's technical critique of the serotonin hypothesis: the monoamine paradigm was never well-validated as a drug target. Schildkraut's 1965 theory acknowledged there was very little evidence that depressed patients had abnormal levels of adrenaline/noradrenaline in their brains. The same was true for serotonin when Lilly started developing Prozac in 1975. It was a plausible target for medicinal chemistry but not a causally validated one. This fundamental problem (drug engineering without validated target) explains why 30 years of SSRI-based treatment has not produced follow-on improvements.

231.quote: the mobilisation of the brain's microglial robocops causes collateral damage to innocent bystanders, to the nerve cells in the surrounding tissue. When the macrophage army is mobilised under shoot-to-kill orders, whether it is in the lung or the joints or the brain, it will always lay waste to the neighbourhood. The brain is at least spared the scarring that can follow chronic inflammation in other parts of the body - the brain doesn't form mechanically distorting scar tissue in the same way that Mrs P's hands were deformed by fibrous contractures around the joints of her fingers. But the brain suffers from the collateral damage of microglial activation in other ways: nerve cells are more likely to die or to shrink in size, synaptic connections between cells are more likely to be rigid than plastic, and the synaptic supply of neurotransmitters like serotonin is likely to be disrupted.
231.content: Neurobiological mechanism of cytokine-induced mood change: peripheral inflammation activates brain microglial cells (brain macrophages) via cytokine signaling across the blood-brain barrier. Activated microglia produce more cytokines themselves, amplifying inflammation in the brain. The collateral damage to neurons includes: increased neuronal death, reduced synaptic plasticity, disrupted neurotransmitter supply (especially serotonin). This is the cellular-level mechanism linking peripheral cytokines to depression-like behavior in animals.

232.quote: Microglial activation also has disadvantageous effects on how nerve cells handle the transmitters that pass signals from one cell to another across the synaptic gap. This is especially clear for serotonin, the neurotransmitter that is targeted by SSRIs. Normally nerve cells make serotonin from a raw material called tryptophan. But the cytokines released by angry microglial cells can instruct nerve cells to use this same material to make other end-products, such as kynurenine. This is bad news in two ways. First, it means that there is less serotonin available for release into synapses, so the normal rhythms of serotonin signalling that are thought to be important in controlling sleep, appetite and mood will be disrupted. Second, kynurenine and many of the other molecules produced instead of serotonin are toxic. They poison nerve cells, making them over-excited and metabolically exhausted, and ultimately killing them.
232.content: Specific molecular mechanism by which cytokines deplete serotonin: activated microglial cells release cytokines that instruct nerve cells to divert tryptophan (the raw material for serotonin synthesis) toward kynurenine production instead. Two effects: (1) less serotonin is synthesized and released, disrupting the signaling on which SSRIs supposedly depend; (2) kynurenine and its downstream metabolites are NEUROTOXIC, poisoning and killing neurons. This provides a molecular bridge between inflammation and depression that runs in the opposite direction to SSRI action - and explains why treatment-resistant depression is particularly likely to be inflamed.

233.quote: if a mouse is injected with BCG, the vaccine against tuberculosis, it passes through a short-term phase of sickness behaviour in the first few days after vaccination but then remains socially isolated from other mice and takes less pleasure in life for many weeks. It looks very much as if the mouse has become chronically depressed as a result of being inflamed.
233.content: Chronic sickness behavior in mice: BCG vaccination produces a short-term acute sickness-behavior phase (first few days), followed by SOCIAL ISOLATION and REDUCED PLEASURE in drinking sweetened water (anhedonia) that lasts for weeks. The anhedonia (via sucrose-preference testing) maps to a core symptom of major depressive disorder. This is the strongest animal-model evidence that persistent inflammation produces a persistent depression-like state rather than just acute illness behavior, and that the behavioral change reflects a genuine motivational/hedonic change rather than passive sickness.

234.quote: Auto-antibodies and cytokines are in circulation throughout the body, not solely concentrated in a few local hotspots. That is why doctors can check the diagnosis of rheumatoid disease by a blood test - cytokines and other inflammatory proteins are increased to concentrations much higher than normal in the blood of a patient like Mrs P. Her whole body was inflamed, not just her joints. And the whole body includes the brain.
234.content: Rheumatoid arthritis case illustration (Mrs P): RA is classically taught as a localized joint disease, but the molecular cause is systemic - auto-antibodies and cytokines circulate throughout the body, not just in inflamed joints. Blood cytokine levels are elevated in RA patients, confirming the systemic inflammation. The question Bullmore retrospectively asks: was Mrs P's depression-and-fatigue profile (present alongside her joint disease) a DIRECT CONSEQUENCE of her systemic inflammation rather than a 'rational' response to her grim prospects? This reframes the comorbidity of depression with inflammatory disease from psychological to biological-cascade.
234.where: Chapter 2 'The Maudsley Hypothesis' - Mrs P rheumatoid arthritis case

235.quote: Atherosclerosis, we were taught in the 20th century, was a thickening of the arteries due to deposits of cholesterol just beneath the lining of the arterial walls. If enough cholesterol accumulated it would block the artery completely; and if that artery happened to be supplying blood to the heart, then the patient would have a heart attack. We learnt about it by analogy to plumbing and that was often how it was treated, by a surgical operation to unblock or bypass the blocked piece of arterial pipe. In the 21st century, medical students are taught a significantly different story: the accumulation of cholesterol triggers an inflammatory reaction in the arterial wall.
235.content: Paradigmatic example of the inflammation-as-cause reframing in medicine generally: atherosclerosis was 20th-century taught as a cholesterol plumbing problem, but 21st-century medical students are taught it as an inflammatory disease. Cholesterol accumulation triggers macrophage activity (foam cells), which spew cytokines, damage neighboring cells, and cause the sticky arterial wall that becomes a clot. 'Having a heart attack isn't a random plumbing disaster; it's often the end product of arterial inflammation.' This is the broader paradigm shift in medicine that Bullmore argues psychiatry has missed.

236.quote: MDD in psychiatric patients, and milder depressive symptoms in the general population, are both robustly associated with increased levels of inflammatory proteins in the blood. That much seems beyond doubt from the growing volume of case-control and epidemiological studies that have been published in the last 20 years. Although a psychiatric diagnosis of MDD is conventionally incompatible with bodily disease, the association between MDD and inflammation is mechanistically compatible with the enormous number of medical patients, hiding in plain sight like Mrs P,
236.content: Epidemiological consensus: both major depressive disorder (MDD) in psychiatric patients and milder depressive symptoms in the general population are robustly associated with increased levels of inflammatory proteins in the blood. This is beyond doubt from the growing case-control and epidemiological literature of the last 20 years. While psychiatric diagnosis of MDD is conventionally incompatible with bodily disease, the association between MDD and inflammation is mechanistically compatible with 'enormous number of medical patients hiding in plain sight' who have both inflammatory disease and depression. This undermines the Cartesian mind/body separation in psychiatric diagnosis.

237.quote: A small group of philosophers of action (e.g., Bratman, 1992; Searle, 1995; Gilbert, 1989; Tuomela, 2007) have investigated how humans put their heads together with others in acts of so-called shared intentionality, or "we" intentionality. When individuals participate with others in collaborative activities, together they form joint goals and joint attention, which then create individual roles and individual perspectives that must be coordinated within them (Moll and Tomasello, 2007).
237.content: Tomasello's central thesis: what makes human thinking unique is its fundamentally cooperative nature. Humans put their heads together with others in acts of shared intentionality - 'we' intentionality - creating joint goals and joint attention that constitute a plural agent. This capacity enables everything from collaborative hunting to cultural institutions. Great apes, despite knowing much about others as intentional agents, do NOT engage in shared intentionality and do NOT form human-like culture. Shared intentionality is the specific human-unique adaptation.

238.quote: There were two key evolutionary steps. The first step, reflecting the focus of social infrastructure theorists such as Mead and Wittgenstein, involved the creation of a novel type of small-scale collaboration in human foraging. Participants in this collaborative foraging created socially shared joint goals and joint attention (common ground), which created the possibility of individual roles and perspectives within that ad hoc shared world or "form of life."
238.content: Tomasello's two-step evolutionary sequence for uniquely human cognition: (1) Joint intentionality - small-scale ad hoc pair collaboration with 'I'/'you' second-personal engagement, emerging from obligate collaborative foraging ~400,000 years ago; (2) Collective intentionality - group-mindedness with in-group strangers, based on conventions/norms/institutions, emerging as populations grew and competed. This maps to two distinct cognitive-capacity profiles: perspectival/symbolic representations with recursive mind reading (joint) vs agent-neutral thinking with cultural common ground (collective). Both steps were driven by ecological pressure forcing cooperative lifeways.

239.quote: In the hypothesis of Tomasello et al. (2012), obligate collaborative foraging became an evolutionarily stable strategy for early humans because of two interrelated processes: interdependence and social selection. The first and most basic point is that humans began a lifestyle in which individuals could not procure their daily sustenance alone but instead were interdependent with others in their foraging activities - which meant that individuals needed to develop the skills and motivations to forage collaboratively or else starve. There was thus direct and immediate selective pressure for skills and motivations for joint collaborative activity (joint intentionality). The second point is that as a natural outcome of this interdependence, individuals began to make evaluative judgments about others as potential collaborative partners: they began to be socially selective, since choosing a poor partner meant less food. Cheaters and laggards were thus selected against, and bullies lost their power to bully.
239.content: Obligate collaborative foraging as evolutionarily stable strategy: interdependence + social selection. Early humans began a lifestyle in which individuals could not procure daily food alone - they were interdependent. This created direct selective pressure for joint-intentionality skills. As a natural outcome, individuals made evaluative judgments about potential collaborative partners - social selection against cheaters and laggards, and against bullies. Critically, individuals had to worry about BOTH evaluating others AND how others were evaluating them (self-image concern) - a uniquely human cognitive preoccupation.

240.quote: The situation these early humans faced is perhaps best modeled by the stag hunt scenario from game theory (Skyrms, 2004). Two individuals have easy access to low-payoff "hares" (e.g., low-calorie vegetation), and then there appears on the horizon a high-payoff but difficult-to-obtain "stag" (e.g., large game) that can be acquired only if individuals abandon their hares and collaborate. Their motivations thus align, because it is in both their interests to work together. The dilemma is thus purely cognitive: since collaboration is mandatory and I am risking my hare, I want to go for the stag only if you do, too. But you only want to go for the stag if I do, too.
240.content: The stag hunt as formal model for early human collaboration: two individuals have easy access to low-payoff hares and see a high-payoff stag that requires joint action.
