Motivations align but the cognitive problem is coordination - I want to go for the stag only if you do, and vice versa. The leader-follower solution that chimpanzees use is unstable when risk is high. Schelling/Lewis showed that coordination requires mutual knowledge / recursive mind-reading. Tomasello's refinement: humans use 'common ground' with recursive decomposition only when perturbations occur. This is the cognitive architecture that distinguishes human from ape cooperation.

241.quote: Thus, Warneken et al. (2006, 2007) had infants of this age engage in a joint activity with an adult, such as obtaining a toy by each operating one side of an apparatus. Then, the adult simply stopped playing her role for no reason. The children were not happy about this and did various things to attempt to reengage their partner. (They did not do this if her stopping was for a good reason; e.g., she had to attend to something else [Warneken et al., 2012].) Interesting, when this same situation was arranged for human-raised chimpanzees, they simply ignored the recalcitrant partner and tried to find ways to achieve the goal on their own.
241.content: Children vs chimps reengagement experiment: Warneken et al. had 14-18 month old human infants engage in joint activity with an adult (operating an apparatus). When the adult stopped playing her role for no reason, children were unhappy and attempted to reengage the partner. When the SAME situation was arranged for human-raised chimpanzees, chimps ignored the partner and tried to complete the goal alone. This dissociation - even at prelinguistic ages, humans expect partners in joint activity to be committed enough to reengage, chimps do not - is a central behavioral marker of joint intentionality.

242.quote: For example, Hamann et al. (2012) had pairs of three-year-old children work together to bring rewards to the top of a step-like structure. The problem was that for one child the reward, surprisingly, became available midway through. Nevertheless, when this happened, the lucky child delayed consumption of her own reward and persevered until the other got hers (i.e., more than they helped the partner in a similar situation in which they were acting individually, without collaboration). Such commitment to the partner suggests that the children constructed a joint goal at the beginning that "we" get the prizes together, and they made whatever adjustments were necessary to realize that joint goal. Again, great apes do not behave in this same way.
242.content: 3-year-old children collaborative commitment study (Hamann 2012): pairs of 3yo children worked together to bring rewards to the top of a step structure. One child's reward, surprisingly, became available midway. The 'lucky' child DELAYED consuming her own reward and PERSEVERED until the other got hers - significantly more than in a parallel non-collaborative individual-action condition. This shows commitment to a joint goal: 'we' get the prizes together, and they make adjustments to realize the joint goal. Chimps in parallel experiments show no such commitment. And Hamann 2011: 3yo children (but not chimps) also committed to dividing spoils equally.

243.quote: Importantly, when children of this same age have it in their common ground with a collaborative partner that each is counting on the other to come through (we are interdependent), they both feel obligated to the other (see Gilbert, 1989, 1990). Thus, Gräfenhain et al. (2009) had preschoolers explicitly agree to play a game with one adult, and then another adult attempted to lure them away to a more exciting game. Although two-year-old children mostly just bolted to the new game straightaway, from three years of age children paused before departing and "took leave," either verbally or by handing the adult the tool they had been using together. The children seemed to recognize that joint goals involve joint commitments, the breaking of which requires some kind of acknowledgment or even apology. No study of this type has ever been done with chimpanzees, but there are no published reports of one chimpanzee taking leave from, making excuses to, or apologizing to another for breaking a joint commitment.
243.content: Taking leave: Gräfenhain 2009 had preschoolers explicitly agree to play a game with one adult; then another adult attempted to lure them to a more exciting game. Two-year-olds mostly bolted to the new game, but from age 3 children paused before departing and 'took leave' - verbally or by handing the adult the shared tool. Children recognized that joint goals involve joint commitments, the breaking of which requires acknowledgment. No published reports of chimpanzees taking leave from, making excuses to, or apologizing to another for breaking a joint commitment exist. This is specific evidence for commitment-as-moral-obligation in joint intentionality.

244.quote: other studies have found that young children, but not chimpanzees, learn important new things about the partner's role as they are collaborating. For example, Carpenter et al. (2005) found that after young children played one role in a collaboration, they could quickly switch to the other, whereas chimpanzees could not do this (Tomasello and Carpenter, 2005).
244.content: Role-switching in collaborative roles: Carpenter 2005 found that young children, after playing one role in a collaboration, could quickly switch to the other role. Chimpanzees could not. This indicates that children attend not just to their own subgoals but to the partner's subgoal AND to the partner attending to them - a specifically recursive level of joint-attention tracking. Fletcher 2012 extended this: 3yo children who had first played role A in collaboration learned role B more easily than children who had only observed - they had learned BOTH roles from their own collaborative experience simultaneously.

245.quote: as a specific form of human collaborative activity and shared intentionality, human cooperative communication involves a set of special intentional and inferential processes - first identified by Grice (1957, 1975) and since elaborated and amended by Sperber and Wilson (1996), Clark (1996), Levinson (2000), and Tomasello (2008). Human communicators conceptualize situations and entities via external communicative vehicles for other persons; these other persons then attempt to determine why the communicator thinks that these situations and entities will be relevant for them.
245.content: Cooperative communication as second-personal process: humans communicators conceptualize situations via external communicative vehicles for other persons; recipients then attempt to determine why the communicator thinks these will be relevant for them. This dialogic process involves not just shared-intentionality motivations but complex recursive inferences about others' intentions toward my intentional states. This form of communication - unique to humans, characteristic even of prelinguistic infant gestures - presupposes a shared conceptual framework (common conceptual ground) AND appreciation of the partner's individual intentions within it. Grounds M11 cooperation AND M3 social bonding through the communication channel.

246.quote: Clark (1996) proposed, as a more realistic account, that humans simply recognize the "common ground" they have with others (e.g., we both know that we both want to go for the stag) and that this is sufficient for making joint decisions toward joint goals. Tomasello (2008) suggested that something like common ground is how people actually operate, but when perturbations occur they often explain them by reasoning that "he thinks that I think he thinks . . ." (typically only a few iterations deep), suggesting an underlying recursive structure.
246.content: Tomasello's characterization of how humans think about each other recursively: attuned to common ground, and decomposing common ground a few recursive layers deep when perturbations occur ('he thinks that I think he thinks...'). Typically only a few iterations deep - not the infinite regress that Lewis/Schelling formalized. This realistic recursive-mind-reading architecture is what supports joint intentionality in practice: most of the time you just know what the shared situation is, but when things go wrong you can reason explicitly about what the partner thinks about your thinking.

247.quote: We may characterize the formation of a joint goal (or joint intention) in more detail as follows (see Bratman, 1992). For you and me to form a joint goal (or joint intention) to pursue a stag together, (1) I must have the goal to capture the stag together with you; (2) you must have the goal to capture the stag together with me; and, critically, (3) we must have mutual knowledge, or common ground, that we both know each other's goal.
247.content: Joint goal formation specification (from Bratman 1992): for you and me to form a joint goal to pursue a stag together, (1) I must have the goal to capture the stag TOGETHER WITH YOU; (2) you must have the goal to capture the stag TOGETHER WITH ME; and critically (3) we must have MUTUAL KNOWLEDGE (common ground) that we both know each other's goal. Each of us wanting separately to capture the stag, even if mutually known, does not count - it would be parallel hunting, not joint hunting. The together-with-the-other structure is essential.

248.quote: Although humans' great ape ancestors were social beings, they lived mostly individualistic and competitive lives, and so their thinking was geared toward achieving individual goals. But early humans were at some point forced by ecological circumstances into more cooperative lifeways, and so their thinking became more directed toward figuring out ways to coordinate with others to achieve joint goals or even collective group goals. And this changed everything.
248.content: Tomasello's framing of ape-cognition vs human-cognition: early humans' great ape ancestors were social beings, but they lived mostly individualistic and competitive lives, and so their thinking was geared toward achieving individual goals. Early humans were FORCED by ecological circumstances into more cooperative lifeways, and their thinking became more directed toward coordinating with others to achieve joint goals or collective group goals. This shift - from individual-competitive to joint-cooperative cognition - 'changed everything'. Thinking itself became fundamentally social.

249.quote: although many animal species can cognitively represent situations and entities at least somewhat abstractly, only humans can conceptualize one and the same situation or entity under differing, even conflicting, social perspectives (leading ultimately to a sense of "objectivity"). Further, although many animals also make simple causal and intentional inferences about external events, only humans make socially recursive and self-reflective inferences about others' or their own intentional states. And, finally, although many animals monitor and evaluate their own actions with respect to instrumental success, only humans self-monitor and evaluate their own thinking with respect to the normative perspectives and standards ("reasons") of others or the group.
249.content: Objective-reflective-normative thinking: the human-unique cognitive profile. Many animals can cognitively represent situations abstractly, but only humans conceptualize the same situation under differing, even CONFLICTING social perspectives (leading to 'objectivity'). Many animals make simple causal/intentional inferences, but only humans make socially RECURSIVE and self-reflective inferences about others' intentional states. Many animals monitor their actions for instrumental success, but only humans self-monitor with respect to the NORMATIVE perspectives and standards ('reasons') of others or the group. These three social differences - perspectival, recursive, normative - yield an identifiably different type of thinking.

250.quote: The second step, reflecting the focus of culture theorists such as Vygotsky and Bakhtin, came as human populations began growing in size and competing with one another. This competition meant that group life as a whole became one big collaborative activity, creating a much larger and more permanent shared world, that is to say, a culture. The resulting group-mindedness among all members of the cultural group (including in-group strangers) was based on a new ability to construct common cultural ground via collectively known cultural conventions, norms, and institutions.
250.content: Collective intentionality (second step): as human populations grew and groups competed, group life as a whole became 'one big collaborative activity' - a culture. The resulting group-mindedness among all members of the cultural group (including in-group strangers) was based on ability to construct common cultural ground via collectively known cultural conventions, norms, and institutions. This shifts from the face-to-face 'I-you' joint-intentionality of the first step to an impersonal 'we-as-group' collective intentionality with conventional communication and cultural institutions. The architectural distinction matters for M11 - humans have BOTH ad hoc joint collaboration AND stable group-mindedness, and these are different cognitive capacities.

251.quote: The SEEKING system (see Chapter 8): This emotional system is a coherently operating neuronal network that promotes a certain class of survival abilities. This system makes animals intensely interested in exploring their world and leads them to become excited when they are about to get what they desire. It eventually allows animals to find and eagerly anticipate the things they need for survival, including, of course, food, water, warmth, and their ultimate evolutionary survival need, sex. In other words, when fully aroused, it helps fill the mind with interest and motivates organisms to
251.content: Panksepp's canonical definition of the SEEKING system: a coherently operating neuronal network that promotes survival by making animals intensely interested in exploring their world and excited when they are about to get what they desire. It drives animals to find and eagerly anticipate food, water, warmth, and sex. When fully aroused, it fills the mind with interest and motivates movement toward resources. In humans, this is 'one of the main brain systems that generates and sustains curiosity, even for intellectual pursuits'. Neuroanatomically the SEEKING system corresponds to the major self-stimulation system from midbrain to cortex, long misconceptualized as a 'reward or reinforcement system'. This is the foundational primary-source definition that load-bears M2 Pursuit/Exploration in Cor.
251.where: Chapter 3 'The Varieties of Emotional Systems in the Brain' pp. ~53

252.quote: A very important neurochemical in this system is dopamine, especially the dopaminergic mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine circuits, which emanate from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) situated at the very back of the hypothalamus (Figure 3.6). These dopamine circuits tend to energize and coordinate the functions of many higher brain areas that mediate planning and foresight (such as the amygdala, nucleus accumbens, and frontal cortex - see next chapter) and promote states of eagerness and directed purpose in both humans and animals.
252.content: Panksepp's specific neuroanatomical claim for SEEKING: dopamine is the key neurochemical, specifically the mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine circuits emanating from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) at the back of the hypothalamus. These dopamine circuits energize and coordinate higher brain areas mediating planning and foresight - amygdala, nucleus accumbens, frontal cortex - and promote states of eagerness and directed purpose in both humans and animals. Amphetamines and cocaine produce their psychic appeal by temporarily overarousing this emotional system; opiates, nicotine, and alcohol also derive hedonic appeal from interacting with it. This is the specific anatomical substrate that load-bears M2 and DA4 (proxy hijacking by stimulant drugs).

253.quote: The RAGE system (see Chapter 10): Working in opposition to SEEKING is a system that mediates anger. RAGE is aroused by frustration and attempts to curtail an animal's freedom of action. It has long been known that one can enrage both animals and humans by stimulating very specific parts of the brain, which parallel the trajectory of the FEAR system. This system not only helps animals defend themselves by arousing fear in their opponents but also energizes behavior when an animal is irritated or restrained. Human anger may get much of its psychic "energy" from this brain system.
253.content: Panksepp's definition of the RAGE system: working in opposition to SEEKING, it mediates anger. RAGE is aroused by frustration and by attempts to curtail an animal's freedom of action. Electrical stimulation of specific brain regions paralleling the FEAR trajectory produces rage in both animals and humans. The system helps animals defend themselves by arousing fear in opponents, AND energizes behavior when an animal is irritated or restrained. Human anger gets much of its psychic 'energy' from this brain system. Brain tumors irritating the circuit cause pathological rage; damage to the system promotes serenity. This is the canonical primary-source definition for M1 Threat Management (rage component).

254.quote: The FEAR system (see Chapter 1 1): A FEAR circuit was probably designed during evolution to help animals reduce pain and the possibility of destruction. When stimulated intensely, this circuit leads animals to run away as if they are extremely scared. With very weak stimulation, animals exhibit just the opposite motor tendency - a freezing response, common when
254.content: Panksepp's definition of the FEAR system: a circuit designed during evolution to help animals reduce pain and the possibility of destruction. Intense stimulation makes animals run away as if extremely scared; weak stimulation produces the opposite motor tendency - freezing, common when animals are placed in circumstances where they have previously been hurt or frightened. Humans stimulated in these same brain areas report being engulfed by intense anxiety. This is the canonical primary-source evidence that fear is not a derived cognitive state but a hardwired affective circuit with specific neuroanatomy. Load-bearing for M1 Threat Management.

255.quote: The PANIC system (see Chapter 14): To be a mammal is to be born socially dependent. Brain evolution has provided safeguards to assure that parents (usually the mother) take care of the offspring, and the offspring have powerful emotional systems to indicate that they are in need of care (as reflected in crying or, as scientists prefer to say, separation calls). The nature of these distress systems in the brains of caretakers and those they care for has only recently been clarified; they provide a neural substrate for understanding many other social emotional processes.
255.content: Panksepp's definition of the PANIC separation-distress system, one of his most distinctive theoretical contributions: to be a mammal is to be born socially dependent. Brain evolution has provided safeguards to ensure parents take care of offspring AND offspring have powerful emotional systems to indicate they need care - reflected in crying (scientifically: separation calls). The nature of these distress systems in the brains of caretakers and those they care for provides a neural substrate for understanding many other social emotional processes. This is load-bearing for M3 Social Bonding and M9 Care/Alloparenting - Panksepp is the primary source for reading attachment distress as a specific affective circuit rather than a learned association.

256.quote: In addition to the preceding primitive systems that are evident in all mammals soon after birth, we also have more sophisticated special-purpose socioemotional systems that are engaged at appropriate times in the lives of all mammals-for instance, those that mediate sexual LUST (see Chapter 12), maternal CARE (see Chapter 13), and roughhousing PLAY (see Chapter 15). Each of these is built around neural complexities that are only provisionally understood. Sexual urges are mediated by specific brain circuits and chemistries that are quite distinct for males and females but appear to share some components such as the physiological and psychological effects of oxytocin, which also promotes maternal motivation.
256.content: Panksepp's identification of three additional special-purpose socioemotional systems beyond the 4 primitive ones: sexual LUST (Ch 12), maternal CARE (Ch 13), and roughhousing PLAY (Ch 15). Sexual urges are mediated by distinct brain circuits and chemistries for males and females but share components such as oxytocin, which also promotes maternal motivation. Maternal behavior circuits remain closely intermeshed with sexuality circuits, suggesting how evolution gradually constructed the basic neural substrates for 'the social contract' - the possibilities for love and bonding - in the mammalian brain. This is load-bearing for M14 Reproductive Motivation, M9 Care/Alloparenting, M4 Social Calibration/Play, and the architectural claim that social bonding evolved as an extension of pre-existing reproductive circuits.

257.quote: The underlying circuits are genetically predetermined and designed to respond unconditionally to stimuli arising from major life-challenging circumstances. These circuits organize diverse behaviors by activating or inhibiting motor subroutines and concurrent autonomic-hormonal changes that have proved adaptive in the face of such life-challenging circumstances during the evolutionary history of the species. Emotive circuits change the sensitivities of sensory systems that are relevant for the behavioral sequences that have been aroused. Neural activity of emotive systems outlasts the precipitating circumstances. Emotive circuits can come under the conditional control of emotionally neutral environmental stimuli. Emotive circuits have reciprocal interactions with the brain mechanisms that elaborate higher decision-making processes and consciousness.
257.content: Panksepp's six methodological criteria for identifying genuine emotional systems in the brain (Figure 3.3): (1) Underlying circuits are genetically predetermined to respond unconditionally to life-challenging stimuli; (2) they organize diverse behaviors by activating/inhibiting motor subroutines and autonomic-hormonal changes; (3) they change sensitivities of sensory systems relevant to the aroused behavioral sequences; (4) their neural activity outlasts precipitating circumstances; (5) they can come under conditional control of emotionally neutral stimuli; (6) they have reciprocal interactions with higher decision-making and consciousness circuits. Plus the seventh psychological criterion: they must generate affective feelings. This is Panksepp's load-bearing methodological framework for distinguishing emotional systems from general-purpose sensorimotor circuits.

258.quote: To evaluate whether rats laugh, we took a simple tickling approach. Listening in to the ultrasonic frequency range at which rats communicate, we rapidly found that friendly tickling induced very high-frequency chirping at about 50 KHz. This response could be provoked more effectively when the tickling occurred at the nape of the neck, where animals normally solicit play, than on the rump, and full body tickling was most effective of all (Figure 15.4). Animals that had been deprived of social contact from weaning at 24 days of age through puberty exhibited more chirping to tickling than littermates that had been allowed two play sessions each day through this interval.
258.content: Panksepp's empirical discovery of rat laughter: listening in the ultrasonic frequency range at which rats communicate, friendly tickling induced very high-frequency chirping at about 50 kHz. The response was most effective when tickling the nape of the neck (where rats normally solicit play) or when full-body tickling was applied. Social-deprived rats exhibited MORE chirping to tickling than littermates allowed daily play sessions; playfulness correlated highly with tickling-induced 'laughter'. Tickling was a positive incentive - rats sought it out and began to chirp to cues associated with it. If this vocalization is homologous to human laughter, 'we may come to understand human joy by studying the circuits that generate such vocalization in rats'. This is Panksepp's primary empirical evidence for M4 PLAY and for cross-species affective homology.

259.quote: especially the endogenous opioid peptides, are already known to modify feeling states in humans and corresponding behavioral changes in animals.
259.content: Panksepp's original discovery linking endogenous opioids to separation distress: brain opioids (especially beta-endorphin and enkephalins) modulate social feelings and separation distress, AND opioids promote social bonding. Oxytocin and opioids work together to inhibit separation distress. This is Panksepp's foundational finding that attachment pain shares neural substrates with physical pain - the 'social pain' hypothesis at the molecular level. Load-bearing for M3 Social Bonding, DA8 Phylogenetic Priority (opioid system is ancient), and for reading depression/grief as dysregulation of an opioid-modulated affective circuit rather than a purely cognitive state.
259.where: Chapter 6 'Neurochemical Maps of the Brain' pp. ~101

260.quote: oxytocin, which mediates various pro-social processes, including maternal behavior and the inhibition of separation distress (Chapters 12 to 14), can yield a tripeptide called PLG (proline-leucine-glycine), which mediates none of the above but has antidepressant effects.
260.content: Panksepp's early summary of oxytocin's pro-social functions: oxytocin mediates various pro-social processes including female sexual response, orgasm, maternal behavior, social memory, and the INHIBITION of separation distress. It is a single neuropeptide that operates across the sexual-maternal-social-bonding domains - exactly the molecular overlap that allows evolution to construct the 'social contract' by repurposing reproductive circuits for broader bonding. This is primary-source evidence for the M14/M9/M3 architectural overlap in Cor's specification.

261.quote: Of course, as mentioned, there is a seventh psychological criterion: The emotional circuits must be able to generate affective feelings, but this is hard to incorporate into the conceptual diagram. I will eventually develop the idea that affect emerges from the many interactions of emotional systems depicted in Figure 3.3 with primal neural mechanisms that represent "the self" (see Chapter 16)
261.content: Panksepp's central theoretical commitment - the seventh psychological criterion: emotional circuits must be able to generate affective feelings. This criterion is 'hard to incorporate into the conceptual diagram' but is the load-bearing claim that distinguishes affective neuroscience from behavioral neuroscience. Panksepp argues affect emerges from interactions of emotional systems with primal neural mechanisms that represent 'the self', particularly midbrain periaqueductal and deep tectal circuits interacting with frontal cortical systems. Arousal of the executive circuit for each emotion is a NECESSARY CONDITION for getting feeling states activated within the brain. Load-bearing for reading M1-M4/M9/M14 outputs as having affective content, not just behavioral output.

262.quote: I will speak of these emotional systems in a variety of ways, using designations such as executive, command, and operating systems, to provide nuances of meaning that may be needed to conceptualize their overall functions. The use of the term executive implies that a neural system has a superordinate role in a cascade of hierarchical controls
262.content: Panksepp's conceptual toolkit for emotional circuits: he calls them 'executive, command, and operating systems' - executive implies a superordinate role in hierarchical controls; command implies the circuit can INSTIGATE a full-blown emotional process (not just correlate with it); operating implies it coordinates and synchronizes multiple subsystems. Together these yield coherent psycho-behavioral and physiological responses that constitute an emotional 'organ system' - an anatomical network of interconnected neurons with endocrine, paracrine, and immune influences. This is the load-bearing architectural framing for why emotional circuits are mechanisms (Cor's M-framework) rather than mere sensorimotor reflexes.

263.quote: The major emotional operating systems are defined primarily by genetically coded neural circuits that generate well-organized behavior sequences that can be evoked by localized electrical stimulation of the brain. Representative behaviors generated by the various systems are indicated, and the approximate locations of the SEEKING, FEAR, and RAGE systems are depicted on a small frontal section through one side of the hypothalamus.
263.content: Panksepp's historical contribution: in his 1982 paper he first distinguished four primary emotional command systems that are organized along discrete but interacting subcortical trajectories (mostly following the medial forebrain bundle). These are depicted in Figure 3.5 (original paper) with approximate anatomical locations for SEEKING, FEAR, and RAGE in the hypothalamus and their interconnections. The 1982 framework was the foundational statement of affective neuroscience as a research program distinct from behavioral or cognitive approaches. This is primary-source citation for the architectural claim that mammalian emotions are subcortically organized, not cortically derived.

264.quote: When this brain system becomes underactive, as is common with aging, a form of depression results. When the system becomes spontaneously overactive, which can happen as a result of various kinds of stress, an animal's behavior becomes excessive and schizophrenic or manic symptoms may follow-especially the "functional" forms of psychosis that can be treated with traditional antipsychotic medications (which all reduce dopamine activity in the brain)
264.content: Panksepp's clinical prediction from the SEEKING-system framework: when the SEEKING brain system becomes UNDERACTIVE (as is common with aging), a form of depression results. When it becomes spontaneously OVERACTIVE (from stress), animal behavior becomes excessive and schizophrenic or manic symptoms may follow - especially the 'functional' forms of psychosis treatable with traditional antipsychotic medications (all of which reduce dopamine activity). This predicts that depression-via-SEEKING-hypofunction is mechanistically distinct from depression-via-PANIC-overactivation (social loss), and provides a specific dopamine-centered prediction for M2 Pursuit/Exploration dysregulation. Load-bearing for reading modern anhedonic depression as a SEEKING-hypoactivation phenotype.

265.quote: there is a great deal of neuropeptide specificity in the coding of behavior, and it is esthetically pleasing to note that we often observe a correspondence between the peripheral functions of these neuropeptides and their role within the brain (Table 6.1). For instance, in the periphery, insulin controls metabolic dispersion of nutrients, while in the brain it helps mediate satiety (see Chapter 9). Likewise, in the periphery, the hormone angiotensin promotes water retention in the kidney, while in the brain it promotes thirst. Thus, many neuropeptide languages highlight the tendency of evolution to reutilize existing elements for new tasks that are harmonious with previous functions.
265.content: Panksepp's observation of evolutionary economy in neuropeptide coding: there is extensive correspondence between the peripheral and central functions of neuropeptides - insulin controls peripheral glucose dispersion AND central satiety; angiotensin controls peripheral water retention AND central thirst; oxytocin controls peripheral birthing and milk letdown AND central maternal acceptance and readiness. Many peptides highlight evolution's tendency to REUTILIZE existing elements for new tasks harmonious with previous functions. This exaptation pattern is load-bearing for the DA8 architectural claim that newer mechanisms (social bonding) are built from older ones (reproductive physiology).

266.quote: We now realize that maternal behavior circuits remain closely intermeshed with those that control sexuality, and this suggests how evolution gradually constructed the basic neural substrates for the social contract (i.e., the possibilities for love and bonding) in the mammalian brain.
266.content: Panksepp's architectural claim about the evolution of social bonding: maternal behavior circuits remain closely intermeshed with those that control sexuality. This suggests how evolution gradually constructed the basic neural substrates for the 'social contract' - 'the possibilities for love and bonding' - in the mammalian brain. Maternal nurturance probably arose gradually from preexisting circuits that initially mediated reproductive behaviors. This is THE foundational architectural claim for why Cor's M3 Social Bonding, M9 Care/Alloparenting, and M14 Reproductive Motivation share substrate - they were built by evolution as extensions and overlays of the same neurochemical machinery, not as independent systems.

267.quote: In addition to the preceding primitive systems that are evident in all mammals soon after birth
267.content: Panksepp's framework of 4 primary emotional command systems: expectancy/SEEKING, RAGE, FEAR, and separation-distress/PANIC. These are organized along discrete but interacting trajectories in the subcortical brain, largely following the medial forebrain bundle. These 4 systems are 'evident in all mammals soon after birth' - they are not cognitive achievements but mammalian hardware inherited from at least 150 million years of mammalian evolution. This is the central DA8 phylogenetic-priority claim: the affective substrate is ancient, pre-cortical, and conserved across all mammals.

268.quote: for separation distress to highlight striking species
268.content: Panksepp notes important species differences in separation-distress systems - they exhibit striking interspecies variability even though the basic circuit is conserved. This calibration variability is important for understanding human-unique attachment patterns: the PANIC system is mammal-universal but its specific tuning (sensitivity thresholds, recovery dynamics, cross-modal signaling) varies with species ecology. For humans, separation distress is tuned for the long juvenile dependency period and for loss of specific attachment figures rather than general social absence. This grounds DA7 Developmental Calibration at the PANIC-circuit level.

269.quote: we now have considerable evidence that opioids participate
269.content: Panksepp's more specific primary-source claim: brain opioids promote the development of food and social attachments, and the inhibition of separation distress. In young animals, opioid agonists reduce separation-distress vocalizations; opioid antagonists increase them. This is the neurochemical bridge from physical pain (classically opioid-modulated) to social pain (separation distress), grounding the architectural claim that social rejection activates the same molecular systems as physical injury. Load-bearing for the M3 cascade connecting social bonds to physical-pain circuitry and for the DA8 phylogenetic-priority claim that attachment evolved by repurposing older pain-modulation systems.

270.quote: In addition to being the deep neural sources of psychic life, emotional circuits achieve their profound influence over the behavior and mental activity of an organism through the widespread effects on the rest of the nervous system. Emotive circuits change sensory, perceptual, and cognitive processing, and initiate a host of physiological changes that are naturally synchronized with the aroused behavioral tendencies characteristic of emotional experience.
270.content: Panksepp's architectural claim about emotion-cognition interaction: emotional circuits achieve their profound influence over behavior and mental activity through widespread effects on the rest of the nervous system. Emotive circuits change sensory, perceptual, and cognitive processing, and initiate physiological changes synchronized with the aroused behavioral tendencies. This is NOT just a one-way emotion→behavior pathway - cognition is PENETRATED by emotional-circuit activity, meaning that 'cognitive' function cannot be cleanly separated from affective-circuit function. Load-bearing for Cor's framing that mechanism outputs (M1-M4, M9, M14) shape perception and attention upstream, not just behavior downstream.

271.quote: Among humans living in foraging societies, a helpful mate and/or alloparents were usually essential for a mother to rear any infant at all. In a surprisingly broad range of creatures, indispensable alloparents provide many of the same forms of care a mother might, protecting and provisioning, even suckling another female's infant in cases where the alloparent is
271.content: Hrdy's core allomothering thesis: Among humans living in foraging societies, a helpful mate and/or alloparents were usually essential for a mother to rear any infant at all. Indispensable alloparents provide many of the same forms of care a mother might - protecting, provisioning, even suckling another female's infant. This is load-bearing for M9 Care/Alloparenting: human infants are NOT raised dyadically, and the mother-as-sole-caregiver framing misses the evolutionary architecture entirely.

272.quote: Ornithologists used to call such assistants "helpers"; primatologists called them "aunts" (after the British "auntie," to designate a female relative or trusted family friend). In 1975, Edward O.Wilson decided it was time for a more dignified designation: allo- (from the Greek for "other than") plus parent.
272.content: Hrdy's 'allomother' term precision: E.O. Wilson coined 'alloparent' in 1975 to replace imprecise 'helpers' (ornithologists) and 'aunts' (primatologists). Hrdy refines further to 'allomothers' - all caretakers OTHER than the mother (whose identity is usually known for sure). The precision matters: in cooperative-breeding species, alloparents play critical roles, allowing mothers to breed at a faster rate than would otherwise be possible. Humans fit this pattern.

273.quote: the dwarf mongoose of East Africa provides a classic example of cooperative breeding. Typically only the oldest female in a large group breeds, but all help her rear her young. Each animal takes a turn as baby-sitter or sentinel, standing upright on the vast arid savanna, vigilantly scanning the horizon for predators.
273.content: Dwarf mongoose as classic cooperative breeding example: Typically only the oldest female in a large group breeds, but all help her rear her young. Each animal takes a turn as babysitter or sentinel. The rule: 'Those who can, breed; kin who can't, help out.' Subordinate females spontaneously lactate to feed their charges. Dominant breeding females ensure allomother availability by killing infants born to subordinates - the alpha female makes giving birth an option not worth the cost. This is a paradigm case for cooperative-breeding biology and for M9.

274.quote: alloparenting is particularly well developed and played a special role in the evolution of our own large-brained, slow-growing, and extraordinarily inventive species.
274.content: Hrdy's alloparenting role in human evolution: alloparenting is particularly well developed and played a special role in the evolution of our own large-brained, slow-growing, and extraordinarily inventive species. This links the cross-species cooperative-breeding finding to the specific human case: our unusually extended juvenile period and large brains require more caloric provisioning than a single mother can provide, making allomothering not a cultural addition but a species architecture.

275.quote: My melding of vocation with family has been supported by a steadfast partner, resilient children, and the generous hearts of alloparents - all the individuals other than me and my husband who helped us rear our children. As I would learn, mothers have worked for as long as our species has existed, and they have depended on others to help them rear their children.
275.content: Hrdy's autobiographical framing: she describes her own reliance on alloparents to melding vocation with family, and grew up herself being reared by a succession of governesses. Her experience - that mothers have worked for as long as our species has existed and depended on others to help rear their children - is the implicit empirical anchor for the broader thesis. This is not mere anecdote but frames the book's central argument that maternal self-sacrifice as a norm is a modern-Western construction, not an evolutionary given.

276.quote: Bowlby demonstrated that babies are genetically programmed to seek and form an attachment to a trusted figure. Secure attachment to one or more trusted caretakers is an essential aspect of emotional development in humans, just as it is in all other primates.
276.content: Hrdy on attachment theory: Bowlby's insights that babies are genetically programmed to seek and form attachment to a trusted figure, and that secure attachment to one or more trusted caretakers is essential for emotional development, rank among the greatest contributions of evolutionary-minded psychologists. BUT Bowlby's original framing (exclusive maternal attachment) produces dilemmas for mothers wanting self-confident children AND lives/careers of their own. Hrdy's refinement: 'one or more trusted caretakers' - plural attachment figures, not a single dyadic bond. This is load-bearing for how M9 Care/Alloparenting integrates with M3 Social Bonding in Cor's architecture.

277.quote: Even in normally gentle and herbivorous primates like langurs and gorillas, other members of the same species can be a threat to infant survival every bit as hazardous as lurking predators. This was a new kind of selective pressure on mothers, one not previously dreamed of.
277.content: Infanticide by males as selective pressure: Even in normally gentle primates like langurs and gorillas, other members of the same species can be a threat to infant survival every bit as hazardous as lurking predators. This creates selective pressure on mothers. Hrdy's specific hypothesis: female langurs' apparently promiscuous mating with invading males (even when pregnant/not ovulating) casts wide the web of possible paternity - males almost never attack infants they might have fathered. Males use past mating relations as a cue to attack or tolerate an infant. This is load-bearing for M14 Reproductive Motivation and for reading female sexuality in light of infanticide risk.

278.quote: In the early 1970s, it was still widely assumed by Darwinians that females were sexually passive and "coy." Female langurs were anything but. When bands of roving males approached the troop, females would solicit them or actually leave their troop to go in search of them. On occasion, a female mated with invaders even though she was already pregnant and not ovulating (something else nonhuman primates were not supposed to do).
278.content: Hrdy's central reframing of female sexuality: In the 1970s Darwinians widely assumed females were sexually passive and 'coy'. Female langurs were anything but - they solicited invading males or left their troop to find them, and mated with invaders even while pregnant and not ovulating. Hrdy's interpretation: mothers were insuring paternity uncertainty as an infanticide-avoidance strategy. This overturns the passive-female Darwinian framing and grounds M14 Reproductive Motivation in a specifically female-agency frame rather than a male-pursuit frame.

279.quote: By casting wide the web of possible paternity, mothers could increase the prospects of future survival of offspring, since males almost never attack infants carried by females that, in the biblical sense of the word, they have "known." Males use past relations with the mother as a cue to attack or tolerate her infant.
279.content: Hrdy's elaboration of the infanticide mechanism: males use past relations with the mother as a cue to attack or tolerate her infant. Mothers who cast wide the web of possible paternity increase the prospects of future survival for their offspring, since males almost never attack infants carried by females they have 'known' in the biblical sense. This is the specific behavioral rule that makes paternity confusion adaptive for mothers - it's not promiscuity as failure of pair-bonding but as insurance against infanticide.

280.content: Hrdy's identification of infanticide as widespread across primate taxa: infanticide by males is documented across many primate species, establishing it as a recurrent evolutionary pressure shaping female reproductive strategy across primates broadly, not a pathological anomaly of a few species. This cross-taxon distribution is load-bearing for P1 Inclusive Fitness and for M14 Reproductive Motivation's architectural shaping by infanticide risk.

281.quote: Clearly, for cooperatively breeding mammals, a female's physical capacity to conceive and bear viable young is only a small part of the equation. She must also be able to carry through with the enterprise - rearing offspring to independence.
281.content: Hrdy on contingent maternal commitment: For cooperatively breeding mammals, a female's physical capacity to conceive and bear viable young is only a small part of the equation. She must also be able to CARRY THROUGH with the enterprise - rearing offspring to independence. This is the foundational argument that maternal investment is context-dependent, not unconditional - mothers evaluate whether circumstances (including alloparent availability, food resources, and infant health) permit successful rearing, and adjust their investment accordingly. Load-bearing for M9 Care/Alloparenting and for reading maternal ambivalence as adaptive rather than pathological.

282.quote: a woman's maternal emotions (those concerned with producing and nurturing offspring and keeping them alive) continued to be viewed as separate from and even antithetical to the rest of her - her sexuality and, particularly, her ambition. Yet the compartmentalized way we have learned to think about these emotions has nothing to do with how they evolved.
282.content: Hrdy on the compartmentalization error: maternal emotions (producing/nurturing/keeping offspring alive) have been viewed as separate from and even antithetical to the rest of a woman - her sexuality and her ambition. This compartmentalized framing has nothing to do with how these emotions evolved. In the ancestral environment, the same female was simultaneously pursuing reproductive goals AND maternal goals AND resource goals AND social-position goals, with all of them integrated rather than competing. The modern fragmentation is cultural, not evolutionary.

283.quote: Here we tested a Constrained total energy expenditure model, in which total energy expenditure increases with physical activity at low activity levels but plateaus at higher activity levels as the body adapts to maintain total energy expenditure within a narrow range. We compared total energy expenditure, measured using doubly labeled water, against physical activity, measured using accelerometry, for a large (n = 332) sample of adults living in five populations. After adjusting for body size and composition, total energy expenditure was positively correlated with physical activity, but the relationship was markedly stronger over the lower range of physical activity. For subjects in the upper range of physical activity, total energy expenditure plateaued, supporting a Constrained total energy expenditure model.
283.content: The constrained total energy expenditure model: total daily energy expenditure (TEE) increases with physical activity at low activity levels but plateaus at higher levels as the body adapts metabolically to maintain TEE within a narrow range. Tested in a multi-population doubly-labeled-water study (n=332 adults from Ghana, Jamaica, Seychelles, South Africa, and the US). Above moderate activity, each additional increment of ~100 counts per minute per day was associated with less than 50 kcal/day increase in TEE. The change point from positive slope to zero was 230 CPM/day. Load-bearing for M13 Energy Regulation: the body is homeostatically buffered against habitual activity variation, and exercise does not produce linear caloric deficits.
283.where: Pontzer et al. 2016 Current Biology 26:410-417, Abstract / Introduction

284.quote: People in less socioeconomically developed populations, including subsistence farmers and traditional hunter-gatherers, have total energy expenditures similar to those in more developed populations despite substantial differences in physical activity. Mammals living in the wild, including non-human primate species, have total energy expenditures similar to captive populations. These population-level comparisons suggest that total energy expenditure is an evolved, species-specific trait that is homeostatically buffered against variation in habitual physical activity.
284.content: Cross-population pattern: people in less socioeconomically developed populations - subsistence farmers and traditional hunter-gatherers - have total energy expenditures similar to those in more developed populations despite substantial differences in physical activity. Non-human mammals in the wild show the same pattern: wild and captive populations have similar TEE. These population-level comparisons suggest that total energy expenditure is an evolved, species-specific trait that is homeostatically buffered against variation in habitual physical activity. This is the foundational empirical pattern that the Constrained TEE model is designed to explain.
284.where: Pontzer et al. 2016, Introduction / Cross-population synthesis

285.quote: We hypothesize that non-muscular physiological activity contributes substantially to activity energy expenditure 2 and its adaptation to physical activity. Human studies and non-human animal models show that energy allocation across a broad range of physiological tasks, including reproductive activity and somatic maintenance, may be reduced when physical activity increases, resulting in decreased activity energy expenditure 2. Indeed, such physical activity-induced reduction in activity energy expenditure 2 could potentially contribute to the beneficial health effects of exercise, reducing energy expenditure on inflammation and detrimental immune system activity.
285.content: Pontzer's non-muscular compensation hypothesis: the component of activity energy expenditure that compensates for increased physical activity is unlikely to be purely muscular. When the analysis limits to subjects above 230 CPM/day, activity energy expenditure 2 (the compensatory component) is too large to be accounted for by reductions in standing, fidgeting, or peripheral limb movement alone. Pontzer hypothesizes that non-muscular physiological activity - reproductive activity, somatic maintenance, inflammation, immune system activity - is reduced when physical activity increases, absorbing the expected caloric deficit. This frames physical activity as a regulator of systemic energy allocation across multiple physiological domains, not merely as direct caloric expenditure.
285.where: Pontzer et al. 2016, Discussion section on activity energy expenditure components

286.quote: As expected, physical activity level, PAL, was greater among Hadza foragers than among Westerners. Nonetheless, average daily energy expenditure of traditional Hadza foragers was no different than that of Westerners after controlling for body size. The metabolic cost of walking and resting were also similar among Hadza and Western groups. The similarity in metabolic rates across a broad range of cultures challenges current models of obesity suggesting that Western lifestyles lead to decreased energy expenditure.
286.content: The Pontzer 2012 Hadza-energetics finding: despite dramatically greater physical activity (Hadza PAL ~1.78-2.26 vs Western PAL ~1.68-1.81), Hadza hunter-gatherers expend no more total daily energy than Western adults after controlling for body size. The metabolic cost of walking and resting are also similar across groups. This contradicted the then-dominant obesity hypothesis that Western lifestyles reduce caloric expenditure and motivated the Constrained TEE model developed in subsequent work. The implication: global obesity cannot be explained by Western sedentarism producing lower daily energy expenditure - Western and hunter-gatherer daily calorie burns are similar, so the obesity difference must lie primarily in energy intake and food composition.
286.where: Pontzer et al. 2012 PLoS ONE 7(7):e40503, Abstract

287.quote: We hypothesize that human daily energy expenditure may be an evolved physiological trait largely independent of cultural differences.
287.content: Pontzer's evolved-trait hypothesis from the 2012 Hadza paper: human daily energy expenditure may be an evolved physiological trait largely independent of cultural differences. This is the theoretical claim that motivated the broader Constrained TEE research program - TEE is not a passive function of behavior but an actively regulated species-typical homeostatic variable. If correct, it reframes the entire energetic basis of obesity: the difference between Hadza and Western adults is not caloric throughput but caloric composition and timing of intake.
287.where: Pontzer et al. 2012 PLoS ONE 7(7):e40503, Abstract

288.quote: Here, we test the hypothesis that the ways in which urban populations rest, rather than the amount of time spent resting, represents an inactivity mismatch with an evolutionarily relevant hunting and gathering lifestyle, and propose that this mismatch may contribute to the negative health impacts of sedentary behavior today.
288.content: The Inactivity Mismatch Hypothesis (Raichlen, Pontzer et al. 2020): Hadza adults spend similar amounts of time in nonambulatory rest as industrialized adults (~9.9 hours/day), but they rest in postures - squatting, kneeling, ground-sitting - that maintain higher lower-limb muscle activity than Western chair-sitting. Measured via thigh-worn accelerometers plus electromyography in the field. The hypothesis: human physiology evolved in a context of high muscle activity across the waking day BOTH through physical activity AND through resting postures with sustained low-level muscle contraction. Modern chair-sitting is the mismatch - not the total amount of rest, but the specific posture during rest.
288.where: Raichlen, Pontzer et al. 2020 PNAS 117(13):7115-7121, Introduction

289.quote: In addition to ground-sitting postures, Hadza individuals also spend a large percentage of their nonambulatory time in squatting (∼18%) and kneeling postures (∼12.5%) that differ from ground sitting by individuals maintaining an elevated buttocks. [...] For soleus, the assisted squat posture (squatting with heels in ground contact and with the buttocks resting on a small rock) elicited significantly higher muscle activity compared with chair sitting.
289.content: The empirical result: Hadza adults spend roughly as much time in nonambulatory rest as industrialized adults (~9.9 hours/day for Hadza vs ~8.8 hours/day for Australian adults in comparison data), with similar average sedentary bout duration (~15 min) and similar numbers of transitions between sitting and standing per day (~50 vs ~38 for European adults). But Hadza nonambulatory time occurs heavily in squatting (~18%) and kneeling (~12.5%) postures that elicit significantly higher muscle activity than chair-sitting. The Hadza data refute the naive 'hunter-gatherers never sit' assumption and reframe the mismatch as about HOW humans rest, not HOW MUCH.
289.where: Raichlen et al. 2020 PNAS, Results section

290.quote: These illnesses are mismatch diseases, defined as diseases that result from our Paleolithic bodies being poorly or inadequately adapted to certain modern behaviors and conditions. I don't think it is possible to overemphasize just how important mismatch diseases are. You are most likely going to die from a mismatch disease. You are most likely to suffer from disabilities caused by mismatch diseases. Mismatch diseases contribute to the bulk of health-care spending throughout the world.
290.content: Lieberman's foundational mismatch-disease framework from The Story of the Human Body (2013). Evolutionary medicine identifies 'mismatch diseases' - illnesses caused by our bodies being poorly or inadequately adapted to certain modern behaviors and conditions. The framework analogizes human mismatch to transplanting a zebra to New England: the organism is still well-adapted for its original environment but the new environment is wrong. Over 50% of healthcare spending worldwide goes toward mismatch diseases. This is the architectural framing for P3 Systematic Mismatch at the chronic-disease-epidemiology scale and the theoretical backbone for Lieberman's subsequent Exercised (2021).
290.where: Lieberman, The Story of the Human Body (2013) Part II opening, pp. ~181

291.quote: The simplest way to classify mismatch diseases is by how a given environmental stimulus has changed. Broadly speaking, most mismatch diseases occur when a common stimulus either increases or decreases beyond levels for which the body is adapted, or when the stimulus is entirely novel and the body is not adapted for it at all. Put simply, mismatches are caused by stimuli that are too much, too little, or too new. For example, as cultural evolution transforms people's diets, some mismatch diseases occur from eating too much fat, others from eating too little fat, and yet others from eating new kinds of fat that the body cannot digest (such as partially hydrogenated fats).
291.content: Lieberman's taxonomy of mismatch causes - 'too much, too little, or too new'. Mismatch diseases occur when a common environmental stimulus either increases or decreases beyond levels for which the body is adapted, or when the stimulus is entirely novel and the body is not adapted for it at all. For diet specifically: some mismatch diseases come from eating too much fat, others from eating too little fat, others from eating new kinds of fat the body cannot digest (partially hydrogenated fats). This classification is load-bearing for M13 Energy Regulation - the mechanism handles each of these three categories differently, and the too-much/too-little/too-new framing helps distinguish among specific M13 cascade failures.
291.where: Lieberman, The Story of the Human Body (2013), Chapter on mismatch classification

292.quote: According to Jared Diamond, farming was the 'worst mistake in the history of the human race.' In spite of having more food, hence more children, than hunter-gatherers, farmers generally have to work harder; they eat a lower-quality diet; they more often confront starvation because their crops occasionally fail from floods, droughts, and other disasters; and they live at higher population densities, which promote infectious diseases and social stress. Farming may have led to civilization and other types of 'progress,' but it also led to misery and death on a grand scale. Most of the mismatch diseases from which we currently suffer stem from the transition from hunting and gathering to farming.
292.content: Lieberman on the farming transition as a foundational mismatch event. Drawing on Jared Diamond's provocative characterization of farming as 'the worst mistake in the history of the human race', Lieberman argues that most modern mismatch diseases stem from the transition from hunting-gathering to farming: more food but lower-quality diet, harder work, more frequent starvation from crop failures, higher population densities driving infectious disease and social stress. The architectural implication for M13: the first major mismatch in the human metabolic environment came roughly 11,000 years ago, predating the industrial and dietary transitions that Exercised focuses on. Load-bearing for reading M13 failure modes as stacked across multiple historical transitions rather than as a single industrial-era problem.
292.where: Lieberman, The Story of the Human Body (2013), Chapter on farming transition

293.quote: We have since found that moderate pressure is key to the massage therapy effects. We massage babies from head to foot (all but their chests and stomachs; they do not want to be touched there, most likely because that is where all the tubes have been inserted). The babies who were massaged gained 47 percent more weight than those not massaged, a significant weight gain.
293.content: Field's foundational premature-infant massage finding: infants massaged from head to foot (excluding chest and stomach where IVs were inserted) gained 47 percent more weight than unmassaged infants. This established touch as a quantifiable developmental input with direct physiological consequences on growth. The initial study motivated the establishment of the Touch Research Institute at the University of Miami School of Medicine in 1992 and launched a research program of over 100 touch/massage studies. Critically, earlier attempts by other researchers had failed to show growth effects because they used light-touch (tickling-like) stimulation; Field's group discovered that moderate pressure is necessary for the physiological response.

294.quote: Several decades ago, Harry Harlow, at the University of Wisconsin, performed a classic experiment on touching monkeys. He built one surrogate mother out of terry cloth and a second surrogate mother out of wire mesh. For some of the monkey infants, the terry-cloth mother provided milk, and the wire mother did not. For others, the condition was reversed. The monkey infants preferred the cloth mother without the milk over the wire mother with milk, suggesting that they needed the touch stimulation as much as, if not more than, the nourishment.
294.content: Field's synthesis of Harlow's foundational primate touch-deprivation work: infant rhesus monkeys preferred a terry-cloth surrogate mother without milk over a wire-mesh mother with milk, suggesting that touch stimulation is at least as important as nourishment. Harlow's experiments showed that infants without any surrogate developed self-clasping behavior, failed to develop normal grooming or reproduction, and had broken immune systems. Suomi's follow-up showed that Plexiglas separation (vision, hearing, smell preserved but no touch) was sufficient to produce these deficits - touch itself was the critical missing stimulation, not the other sensory modalities. This is the primary-source chain Field uses to ground touch as a distinct regulatory input in R1's architecture.
294.where: Field, Touch (2014) Chapter 3 'Touch in Early Development', pp. ~47

295.quote: Sidney Jourard, a University of Florida psychologist, visited cafés in different parts of the world and recorded the number of times two people who were sharing coffee touched each other. In London, the tally was 0; in Gainesville, Florida, 2; in Paris 110; and in San Juan, Puerto Rico, more than 180. Most sociologists would agree that societies like those in the Mediterranean countries (e.g., Spain, France, Italy, Greece, Turkey, Egypt) are contact societies, whereas the more northern societies in countries such as Holland, Great Britain, and the United States are not.
295.content: Jourard's cross-cultural café-touch observations, reported by Field: in cafés where two people shared coffee, the number of physical contacts in one hour varied from 0 (London) to 2 (Gainesville Florida) to 110 (Paris) to more than 180 (San Juan Puerto Rico). This documents the dramatic cross-cultural variation in touch frequency and grounds the 'touch hunger' framing that Field extends to industrialized screen-mediated life. The cross-cultural data also ground R1's architectural claim that the touch input has a wide tolerance range but a floor below which developmental and regulatory deficits appear.
295.where: Field, Touch (2014) Chapter 2 'Touch as Communication', pp. ~24-25

296.quote: The skin is the first and the largest sense organ to develop prenatally. The fetus is suspended in amniotic fluid and receives active stimulation from the fluid and the mother and others as they touch her abdomen. The fetus becomes increasingly active as this happens. The fetus also touches itself by thumb sucking and grasping the umbilical cord. The fetus gets a continuous massage for the entire nine months from both the amniotic fluid and the mother's insides. In addition, a pregnant woman naturally massages her baby in the womb. Touch alters oxytocin (an estrogen-dependent chemical), which relaxes the individual, promotes touch, encourages bonding, triggers milk letdown during breastfeeding, and sets off the uterine contractions that accompany childbirth.
296.content: Field's phylogenetic framing of touch as the first sense organ. The skin is the largest sense organ because it is the largest organ in the body - the 'first and largest sense organ to develop prenatally'. The fetus receives continuous touch stimulation in utero from amniotic fluid, maternal internal movement, and external touch to the mother's abdomen. Touch alters oxytocin, which relaxes the individual, promotes touch (positive feedback), encourages bonding, triggers milk letdown during breastfeeding, and initiates uterine contractions during childbirth. This is the architectural grounding for R1 Touch as a phylogenetically ancient regulatory input distinct from vision and hearing, with downstream effects on M9 Care/Alloparenting and M3 Social Bonding via oxytocin.
296.where: Field, Touch (2014) Chapter 3 'Touch in Early Development', pp. ~49

297.quote: we have conducted an experimental research program over the last eight years, exploring the hypothesis that the human mind contains algorithms (specialized mechanisms) designed for reasoning about social exchange. The topic of reasoning about social exchange was selected for several reasons. In the first place, as we will discuss, many aspects of the evolutionary theory of social exchange (also sometimes called cooperation, reciprocal altruism, or reciprocation) are relatively well developed and unambiguous.
297.content: Cosmides and Tooby's foundational argument for domain-specific reasoning: the human mind contains algorithms specialized for reasoning about social exchange. Social exchange was chosen as the target domain because the evolutionary theory of reciprocal altruism is mathematically well-developed, and because social exchange behavior is universal across human cultures (including hunter-gatherer cultures) AND present in our nearest primate relatives, indicating that cognitive adaptations for social exchange were present in the hominid lineage at least back to the common ancestor with chimpanzees ~5-10 million years ago. This establishes the Pleistocene depth required for a genuine cognitive adaptation rather than a culturally-transmitted pattern.
297.where: Cosmides & Tooby, 'Cognitive Adaptations for Social Exchange', in Barkow Cosmides Tooby (eds.) The Adapted Mind (1992)

298.quote: In this dialogue, reasoning has served as the paradigm case of the 'general-purpose' psychological process: It has been viewed as preeminently characteristic of those processes that are purportedly the central engine of the human mind. Even vigorous advocates of modularity have held so-called central processes, such as reasoning, to be general-purpose and content-independent. Consequently, we felt that reasoning about social exchange offered an excellent opportunity to cut to the quick of the controversy. If even human reasoning, the doctrinal 'citadel' of the advocates of content-free, general-purpose processes, turns out to include a large number of content-dependent cognitive adaptations, then the presumption that psychological mechanisms are characteristically domain-general and originally content-free can no longer be accorded privileged status.
298.content: Cosmides & Tooby's direct challenge to the general-purpose-reasoning citadel: if even human reasoning - traditionally held as the paradigm case of content-free, general-purpose cognition - turns out to include content-dependent cognitive adaptations, then the assumption that psychological mechanisms are characteristically domain-general and originally content-free can no longer be accorded privileged status. This is the specific argumentative move the Wason selection task cheater-detection finding is designed to make: by showing that humans reason about social-exchange problems fundamentally differently than isomorphic abstract problems, it forces the conclusion that reasoning is not a single general-purpose faculty. Load-bearing for P2 Domain-Sensitive Interacting Adaptations.
298.where: Cosmides & Tooby, Adapted Mind Ch. 3, chapter-opening argument

299.quote: The Standard Social Science Model requires an impossible psychology. Results out of cognitive psychology, evolutionary biology, artificial intelligence, developmental psychology, linguistics, and philosophy converge on the same conclusion: A psychological architecture that consisted of nothing but equipotential, general-purpose, content-independent, or content-free mechanisms could not successfully perform the tasks the human mind is known to perform or solve the adaptive problems humans evolved to solve - from seeing, to learning a language, to recognizing an emotional expression, to selecting a mate, to the many disparate activities aggregated under the term 'learning culture'. It cannot account for the behavior observed, and it is not a type of design that could have evolved.
299.content: Tooby & Cosmides's Standard Social Science Model (SSSM) critique from the Adapted Mind opening chapter. The SSSM is the consensus view of the nature of social and cultural phenomena that served for a century as the intellectual framework for psychology and the social sciences - and their claim of autonomy from the rest of science. The SSSM requires an impossible psychology: a cognitive architecture consisting only of equipotential, general-purpose, content-independent mechanisms could not successfully perform tasks the human mind is known to perform (seeing, language learning, emotional expression recognition, mate selection, cultural learning) or solve the adaptive problems humans evolved to solve. The Cor framework inherits Tooby & Cosmides's rejection of the SSSM as the architectural basis for P2.
299.where: Tooby & Cosmides, 'The Psychological Foundations of Culture' in Barkow Cosmides Tooby (eds.) The Adapted Mind (1992)

300.quote: people move their facial muscles in many different ways, not one consistent way, when feeling an instance of the same emotion category. Large meta-analyses conclude that a single emotion category involves different bodily responses, not a single, consistent response. Brain circuitry operates by the many-to-one principle of degeneracy: instances of a single emotion category, such as fear, are handled by different brain patterns at different times and in different people. Conversely, the same neurons can participate in creating different mental states (one-to-many).
300.content: Barrett's comprehensive meta-analysis of brain-imaging, facial EMG, and autonomic nervous system studies finds no consistent physical fingerprint for any single emotion. Facial muscles move in many different ways for the same emotion category. Bodily responses vary across instances. Brain circuitry operates by degeneracy (many-to-one: different neural patterns produce the same emotion category) and core systems (one-to-many: the same neurons participate in different mental states). Variation, not uniformity, is the norm across all three measurement domains.

301.quote: In every waking moment, your brain uses past experience, organized as concepts, to guide your actions and give your sensations meaning. When the concepts involved are emotion concepts, your brain constructs instances of emotion.
301.content: Barrett's formal definition of the theory of constructed emotion: the brain uses past experience organized as concepts to guide actions and give sensations meaning. When emotion concepts are active, the brain constructs instances of emotion. Emotions are not triggered reactions but active constructions from interoceptive sensations, conceptual knowledge, and contextual predictions.

302.quote: Degeneracy means "many to one": many combinations of neurons can produce the same outcome. In the quest to map emotion fingerprints in the brain, degeneracy is a humbling reality check.
302.content: The principle of degeneracy in emotion: different combinations of neurons can produce the same emotional outcome (many-to-one). Barrett's lab demonstrated this in brain-imaging studies where men and women reported equivalent feelings of arousal but showed different neural patterns - women's arousal was more strongly linked to the anterior insula, men's to visual cortex. The same subjective experience was associated with different patterns of neural activity.

303.quote: Simple pleasant and unpleasant feelings come from an ongoing process inside you called interoception. Interoception is your brain's representation of all sensations from your internal organs and tissues, the hormones in your blood, and your immune system. Think about what's happening within your body right this second. Your insides are in motion. Your heart sends blood rushing through your veins and arteries. Your lungs fill and empty. Your stomach digests food. This interoceptive activity produces the spectrum of basic feeling from pleasant to unpleasant, from calm to jittery, and even completely neutral.
303.content: Interoception - the brain's representation of all sensations from internal organs, tissues, hormones, and the immune system - produces the spectrum of basic feeling from pleasant to unpleasant, calm to jittery. Interoception is a core ingredient of emotion, but these feelings are simpler than full-blown emotional experiences. The brain uses interoceptive predictions to regulate the body budget (allostasis) and creates meaning from these sensations via concepts.

304.quote: Why is this relevant to emotion? Because every brain region that's claimed to be a home of emotion in humans is a body-budgeting region within the interoceptive network. These regions, however, don't react in emotion. They don't react at all. They predict, intrinsically, to regulate your body budget. They issue predictions for sights, sounds, thoughts, memories, imagination, and, yes, emotions. The idea of an emotional brain region is an illusion caused by the outdated belief in a reactive brain. Neuroscientists understand this today, but the message hasn't trickled down to many psychologists, psychiatrists, sociologists, economists, and others who study emotion.
304.content: Every brain region historically claimed as a home of emotion is actually a body-budgeting region within the interoceptive network. These regions do not react in emotion - they predict intrinsically to regulate the body budget, issuing predictions for sights, sounds, thoughts, memories, imagination, and emotions. The notion of a dedicated emotional brain region is an illusion caused by the outdated belief in a reactive brain.

305.quote: Through prediction, your brain constructs the world you experience. It combines bits and pieces of your past and estimates how likely each bit applies in your current situation.
305.content: The brain constructs the world you experience through prediction. Intrinsic brain activity - millions of nonstop predictions - is the brain's primary mode of operation. Past experience, organized as concepts, generates predictions that are tested against incoming sensory input. Events in the world merely tune these predictions rather than triggering responses. Evolution literally wired the brain for efficient prediction: 90 percent of connections entering primary visual cortex carry predictions from other brain regions, not sensory input from the world.

306.quote: Likewise, emotions are social reality. A physical event like a change in heart rate, blood pressure, or respiration becomes an emotional experience only when we, with emotion concepts that we have learned from our culture, imbue the sensations with additional functions by social agreement.
306.content: Emotions are social reality - not physical reality. A physical event like a change in heart rate or blood pressure becomes an emotional experience only when emotion concepts, learned from culture, imbue the sensations with additional functions by social agreement. Barrett draws an analogy to cupcakes and muffins: chemically identical baked goods distinguished only by the cultural category applied. Words and concepts from culture shape brain wiring and physical changes during emotion.

307.quote: A chronically imbalanced body budget acts like fertilizer for disease. In the last twenty years, it has become clear that the immune system is an ingredient in far more illnesses than you might expect, including diabetes, obesity, heart disease, depression, insomnia, reduced memory, and other "cognitive" functions related to premature aging and dementia.
307.content: A chronically imbalanced body budget acts like fertilizer for disease. Immune system involvement in far more illnesses than expected has become clear in the last twenty years: diabetes, obesity, heart disease, depression, insomnia, reduced memory, premature aging, and dementia all involve inflammatory processes. When the body budget is chronically unbalanced, cortisol excess leads to inflammation, which crosses into the brain, reshapes brain structure (particularly the interoceptive network), interferes with neural connections, kills neurons, and impairs attention and memory.

308.quote: My view is that some major illnesses considered distinct and "mental" are all rooted in a chronically unbalanced body budget and unbridled inflammation. We categorize and name them as different disorders, based on context, much like we categorize and name the same bodily changes as different emotions.
308.content: Barrett proposes that major illnesses considered distinct and mental - chronic stress, chronic pain, anxiety, depression - are all rooted in a chronically unbalanced body budget and unbridled inflammation. Different disorders share symptoms, cause atrophy in the same brain regions, their sufferers exhibit low emotional granularity, and the same medications are prescribed across disorders. These illnesses do not have firm boundaries in nature; like emotions, they are constructed categories applied to the same highly variable biological processes.

309.quote: Words seed your concepts, concepts drive your predictions, predictions regulate your body budget, and your body budget determines how you feel. Therefore, the more finely grained your vocabulary, the more precisely your predicting brain can calibrate your budget to your body's needs.
