In fact, people who exhibit higher emotional granularity go to the doctor less frequently, use medication less frequently, and spend fewer days hospitalized for illness.
309.content: Emotional granularity - the ability to construct finer-grained emotional experiences - has direct health consequences. Words seed concepts, concepts drive predictions, predictions regulate the body budget, and the body budget determines how you feel. The more finely grained the vocabulary, the more precisely the predicting brain can calibrate the body budget to actual needs. People who exhibit higher emotional granularity go to the doctor less frequently, use medication less frequently, and spend fewer days hospitalized for illness.

310.quote: So consider what happens if you're in a stressful social situation, like when a clique of coworkers suddenly stops inviting you to join them at lunch, or when friends read your text messages but don't answer. As per normal, your brain predicts you need fuel that your body doesn't require, temporarily impacting your budget. But what if the social situation doesn't resolve quickly? What if this social rejection is your life every day? Your body stays on alert, flush with cortisol and cytokines. Now your brain starts treating your body as if it were sick or damaged, and chronic inflammation sets in.
310.content: Social rejection as chronic body-budget crisis: when social exclusion becomes a daily reality (coworkers stop inviting you to lunch, friends read your texts but do not answer), the brain continuously predicts fuel needs the body does not require. Cortisol and cytokines stay elevated. The brain treats the body as if it were sick or damaged, and chronic inflammation sets in. Inflammation in the brain affects predictions that manage the body budget, driving the budget into overdraft and creating a vicious cycle of worsening misregulation.

311.quote: stress doesn't come from the outside world. You construct it.
311.content: Stress is constructed via the same brain mechanisms that construct emotion. In both cases the brain issues predictions about the body budget in relation to the outside world and makes meaning via concepts. The interoceptive network and the control network play the same roles in stress and emotion construction. The ascending and descending pathways between brain and body are identical. What differs is the end result - whether the brain categorizes sensations as stressful or emotional.

312.quote: Cumulative imbalance in the body budget - say, from growing up in adversity, where you don't feel safe or are deprived of basic necessities like nutritious food, quiet time to sleep, and so on - also changes the structure of your interoceptive network, rewiring your brain and reducing its ability to accurately regulate your body budget. All it takes are a couple of highly negative experiences for children to feel like they are living in a combat zone, reducing the size of their body-budgeting regions by the time they reach adulthood.
312.content: Cumulative body-budget imbalance from growing up in adversity - without safety, nutritious food, or quiet time to sleep - changes the structure of the interoceptive network, rewiring the brain and reducing its ability to regulate the body budget. A couple of highly negative childhood experiences can reduce the size of body-budgeting regions by adulthood. Growing up in a harsh or chaotic family, with conflict or verbal criticism, increases inflammation in adolescent girls. Children bullied in childhood show low-grade inflammation persisting into adulthood, predisposing them to psychiatric and physical diseases.

313.quote: In the theory of constructed emotion, however, the dividing line between brain and world is permeable, perhaps nonexistent. Your brain's core systems combine in various ways to construct your perceptions, memories, thoughts, feelings, and other mental states.
313.content: In the theory of constructed emotion, the dividing line between brain and world is permeable, perhaps nonexistent. The brain models the world through prediction and simulation; interoceptive predictions produce feelings of affect, influence every action, and determine what the organism cares about. At the same time, the outside world wires the brain: as an infant, sensory input seeds the earliest concepts; as language develops, the brain hardwires itself to the social world. Culture is not amorphous - it helped wire the brain, and behavior in turn wires the brains of the next generation.

314.quote: every thought, memory, emotion, or perception that you construct in your life includes something about the state of your body. Your interoceptive network, which regulates your body budget, is launching these cascades. Every prediction you make, and every categorization your brain completes, is always in relation to the activity of your heart and lungs, your metabolism, your immune function, and the other systems that contribute to your body budget.
314.content: Every thought, memory, emotion, or perception includes something about the state of the body. The interoceptive network, which regulates the body budget, launches the prediction cascades underlying all mental states. Every prediction and categorization occurs in relation to the activity of the heart, lungs, metabolism, immune function, and other body-budget systems. This means no mental state is purely cognitive or purely emotional - all are embodied through interoceptive prediction.

315.quote: This environment I propose to term the system's 'environment of adaptedness'. Only within its environment of adaptedness can it be expected that a system will work efficiently. In any other environment it cannot be expected to do so. In some such cases a system may in fact work reasonably well; in others it does not work at all; and in others again it gives rise to behaviour that is at best unusual and at worst positively unfavourable to survival.
315.content: Bowlby's concept of the environment of adaptedness: every behavioral system has a particular environment to which it is adapted. Only within this environment can the system work efficiently. In any other environment it may work reasonably well, give rise to unusual behavior, or produce outcomes positively unfavourable to survival. Each species and each system within a species has its own environment of adaptedness, defined in terms of specific variables.

316.quote: During it the young child appears acutely distressed at having lost his mother and seeks to recapture her by the full exercise of his limited resources. He will often cry loudly, shake his cot, throw himself about, and look eagerly towards any sight or sound which might prove to be his missing mother.
316.content: Bowlby's three-phase separation response in young children: protest (acute distress, crying, seeking the missing mother), despair (increasing hopelessness, withdrawal, deep mourning), and detachment (apparent recovery that masks emotional disengagement). The protest phase involves active attempts to recapture the mother; despair involves withdrawal and monotonous crying; detachment involves accepting care from others while showing striking absence of attachment behavior toward the mother on her return.

317.quote: What an animal requires is something more like a working model of its environment. The use to which a model in the brain is put is to transmit, store, and manipulate information that helps in making predictions as to how what are here termed set-goals can be achieved.
317.content: Bowlby's internal working model concept: the brain provides not merely a static map but a working model of the environment. This model transmits, stores, and manipulates information to generate predictions about how set-goals can be achieved. The working model concept explains how the child builds and updates mental representations of the attachment figure's availability and responsiveness, which then guide future attachment behavior.

318.quote: there is good evidence, derived from observations of many species of bird and mammal, that an isolated animal is much more likely to be attacked and seized by a predator than is an animal that stays bunched together with others of its kind. Secondly, attachment behaviour is elicited particularly easily and intensely in animals which, by reason of age, size, or condition, are especially vulnerable to predators, for example the young, pregnant females, the sick. Thirdly, attachment behaviour is always elicited at high intensity in situations of alarm, which are commonly situations when a predator is either sensed or suspected. No other theory fits these facts.
318.content: The biological function of attachment behavior is protection from predators. Three facts support this: (1) isolated animals are much more likely to be attacked by predators than animals that stay with others; (2) attachment behavior is most easily and intensely elicited in individuals especially vulnerable to predators - the young, pregnant females, the sick; (3) attachment behavior is always elicited at high intensity in situations of alarm when a predator is sensed or suspected. The paradoxical finding that punishment strengthens rather than weakens attachment is explained by this anti-predator function.

319.quote: Because the bias of a child to attach himself especially to one figure seems to be well established and also to have far-reaching implications for psychopathology, I believe it merits a special term. In the earlier paper I referred to it as 'monotropy'.
319.content: Bowlby coins the term monotropy for the child's bias to attach especially to one figure, noting this bias is well-established and has far-reaching implications for psychopathology. While children form multiple attachments, there is a strong tendency to direct attachment behavior principally toward one person - the principal attachment figure.

320.quote: The theory of secondary drive holds that a liking to be with other members of the species is a result of being fed by them.
320.content: Bowlby's critique of secondary drive theory: the theory that attachment to the mother is secondary to feeding (that the child learns to like the mother because she feeds it) is rejected. Bowlby argues attachment is a primary motivational system independent of feeding, as demonstrated by Harlow's rhesus monkey experiments and by the observation that punishment paradoxically strengthens rather than weakens attachment.

321.quote: the central concepts are those of behavioural systems and their control, of information, negative feedback, and a behavioural form of homeostasis. The more complex forms of instinctive behaviour are regarded as resulting from the execution of plans that, depending on the species, are more or less flexible.
321.content: Bowlby's behavioral systems model: instinctive behavior operates through control systems using behavioral homeostasis. The central concepts are behavioral systems and their control, information, negative feedback, and homeostatic regulation. Complex instinctive behavior results from the execution of plans that, depending on species, are more or less flexible. Plan execution is initiated by receipt of information from sense organs and guided by continuous reception of feedback from results of action taken.

322.quote: some of the infants who seemed most solidly attached to their mothers displayed little protest behaviour or separation anxiety, but rather showed the strength of their attachment to the mother through their readiness to use her as a secure base from which
322.content: Ainsworth's secure base concept as reported by Bowlby: some infants who seemed most solidly attached to their mothers displayed little protest behavior or separation anxiety. Instead, they showed the strength of their attachment through their readiness to use the mother as a secure base from which to explore. This redefines secure attachment not as constant proximity-seeking but as confident exploration enabled by the availability of the attachment figure.

323.quote: The existence of sensitive periods in early life during which the form to be taken by an adult's instinctive behaviour is in great part determined is yet another characteristic of instinctive behaviour to which Freud drew attention. In the psychoanalytic tradition it is represented in the concepts of fixation and of stage in libidinal organisation.
323.content: Sensitive periods in attachment development: Bowlby draws attention to the existence of sensitive periods in early life during which the form of adult instinctive behavior is largely determined. In the psychoanalytic tradition this is represented in the concepts of fixation and stage in libidinal organization. The sensitive period concept explains why early attachment experiences have disproportionate influence on later relationship patterns.

324.quote: Thus, when mother is called away a child's attachment behaviour is likely to be elicited and his exploratory behaviour inhibited; conversely, when a child explores too far, a mother's care behaviour is likely to be elicited and whatever else she is doing to be inhibited. In a happy couple these four classes of behaviour occur and progress together in harmony. But risk of conflict is ever-present.
324.content: Attachment behavior as one of four interacting classes in mother-child interaction: (a) the child's attachment behavior, (b) the child's exploratory behavior and play (antithetic to attachment), (c) the mother's caretaking behavior, and (d) the mother's behavior antithetic to care. When the mother is called away, the child's attachment behavior is elicited and exploratory behavior inhibited; when the child explores too far, the mother's care behavior is elicited. In a happy couple these four classes occur in harmony, but risk of conflict is ever-present.

325.quote: the antithesis 'innate versus acquired' is unreal. Just as area is a product of length multiplied by width so every biological character, whether it be morphological, physiological, or behavioural, is a product of the interaction of genetic endowment with environment. Terms like innate and acquired must therefore be cast into limbo and a new terminology employed.
325.content: The innate-acquired antithesis is unreal. Every biological character - morphological, physiological, or behavioral - is a product of the interaction of genetic endowment with environment. Bowlby adopts Hinde's terminology: characters little influenced by environmental variation are 'environmentally stable'; those much influenced are 'environmentally labile.' Attachment behavior has both stable and labile components - the basic behavioral system is species-typical but its organization is shaped by developmental experience.

326.quote: A large body of observational data from the Wisconsin laboratories indicates that heterosexual behaviour is greatly influenced by early experience, and the failure of infants to form effective infant-infant affectional relations delays or destroys adequate adult heterosexual behaviour
326.content: Harlow's deprivation experiments with rhesus monkeys: infants reared in social environments differing greatly from the environment of evolutionary adaptedness show severe disruption. Failure to form effective infant-infant affectional relations delays or destroys adequate adult heterosexual behavior. Even monkeys with adequate peer play but no maternal experience show considerable individual differences in adult social and sexual competence.

327.quote: loss of mother-figure, either by itself or in combination with other variables yet to be clearly identified, is capable of generating responses and processes that are of the greatest interest to psychopathology. Not only so, but these responses and processes, we concluded, are the very same as are known to be active in older individuals who are still disturbed by separations that they suffered in early life.
327.content: Loss of the mother-figure generates responses and processes of the greatest interest to psychopathology. These responses are the very same as those active in older individuals still disturbed by early separations. On one hand: excessive demands on others, anxiety and anger when demands are unmet (dependent and hysterical personalities). On the other: blockage in the capacity to make deep relationships (affectionless and psychopathic personalities).

328.quote: the young child's hunger for his mother's love and presence is as great as his hunger for food, and that in consequence her absence inevitably generates 'a powerful sense of loss and anger'.
328.content: The young child's hunger for the mother's love and presence is as great as hunger for food, and her absence inevitably generates a powerful sense of loss and anger. This framing establishes attachment as a primary motivational need on par with nutrition - not secondary to it - and positions separation distress as a necessary consequence of the attachment system's design rather than a sign of weakness or pathology.

329.quote: close examination reveals that the different signalling components of attachment behaviour are far from being interchangeable; rather, each is found to be distinctive and to be complementary to each of the others.
329.content: Signalling components of attachment behavior - including crying - are distinctive and complementary, not interchangeable. Crying takes several different forms elicited by different conditions: crying from hunger builds slowly and becomes rhythmical; crying from pain is loud from the start with a sudden long initial cry. Different signal types elicit different components of maternal behavior, demonstrating that attachment signaling is a differentiated communication system.

330.quote: The cortex and limbic system are not separate, as scads of axonal projections course between the two. Crucially, those projections are bidirectional - the limbic system talks to the cortex, rather than merely being reined in by it.
330.content: The frontal cortex is bidirectionally enmeshed with the limbic system. Nauta's landmark discovery showed the frontal cortex is a quasi member of the limbic system, not a hierarchical controller standing above it. In different circumstances the frontal cortex and limbic system stimulate or inhibit each other, collaborate and conflict. The false dichotomy between thought and feeling is a neuroscientific error.

331.quote: while the acute stress response involves enhanced immunity, chronic stress suppresses immunity, increasing vulnerability to some infectious diseases.
331.content: The acute stress response involves enhanced immunity, but chronic stress suppresses immunity, increasing vulnerability to infectious diseases. We get sick not from failing to activate the stress response but from activating it too often, too long, and for purely psychological reasons. The beneficial effects of stress (fight-or-flight for seconds to minutes) become damaging on the sustained timescale of chronic psychological stress.

332.quote: Testosterone was administered to the middle-ranking male in each group (say, rank number 3 out of five), increasing their levels of aggression. Does this mean that these guys, stoked on 'roids, started challenging numbers 1 and 2 in the hierarchy? No. They became aggressive jerks to poor numbers 4 and 5. Testosterone did not create new social patterns of aggression; it exaggerated preexisting ones.
332.content: Testosterone does not create aggression - it amplifies preexisting social patterns. In talapoin monkeys, testosterone given to middle-ranking males did not make them challenge higher-ranking individuals; it made them more aggressive to lower-ranking ones. In humans, testosterone does not raise baseline amygdala activity but boosts amygdala response to angry faces specifically. Testosterone makes subjects more punitive when provoked, enhancing 'vengeful reactive aggression' rather than creating new social patterns.

333.quote: In another study subjects waited an unknown length of time to receive a shock. This lack of predictability and control was so aversive that many chose to receive a stronger shock immediately. And in the others the period of anticipatory dread increasingly activated the amygdala.
333.content: Lack of predictability and control over stressors is so aversive that subjects chose to receive a stronger shock immediately rather than wait an unknown time for a weaker one. The period of anticipatory dread increasingly activated the amygdala.

334.quote: This domain of epigenetics was uncovered in a landmark 2004 study by Meaney and colleagues, one of the most cited papers published in the prestigious journal Nature Neuroscience. They had shown previously that offspring of more "attentive" rat mothers (those that frequently nurse, groom, and lick their pups) become adults with lower glucocorticoid levels, less anxiety, better learning, and delayed brain aging.
334.content: Meaney's landmark 2004 study demonstrated that maternal care style in rats produces epigenetic changes in offspring's stress response genes. Offspring of more attentive mothers (frequent nursing, grooming, licking) become adults with lower glucocorticoid levels, less anxiety, better learning, and delayed brain aging. These changes are epigenetic - mothering style alters gene regulation in pups' brains. Remarkably, such pups as adults become more attentive mothers themselves, passing the trait epigenetically to the next generation.

335.quote: What is social play in the young? Writ large, it's an array of behaviors that train individuals in social competence. Writ medium, it's fragments of the real thing, bits and pieces of fixed action patterns, a chance to safely try out roles and improve motor skills. Writ small and endocrine, it's a demonstration that moderate and transient stress - "stimulation" - is great. Writ small and neurobiological, it's a tool for deciding which excess synapses to prune.
335.content: Social play in the young is an array of behaviors that train individuals in social competence. It consists of fragments of real behavioral patterns - a chance to safely try out roles and improve motor skills. Endocrinologically, play demonstrates that moderate transient stress (stimulation) is beneficial. Neurobiologically, play is a tool for deciding which excess synapses to prune. Play is universal among socially complex species, peaking at puberty. A child deprived of or disinterested in play rarely has a socially fulfilling adult life.

336.quote: Korean and European American subjects observed pictures of either in- or out-group members in pain. All subjects reported more subjective empathy and showed more activation of Theory of Mind brain regions (i.e., the temporoparietal junction) when observing in-group members, but the bias was significantly greater among Korean subjects.
336.content: In-group empathy bias is stronger in collectivist than individualist cultures. Korean and European American subjects showed more empathy and Theory of Mind activation for in-group members in pain, but the bias was significantly greater among Korean subjects. Both individualist and collectivist cultures denigrate out-groups, but only individualist cultures inflate assessments of their own group - East Asians do not need to puff up their own group to view others as inferior.

337.quote: Which raises a third fundamental, alongside individual selection and kin selection: reciprocal altruism. "I'll scratch your back if you scratch mine. I'd rather not actually scratch yours if I can get away with it. And I'm watching you in case you try the same."
337.content: Reciprocal altruism: cooperation among unrelated organisms where each incurs a fitness cost to enhance the other's fitness with expectation of reciprocation. Trivers (1971) laid out the evolutionary logic. Unrelated animals frequently cooperate - fish school, birds fly in formation, meerkats give alarm calls, vampire bats feed one another's babies, primates groom one another and share meat. Cooperation evolves because many hands lighten the load, but it creates the problem of cheater detection.

338.quote: Just as prenatal testosterone exposure generates an adult brain that is more sensitive to environmental triggers of aggression, excessive prenatal glucocorticoid exposure produces an adult brain more sensitive to environmental triggers of depression and anxiety.
338.content: Prenatal glucocorticoid exposure produces organizational effects on fetal brain construction, decreasing growth factors, neurons, and synapses. Just as prenatal testosterone exposure generates an adult brain more sensitive to aggression triggers, excessive prenatal glucocorticoid exposure produces an adult brain more sensitive to environmental triggers of depression and anxiety. Stressed mothers secrete glucocorticoids that enter fetal circulation with the same consequences as postnatal stress.

339.quote: glucocorticoids decrease activation of the (cognitive) medial PFC during processing of emotional faces. Collectively, stress or glucocorticoid administration decreases accuracy when rapidly assessing emotions of faces.
339.content: Chronic stress literally eats away at interoceptive and control networks. It causes the amygdala to expand while the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex atrophy. Glucocorticoids decrease activation of the cognitive medial PFC during emotional processing, decreasing accuracy when rapidly assessing emotions. During sustained stress, the systems that should regulate the stress response are themselves damaged by the stress response - a vicious cycle of worsening misregulation.

340.quote: the worst stress-related health typically occurs in middle management, with its killer combo of high work demands but little autonomy - responsibility without control.
340.content: Subordinate organisms are typically the most stressed and unhealthy. Lab rodents, primates from rhesus monkeys to lemurs, hamsters, guinea pigs, wolves, rabbits, pigs, fish, and sugar gliders all show that subordinate individuals have elevated resting glucocorticoids - chronic activation of the stress response even in the absence of acute stressors. The worst stress-related health in humans occurs in middle management, with its killer combination of high work demands but little autonomy - responsibility without control.

341.quote: The amygdala is particularly sensitive to unsettling circumstances that are social. Stable rankings activated parts of the frontal cortex that we'll soon consider. Instability activated the frontal cortex plus the amygdala. Being unsure of your place is unsettling.
341.content: The amygdala is particularly sensitive to social uncertainty. When a male monkey's social position is threatened by a rival, amygdala activation correlates not with aggression or testosterone but with anxiety (teeth chattering, self-scratching). In humans, unstable social rankings activate both the frontal cortex and amygdala, while stable rankings activate only the frontal cortex. Being unsure of your social place is unsettling - rank uncertainty, not rank itself, drives threat-system activation.

343.quote: Childhood abuse, for example, causes epigenetic changes in hundreds of genes in the human hippocampus. Moreover, Stephen Suomi of the National Institutes of Health and Szyf found that mothering style in monkeys has epigenetic effects on more than a thousand frontocortical genes.
343.content: Childhood abuse causes epigenetic changes in hundreds of genes in the human hippocampus. Mothering style in monkeys has epigenetic effects on more than a thousand frontocortical genes. Hormonal responses to fetal and childhood experiences have epigenetic effects on genes related to BDNF, the vasopressin and oxytocin system, and estrogen sensitivity, with effects pertinent to adult cognition, personality, emotionality, and psychiatric health.

344.quote: Moreover, sustained stress and glucocorticoid exposure enhance LTP and suppress LTD in the amygdala, boosting fear conditioning, and suppress LTP in the frontal cortex. Combining these effects - more excitable synapses in the amygdala, fewer ones in the frontal cortex - helps explain stress-induced impulsivity and poor emotional regulation.
344.content: Sustained stress and glucocorticoid exposure enhance LTP and suppress LTD in the amygdala while suppressing LTP in the frontal cortex. This combination - more excitable synapses in the amygdala, fewer in the frontal cortex - helps explain stress-induced impulsivity and poor emotional regulation.

345.quote: the Smoke Detector Principle. Most of the responses that cause human suffering are unnecessary in the individual instance but still perfectly normal because they have low costs but protect against huge possible losses. They are like false alarms from smoke detectors. The occasional wail when you burn the toast is worth it to ensure that you are warned
345.content: The Smoke Detector Principle: most defensive responses that cause human suffering are unnecessary in the individual instance but perfectly normal because they have low costs but protect against huge possible losses. They are like false alarms from smoke detectors - the occasional wail when you burn toast is worth it to ensure warning about every real fire. This explains why it is usually safe to use drugs to block vomiting and pain - most instances are false alarms.

346.quote: People seek help mainly for symptoms, not diseases. Pain, fever, malaise, cough, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are protective responses. So are anxiety, jealousy, anger, and low mood. They are set off when something bad is happening. They are unpleasant but useful.
346.content: Defensive responses such as pain, fever, cough, nausea, anxiety, jealousy, anger, and low mood are protective responses, not diseases. They are set off when something bad is happening. They are unpleasant but useful.

347.quote: An evolutionary view explains why we have desires, why we can't satisfy them, and why it is so hard to set them aside: our brains were shaped to benefit our genes, not us.
347.content: An evolutionary view explains why we have desires, why we cannot satisfy them, and why it is so hard to set them aside: our brains were shaped to benefit our genes, not us. Most suffering is emotional suffering. Anxiety and low mood exist for the same reason as pain and nausea - because they are useful in certain situations. They are often excessive for good evolutionary reasons.

348.quote: Organisms try to get sex, power, and resources and to avoid danger and loss. Pursuing these goals gives rise to a set of defined situations. Each one poses different adaptive challenges that shape a different emotional state. Opportunity arouses enthusiasm. Success arouses joy. Threat arouses anxiety. Loss arouses sadness.
348.content: Four situations that arise in goal pursuit map to four emotions: opportunity arouses enthusiasm, success arouses joy, threat arouses anxiety, loss arouses sadness. Organisms try to get sex, power, and resources and to avoid danger and loss. Each situation poses different adaptive challenges that shape a different emotional state. The scheme can be expanded by adding emotions for alternative outcomes - disappointment when pursuit fails, relief when threat is avoided.

349.quote: The core problem for psychiatric diagnosis is the lack of a perspective on normal useful functions that physiology provides for the rest of medicine. Internal medicine doctors know the functions of the kidneys. They don't confuse protective defenses such as cough and pain with diseases such as pneumonia and cancer. Psychiatrists lack a similar framework for the utility of stress, sleep, anxiety, and mood, so psychiatric diagnostic categories remain confusing and crude.
349.content: The core problem for psychiatric diagnosis is the lack of a perspective on normal useful functions that physiology provides for the rest of medicine. Internal medicine doctors know kidney functions and do not confuse protective defenses (cough, pain) with diseases (pneumonia, cancer). Psychiatrists lack a similar framework for the utility of stress, sleep, anxiety, and mood, so diagnostic categories remain confusing and crude. Anxiety and low mood are useful normal responses - it is time to give up the fantasy that each mental disorder has a specific cause.

350.quote: While attributing specific functions to specific mood states is a mistake, the capacity for mood can be said to have a general function: mood reallocates investments of time, effort, resources, and risk taking to maximize Darwinian fitness in situations of varying propitiousness. High and low moods adjust cognition and behavior to cope with propitious and unpropitious situations.
350.content: Mood reallocates investments of time, effort, resources, and risk taking to maximize Darwinian fitness in situations of varying propitiousness. High and low moods adjust cognition and behavior to cope with propitious and unpropitious situations. Attributing specific functions to specific mood states is a mistake - the capacity for mood has a general function as a resource-allocation system.

351.quote: Many of our current health problems result from the environments we have created to satisfy our desires. Most people in developed societies live better now physically than the kings and queens of just a century ago. We have a surfeit of delicious food, protection from the elements, time for leisure, and relief from pain. These accomplishments are spectacular, but they also cause most chronic disease.
351.content: Many current health problems result from environments created to satisfy our desires. Most people in developed societies live better physically than kings and queens of a century ago - surfeit of delicious food, protection from elements, leisure time, relief from pain. These accomplishments are spectacular but they also cause most chronic disease. The mismatch between our evolved bodies and the environments we have created is a major source of illness.

352.quote: systems that regulate protective responses such as vomiting and pain turn the response on whenever the benefits are greater than the costs, even if that means false alarms. The costs of such responses tend to be low compared to the benefits of avoiding danger. So when danger may or may not be present, the small cost of a response ensures protection against a much larger harm. That is why we put up with false alarms from smoke detectors. It is why we can safely use medications to block responses such as vomiting and pain. And it is why useless anxiety is so common.
352.content: The Smoke Detector Principle explains why useless anxiety is so common. Systems that regulate protective responses turn the response on whenever the benefits are greater than the costs, even if that means false alarms. The costs of such responses tend to be low compared to the benefits of avoiding danger, so when danger may or may not be present, the small cost of a response ensures protection against a much larger harm.

353.quote: We want so badly to be important, rich, loved, admired, attractive, and powerful. For what? The good feelings from succeeding are just about balanced by the bad feelings from failure. Our emotions benefit our genes far more than they do us.
353.content: Our emotions benefit our genes far more than they do us. We want so badly to be important, rich, loved, admired, attractive, and powerful - but the good feelings from succeeding are just about balanced by the bad feelings from failure. The emotional system is calibrated not for individual happiness but for gene propagation, which explains why suffering is inherent rather than accidental.

354.quote: Nearly everyone has wondered why human life is so full of suffering. Part of an answer is that natural selection shaped emotions such as anxiety, low mood, and grief because they are useful. More of an answer comes from recognizing that our suffering often benefits our genes.
354.content: Natural selection shaped emotions such as anxiety, low mood, and grief because they are useful. More of an answer to why life is full of suffering comes from recognizing that our suffering often benefits our genes. Nearly everyone has wondered why human life is so full of suffering - an evolutionary perspective provides the first satisfying scientific explanation.

355.quote: Sometimes low mood should be respected as normal and useful to help adjust a person's motivation and life directions. However, often the situation can't be changed. The loss of a friend, continuing abuse, inability to get a job, trying every night to help a child get off drugs, finding no relief from chronic pain - those are good reasons, but the resulting bad feelings are harmful even if they are normal.
355.content: Low mood can be (1) normal and useful for adjusting motivation, (2) normal but harmful because the situation cannot be changed (loss, abuse, chronic pain), (3) normal but useless because of the Smoke Detector Principle, (4) normal but useless because we live in environments so different from those we evolved in, or (5) caused by abnormalities in the mood regulation system. Clinicians should take the same medical approach to low mood as to physical pain: find the cause and fix it, but always relieve suffering.

356.quote: There are good reasons for bad feelings. Anxiety and depression are often excessive because they benefit genes at our expense, because of the Smoke Detector Principle, because we live in modern environments, and because regulation mechanisms are intrinsically vulnerable.
356.content: Nesse's resolution: there are good reasons for bad feelings. Anxiety and depression are often excessive because (1) they benefit genes at our expense, (2) the Smoke Detector Principle, (3) we live in modern environments, and (4) regulation mechanisms are intrinsically vulnerable. Some disorders have specific brain causes; others are syndromes like kidney failure with many possible causes. Top-down and bottom-up causes interact to create tangled webs - this is not confusion, it is reality.

357.quote: Low moods prevent us from wasting effort in pursuit of unreachable goals, but they often escalate into pathological depression.
357.content: Low mood prevents us from wasting effort in pursuit of unreachable goals, but it often escalates into pathological depression. The signal is functionally adaptive - it indicates that current strategies are failing and effort should be redirected - but the signal itself can become the problem when the mood regulation system cannot disengage.

358.quote: There is nothing normal or useful about psychotic depression or mania. Both are serious diseases that result from broken mood regulation mechanisms.
358.content: There is nothing normal or useful about psychotic depression or mania. Both are serious diseases that result from broken mood regulation mechanisms. Nesse explicitly distinguishes these from normal-but-excessive low mood - the mood regulation system itself is damaged, not just producing adaptive but unwanted signals.

359.quote: Panic disorder is caused by false alarms in the emergency response system. The system has been honed to speed escape when life-threatening danger may be present. You are thirsty on the ancient African savanna and a watering hole is just ahead, but you hear a noise in the grass. It could be a lion, or it might just be a monkey. Should you flee?
359.content: Panic disorder is caused by false alarms in the emergency response system. The system has been honed to speed escape when life-threatening danger may be present. On the ancient African savanna, a noise near a watering hole could be a lion or a monkey - the expected cost calculation (100 calories for fleeing vs. death for not fleeing when it IS a lion) means panic should be triggered whenever the probability of danger exceeds a tiny threshold. This cost asymmetry explains why panic attacks occur in objectively safe modern environments.

360.quote: Unlike much of the world today, and most people who have ever lived, we WEIRD people are highly individualistic, self-obsessed, control-oriented, nonconformist, and analytical. We focus on ourselves - our attributes, accomplishments, and aspirations - over our relationships and social roles.
360.content: WEIRD people are psychologically peculiar: highly individualistic, self-obsessed, control-oriented, nonconformist, and analytical. They focus on attributes, accomplishments, and aspirations over relationships and social roles. They see themselves as unique beings, not as nodes in a social network. They prefer a sense of control and making their own choices. They are less willing to conform when this conflicts with their own beliefs. Yet paradoxically, WEIRD people tend to stick to impartial rules and are quite trusting, honest, and cooperative toward strangers.

361.quote: Throughout most of human history, people grew up enmeshed in dense family networks that knitted together distant cousins and in-laws. In these regulated-relational worlds, people's survival, identity, security, marriages, and success depended on the health and prosperity of kin-based networks, which often formed discrete institutions known as clans, lineages, houses, or tribes.
361.content: Throughout most of human history, people grew up enmeshed in dense family networks of distant cousins and in-laws. Survival, identity, security, marriages, and success depended on kin-based networks (clans, lineages, houses, tribes). People were endowed with inherited obligations, responsibilities, and privileges in relation to others in a dense social web. This social interdependence bred emotional interdependence, leading people to strongly identify with in-groups and make sharp in-group/out-group distinctions.

362.quote: This evolving proto-WEIRD psychology gradually laid the groundwork for the rise of impersonal markets, urbanization, constitutional governments, democratic politics, individualistic religions, scientific societies, and relentless innovation.
362.content: One sect of Christianity drove the spread of social norms that dramatically altered marriage, families, inheritance, and ownership in parts of Europe over centuries. This transformation of family life initiated psychological changes that spurred new forms of urbanization and fueled impersonal commerce. An evolving proto-WEIRD psychology laid the groundwork for impersonal markets, constitutional governments, democratic politics, individualistic religions, scientific societies, and relentless innovation.

363.quote: Individualism is best thought of as a psychological cluster that allows people to better navigate WEIRD social worlds by calibrating their perceptions, attention, judgments, and emotions.
363.content: Individualism is a psychological cluster that calibrates perceptions, attention, judgments, and emotions for navigating WEIRD social worlds. Most populations reveal psychological packages that similarly fit their societies' institutions, technologies, environments, and languages. The psychology-institution fit is bidirectional - institutions shape psychology through cultural learning, and psychology shapes which institutions can emerge and persist.

364.quote: WEIRD people do conform to others, and this is what surprised Solomon. Only about one-quarter of his participants were never influenced by their peers. WEIRD people, however, conform less than all the other populations that have been studied.
364.content: WEIRD people conform less than all other studied populations, but they do still conform. Cross-cultural studies show substantial variation in conformity across countries, with WEIRD undergraduate samples at the low end. The reduced conformity in WEIRD populations reflects the dismantling of kin-based social pressure and the institutional promotion of individual autonomy.

365.quote: The data, from over 20,000 participants in 30 countries, confirm that in places where people actually do trust strangers in anonymous experimental settings, they also tend to say, when asked the GTQ, that most people can be trusted.
365.content: Impersonal trust and cooperation with strangers: in places where people actually trust strangers in anonymous experimental settings, they also report trusting most people in surveys. Impersonal prosociality includes motivations and strategies for punishing those who break impartial norms. This trust-among-strangers is a WEIRD psychological feature that evolved alongside impersonal market institutions.

366.quote: Shame is rooted in a genetically evolved psychological package that is associated with social devaluation in the eyes of others.
366.content: Shame is rooted in a genetically evolved psychological package associated with social devaluation in the eyes of others. In regulated-relational societies, shame can be experienced vicariously - a crime by one person brings shame to parents, siblings, and distant relations. The reverberation of shame through kin networks creates collective accountability. WEIRD societies shifted from shame-based to guilt-based moral psychology as kin networks dissolved.

367.quote: We have evolved genetically to learn adaptively in ways that calibrate our minds and behavior to the environments we encounter. Specifically, our evolved capacities for cultural learning have been honed to figure out who to learn from, what to learn, and when to use cultural learning over other informational sources like individual experience or innate intuitions.
367.content: We have evolved genetically to learn adaptively in ways that calibrate our minds and behavior to the environments we encounter. Our evolved capacities for cultural learning have been honed to figure out who to learn from, what to learn, and when to use cultural learning over other information sources like individual experience or innate intuitions.

368.quote: By selectively attending to particular kinds of ideas and individuals under particular circumstances, our cultural learning abilities adaptively rewire our brains and biology to better calibrate them for navigating our culturally constructed worlds.
368.content: Cultural learning rewires brains and biology. When learners watch others, they actively calibrate neurocircuitry in ways that move perceptions, preferences, behaviors, and judgments closer to those of chosen models. By selectively filtering and recombining beliefs, practices, techniques, and motivations acquired from others, cultural learning abilities adaptively rewire brains to better calibrate them for navigating culturally constructed worlds.

369.quote: The banning of sororate and levirate marriages were among the first actions taken as the Church began to restructure European families.
369.content: The Church's Marriage and Family Program (MFP) restructured European families by banning cousin marriage, levirate and sororate marriage, adoption, and polygyny. Starting as early as 315 CE with the Synod of Neocaesarea banning men from marrying a dead brother's wife, these prohibitions systematically dismantled the kin-based institutions that had organized human social life for millennia.

370.quote: Often, especially in formerly non-state societies, the newly transplanted institutions created a misfit with people's cultural psychology, leading to poorly functioning governments, economies, and civil societies.
370.content: Impersonal institutions (representative governments, universities, social safety nets) evolved in Europe and have been exported to numerous populations. Often, especially in formerly non-state societies, newly transplanted institutions create a misfit with people's cultural psychology, leading to poorly functioning governments, economies, and civil societies. The institutional-psychological mismatch produces systemic dysfunction.

371.quote: In effect, it is the rank and file who are on top, and the would-be alphas who remain under their thumbs. The fact that the occasional successful intimidator can rise to tyrannize these egalitarians for a time does not negate the characterization, for the group's next move is to dominate the dominator by removing him.
371.content: Reverse dominance hierarchy: the rank and file are on top, and would-be alphas remain under their thumbs. When an occasional intimidator rises to tyrannize, the group's next move is to dominate the dominator by removing him. This is the fundamental political structure of human forager bands - not the absence of hierarchy but the active suppression of dominance by coalitions of subordinates.

372.quote: The most frequent type of power coalition in egalitarian bands consists of the entire adult community coalescing against a deviant. In addition to the proscription of bullying by upstarts, all foragers are opposed to incest, murder within the group, and undue selfish use of deception.
372.content: The entire moral community coalesces against deviants. All foragers oppose incest, murder within the group, and undue selfish use of deception. The most frequent type of power coalition in egalitarian bands consists of the entire adult community acting collectively against a deviant. The threat of sanctions (including ostracism and execution) keeps power seekers in their place. When upstartism becomes active, so does the moral community - it unites preemptively and assertively.

373.quote: In effect, the band keeps a dossier on every individual, noting positive and negative points. Group members exercise the right to take action if a deviant begins to intimidate other group members individually - or threatens the social equilibrium of the group or its very ability to function.
373.content: Gossip as information processing and social control: the band keeps a dossier on every individual, noting positive and negative points. Types of deviance that all groups watch for include murder, deception, theft, and stinginess. Everyone knows gossiping is constantly taking place and anyone can be a target - this knowledge serves as a deterrent, for most foragers worry about the opinion of their peers and try to exert self-control accordingly.

374.quote: I proposed that leveling mechanisms may be necessary because, as with chimpanzees, underlying dominance and submission tendencies facilitate competition among individuals and constitute a powerful force for hierarchy in group life.
374.content: Leveling mechanisms may be necessary because underlying dominance and submission tendencies facilitate competition among individuals and constitute a powerful force for hierarchy in group life. Humans have innate dominance tendencies that must be actively suppressed through egalitarian leveling. The tension between the impulse to dominate and the egalitarian ethos is a fundamental feature of human political psychology.

375.quote: those who have things of value but do not give are subject to social control through gossip, ridicule or ostracism.
375.content: Social control through gossip, ridicule, and ostracism targets free-riders: those who have things of value but do not give are subject to social control. Bullying free-riders are handled by egalitarian sanctioning. Other free-riders take advantage by being lazy, feigning injury, or secretly consuming meat they have killed. Much of the enforcement investment involves gossiping, which brings individual reproductive benefits through rewarding social interaction and exchange of information about subsistence.

376.quote: How can cheerful, altruistic cooperators, people guided by generous feelings and positive expectations about cooperation, avoid being exploited by lazy slackers and outright cheaters, or by opportunistic bullies who take advantage of situations by force? To whatever degree the cooperating altruists in a group can be successful in circumventing such losses, it becomes far, far easier to explain the natural selection of altruistic traits.
376.content: How can altruistic cooperators avoid exploitation by lazy slackers, outright cheaters, and opportunistic bullies? To whatever degree cooperating altruists can successfully circumvent such losses, it becomes far easier to explain the natural selection of altruistic traits. Free-rider suppression is the mechanism that makes group selection for cooperation viable - without it, selfish individuals would always outcompete altruists within groups.

377.quote: Stigmatized roles such as 'cheater' or 'selfish bully' are labeled (and sanctioned) to make the system work in spite of predictable conflicts. This moralistic approach works reasonably well in curbing individual selfishness or tendencies to dominate, precisely because the group knows how to become aggressive in dealing with those it labels as deviants.
377.content: Moral enforcement of sharing: the meat-sharing habit of nomadic foragers is transformed by language and morality so that definitive rules exist. Stigmatized roles such as 'cheater' or 'selfish bully' are labeled and sanctioned to make the system work despite predictable conflicts. An armed group can be exceedingly dangerous to any deviant - even the most powerful hunter - and hunters are always armed.

378.quote: In humans, it seems safe to assume that the larger the brain, the greater the degree of political intelligence and the higher the probability that subordinate coalitions could definitively suppress alpha-type behavior. Humans were ready to form moral communities and reverse their dominance hierarchies 100,000 years ago, and probably considerably earlier.
378.content: The earliest human precursor was likely an African ape that formed political coalitions enabling the rank and file to whittle away at alpha powers. By the Late Paleolithic, humans possessed an egalitarian ethos and political order similar to present-day hunting bands. The larger the brain, the greater the political intelligence and the higher the probability that subordinate coalitions could suppress alpha-type behavior. Humans were ready to form moral communities and reverse their dominance hierarchies 100,000 years ago, probably earlier.

379.quote: We have underestimated just how important shared care and provisioning of offspring by group members other than parents have been in shaping prosocial impulses.
379.content: We have underestimated how important shared care and provisioning by group members other than parents have been in shaping prosocial impulses. Without shared care and provisioning, all intergroup strategizing and strife would have been evolutionarily speaking signifying nothing. Cooperative breeding - where there is shared care and provisioning of young - is the key innovation that made human-level prosociality possible.

380.quote: 'Cooperative breeding' refers to any species with alloparental assistance in both the care and provisioning of young.
380.content: Cooperative breeding refers to any species with alloparental assistance in both care and provisioning of young. Unlike mothers among other African apes who nurtured infants alone, early hominin mothers relied on groupmates to protect, care for, and provision their slow-maturing children. This mode of child-rearing had profound psychological implications for the ape line leading to Homo sapiens.

381.quote: Of all the attachments mammalian babies form, none is more powerful than that between baby primates and their mothers. The emotional ties that bind ape mothers to their infants and infants to their mothers are unusually long-lasting.
381.content: Of all attachments mammalian babies form, none is more powerful than that between baby primates and their mothers. The emotional ties binding ape mothers to infants and infants to mothers are unusually long-lasting. But in cooperatively breeding humans, this dyadic bond is embedded in a wider network of allomaternal attachments that share the regulatory burden.

382.quote: A quick survey of available ethnography indicates how widespread shared care is among foraging peoples.
382.content: Ethnographic survey of shared care among foraging peoples: !Kung San babies have available the mother's entire social world with intense face-to-face interactions from girls. Trobriand Islanders routinely share infants who are suckled by lactating allomothers. Hadza babies under four are held by mothers 69% of the time and by allomothers the rest. These mothers trust others and allow them to take infants shortly after birth.

383.quote: Attacks from conspecifics (both infanticide and deaths due to lethal raids by bands of males from neighboring groups) are major sources of mortality.
383.content: In chimpanzees, attacks from conspecifics - including infanticide and lethal raids by bands of males from neighboring groups - are major sources of mortality.

384.quote: Chimpanzees perform best on tests requiring a rudimentary theory of mind when they are in competitive situations.
384.content: Chimpanzees perform best on tests requiring rudimentary theory of mind when they are in competitive situations. But human children develop robust theory of mind in cooperative contexts - because in a cooperatively breeding species, infants who could read the intentions of multiple caregivers had a survival advantage. Human mind-reading evolved not for competition but for navigating the cooperative breeding network.

385.quote: Extrapolating from the relationship for monkeys and apes gives a group size of about 150 - the limit on the number of social relationships that humans can have, a figure that is now graced by the title Dunbar's Number.
385.content: The social brain hypothesis: there is a strong correlation between group size (social world complexity) and neocortex size in primates. Extrapolating gives a human group size of about 150 - the limit on the number of social relationships humans can maintain, now known as Dunbar's Number. The need to live in larger groups drove the evolution of large brains in primates.

386.quote: Monkey grooming is not about removing fleas. Rather, it is about the intimacy of massage. The physical stimulation of the skin triggers the release of endorphins in the brain.
386.content: Primate grooming is not about removing fleas - it is about the intimacy of massage. Physical stimulation of the skin triggers endorphin release in the brain. Low-level pain associated with generalized stresses is dealt with by the endorphin system, creating a sense of wellbeing and relaxed contentedness. Grooming is the mechanism through which primate social bonds are maintained.

387.quote: Laughter - and I mean deep belly laughter, not the polite titters that tinkled among T.S. Eliot's teacups - is an extremely effective releaser of endorphins, probably because the physical effort of laughter's heaving chest is quite hard work for the muscles.
387.content: Laughter - deep belly laughter, not polite titters - is an extremely effective releaser of endorphins, probably because the physical effort is hard work for the muscles. Communal laughter creates a sense of bondedness that goes beyond tension release. Language evolved as a form of grooming at distance - 'I'd rather be here with you than over there with Jennifer.'

388.quote: The suggestion that female-female bonding, based on knowledge of the relationships of other individuals, was more important fits much better with views about the structure of nonhuman primate societies where relationships between females are all-important.
388.content: Language evolved in the context of social bonding between females. Female-female bonding based on knowledge of others' relationships was more important than male-male bonding in driving language evolution. This fits with primate societies where relationships between females are all-important for group cohesion and infant survival.

389.quote: This is an example of biased cultural transmission, which occurs when people tend to acquire some cultural variants rather than others.
389.content: Biased cultural transmission: people tend to acquire some cultural variants rather than others. Biases may be innate preferences or cultural preferences acquired in earlier social learning. Conformist bias (When in Rome, do as the Romans do) makes evolutionary sense because adaptive behavior tends to become more common than maladaptive behavior. Prestige bias: people grant prestige to those perceived as having superior cultural variants, compensating them for the privilege of imitation.

390.quote: Moralistic punishment is more effective in supporting large-scale cooperation than reciprocity for two reasons.
390.content: Moralistic punishment is more effective than reciprocity at supporting large-scale cooperation. Punishment takes forms including reduced status, fewer friends, and fewer mating opportunities. In groups where a norm is common, people who violate it are punished. When newcomers arrive, they rapidly learn local norms and maintain them despite different evolved psychology. Cultural group selection - tribes with cooperation-promoting norms outcompete those without.

391.quote: Darwin said, 'A tribe including many members who, from possessing in a high degree the spirit of patriotism, fidelity, obedience, courage, and sympathy, were always ready to aid one another, and to sacrifice themselves for the common good, would be victorious over most other tribes.'
391.content: Darwin's group selection insight: a tribe with many members possessing patriotism, fidelity, obedience, courage, and sympathy who sacrifice for the common good would be victorious over most other tribes. The Nuer-Dinka case demonstrates cultural group selection in practice: cultural differences in norms meant the Nuer could cooperate in larger groups, enabling territorial expansion at the Dinka's expense.

392.quote: Adopting a Darwinian approach to culture does not mean that you have to also believe that culture is made of miniscule, genelike particles that are faithfully replicated during cultural transmission.
392.content: Adopting a Darwinian approach to culture does not mean believing culture is made of miniscule genelike particles faithfully replicated during transmission. Evidence suggests cultural variants are sometimes somewhat genelike, while at other times decidedly not. The dual-inheritance framework treats cultural and genetic inheritance as two parallel but interacting evolutionary systems with different transmission properties.

393.quote: the ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven emotional, or affective, systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy). Each of these systems controls distinct but specific types of behaviors associated with many overlapping physiological changes.
393.content: The ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven emotional systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy). Each controls distinct behaviors with overlapping physiological changes and generates distinct types of affective consciousness. When stimulated in humans, people always experience intense emotional feelings. Capitalizations indicate that real physical and distinct networks for these emotions exist in mammalian brains.

394.quote: primal emotional systems are made up of neuroanatomies and neurochemistries that are remarkably similar across all mammalian species. This suggests that these systems evolved a very long time ago and that at a basic emotional and motivational level, all mammals are more similar than they are different.
394.content: Primal emotional systems are made up of neuroanatomies and neurochemistries remarkably similar across all mammalian species. This suggests these systems evolved a very long time ago and that at a basic emotional and motivational level, all mammals are more similar than different. Deep in the ancient affective recesses of our brains, we remain evolutionarily kin. The same neural paths and brain chemicals that arouse each of these seven systems are found within all mammals.

395.quote: these affective substrates are "archaeological treasures" - multi-faceted "jewels" of mind that embody our capacity for affective experience, a capacity that we still share with our animal cousins.
395.content: These affective substrates are archaeological treasures - multi-faceted jewels of mind that embody our capacity for affective experience, a capacity we still share with our animal cousins. However, as humans, we have higher brain expansions that allow us to think deeply about our nature and our options to live more cerebrally, culturally, and creatively. We can bite our tongues when angry, but many choose not to.

396.quote: Sexual gratification, arising from our capacity for LUST, feels good in a rather different way from the joys of rough-and-tumble PLAY or the tender bliss of caressing, nurturing, and CAREing for one's infant. FEAR is an entirely different kind of emotional 'pain' than frustrated RAGE; both differ from the PANICked misery of social isolation.
396.content: Sexual gratification from LUST feels good in a different way from the joys of rough-and-tumble PLAY or the tender bliss of caressing and CARing for an infant. FEAR is an entirely different kind of emotional pain than frustrated RAGE; both differ from the panicked misery of social isolation (PANIC/GRIEF). These diverse affects provide guidance for living due to the survival-enhancing advantages each conferred over evolution. Affects are ancestral memories of how effectively we play the game of survival and reproduction.

397.quote: The SEEKING, or expectancy, system is characterized by a persistent exploratory inquisitiveness. This system engenders energetic forward locomotion - approach and engagement with the world - as an animal probes into the nooks and crannies of interesting places, objects, and events in ways that are characteristic of its species.
397.content: The SEEKING system is characterized by persistent exploratory inquisitiveness. It engenders energetic forward locomotion - approach and engagement with the world - as animals probe nooks and crannies of interesting places, objects, and events. This system holds a special place among emotional systems because to some extent it plays a dynamic supporting role for all of the other emotions.

398.quote: Affective neuroscience has made a fresh start by proceeding from the bottom up, without denigrating our unique human abilities, and it is offering both a new vision of mental origins and new data to back up such assertions.
398.content: The triangulation approach of affective neuroscience links the affective mind to animal brains by triangulating among (i) subjective mental states (most easily studied in humans), (ii) brain functions (more easily studied in animals), and (iii) natural instinctual emotional behaviors that all young mammals must exhibit early in life to survive. This bottom-up approach offers both a new vision of mental origins and new data.

399.quote: FEAR is an inborn capacity of the mammalian brain. However, FEAR, just like all other basic emotions, rapidly gets enmeshed with world events as it comes to be regulated by learning and encoded in our conscious minds.
399.content: FEAR is an inborn capacity of the mammalian brain that rapidly gets enmeshed with world events through learning. Most basic emotions need not be expressed immediately after birth. Some - including CARE, LUST, and PLAY - come online long after others such as SEEKING, RAGE, and FEAR. The developmental timing reflects phylogenetic priority: the oldest and most survival-critical systems activate earliest.

400.quote: But primates are unusual. Instead of decamping after they mate, fathers in most species in the order Primates remain year-round in the same social group as the mothers of their offspring.
400.content: Primates are unusual: instead of decamping after mating, fathers in most primate species remain in the same social group year-round. In New World monkeys like titi and night monkeys, fathers are primary attachment figures - infants are more attached to fathers than mothers. This establishes paternal care as an ancestral primate capacity, not a modern cultural invention.

401.quote: One widely accepted tenet of life history theory is that, across species, those with bigger babies relative to the mother's body size will also tend to exhibit longer intervals between births because the more babies cost the mother to produce, the longer she will need to recoup before reproducing again. Yet humans - like marmosets - provide a paradoxical exception to this rule.
401.content: Humans produce the largest, slowest-maturing, most costly babies of any primate yet breed the fastest (every 3-4 years vs. 6-8 years for other apes). This paradox requires approximately 13 million calories per child from birth to independence. The only way this is possible is through alloparental provisioning - mothers cannot meet these costs alone. Life-history theory predicts longer birth intervals for costlier offspring; cooperative breeding is what breaks this constraint.

402.quote: for their pronounced ambivalence toward newborns and their extremely contingent maternal commitment. Infants have adapted, as we will see later, with special traits for attracting the attention of potential caretakers.
402.content: Humans display pronounced ambivalence toward newborns and extremely contingent maternal commitment. Unlike the steady investment other great ape mothers show, human mothers assess whether conditions support successful rearing before committing fully. Infants have adapted with special traits - cuteness, prolonged eye contact, social smiling - for attracting attention from potential caretakers. Maternal commitment is conditional on perceived alloparental support.

403.quote: When politicians lament the 'decline of the family,' they have in mind departures from the nuclear family: a man, his wife, and their biological children. However, the template for this kind of family dates back only a century or so, at most to Victorian times.
403.content: The idealized nuclear family (breadwinner father, homemaker mother, biological children) dates back only about a century, to Victorian times at most. In American contexts, it became the template only in the 1950s. This family structure is a historical aberration - for the vast majority of human history, children were raised in extended kin networks with multiple allomaternal caregivers. The 'decline of the family' that politicians lament is actually a departure from an extremely brief historical norm.

404.quote: The innermost group consists of about three to five people.
404.content: Friendship circles nest in a sequence scaling by factors of approximately three: innermost 5 (close confidants who provide emotional and physical support), then 15 (sympathy group, roughly jury size), 50 (typical hunter-gatherer overnight camp), 150 (Dunbar number, clan/tribal size), with additional layers at 500 and 1500. Each layer represents a qualitatively different type of social relationship with different obligations and investment requirements.

405.quote: It was most likely a form of chorusing, a kind of communal singing without the words. Its function, I think, was to generate the same kind of surge of endorphins as that produced during grooming.
405.content: Communal singing and music evolved as a bonding mechanism to generate endorphin surges when time constraints on social grooming became prohibitive in larger groups. Music was most likely a form of chorusing - communal singing without words - that preceded language. Its function was to generate the same endorphin surge as grooming but for multiple individuals simultaneously, solving the time-budget problem of maintaining bonds in groups beyond 50.

406.quote: Kinship provides a surprisingly deep and sometimes unrecognised framework for our social life, not just in traditional small-scale societies, but for us today as well.
406.content: Kinship provides a deep and often unrecognized framework for social cooperation, not just in traditional small-scale societies but in modern WEIRD contexts as well. Extended family networks function as migration facilitators, employment networks, and mutual-aid systems - illustrating that kin-based cooperation remains active even in supposedly individualistic societies.

407.quote: Facebook, MySpace and Bebo. Darwin and his contemporaries could not have conceived of such things, even in their wildest dreams.
407.content: Social media breaks through time and geography constraints but creates perverse competition in friend counts. Most users know little about connections beyond approximately 200. The limits of online friendship reveal the constraint that Dunbar's number reflects - not communication bandwidth but cognitive capacity for maintaining genuine relationships. Digital tools extend reach but cannot expand the social brain's processing limit.

408.quote: The tribal social instincts result from the gene-culture co-evolution of tribal-scale societies by the process described above. Consequently, humans are able to make common cause with a sizable, culturally defined set of distantly related individuals, a form of social organization that is absent in other primates.
408.content: Tribal social instincts result from gene-culture coevolution of tribal-scale societies. Humans are able to make common cause with a sizable, culturally defined set of distantly related individuals - a form of social organization absent in other primates. These instincts equip humans with the psychological machinery for in-group cooperation, out-group vigilance, and norm-governed behavior in groups of 50-500.

409.quote: Tribal instincts cause people to use symbolic markers to define the boundaries of in-groups and establish, for example, who is eligible for empathy, who should excite suspicion, and, in some horrible cases, who should be killed.
409.content: Symbolic markers of group boundaries motivate important behavior. Tribal instincts cause people to use symbolic markers to define who is eligible for empathy, who should excite suspicion, and in some cases who should be killed. Small differences in arrow styles, dress, or dialect become psychologically salient signals of group membership. People essentialist ethnic groups as species-like categories.

410.quote: You are engaged in maladaptive behavior right now.
410.content: Modern middle-class reproductive restraint is a striking maladaptation: professional status-seeking consumes resources (time, money, effort) needed for reproduction. Evolved psychology for status competition in Pleistocene tribal contexts now causes fitness loss in modern economies. People prioritize career advancement, education, and consumption over reproduction - the very success of cultural transmission mechanisms (prestige bias, conformist bias) producing behaviors that reduce genetic fitness.

411.quote: In the section that follows, we describe what seem to us to be the main work-around mechanisms, and the conflicts, compromises, and modes of failure that each entails.
411.content: Complex societies employ institutional work-arounds to simulate tribal-scale relationships: hierarchical command backed by force, segmentary hierarchy, and symbolic in-group marking. Each work-around creates predictable conflicts and failure modes - elite exploitation from hierarchical command, subgroup factionalism from segmentary structure, and fundamentalism from symbolic marking. These are not design flaws but inherent consequences of scaling tribal instincts beyond their natural range.

412.quote: We get sick from chronic diseases by doing what we evolved to do but under conditions for which our bodies are poorly adapted, and we then pass on those same conditions to our children, who also then get sick.
412.content: Humans get sick from chronic diseases by doing what they evolved to do but under conditions their bodies are poorly adapted to, then pass those conditions to their children in a vicious cycle. Lieberman calls this dysevolution - an intergenerational feedback loop where mismatch diseases persist because modern environments prevent natural selection from eliminating the underlying susceptibilities.

413.quote: Humans evolved to be prone to obesity not because excess fat makes us healthy, but because it increases fertility. Along the same lines, our species' proclivities to be worried, anxious, and stressed cause much misery and unhappiness, but they are ancient adaptations to avoid or cope with danger.
413.content: Humans evolved to be prone to obesity not because excess fat makes us healthy but because it increases fertility. Anxiety, worry, and stress cause misery and unhappiness but they are ancient adaptations to avoid or cope with danger. The mismatch hypothesis - that human bodies were adapted for very different conditions - is the core of evolutionary medicine.

414.quote: diabetes is a growing problem because human bodies, like those of captive primates, were adapted primarily for very different conditions that render us inadequately adapted to cope with modern diets and physical inactivity.
414.content: Type 2 diabetes is a mismatch disease: human bodies, like captive primates, were adapted for very different conditions and are inadequately adapted to cope with modern diets and physical inactivity. The answer does not lie solely in cellular and genetic mechanisms but in the evolutionary mismatch between ancestral and modern environments.

415.quote: Farming brought many advantages but also caused many serious problems. Farming enabled humans to have more food, hence more children, but also required new forms of work, transformed diets, and opened a Pandora's box of diseases and social ills.
415.content: Farming brought many advantages but also caused serious problems. It enabled more food and hence more children, but also required new forms of work, transformed diets, and opened a Pandora's box of diseases and social ills. The agricultural revolution was the first major dysevolution event - the transition from foraging to farming created the first systematic mismatch between human bodies and their environment.

416.quote: The babies who were massaged gained 47 percent more weight than those not massaged, a clearly significant weight gain.
416.content: Moderate-pressure massage therapy causes preterm infants to gain more weight, leave tube feeding earlier, perform better on neurological examinations, and be discharged earlier at lower hospital cost. The mechanism involves stimulation of pressure receptors leading to increased vagal activity. Increased serotonin and decreased substance P may mediate the pain-alleviating effects of touch.

417.quote: Tana was raised in a Romanian orphanage. At age seven, relief workers found her all skin and bones and only half the height of a normal child her age.
417.content: Touch deprivation in Romanian orphanages produced devastating consequences: children were skeletal, half normal height, unable to walk or run. After months of regular nutrition and massage therapy, orphanage children recovered physically - illustrating that touch is not merely pleasant but a biological necessity for normal development. Touch deprivation produces growth hormone suppression and immune dysfunction.

418.quote: Many human cultures know the primary value of touch. In some primitive cultures, for example, people live skin-to-skin with virtually everyone.
