538.content: Cloth mother serves as secure base for exploration. When frightened by novel stimuli, infants consistently fled to cloth mother regardless of food source. In open-field tests with cloth mother present, emotionality scores reduced by half. Without any mother, infants froze in crouched positions. Wire mother provided zero comfort function in any fear test.

539.quote: this interval of delay depresses the intensity of the affectional response below that of the infant monkeys that were surrogate-mothered from birth onward.
539.content: Late-adopted controls (surrogates introduced at day 250) reached ~9 hours daily contact within 10 days but behavioral intensity remained lower than birth-reared animals. This demonstrates a sensitive period for attachment formation - delay depresses the intensity of affectional response.

540.quote: a baby monkey raised on a bare wire-mesh cage floor survives with difficulty, if at all, during the first five days of life.
540.content: Infant monkeys raised on bare wire-mesh cage floors survived with difficulty during the first 5 days of life. Adding a wire-mesh cone improved survival. Covering the cone with terry cloth produced husky, healthy, happy babies. This demonstrates that tactile comfort is not merely a preference but a survival-critical input.

541.content: Total social isolation from birth produces devastating behavioral deficits scaling with duration. 3-month isolates slowly recovered with minimal long-term damage (one died of emotional anorexia). 6-month isolates showed severe deficits in virtually every aspect of social behavior - no contact play, only limited recovery. 12-month isolates were almost obliterated socially - zero activity play, persistent fear, no positive social behavior.

542.content: Upon release from isolation, monkeys entered a state of emotional shock characterized by autistic self-clutching and rocking, blank staring, cage circling, and self-mutilation. When placed with normal peers, isolated monkeys sat huddled in corners and were bullied. Recovery possible with younger therapist monkeys who engaged in clinging and simple play without aggression.
542.where: PNAS 54(1):90-97, post-isolation behavior and recovery sections

543.quote: This work has pinpointed the amygdala as an important component of the system involved in the acquisition, storage, and expression of fear memory.
543.content: Dual pathway model for threat information reaching the amygdala. The low road (thalamo-amygdala, ~150-200ms) provides quick, coarse processing of simple stimulus features enabling immediate defensive responses before conscious identification. The high road (thalamo-cortico-amygdala, ~300ms) provides detailed, complex evaluation through sensory cortex and can override false alarms. Both converge on the lateral nucleus.
543.where: Annual Review of Neuroscience 23:155-184. DOI: 10.1146/annurev.neuro.23.1.155. PMID: 10845062

544.content: Amygdala functional architecture: lateral nucleus (LA) is the sensory interface where CS and US converge (synaptic plasticity encodes fear memories via LTP); central nucleus (CE) is the principal output for expression of conditioned fear, projecting to PAG (freezing), lateral hypothalamus (autonomic), and BNST (endocrine). Lesion studies confirm functional dissociation of these output pathways.
544.where: Annual Review of Neuroscience 23:155-184, amygdala architecture section

545.content: Fear conditioning involves calcium influx during CS-US pairing at lateral nucleus synapses, with subsequent gene expression and protein synthesis stabilizing long-term fear memories. LTP can be induced in the lateral nucleus by stimulating auditory thalamus. Findings from rodent fear conditioning apply to the human brain via functional neuroimaging and lesion studies.
545.where: Annual Review of Neuroscience 23:155-184, cellular mechanisms section

546.quote: I, and others, have called the brain system that detects and responds to threats the fear system. This was a mistake that has led to much confusion.
546.content: LeDoux revises his terminology: calling the threat-detection system a fear system was a mistake that led to confusion, because people assume a fear system produces conscious fear. He now distinguishes defensive survival circuits (subcortical, nonconscious, conserved across vertebrates with invertebrate analogues) from conscious fear (a cognitive construction arising from multiple neural ingredients).

547.content: Evidence for unconscious threat processing: subliminal threat stimuli elicit physiological responses without awareness; conditioning occurs without CS-US contingency awareness; amygdala activates to subliminal stimuli; hippocampal damage disrupts explicit memory but NOT fear conditioning (amygdala damage produces opposite pattern); blindsight patients show body responses to unseen threats; bilateral amygdala damage does NOT eliminate conscious fear - proving neither amygdala activity nor amygdala-controlled responses are necessary for fearful feelings.

548.quote: The feeling of fear occurs in the same way as the feeling of compassion or pride--through cognitive processing of neural raw materials.
548.content: Fear as cognitive construction: conscious fear emerges from multiple neural ingredients (survival circuit activation, brain arousal, body feedback, memories, predictions) much as a soup's character emerges from raw materials. Some fears involve no survival circuit activation (social anxiety, existential concerns). Proposed terminology: replace fear conditioning with threat conditioning, fear system with defensive survival circuit, restrict fear exclusively to conscious experience.

549.quote: An evolved module for fear elicitation and fear learning with 4 characteristics is proposed.
549.content: Evolved fear module with four characteristics: (a) preferentially activated by phylogenetically relevant stimuli (snakes, spiders, angry faces) in aversive contexts; (b) activation is automatic and pre-attentive; (c) relatively impenetrable to cognitive control (resistant to verbal instruction); (d) originates in dedicated amygdala-centered neural circuitry. Module mediates emotional fear learning dissociable from cognitive learning of stimulus relationships.

550.quote: The fear module is assumed to mediate an emotional level of fear learning that is relatively independent and dissociable from cognitive learning of stimulus relationships.
550.content: Visual search reveals pre-attentive threat detection: snake/spider targets among flower/mushroom distractors detected faster (~615ms) than reverse (~704ms). Fear-relevant detection unaffected by display size (parallel/pop-out processing, slope ~6ms/item). Fear-irrelevant targets show serial search (slope ~15ms/item). Conditioning to fear-relevant stimuli resists verbal instruction to extinguish; backward-masked fear-relevant conditioned stimuli elicit electrodermal responses without conscious awareness.
550.where: Psychological Review 108(3):483-522 and Öhman, Flykt & Esteves 2001 visual search study

551.content: Monkey observational conditioning demonstrates prepared learning: lab-reared rhesus monkeys with no snake experience acquired fear of snakes and crocodiles (fear-relevant) through watching fearful models, but did NOT acquire fear of flowers or rabbits (fear-irrelevant) through the same procedure. This demonstrates selective associations operating even through vicarious/observational learning, not just direct conditioning.
551.where: Psychological Review 108(3):483-522, citing Cook & Mineka studies

552.content: The Strange Situation paradigm: 8 episodes (~21 min) of separation and reunion in a novel room. Three attachment classifications identified: Type B (Secure, ~65-70%) - uses mother as secure base, distressed at separation, seeks contact at reunion, quickly soothed. Type A (Avoidant, ~21%) - conspicuous avoidance at reunion, ignores mother, minimal contact-maintaining. Type C (Ambivalent/Resistant, ~14%) - clingy before separation, intensely distressed during, simultaneously seeks and resists contact at reunion.
552.where: Patterns of Attachment (1978). DOI: 10.4324/9781315802428. Book, not freely available.

553.content: The sensitivity hypothesis: maternal sensitivity to infant signals throughout the first year predicts attachment classification. Securely attached infants had consistently responsive mothers. Avoidant infants had rejecting mothers with aversion to close bodily contact. Ambivalent infants had inconsistently responsive mothers. Five behavioral dimensions scored on 1-7 scale: proximity seeking, contact maintaining, avoidance, resistance, search behavior.
553.where: Patterns of Attachment (1978), sensitivity and scoring chapters

554.quote: an essential part of the ground plan of the human species--as well as that of many other species
554.content: Attachment is an essential part of the biological ground plan of the human species. Hunter-gatherer societies show much more mother-infant contact than Western societies. Humans evolved as a species in which infants are carried and fed at frequent intervals. When attachment behavior is intensely activated, it is close bodily contact that is specifically required - not proximity alone.
554.where: American Psychologist 34(10):932-937. DOI: 10.1037//0003-066x.34.10.932. Full text via Smith College.

555.quote: Mothers of the securely attached (Group B) babies were, throughout the first year, more sensitively responsive to infant signals than were the mothers of the two anxiously attached groups.
555.content: Feeding does not determine attachment. No evidence that methods of feeding significantly affected infant development. Instead, sensitive maternal responsiveness to infant signals determines attachment security. Securely attached infants develop working models of mother as accessible and responsive - therein lies security. Insecurely attached infants whose signals were disregarded have no basis for believing mother is responsive, consequently they are anxious.
555.where: American Psychologist 34(10):932-937, sensitivity and working models section

556.quote: Fostering the growth of secure attachment facilitates rather than hampers the growth of healthy self-reliance.
556.content: Secure attachment facilitates rather than hampers independence. Babies responding positively to close bodily contact also respond positively to being put down and move into exploratory play. Longitudinal follow-up: secure infants became more cooperative, more competent with peers, more curious, more self-directed, and more ego-resilient. Avoidant infants remained more aggressive and noncompliant. Ambivalent infants were more easily frustrated and less persistent.

557.quote: This article explores the possibility that romantic love is an attachment process--a biosocial process by which affectional bonds are formed between adult lovers, just as affectional bonds are formed earlier in life between human infants and their parents.
557.content: Adult romantic love is an attachment process: affectional bonds form between adult lovers just as between infants and parents. Three adult attachment styles parallel Ainsworth's infant categories. Distribution: ~56% secure, ~25% avoidant, ~19% anxious-ambivalent (N=620 in Study 1), closely matching infant distributions (~62/23/15%). Secure adults describe relationships as happy, friendly, trusting. Avoidant adults fear closeness and doubt romantic love exists. Anxious adults experience love as obsessive with constant abandonment worry.

558.quote: attachment style is related in theoretically meaningful ways to mental models of self and social relationships and to relationship experiences with parents.
558.content: Attachment style is related to mental models of self and relationships and to childhood relationship memories. Secure adults recall parents as respectful and accepting. Anxious adults remember intermittently available parents. Avoidant adults recall critical and distant parents. Continuity of style is due in part to Bowlby's internal working models - cognitive representations of self and others formed in early relationships that persist and shape adult relational patterns.

559.quote: Thus, critically, the troop's unique culture was being adopted by new males joining the troop.
559.content: Forest Troop natural experiment: bovine tuberculosis selectively killed the most aggressive males (46% of adult males who competed at a garbage dump), leaving atypically unaggressive survivors with a >2:1 female-to-male ratio. A decade later (1993-96), when NO original males remained, the low-aggression culture persisted: relaxed dominance hierarchy, reduced male-to-female aggression, more male-female grooming, closer proximity to females/infants.
559.where: PLoS Biology 2(4):e106. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pbio.0020106. PMC387274. Full text.

560.quote: subordinate F93-96 males did not have elevated basal glucocorticoid levels.
560.content: Subordinate males in Forest Troop did NOT show the elevated basal glucocorticoid levels typical of low-ranking baboons in other troops. When injected with an anxiety-inducing drug (beta-carboline), low-ranking Forest Troop males showed no anxiety-related behavioral changes, while controls showed significant increases. The stress-rank gradient was eliminated by the social culture change.
560.where: PLoS Biology 2(4):e106, physiological results. Full text.

561.quote: F93-96 females did not seem to treat transfer males in a contingent manner
561.content: Cultural transmission mechanism: resident females were the key. Transfer males arrived as aggressive as those joining control troops. But Forest Troop females had shorter latency to groom/present to newcomers and were unconditionally more affiliative - not contingent on newcomer behavior. The pattern was NOT an artifact of sex ratio: five other troops with similar ratios resembled controls, not Forest Troop.
561.where: PLoS Biology 2(4):e106, transmission analysis. Full text.

562.quote: I first consider whether it is high- or low-ranking animals that are most stressed in a dominance hierarchy; this turns out to vary as a function of the social organization in different species and populations.
562.content: Whether high or low rank is most stressful depends on social organization. In despotic/unstable hierarchies, subordinates bear disproportionate chronic stress with elevated glucocorticoids. In stable/egalitarian systems, the stress-rank relationship diminishes or reverses. Subordinate rank associates with atherosclerosis, impaired immunity, reduced fertility, and hippocampal atrophy - all mediated through sustained glucocorticoid exposure.

563.content: Human application: like subordinate primates, lower-SES humans show elevated basal cortisol, impaired immune function, and accelerated cardiovascular disease. The Whitehall studies of British civil servants show employment grade predicts health outcomes independent of traditional risk factors (smoking, cholesterol, blood pressure account for less than a third of the social gradient in CVD).

564.content: The glucocorticoid cascade hypothesis: chronic stress produces elevated glucocorticoids that damage hippocampal neurons. Because the hippocampus mediates inhibition of the HPA axis, hippocampal damage creates a positive feedback loop: more cortisol → more hippocampal damage → less cortisol suppression → even more cortisol. Three types of damage: reversible dendritic atrophy (weeks), neurotoxicity (months), and neuroendangerment (impaired survival of neurological insults).

565.quote: Out of 1000 episodes of flight at this response threshold, on the average, 999 will be false alarms and only 1 will be flight from an actual predator.
565.content: The smoke detector principle formalized via signal detection theory. For all-or-none defenses, expression is optimal whenever p(Harm) > Cost_defense/Cost_harm. With a 1000:1 cost ratio (300 kcal flight vs 300,000 kcal predator attack), the optimal threshold produces 999 false alarms per 1 genuine escape. These false alarms are completely normal products of an optimal system, not dysfunction.
565.where: Evolution and Human Behavior 26(1):88-105. DOI: 10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2004.08.002. Full text via UMich PDF.

566.quote: natural selection will tend to shape systems that err on the side of excessive defensive expression.
566.content: Graded defenses (fever, anxiety, fatigue) have a non-intuitive optimum: the optimal level is where marginal cost of additional defense exceeds marginal benefit, NOT where total costs equal total danger. Skewed payoff curves create additional over-expression bias: being 7 units below optimum costs 1.6 units extra, but being 0.7 above costs only 0.3 extra. Selection shapes systems that err on the side of excessive defense.
566.where: Evolution and Human Behavior 26(1):88-105, graded defense analysis. Full text.

567.quote: Individuals who experience a panic attack react as if they had encountered a real danger, subsequently becoming not only more cautious but also more susceptible to additional attacks.
567.content: Repeated danger exposure may adaptively lower response thresholds, creating vulnerability to runaway positive feedback. Panic disorder exemplifies this: individuals experiencing a panic attack react as if they encountered real danger, becoming more cautious and more susceptible to additional attacks. The clinical condition is an extreme of normal threshold-lowering, not a qualitatively different pathology.
567.where: Evolution and Human Behavior 26(1):88-105, threshold dynamics section. Full text.

568.quote: The cost of a false alarm--vomiting when no toxin is truly present--is only a few calories. But the penalty for a single missed authentic alarm--failure to vomit when confronted with a toxin--may be death.
568.content: Five categories of evolutionary explanations for disease vulnerability: (1) defenses that are actually adaptive (pain, fever, cough, anxiety, vomiting); (2) conflicts with other organisms (pathogens, predators); (3) novel environments to which selection has not yet adapted; (4) trade-offs between benefits and costs (e.g., sickle cell); (5) constraints on natural selection leaving suboptimal designs. Symptoms like fever are carefully regulated rises in the thermostat set point, not mere metabolic byproducts.
568.where: Scientific American 279(5):86-93. DOI: 10.1038/scientificamerican1198-86. Full text via UMich PDF.

569.quote: our poor decisions about diet and exercise are made by brains shaped to cope with an environment substantially different from the one our species now inhabits.
569.content: Blocking evolved defenses can cause harm. Shigella study: patients taking antidiarrheal drugs stayed sick longer with more complications than placebo. Iron supplementation in Africa increased infectious disease (amebiasis) by removing iron-withholding defense. Drug vulnerability exists because plants evolved defensive compounds (nicotine, cocaine, opium) targeting insect nervous systems, and shared evolutionary heritage means these affect human systems too.
569.where: Scientific American 279(5):86-93, defense-blocking section. Full text.

570.quote: Seeking answers to all four of Tinbergen's questions expands explanations beyond mechanisms to also describe a trait's development, evolutionary history and adaptive significance.
570.content: Tinbergen's four questions organized into a 2×2 framework: proximate vs evolutionary crossed with synchronic (single form) vs diachronic (sequence). Mechanism (what is the structure?) and ontogeny (how does it develop?) are proximate. Adaptive significance (how have variations influenced fitness?) and phylogeny (what is the evolutionary history?) are evolutionary. All four are needed for a complete explanation of any biological trait.
570.where: Evolution, Medicine, and Public Health 2019(1):2. DOI: 10.1093/emph/eoy035. PMC6343817. Full text (open access).

571.quote: Those which I believe we can identify at present are sucking, clinging, and following, in all of which the baby is the principal active partner, and crying and smiling in which his behaviour serves to activate maternal behaviour.
571.content: Attachment is primary, not secondary to feeding. Bowlby proposed five component instinctual responses - sucking, clinging, following (baby is active partner) and crying, smiling (activate maternal behavior) - all primary and initially independent, becoming integrated and focused on one mother figure during the second six months of life. This broke with Freudian secondary drive theory.

572.quote: Children will cling even to mothers who are continually cross and sometimes cruel to them. The attachment of the small child to his mother seems to a large degree independent of her personal qualities.
572.content: Children attach to cruel mothers: the attachment of the small child to the mother seems largely independent of her personal qualities. This observation is incompatible with secondary drive (feeding-based reinforcement) models. Bowlby drew on ethology (Lorenz's imprinting, Harlow's contact comfort) and proposed monotropy: the tendency for instinctual responses to be directed toward a particular individual, not promiscuously.

573.content: Protest-despair-detachment: three-phase response to separation from attachment figure. Protest = active attempts to recover the figure (crying, searching, resistance to comforting by others). Despair = withdrawal, hopelessness, reduced activity. Detachment = apparent indifference if caregiver does not return. Based on Robertson's hospital observations and Bowlby's theoretical framework.
573.where: Attachment and Loss Vol 2 (1973), Part I: Security, Anxiety, and Distress

574.content: Ethological theory of fear: fear responses to natural clues to danger (strangers, strange environments, rapid approaches, darkness, loud noises, being alone) are part of basic behavioral equipment, not learned. Separation anxiety is reframed as natural: it is no less natural to feel afraid when lines of communication with a safe base are threatened than when something alarming appears. Agoraphobia is reframed as anxious attachment, not fear of open spaces.
574.where: Attachment and Loss Vol 2 (1973), Part II: An Ethological Approach to Human Fear, Ch. 8-11, 17-18

575.content: Anger as functional attachment behavior: anger in response to separation is not aggression but protest - a signal to communicate distress and motivate the attachment figure to return. Secure attachment promotes independence and self-reliance, not dependence. Anxious attachment (insecure base) creates heightened susceptibility to fear and anxiety through unreliable caregiver availability.
575.where: Attachment and Loss Vol 2 (1973), Ch. 16 (Anger, Anxiety, Attachment), Ch. 20 (Secure Attachment and Self-reliance)

576.quote: mischaracterizes important avenues of causation, induces researchers to study complexly chaotic and unordered phenomena, and misdirects study away from areas where rich principled phenomena are to be found
576.content: The Standard Social Science Model (SSSM) critique: Tooby and Cosmides identify the dominant 20th-century metatheory as assuming (a) blank-slate psychology, (b) general-purpose brain, (c) culture programs behavior without constraint, (d) content-independent, equipotential learning mechanisms. They replace this with the Integrated Causal Model: the mind comprises domain-specific evolved mechanisms that interact with environment/culture, and culture itself derives from and is constrained by universal human nature.
576.where: The Adapted Mind (1992), ch. 1, pp. 19-136. CEP UCSB PDF exists but image-scanned.

577.quote: The EEA is not a place or a habitat, or even a time period. Rather, it is a statistical composite of the adaptation-relevant properties of the ancestral environments
577.content: The EEA formalization: the environment of evolutionary adaptedness is not a place, habitat, or time period, but a statistical composite of the adaptation-relevant properties of ancestral environments encountered by members of a species over evolutionary time. Biological mechanisms embody information about stably recurring properties of ancestral worlds. The Pleistocene (2.5M-10K ya) is the primary reference period, with agriculture creating insufficient time for major psychological adaptation.
577.where: The Adapted Mind (1992), pp. 19-136, EEA section

578.quote: both the genes and the developmentally relevant environment are the product of evolution
578.content: Domain-specificity is superior to domain-general learning because: (1) general mechanisms must solve problems from scratch through costly trial-and-error, while specific mechanisms come pre-equipped with content; (2) combinatorial explosion - without domain-specific constraints, organisms face exponentially growing behavioral options; (3) the frame problem - general systems face infinite regress excluding irrelevant information, while modules solve this through information encapsulation. Nature/nurture is replaced by open vs closed developmental programs, both genetically encoded.
578.where: The Adapted Mind (1992), pp. 19-136, domain-specificity arguments

579.quote: In order to successfully engage in social exchange--cooperation between two or more individuals for mutual benefit--humans must be able to solve a number of complex computational problems, and do so with special efficiency
579.content: Wason selection task reveals domain-specific reasoning about social exchange. Abstract conditional rules yield 5-30% correct detection of violations. Social contract rules (if you take benefit B, you must meet requirement R) yield 65-80% correct - despite identical logical structure. Cheater detection is operationally defined: agent takes rationed benefit, fails to meet requirement, acts intentionally. The mechanism does not detect all rule violations, only those revealing intentional cheating.

580.content: Parametric decomposition of cheater detection: a 2×2×2 design manipulating benefit, intention, and ability shows each factor independently drops performance ~20 percentage points. All three present: 64% correct. Two present: ~46%. One: ~26%. None: ~26%. Effects are additive and independent (ANOVA: Benefit F=7.30 p=0.007; Intention F=10.22 p=0.002; Ability F=4.87 p=0.028). Social exchange activates nonstandard inference rules that diverge sharply from first-order logic.
580.where: Cognition 31(3):187-276 and extended work in Cosmides, Barrett & Tooby 2010 PNAS

581.quote: A superordinate program that evolved to coordinate the activity of other programs in the solution of typical adaptive problems
581.content: Emotions are superordinate programs that evolved to coordinate the activity of other programs in solving typical adaptive problems. They simultaneously orchestrate perception, attention, inference, learning, memory, goal choice, motivational priorities, physiological reactions, motor behaviors, and behavioral decision making - activating certain systems and deactivating others to prevent chaos of competing systems operating simultaneously.
581.where: Handbook of Emotions 3rd ed (2008), pp. 114-137. CEP UCSB PDF exists but not parseable.

582.quote: You may suddenly hear with far greater clarity sounds that bear on the hypothesis that you are being stalked, but that ordinarily you would not perceive or attend to, such as creaks or rustling
582.content: Fear example: when sensing a stalker, the emotion simultaneously (a) shifts perception to hear threat-relevant sounds with greater clarity, (b) reprioritizes goals so safety overrides all else, (c) triggers physiological preparation - dry mouth (digestion shutdown), blood to lower body, expanded visual field, increased breathing, (d) retrieves threat-relevant memories. Internal regulatory variables (IRVs) set thresholds, adjust weights, and calibrate responses across all these systems simultaneously.
582.where: Handbook of Emotions 3rd ed (2008), pp. 114-137, fear example

583.content: Ancestral work was characteristically small-group, embodied, skill-based, and autonomy-rich. Psychological adaptations for work - cognitive mechanisms for toolmaking, resource acquisition, learning, and cooperative production - evolved in the context of small networks of hunter-gatherers where effort-outcome links were visible and physical.

584.content: Digital work exacerbates evolutionary mismatch through multiple simultaneous channels: sedentarism replacing embodied activity, always-on connectivity disrupting circadian boundaries, electronic surveillance replacing autonomy, remote/distributed work weakening face-to-face social bonds, and abstract screen-mediated tasks replacing tangible effort-outcome feedback. These mismatches are predicted to increase chronic work stress and related physical and mental health problems.

585.content: Some features of digital work may be more matched with ancestral work conditions than traditional industrial/office work: flexible scheduling restoring autonomy over time allocation, broader access to skill-learning and collaboration networks, and potential for reduced commuting allowing more time for non-work regulatory needs. Digital work is a mixed mismatch profile, not a uniformly mismatched one.

586.content: Organizational interventions for digital work should be grounded in mismatch logic: restore movement breaks, protect circadian boundaries (right to disconnect), design for team sizes within Dunbar-range cooperation thresholds, increase decision latitude and visible effort-outcome links, and create physical co-presence opportunities for distributed teams.

587.content: Electronic monitoring and algorithmic management in digital work environments reduce worker decision latitude, triggering M6 controllability failure (learned helplessness default). Combined with status-threat from visible performance metrics and always-on availability expectations activating M1 without resolution, this creates a chronic stress profile consistent with allostatic load accumulation.

588.content: Many distinctively human cognitive and behavioral traits - language fluency, art, music, humor, creativity, generosity, moral judgment - evolved as fitness indicators under sexual selection (mate-choice pressure), not solely as survival adaptations under natural selection. Sexual selection broadens the set of selection pressures shaping the human motivational and cognitive architecture beyond survival to include mate-choice display and discrimination.

589.content: Consumer goods function substantially as fitness-indicator proxies: signaling intelligence, conscientiousness, openness, stability, and mate value rather than delivering the underlying benefits (mate access, belonging, status-resolution) that the signaling machinery evolved to obtain. Luxury consumption, branded goods, and status markers are industrialized exploitation of mate-choice and status-monitoring mechanisms. Consumers chase proxies that activate these systems without resolving the conditions the systems were selected to track.

590.content: Common mental disorders with high heritability and substantial fitness cost are best explained by polygenic mutation-selection balance - many rare mildly deleterious alleles distributed across large mutational target sizes - rather than by ancestral neutrality or balancing selection. This model accounts for the observed pattern of prevalence, heritability, and fitness cost better than pure-adaptive accounts, and implies that a substantial fraction of heritable mental disorder burden reflects mutational load rather than adaptive tradeoff.

591.quote: It does not pretend to be a complete account of human mental evolution, because it addresses only those psychological adaptations manifest in sexual courtship.
591.content: Miller's sexual-selection argument is explicitly scope-limited. He says it does NOT explain: adaptations shared with other primates (foraging, predator avoidance, parenting), the nature of consciousness, the dynamics of cultural change, or traits better explained by natural selection, kin selection, or reciprocal altruism. The argument applies to self-ornamentation, display, status, ideology, fashion, and aesthetics - to psychological adaptations manifest in sexual courtship. Miller also flags: minimal sexual dimorphism in human mental traits puzzles the classic "choosy-female, displaying-male" model and requires mutual-choice sexual selection models; sexual selection theory itself remains "very much under development"; empirical support is "patchy"; the theory risks over-emphasizing courtship functions of language and creative intelligence while neglecting their other fitness benefits.

592.content: The two theoretical mechanisms Miller invokes for how courtship traits evolved: (1) Zahavi's handicap principle - costly ornaments reliably signal fitness because low-fitness pretenders cannot afford the costly display, forcing honesty through wastefulness; (2) Fisher's runaway selection - mate preferences become genetically linked to ornaments, creating positive-feedback escalation of trait complexity. Mental traits function as either direct fitness indexes (intelligence correlates intrinsically with fitness) or as handicaps (costly displays revealing hidden quality). Psychological biases including "novelty-seeking and pleasure-seeking" shape ornament design.

593.content: Miller frames consumer signaling specifically around the "Central Six" personality dimensions: general intelligence plus the Big Five (openness, conscientiousness, agreeableness, stability, extraversion). These are the traits consumers attempt to display via purchases, and personality research on the Big Five is presented as directly applicable to consumer behavior. This gives a specific mapping: consumer goods = signaling vehicles for Central Six traits = proxies for mate-choice and friend-selection mechanisms that evolved to read these traits in conspecifics.

594.content: Keller & Miller adjudicate between the three evolutionary genetic models using specific empirical criteria: (1) observed prevalence rates of common mental disorders in populations, (2) fitness costs associated with the disorders, (3) likely rarity of susceptibility alleles, (4) increased risks of mental disorders associated with brain trauma, (5) increased risks associated with inbreeding, and (6) increased risks associated with paternal age. They argue only polygenic mutation-selection balance fits all six patterns simultaneously, because brain-trauma/inbreeding/paternal-age effects are specifically predicted by a many-rare-mildly-deleterious-alleles model and do not fit ancestral-neutrality or balancing-selection models.

595.quote: The attachments created within AI companions promise intimacy and connection, yet structurally foreclose the possibility of genuine reciprocal relationships in which the user’s human autonomy is respected.
595.content: Muldoon & Parke's 'cruel companionship' thesis: AI companions activate the human social-bonding response - the evolved tendency to treat a responsive interlocutor as a social being - while structurally foreclosing the genuine reciprocal relationship that would resolve it. Being incapable of genuine understanding, mutual vulnerability, or embodied presence, the companion fires the bonding cue but supplies none of the resolving function, leaving users 'trapped in a cycle of emotional engagement with an app that cannot fulfil their human needs.' Theoretical (political-economy / cultural-studies), not empirical.
595.where: §'Cruel companionship', pp. 9-10 (canonical quote); cue-activation claim at §'The rise of AI companions', pp. 4-5

596.quote: Users may begin with the intention of seeking platonic companionship but gradually develop romantic or sexual attachments, partly because these systems are designed to deepen emotional engagement over time.
596.content: Supports the pair-bond / romantic-sexual slice of M14's proxy floor only: Muldoon & Parke treat AI companions as vehicles for romantic and sexual attachment that simulate a partner while structurally foreclosing a genuine reciprocal relationship. PAIR-BOND SLICE ONLY - the paper says nothing about the desire or attraction subsystems, sexual fulfilment, or reproduction, and does not address M14's full three-system (desire / attraction / pair-bonding) scope.

597.quote: We contrast this signaling view with the idea that moral disgust has a function in causing people to avoid some set of objects, behaviors, or people, as is the case with pathogen and sexual disgust.
597.content: Tybur et al.'s evolutionary-computational framework treats pathogen, sexual, and moral disgust as three FUNCTIONALLY DISTINCT adaptations with distinct information-processing systems, not one mechanism misfiring. Moral disgust is theorized as a condemnation-coordination/signaling adaptation (building on DeScioli & Kurzban) that shares with pathogen disgust primarily the EXPRESSIVE (facial/vocal) component; the defining pathogen "do not touch"/avoidance motivation is absent - moral disgust instead covaries with approach-motivated anger and the desire to punish. The authors explicitly contrast their signaling account with the view that moral disgust functions to cause avoidance "as is the case with pathogen and sexual disgust," and flag the moral domain as the least settled of the three ("little consensus about the measurement, function, and even existence"; treatment "necessarily more exploratory"). Their one causal claim - that activating pathogen/sexual disgust raises moral-wrongness judgments - is framed as disgust being ONE limited input to a SEPARATE strategic rule-endorsement system ("we do not suggest that disgust serves as an input to every moral judgment"), and is evidenced by the Schnall/Eskine/Wheatley-Haidt/Moretti priming studies that Landy & Goodwin (2015, ext105) meta-analyze to d≈-0.01 after publication-bias correction. Net: the canonical framework supports a shared-machinery / functionally-distinct reading and does NOT establish moral disgust as a confirmed lower rung of the pathogen-disgust mechanism - confirming M12's moral-tier demotion while authoritatively grounding the three-domain disgust structure.
597.where: Psychological Review 120(1):65-84. Quote from "Disgust as Output of Moral Cognition" subsection (p. 76). Three-domain thesis: Abstract (p. 65) and "An Evolutionary View of Emotion" (p. 67).

598.quote: An "ego" (the naming person) is 44.2 times (95% C.I. 37.6 to 51.4) more likely to name an "alter" (the named person) in the campmate network, and 14.3 times (95% C.I. 12.2 to 16.4) more likely to name an alter in the gift network, if the alter reciprocated the social tie by also naming the ego as a friend
598.content: Hadza campmate/gift networks show strong dyadic reciprocity even though nominations are private and controlling for kin ties.

599.quote: in both the campmate and gift networks, social ties are significantly more likely when two people are similar in age, height, weight, body fat, and handgrip strength.
599.content: Homophily in Hadza social ties runs on age and physical/condition traits (the "shuffle" is similarity-driven, not random).

600.quote: social distance appears to be as important as genetic relatedness and physical proximity in explaining assortativity in cooperation
600.content: Cooperative assortment in Hadza networks: similarity in cooperation extends to two degrees, and social distance rivals genetic relatedness in explaining it (kinship is not the sole glue).

601.quote: first-order relatives make up less than 10% of residential camps
601.content: Within-camp relatedness is low: most co-residents are not first-order kin.

602.quote: Across the three intervals, the mean proportion of repeated campmates was 12.1%.
602.content: Across 6 years / 4 waves, Hadza camps continuously dissolve and reconstitute: only ~12% of campmates repeat year-over-year (implying ~88% annual turnover), yet cooperative assortment persists.

603.quote: The Hadza live in temporary camps that average about 30 individuals.
603.content: Hadza camp size centers near 30 individuals, composed of several unrelated nuclear families.

604.quote: Every 4-8 weeks entire camps shift location usually in response to resource availability.
604.content: Camp membership is fission-fusion: entire camps relocate on a weeks timescale, so the group as a unit does not persist.

605.quote: Relatedness within camps is low with primary kin comprising, on average, 1.43 and 1.93 of men and women's campmates respectively.
605.content: Direct relatedness measure: primary kin are a small minority of a camp.

606.quote: Among the Ache and Hadza, frequent visiting and long lifespans mean that adults typically interact with more than three hundred same-sex adults during their lifetimes. This implies a social universe of about a thousand individuals, when opposite-sex adults and children are included.
606.content: Among Ache and Hadza foragers, lifetime same-sex interaction exceeds 300 adults, implying a lifetime "social universe" of about a thousand individuals once opposite-sex adults and children are included.

607.quote: Precontact Northern Ache men, for example, are expected to have hunted with 206 men, conversed with 290 men, and watch tool making by 302 different men in a lifetime (Table S16 in File S1). Eastern Hadza men are expected to converse with 427 other Hadza men, hunt with 303 men, and watch tool making by 395 different men in a lifetime. In contrast, chimpanzees living in typical communities of 11 adult males are expected to interact with a mean of only 21 other adult males in a lifetime
607.content: Per-activity lifetime interaction counts for Ache/Hadza men (hundreds of partners) vs ~21 for male chimpanzees: lifetime human social universe is an order of magnitude larger.

608.quote: Additionally, close companions often interact with a somewhat different set of individuals, so that the total number of indirect interactants that each individual hears about repeatedly in detailed stories, and could expect to possibly meet some time during their lifetime is clearly more than 1,000. This is a much higher number of individually known social interactants than reported for any other primate, and possibly more than any other species on earth. It is also much greater than the predicted 150 significant social interactants (known as “Dunbar's number”) that was extrapolated from primate brain by social group size regressions
608.content: The lifetime pool of individually-known interactants is clearly >1,000 - which Hill et al. explicitly note is far above the ~150 figure (the Dunbar number) that was extrapolated from primate brain / social-group-size regressions.

609.quote: Here we show that electrical lighting and the constructed environment is associated with reduced exposure to sunlight during the day, increased light exposure after sunset, and a delayed timing of the circadian clock as compared to a summer natural 14h40min:9h20min light-dark cycle camping. Furthermore, we find that after exposure to only natural light, the internal circadian clock synchronizes to solar time such that the beginning of the internal biological night occurs at sunset and the end of the internal biological night occurs before wake time just after sunrise.
609.content: After exposure to only natural light, the internal circadian clock synchronizes to solar time: biological night begins at sunset and ends just after sunrise; electrical lighting is associated with a delayed clock.

610.quote: Following the week of exposure to natural lighting, all measured markers of internal circadian time were ~2h earlier (Fig 3., all p<0.01; Bonferroni correction required p<0.0167, one tailed) and remarkably, melatonin onset occurred on average near sunset, the melatonin midpoint occurred in the middle of the solar night, and melatonin offset occurred before wake time just after sunrise. Sleep timing was related to circadian timing after electrical lighting-constructed conditions and less so after exposure to only natural light (Supplemental information Table S1 and Fig. S2). The advance in timing of melatonin onset was significantly larger than changes in sleep start and wake times which changed by ~1.2h (Fig. 3, both p<0.02; Bonferroni correction required p<0.025, two tailed). Weekly sleep duration (6.7±0.9h electrical versus 6.8h±0.7h natural lighting; p=0.268, twotailed) and sleep efficiency (87.6±5.6% electrical versus 87.0±4.6% natural lighting; p=0.49, two-tailed) did not significantly change indicating that a change in sleep amount or efficiency did not contribute to the current findings.
610.content: One week of natural light advanced all circadian markers ~2h (melatonin onset near sunset) while sleep duration and efficiency were statistically unchanged: the change was in circadian PHASE/timing, not sleep amount.

611.quote: Natural sunlight is a stronger environmental zeitgeber or time cue for the internal circadian clock than is electrical lighting in the constructed environment.
611.content: Natural sunlight is a stronger circadian zeitgeber than electrical lighting in the constructed environment.

612.quote: We have previously shown that exposure to a natural summer 14 hr 40 min:9 hr 20 min light-dark cycle entrains the human circadian clock to solar time, such that the internal biological night begins near sunset and ends near sunrise [1]. Here we show the beginning of the biological night and sleep occur earlier after a week exposure to a natural winter 9 hr 20 min:14 hr 40 min light-dark cycle as compared to the modern electrical lighting environment.
612.content: Replicates and extends Wright 2013: natural light entrains the clock so the biological night begins near sunset and ends near sunrise; under a natural WINTER light-dark cycle the biological night and sleep occur earlier than under modern electrical lighting.

613.quote: After exposure to the natural light-dark cycle while weekend camping, melatonin onset and midpoint were ~1.4 hr and ~1.0 hr earlier within the same participants compared to the weekday (p<0.01; with large and medium effect sizes for condition [η2G = 0.45 and 0.20, respectively]), despite no change in sleep timing.
613.content: A single weekend of natural-light camping advanced melatonin onset/midpoint ~1.4h/~1.0h within the same participants DESPITE no change in sleep timing: circadian phase, not sleep amount, is the variable that moves.

614.quote: others have reported later circadian and/or sleep timing in Brazilian rubber tappers [2] and in hunter-gatherers from the indigenous Toba/Qom in the Argentinean Chaco with access to electrical lighting compared to those from the same communities without access to electrical lighting
614.content: Convergent field evidence: indigenous Toba/Qom hunter-gatherers and Brazilian rubber-tappers WITH electrical lighting show later circadian/sleep timing than same-community members WITHOUT it.

615.quote: Moreover, infants and mothers are induced to awaken by an arousal exhibited by the other (within seconds) therein creating interconnected, mutually dependent, synchronous arousals [1, 2].
615.content: Cosleeping mother and infant induce arousals in one another within seconds, creating interconnected, mutually-dependent, synchronous arousals (nighttime physiological co-regulation).

616.quote: the behavior can be seen to be intimately linked to underlying EEGs, breathing patterns, changes in sleep architecture, body temperature and linked simultaneously to maternal physiological and behavioral events [5].
616.content: Across the sleep period, cosleeping infant behavior is intimately linked to underlying EEG, breathing patterns, sleep architecture, and body temperature, coupled simultaneously to maternal physiological and behavioral events.

617.quote: as bedsharing safety is determined specifically by how it is practiced and by whom and what adverse factors could be associated
617.content: McKenna himself stresses that bedsharing safety depends entirely on how it is practiced and on adverse co-factors - the live SIDS/safety contestation that keeps co-sleeping from being a clean "ancestral good".

618.quote: At discharge or 40 to 41 weeks' postmenstrual age: "KMC was associated with a statistically significant reduction in the risk of mortality (risk ratio [RR] 0.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.39 to 0.92; eight trials, 1736 infants)." At latest follow-up: "KMC was associated with a significantly decreased risk of mortality (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.95; 12 trials, 2293 infants; moderate-quality evidence)."
618.content: Cochrane meta-analysis of kangaroo mother care (KMC) vs conventional care in low-birthweight infants. In STABILIZED LBW infants, KMC significantly reduced the risk of mortality at discharge or 40-41 weeks postmenstrual age (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.39-0.92; 8 trials, 1736 infants) and at latest follow-up (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48-0.95; 12 trials, 2293 infants; moderate-quality evidence). RR 0.60 is the source of the frequently cited ~40% KMC mortality reduction (1 - 0.60). KMC also reduced nosocomial infection and hypothermia and improved growth and breastfeeding. This is corpus grounding for the claim that continuous skin-to-skin (C-tactile) contact is a mortality-level regulatory input for the preterm/LBW infant, not a comfort measure - the basis of R1 and of empirical demonstration ED9.

619.quote: Our analyses on complementary datasets using different methods yield wildly different numbers. Bayesian and generalized least-squares phylogenetic methods generate approximations of average group sizes between 69-109 and 16-42, respectively. However, enormous 95% confidence intervals (4-520 and 2-336, respectively) imply that specifying any one number is futile. A cognitive limit on human group size cannot be derived in this manner.
619.content: Redoing the neocortex-ratio-to-group-size regression that produced 'Dunbar's number' with modern phylogenetic comparative methods (Bayesian and generalized least-squares) on complementary primate datasets yields wildly unstable human estimates: point estimates of 69-109 (Bayesian) and 16-42 (GLS), with 95 percent confidence intervals of 4-520 and 2-336 respectively. No single number is statistically supportable; a cognitive limit on human group size cannot be derived this way. CHALLENGE to the precise ~150 figure as a cognitive ceiling, cited to Dunbar 1992's neocortex-ratio extrapolation (ext 483).

620.quote: the self-esteem system monitors others' reactions and alerts the individual to the possibility of social exclusion
620.content: Five studies supported the sociometer model: state self-esteem functions as an internal gauge that continuously tracks the individual's perceived relational value (social inclusion versus exclusion) and falls when cues signal potential social devaluation. Self-esteem is the read-out of the monitor rather than an end to be maximized; people act to protect standing. Supplies the measurement axis of M5 - how the organism reads its own position - which the mechanism previously lacked. (Relational value spans both belonging (M3) and rank (M5); tagged to M5 as the standing-monitor per this ingestion pass.)

621.quote: The sociometer system would serve its purpose if it simply assured that the person maintained sufficient social connections with a relatively small set of personally significant people
621.content: The sociometer is calibrated to a small, bounded set of personally significant others rather than to an unbounded audience, and it responds primarily to exclusion (a deprivation state) rather than to ever-greater inclusion: in Studies 3 and 4, exclusion for personal reasons lowered state self-esteem while inclusion produced no matching rise, and random exclusion did not lower it. Directly supports M5's resolution condition that the monitored reference group is bounded and personally known, and M5's mismatch prediction that global mediated audiences over-drive a monitor built for a small group.

622.quote: The finding that Dominance and Prestige can coexist within social groups as viable rank-promoting strategies suggests that human social hierarchies are multidimensional.
622.content: Two experimental studies of hierarchy formation among previously unacquainted people showed that Dominance (using force and intimidation to induce fear) and Prestige (sharing expertise and know-how to gain freely conferred respect) are near-orthogonal (mean correlation close to zero) yet each independently secures real rank: greater perceived influence, greater actual influence over group decisions, and more visual attention from others. Dominance produced influence even where dominant individuals were rated less likable, so influence is separable from liking. Establishes M5's earned-prestige-versus-coerced-dominance distinction as a measurable feature of live human groups rather than a purely theoretical claim, and shows coerced dominance is a partial resolver of rank rather than a non-resolver.

623.quote: Prestigious but not dominant men marry wives who first give birth at earlier ages, which multivariate analysis suggests is the strongest pathway between status and fitness in this population.
623.content: Among Tsimane forager-horticulturalists (Bolivia), both dominance (men more likely to win a dyadic physical confrontation) and prestige (men with more community-wide influence) associate with higher fertility, via different pathways: dominant men have higher intra-marital fertility for their age, while prestigious men show both higher intra-marital fertility and lower offspring mortality. Prestige is the strongest single pathway from status to fitness in this population. Both routes elicit allies' support and competitors' deference but do not buy extra provisioning. Non-WEIRD cross-cultural replication that the dominance/prestige distinction is real and carries genuine fitness consequences, grounding the inclusive-fitness (P1) basis of M5.

624.quote: Measures of prestige and dominance were largely independent, and although both predicted leader status, prestige was more important.
624.content: Among the Chabu (recently settled Ethiopian hunter-gatherers), peer-rated prestige and dominance were largely independent, and although both predicted elected leader status, prestige was clearly more important (dominance's effect was weaker and sensitive to the statistical prior). Most leadership traits covaried strongly, indicating a general leadership/respect factor, and women as well as men held elected leadership. Supports M5's earned-prestige-preferred clause in a non-WEIRD small-scale society and confirms the biased-social-learning (Mentor-salience) prediction of the Henrich & Gil-White model.

627.quote: Circadian misalignment, when subjects ate and slept ≈12 h out of phase from their habitual times, systematically decreased leptin (−17%, P < 0.001), increased glucose (+6%, P < 0.001) despite increased insulin (+22%, P = 0.006), completely reversed the daily cortisol rhythm ( P < 0.001), increased mean arterial pressure (+3%, P = 0.001), and reduced sleep efficiency (−20%, P < 0.002). Notably, circadian misalignment caused 3 of 8 subjects (with sufficient available data) to exhibit postprandial glucose responses in the range typical of a prediabetic state.
627.content: Landmark controlled human experiment (N=10) using a 28-h forced-desynchrony day to isolate circadian misalignment from behavior. With subjects eating and sleeping about 12 h out of phase, leptin fell 17 percent, glucose rose 6 percent despite a 22 percent rise in insulin, the daily cortisol rhythm fully reversed, mean arterial pressure rose 3 percent, and sleep efficiency dropped 20 percent; 3 of 8 subjects reached postprandial glucose in the prediabetic range. Direct causal human evidence that circadian misalignment, as in shift work and jet lag, produces adverse cardiometabolic change independent of the amount of sleep or food.

628.quote: Here we show - by using two 8-d laboratory protocols - that short-term circadian misalignment (12-h inverted behavioral and environmental cycles for three days) adversely affects cardiovascular risk factors in healthy adults. Circadian misalignment increased 24-h systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) by 3.0 mmHg and 1.5 mmHg, respectively.
628.content: Controlled human study (two 8-day protocols with a rapid 12-h inversion simulating night-shift misalignment) showing circadian misalignment raised 24-h systolic and diastolic blood pressure by 3.0 and 1.5 mmHg, driven mainly by higher blood pressure during sleep opportunities (systolic +5.6 mmHg), and lowered wake cardiac vagal modulation by 8 to 15 percent. Direct causal human evidence that misalignment itself raises cardiovascular risk factors, helping explain shift-work hypertension.

629.quote: Circadian misalignment increased 24-h serum interleukin-6, C-reactive protein, resistin, and tumor necrosis factor-α levels by 3-29%.
629.content: In the same misalignment protocol, circadian misalignment raised 24-h inflammatory markers (interleukin-6, C-reactive protein, resistin, and tumour necrosis factor-alpha) by 3 to 29 percent. Human evidence that circadian misalignment drives systemic inflammation, coupling the circadian system (M7) to immune regulation (M8) and giving a mechanism for shift-work cardiovascular and immune risk.

630.quote: Contrary to expectations, we found that half of the maximal phase-delaying response achieved in response to a single episode of evening bright light (∼9000 lux (lx)) can be obtained with just over 1 % of this light (dim room light of ∼100 lx). The same held true for the acute suppressive effects of light on plasma melatonin concentrations. This indicates that even small changes in ordinary light exposure during the late evening hours can significantly affect both plasma melatonin concentrations and the entrained phase of the human circadian pacemaker.
630.content: Dose-response study of the human circadian pacemaker to evening light. Half of the maximal phase delay and half of the maximal melatonin suppression produced by bright evening light (about 9000 lux) were obtained with just over 1 percent of that intensity, about 100 lux of dim room light, both following a logistic dose-response curve. Ordinary indoor evening light is therefore enough to suppress melatonin and shift circadian phase, putting M7's indoor (ATTENUATED) and evening-screen (DEFEATED) rungs on direct dose-response evidence.

631.quote: The resultant PRC of the midpoint of the melatonin rhythm revealed a characteristic type 1 PRC with a significant peak-to-trough amplitude of 5.02 h. Phase delays occurred when the light stimulus was centred prior to the critical phase at the core body temperature minimum, phase advances occurred when the light stimulus was centred after the critical phase, and no phase shift occurred at the critical phase.
631.content: Definitive characterization of the human phase-response curve (PRC) to single bright-light pulses. Light before the core-body-temperature minimum delays the clock, light after it advances the clock, and there is no phase shift exactly at the critical phase; the melatonin-midpoint PRC has a peak-to-trough amplitude of 5.02 h with no prolonged photic dead zone during the subjective day. Grounds the core M7 claim that light is the entraining signal and that its effect is timing-dependent, so mistimed evening light actively mis-sets the clock.

632.quote: Shift work is associated with vascular events, which may have implications for public policy and occupational medicine.
632.content: Systematic review and meta-analysis of shift work and vascular events (34 studies, 2,011,935 people). Shift work was associated with myocardial infarction (risk ratio 1.23, 95 percent CI 1.15 to 1.31), ischaemic stroke (1.05, 1.01 to 1.09), and any coronary event (1.24, 1.10 to 1.39); population attributable risks at Canadian shift-work prevalence were about 7.0 percent for MI and 7.3 percent for coronary events. First shift-work epidemiology in M7's base, directly evidencing the shift-work (MINIMAL) rung. It also cuts on the flagged PARTIAL-versus-MINIMAL ordering: shift work is tied to hard cardiovascular endpoints, more severe than social jetlag's BMI-only association, supporting shift work as the more severe rung.

633.quote: The distribution’s mean value is systematically different with age, shifting later during adolescence, showing a peak in ‘lateness’ at ~19 years, and shifting earlier thereafter. Men are typically later chronotypes than women before 40, but earlier types after 40.
633.content: First nationally representative estimate of the US chronotype distribution, from 12 years of American Time Use Survey diaries (n=53,689, chronotype = weekend mid-sleep). Chronotype is near-normally distributed and spans almost 10 hours; the mean shifts later through adolescence to a peak in lateness at about 19 years and earlier thereafter, and men are later chronotypes than women before 40 but earlier after. Adolescents are on average the latest chronotypes, which the authors note supports later school start times. Grounds M7's social-jetlag (PARTIAL) rung: fixed social and school schedules collide with a wide, developmentally shifting range of internal circadian phase, and the resolution condition is aligning schedule to internal time.

634.quote: Our findings suggest that T mediates tradeoffs between mating and parenting in humans, as seen in other species in which fathers care for young.
634.content: Longitudinal study of 624 Filipino men followed 4.5 years (Cebu cohort). Single nonfathers with high waking testosterone at baseline were more likely to become partnered fathers by follow-up. Men who became partnered fathers then showed large declines in waking (median -26%) and evening (median -34%) testosterone, significantly exceeding the declines of men who stayed single nonfathers. Fathers reporting 3 or more hours of daily childcare had lower testosterone at follow-up than fathers not involved in care. Testosterone and reproductive strategy are bidirectional in human males: high testosterone predicts mating success, then testosterone drops when men take up direct care of offspring.
634.where: PNAS 108(39):16194-16199. Abstract + Results, full text via PMC3182719.

635.quote: Among all fathers, time spent in direct childcare was linked with the degree of amygdala-STS connectivity.
635.content: fMRI study of 89 first-time parents in three groups: primary-caregiving mothers, secondary-caregiving fathers, and primary-caregiving fathers raising infants without maternal involvement. All parents activated a shared global parental caregiving network integrating emotional processing and mentalizing circuits. Primary-caregiving fathers showed amygdala activation comparable to primary-caregiving mothers alongside father-typical superior temporal sulcus activation, and amygdala-STS connectivity scaled with time spent in direct childcare across all fathers. The care network is shared across sexes and its recruitment tracks caregiving experience.
635.where: PNAS 111(27):9792-9797. Abstract + Results, full text via PMC4103311.

636.quote: Our assessment is that studies using more rigorous designs continue to find negative effects of father absence on offspring well-being, although the magnitude of these effects is smaller than what is found using traditional cross-sectional designs.
636.content: Systematic review of father-absence studies restricted to causal-inference designs: lagged dependent variable models, growth curve models, individual and sibling fixed effects, natural experiments, and propensity score matching. Rigorous designs continue to find negative effects of father absence on offspring wellbeing, with smaller magnitudes than traditional cross-sectional estimates. Evidence is strongest and most consistent for high school graduation, social-emotional adjustment in childhood, and adult mental health.
636.where: Annual Review of Sociology 39:399-427. Abstract + Conclusion, full text via PMC3904543.

637.quote: We report a meta-analysis of twin correlations and reported variance components for 17,804 traits from 2,748 publications including 14,558,903 partly dependent twin pairs, virtually all published twin studies of complex traits. Estimates of heritability cluster strongly within functional domains, and across all traits the reported heritability is 49%.
637.content: Polderman and colleagues aggregate virtually the entire twin literature: twin correlations and reported variance components for 17,804 traits from 2,748 publications, covering 14,558,903 partly dependent twin pairs. Across all traits the reported heritability is 49%, and heritability estimates cluster strongly within functional domains. This is the twin-design leg of the C15 triangulation: individual variation in every measured behavioral and psychological trait domain is substantially heritable.

638.quote: The meta-analyses of all traits yielded an average rMZ of 0.636 (s.e.m. = 0.002) and an average rDZ of 0.339 (s.e.m. = 0.003). The reported heritability (h2) across all traits was 0.488 (s.e.m. = 0.004), and the reported estimate of shared environmental effects (c2) was 0.174 (s.e.m. = 0.004)
638.content: The pooled twin correlations across all traits: monozygotic 0.636 versus dizygotic 0.339, the classic roughly-double MZ resemblance that signals additive genetic influence. Reported heritability across all traits is 0.488 and the reported shared-environment component is 0.174. For a majority (69%) of traits the observed correlations are consistent with a parsimonious model in which twin resemblance is due solely to additive genetic variation. Quantifies DA10's heritable-ranges claim at the scale of the whole literature, and simultaneously shows half the variance is not additive-genetic.

639.quote: We estimated the proportion of variance for human height explained by 294,831 SNPs genotyped on 3,925 unrelated individuals using a linear model analysis, and validated the estimation method by simulations based upon the observed genotype data. We show that 45% of variance can be explained by considering all SNPs simultaneously. Thus, most of the heritability is not missing but has not previously been detected because the individual effects are too small to pass stringent significance tests.
639.content: The founding GCTA result: estimating genetic variance directly from 294,831 common SNPs genotyped in 3,925 unrelated individuals recovers 45% of the variance in height, with no twin or family structure anywhere in the design. Heritability estimated by twin and family designs is real and hiding in many variants of individually small effect rather than missing. This is the molecular leg of C15, a method family fully independent of the other two; the SNP-heritability approach has since been replicated across traits and cohorts throughout complex-trait genetics.

640.quote: First Law. All human behavioral traits are heritable. Second Law. The effect of being raised in the same family is smaller than the effect of genes. Third Law. A substantial portion of the variation in complex human behavioral traits is not accounted for by the effects of genes or families.
640.content: Turkheimer's canonical compression of five decades of behavior-genetic findings into three laws. For DA10 the first law states the heritable-variation claim across all human behavioral traits; the second and third laws carry the guard rail: shared family environment accounts for less variance than genes, and a substantial residual is accounted for by neither, so heritability describes population variance partitioning, not individual determinism. Later quantitatively confirmed at scale by Polderman et al. 2015.

641.quote: Finally, we note that four of the top-10 findings (2, 7, 8 and 9) are about environmental influences rather than genetic influences. By using genetically sensitive designs such as twin studies, behavioral genetics has revealed almost as much about the environment as about genetics.
641.content: Plomin, DeFries, Knopik and Neiderhiser's top-ten list opens with the first-law finding: all psychological traits show significant and substantial genetic influence, across cognitive abilities, psychopathology and personality, corroborated across twin, family, and adoption designs with cross-national replication. The adoption/family-design leg of C15: genetic influence on parameter variation appears whether resemblance is measured in twins, in adoptees and their birth parents, or in extended families. The same review notes that four of the ten findings are about environmental influence, which is DA10's guard rail from inside behavior genetics itself.

642.quote: The affective neuroethological perspective presented here, views the ML-DA system in terms of its ability to activate an instinctual emotional appetitive state (SEEKING) evolved to induce organisms to search for all varieties of life-supporting stimuli and to avoid harms.
642.content: The Panksepp-school statement of what M2 is: the mesolimbic dopamine system activates an instinctual appetitive SEEKING state that induces organisms to search for all varieties of life-supporting stimuli. SEEKING is the general-purpose engagement disposition of the awake animal rather than a response to a specific deficit signal, which is why its activation profile is not homeostatic in the M13 sense: no single tissue variable builds pressure and terminates it.

643.quote: Phasic DA transmission is the short-lasting and impulse-dependent release that appears as a consequence of neural burst firing (Gonon, 1988; Suaud-Chagny et al., 1992). Following such bursts, high levels of DA molecules are released into the synaptic cleft at up to mM concentration (Garris et al., 1994), and then rapidly removed via a re-uptake system (Floresco et al. 2003). To the contrary, tonic DA levels are diffused in the extracellular space outside the synaptic clefts, but exist in very small concentrations (in the nM range), and change relatively slowly (Grace, 2000).
643.content: The physiological basis for M2's mixed activation profile: dopamine transmission runs in two modes. Phasic release is short-lasting, impulse-dependent, cue and reward-prediction locked; tonic extracellular dopamine sits at low concentration and changes slowly, carrying a background level of appetitive engagement that varies with state (sleep-wake, arousal). For activation_class this grounds tonic_baseline as M2's primary class with event_triggered phasic spikes as secondary; the phasic incentive-salience side is already carried in C6 by Berridge.
643.where: Section 2.5, Electric activity of DA cells

644.quote: Sexual incentive stimuli activate sexual motivation and heighten the level of general arousal. The sexual motive may induce the individual to approach the incentive, and eventually to initiate sexual acts.
644.content: The incentive-motivation account of M14: sexual motivation is activated by external sexual incentive stimuli interacting with a central motive state; it is not a homeostatic reservoir in which unexpended sexual energy accumulates as an internal need. The review endorses Beach's rejection of an internal origin ("sexual motivation is active only in the presence of an external stimulus") and builds the modern model on Bindra and Toates incentive theory. No tissue deficit accumulates during abstinence; desire follows cue-triggered arousal rather than spontaneous internal pressure. For activation_class: event_triggered (incentive), not homeostatic.

645.quote: Thus, in rats and humans there is no doubt that testicular hormones, either directly or via aromatization, are in charge of the control of the long-term activity of the sexual central motive state.
645.content: Hormones set the gain, not the pressure: in rats and humans, testicular hormones control the long-term activity level of the sexual central motive state (in men via androgen receptors directly; in rats partly via aromatization to estrogens), while short-term variation in sexual motivation is driven by incentive stimuli, not by hormone fluctuation. The same structure is proposed for women (androgens needed for basic long-term activity of the central motive state). This is the hormonal gain-modulation half of M14's activation profile: testosterone tunes cue-sensitivity; cues do the triggering.
645.where: Section on endocrine control of the central motive state

646.quote: Several of the men, like Max Kampelman, agreed that nearly immediately after semistarvation began, all interest in women and dating was lost: "I can tell you, the sex drive disappeared. There was none."
646.content: The Minnesota Starvation Experiment (Keys, 1944-45, 36 conscientious objectors under controlled semi-starvation) documents reproductive-axis shutdown under sustained energy deficit: sexual interest collapsed almost immediately once semi-starvation began, while food became the dominant preoccupation and social engagement narrowed. Evidence that an unresolved M13 deficit suppresses M14, supporting state-dependent drive priority: DA8 priority relations behave as slope functions of current state rather than a fixed order.
646.where: Section on the psychological effects of semistarvation, participant interviews

findings.quote: Degeneracy means "many to one": many combinations of neurons can produce the same outcome. In the quest to map emotion fingerprints in the brain, degeneracy is a humbling reality check.
findings.content: The principle of degeneracy in emotion: different combinations of neurons can produce the same emotional outcome (many-to-one). Barrett's lab demonstrated this in brain-imaging studies where men and women reported equivalent feelings of arousal but showed different neural patterns - women's arousal was more strongly linked to the anterior insula, men's to visual cortex. The same subjective experience was associated with different patterns of neural activity.

findings.quote: Moreover, sustained stress and glucocorticoid exposure enhance LTP and suppress LTD in the amygdala, boosting fear conditioning, and suppress LTP in the frontal cortex. Combining these effects - more excitable synapses in the amygdala, fewer ones in the frontal cortex - helps explain stress-induced impulsivity and poor emotional regulation.
findings.content: Sustained stress and glucocorticoid exposure enhance LTP and suppress LTD in the amygdala while suppressing LTP in the frontal cortex. This combination - more excitable synapses in the amygdala, fewer in the frontal cortex - helps explain stress-induced impulsivity and poor emotional regulation.

findings.quote: As to the functional consequences of structural remodeling in hippocampus, repeated stress can impair hippocampal-dependent behaviors in a manner that is reversible, along with dendritic shrinkage in the CA3 region, within days or weeks after the termination of the stressor. This supports the notion that the remodeling is not brain damage but a form of adaptive plasticity that may also protect the hippocampus from permanent excitotoxic damage.
findings.content: The brain is the central organ of stress and adaptation to stress because it perceives and determines what is threatening, as well as the behavioral and physiological responses to the stressor. The adult, as well as developing brain, possess a remarkable ability to show reversible structural and functional plasticity in response to stressful and other experiences, including neuronal replacement, dendritic remodeling, and synapse turnover. This is particularly evident in the hippocampus. The amygdala and the prefrontal cortex, brain regions involved in anxiety and fear, mood, cognitive function and behavioral control, also show structural plasticity. Repeated stress can impair hippocampal-dependent behaviors in a manner that is reversible, along with dendritic shrinkage in the CA3 region, within days or weeks after the termination of the stressor. This supports the notion that the remodeling is not brain damage but a form of adaptive plasticity that may also protect the hippocampus from permanent excitotoxic damage.

findings.quote: The RAGE system (see Chapter 10): Working in opposition to SEEKING is a system that mediates anger. RAGE is aroused by frustration and attempts to curtail an animal's freedom of action. It has long been known that one can enrage both animals and humans by stimulating very specific parts of the brain, which parallel the trajectory of the FEAR system. This system not only helps animals defend themselves by arousing fear in their opponents but also energizes behavior when an animal is irritated or restrained. Human anger may get much of its psychic "energy" from this brain system.
findings.content: Panksepp's definition of the RAGE system: working in opposition to SEEKING, it mediates anger. RAGE is aroused by frustration and by attempts to curtail an animal's freedom of action. Electrical stimulation of specific brain regions paralleling the FEAR trajectory produces rage in both animals and humans. The system helps animals defend themselves by arousing fear in opponents, AND energizes behavior when an animal is irritated or restrained. Human anger gets much of its psychic 'energy' from this brain system. Brain tumors irritating the circuit cause pathological rage; damage to the system promotes serenity. This is the canonical primary-source definition for M1 Threat Management (rage component).

findings.quote: The FEAR system (see Chapter 1 1): A FEAR circuit was probably designed during evolution to help animals reduce pain and the possibility of destruction. When stimulated intensely, this circuit leads animals to run away as if they are extremely scared. With very weak stimulation, animals exhibit just the opposite motor tendency - a freezing response, common when
findings.content: Panksepp's definition of the FEAR system: a circuit designed during evolution to help animals reduce pain and the possibility of destruction. Intense stimulation makes animals run away as if extremely scared; weak stimulation produces the opposite motor tendency - freezing, common when animals are placed in circumstances where they have previously been hurt or frightened. Humans stimulated in these same brain areas report being engulfed by intense anxiety. This is the canonical primary-source evidence that fear is not a derived cognitive state but a hardwired affective circuit with specific neuroanatomy. Load-bearing for M1 Threat Management.

findings.quote: fear responses reside in ancient neural circuits that evolved long before the full development of the neocortex
findings.content: Experiments assessing visual detection latencies have confirmed that when people are shown large sets of stimulus pictures, snakes automatically capture their visual attention, regardless of how many distractor stimuli are present. Fear responses can be learned and activated, even when backward masking prevents images of snakes from reaching higher cortical processing. This indicates that fear responses reside in ancient neural circuits that evolved long before the full development of the neocortex. Humans and higher primates have a fear module that evolved to reduce recurrent threats posed by dangerous and potentially lethal animals.
findings.where: Chapter 3, 'Methods of Evolutionary Sciences,' pp. 130-131 (Öhman & Mineka program citations)

findings.quote: An evolved module for fear elicitation and fear learning with 4 characteristics is proposed.
