findings.content: Evolved fear module with four characteristics: (a) preferentially activated by phylogenetically relevant stimuli (snakes, spiders, angry faces) in aversive contexts; (b) activation is automatic and pre-attentive; (c) relatively impenetrable to cognitive control (resistant to verbal instruction); (d) originates in dedicated amygdala-centered neural circuitry. Module mediates emotional fear learning dissociable from cognitive learning of stimulus relationships.

findings.quote: The fear module is assumed to mediate an emotional level of fear learning that is relatively independent and dissociable from cognitive learning of stimulus relationships.
findings.content: Visual search reveals pre-attentive threat detection: snake/spider targets among flower/mushroom distractors detected faster (~615ms) than reverse (~704ms). Fear-relevant detection unaffected by display size (parallel/pop-out processing, slope ~6ms/item). Fear-irrelevant targets show serial search (slope ~15ms/item). Conditioning to fear-relevant stimuli resists verbal instruction to extinguish; backward-masked fear-relevant conditioned stimuli elicit electrodermal responses without conscious awareness.
findings.where: Psychological Review 108(3):483-522 and Öhman, Flykt & Esteves 2001 visual search study

findings.content: Evidence for unconscious threat processing: subliminal threat stimuli elicit physiological responses without awareness; conditioning occurs without CS-US contingency awareness; amygdala activates to subliminal stimuli; hippocampal damage disrupts explicit memory but NOT fear conditioning (amygdala damage produces opposite pattern); blindsight patients show body responses to unseen threats; bilateral amygdala damage does NOT eliminate conscious fear - proving neither amygdala activity nor amygdala-controlled responses are necessary for fearful feelings.

findings.quote: Over 60 years ago, Selye recognized the paradox that the physiologic systems activated by stress can not only protect and restore but also damage the body.
findings.content: Allostasis is the ability to achieve stability through change - the body's active adjustment to anticipated demands. Unlike homeostasis (maintaining constant internal conditions), allostasis recognizes that the body actively shifts its operating parameters in response to predicted demands. The cost of this active adjustment, when chronically required, is allostatic load. Selye recognized 60 years earlier that stress mediators can both protect and damage - McEwen's contribution is formalizing this paradox.

findings.quote: a territory-holding male of this species would threaten a mere bundle of red feathers much more readily than a complete mounted young robin which showed all the characteristics of a robin except the red breast. Again, the red breast is the effective stimulus
findings.content: A territory-holding male English robin will threaten a mere bundle of red feathers much more readily than a complete mounted young robin which shows all the characteristics of a robin except the red breast. The red breast alone is sufficient to release the threat response; the rest of the bird is irrelevant. The male's aggression system runs on a single feature of the stimulus, not on a species-level recognition.
findings.where: Chapter III, 'Sign stimuli,' robin example, p. 28, Fig. 21

findings.quote: Clearly lesions of higher areas do not diminish the emotional responses from lower areas, while damage to lower areas can dramatically compromise emotional actions generated from higher areas.
findings.content: Lower subcortical regions, especially the periaqueductal gray (PAG), are more important for generating emotional feelings than cortical regions. Three key properties of the PAG: (1) lowest ESB energy to obtain powerful emotional changes, (2) smallest brain damage compromising consciousness, (3) most massive convergence of brain emotional systems. Lesions of higher areas do not diminish emotional responses from lower areas, while damage to lower areas dramatically compromises emotional actions generated from higher areas.

findings.quote: This work has pinpointed the amygdala as an important component of the system involved in the acquisition, storage, and expression of fear memory.
findings.content: Dual pathway model for threat information reaching the amygdala. The low road (thalamo-amygdala, ~150-200ms) provides quick, coarse processing of simple stimulus features enabling immediate defensive responses before conscious identification. The high road (thalamo-cortico-amygdala, ~300ms) provides detailed, complex evaluation through sensory cortex and can override false alarms. Both converge on the lateral nucleus.
findings.where: Annual Review of Neuroscience 23:155-184. DOI: 10.1146/annurev.neuro.23.1.155. PMID: 10845062

findings.quote: Emotions seem to arise ultimately from hard-wired neural circuits in the visceral-limbic brain that facilitate diverse and adaptive behavioral and physiological responses to major classes of environmental challenges.
findings.content: Emotions arise from hard-wired neural circuits in the visceral-limbic brain, not from cortical constructions. These circuits facilitate diverse adaptive responses to major classes of environmental challenges. Theoretically guided studies of the animal brain can reveal how primitive emotions are organized in the human brain, and conversely, human introspective access can generate hypotheses for animal brain research.

Amygdala functional architecture: lateral nucleus (LA) is the sensory interface where CS and US converge (synaptic plasticity encodes fear memories via LTP); central nucleus (CE) is the principal output for expression of conditioned fear, projecting to PAG (freezing), lateral hypothalamus (autonomic), and BNST (endocrine). Lesion studies confirm functional dissociation of these output pathways.
findings.where: Annual Review of Neuroscience 23:155-184, amygdala architecture section

findings.content: Fear conditioning involves calcium influx during CS-US pairing at lateral nucleus synapses, with subsequent gene expression and protein synthesis stabilizing long-term fear memories. LTP can be induced in the lateral nucleus by stimulating auditory thalamus. Findings from rodent fear conditioning apply to the human brain via functional neuroimaging and lesion studies.
findings.where: Annual Review of Neuroscience 23:155-184, cellular mechanisms section

findings.content: Monkey observational conditioning demonstrates prepared learning: lab-reared rhesus monkeys with no snake experience acquired fear of snakes and crocodiles (fear-relevant) through watching fearful models, but did NOT acquire fear of flowers or rabbits (fear-irrelevant) through the same procedure. This demonstrates selective associations operating even through vicarious/observational learning, not just direct conditioning.
findings.where: Psychological Review 108(3):483-522, citing Cook & Mineka studies

findings.quote: The cortex and limbic system are not separate, as scads of axonal projections course between the two. Crucially, those projections are bidirectional - the limbic system talks to the cortex, rather than merely being reined in by it.
findings.content: The frontal cortex is bidirectionally enmeshed with the limbic system. Nauta's landmark discovery showed the frontal cortex is a quasi member of the limbic system, not a hierarchical controller standing above it. In different circumstances the frontal cortex and limbic system stimulate or inhibit each other, collaborate and conflict. The false dichotomy between thought and feeling is a neuroscientific error.

findings.quote: In another study subjects waited an unknown length of time to receive a shock. This lack of predictability and control was so aversive that many chose to receive a stronger shock immediately. And in the others the period of anticipatory dread increasingly activated the amygdala.
findings.content: Lack of predictability and control over stressors is so aversive that subjects chose to receive a stronger shock immediately rather than wait an unknown time for a weaker one. The period of anticipatory dread increasingly activated the amygdala.

findings.quote: Just as prenatal testosterone exposure generates an adult brain that is more sensitive to environmental triggers of aggression, excessive prenatal glucocorticoid exposure produces an adult brain more sensitive to environmental triggers of depression and anxiety.
findings.content: Prenatal glucocorticoid exposure produces organizational effects on fetal brain construction, decreasing growth factors, neurons, and synapses. Just as prenatal testosterone exposure generates an adult brain more sensitive to aggression triggers, excessive prenatal glucocorticoid exposure produces an adult brain more sensitive to environmental triggers of depression and anxiety. Stressed mothers secrete glucocorticoids that enter fetal circulation with the same consequences as postnatal stress.

findings.quote: The amygdala is particularly sensitive to unsettling circumstances that are social. Stable rankings activated parts of the frontal cortex that we'll soon consider. Instability activated the frontal cortex plus the amygdala. Being unsure of your place is unsettling.
findings.content: The amygdala is particularly sensitive to social uncertainty. When a male monkey's social position is threatened by a rival, amygdala activation correlates not with aggression or testosterone but with anxiety (teeth chattering, self-scratching). In humans, unstable social rankings activate both the frontal cortex and amygdala, while stable rankings activate only the frontal cortex. Being unsure of your social place is unsettling - rank uncertainty, not rank itself, drives threat-system activation.

findings.quote: Although the brain is highly responsive to perceived threat, even simple handholding can substantially attenuate threat responses.
findings.content: SBT describes two mechanisms for social regulation: risk distribution (safety in numbers) and load sharing (distribution of effort toward shared goals). During supportive handholding, the threat-responsive brain returns to a baseline state of relative calm - not through activation of regulatory circuitry but through decreased perceived demand. The brain encodes relational partners as extensions of the self, effectively pooling bioenergetic resources.

findings.quote: Acute and chronic stress cause an imbalance of neural circuitry subserving cognition, decision making, anxiety and mood that can increase or decrease expression of those behaviors and behavioral states. In the short term, such as for increased fearful vigilance and anxiety in a threatening environment, these changes may be adaptive; but, if the danger passes and the behavioral state persists along with the changes in neural circuitry, such maladaptation may need intervention
findings.content: Acute and chronic stress cause an imbalance of neural circuitry subserving cognition, decision making, anxiety and mood that can increase or decrease expression of those behaviors and behavioral states. In the short term, such as for increased fearful vigilance and anxiety in a threatening environment, these changes may be adaptive; but, if the danger passes and the behavioral state persists along with the changes in neural circuitry, such maladaptation may need intervention with a combination of pharmacological and behavioral therapies. Chronic restraint stress causes dendritic shortening in medial prefrontal cortex but produces dendritic growth in neurons of the basolateral amygdala - opposite structural effects in interconnected regions, reflecting different functional roles under sustained stress.
findings.where: Introduction and Section 2.4, 'Prefrontal cortex and amygdala,' pp. 3-4

findings.quote: Offspring of mothers that showed high levels of LG and ABN were found to have differences in DNA methylation, as compared to offspring of low-LG-ABN mothers.
findings.content: The specific epigenetic mechanism involves altered methylation at the NGFI-A transcription factor binding site in the GR promoter, changing GR expression in the hippocampus. This alters the negative feedback sensitivity of the HPA axis - high-LG offspring have more hippocampal GR, stronger negative feedback, and lower baseline glucocorticoid levels. The effect cascades: lower baseline stress hormones → less anxiety → better learning → delayed brain aging.

findings.quote: It is a striking fact that displacement activities often occur in a situation in which the fighting drive and the drive to escape are both activated.
findings.content: Displacement activities occur when two incompatible drives are simultaneously activated - for example, when fighting drive and escape drive conflict at a territory boundary, animals perform apparently irrelevant behaviors like preening or feeding. These activities reveal the competing motivational programs underlying behavior and demonstrate that behavior is not a simple stimulus-response chain but emerges from the interaction of multiple motivational systems.

Although the brain is highly responsive to perceived threat, even simple handholding can substantially attenuate threat responses. These effects are potentiated by higher relationship quality, intimacy, and higher perceived mutuality. Critically, the likeliest mechanisms linking social support to diminished threat responding - regulatory circuits within the prefrontal cortex - are not more activated by support provision as originally hypothesized, but less so. During supportive handholding in particular, the threat responsive brain appears to return to a baseline state of relative calm, suggesting the difference is attributable less to the activation of regulatory circuitry and more to a decrease in perceived demand associated with the threat, a decrease proportional to the increase in resources brought to bear by the relational partner.
findings.where: Section 'Risk, effort, and the expanded self,' pp. 88-89

findings.quote: In our studies, the lonely, both young and old, perceived the hassles and stresses of everyday life to be more severe than did their nonlonely counterparts, even though the objective stressors they encountered were essentially the same. Compounding the problem, the lonely found the small social uplifts of everyday life to be less intense and less gratifying.
findings.content: In our studies, the lonely, both young and old, perceived the hassles and stresses of everyday life to be more severe than did their nonlonely counterparts, even though the objective stressors they encountered were essentially the same. The lonely also found the small social uplifts of everyday life to be less intense and less gratifying. The presence of and interaction with other people in their lives did not cause them to rate the severity of everyday stressors any less intensely.
findings.where: Chapter 6 'The Wear and Tear of Loneliness,' Pathway 3 'Perceived Stress and Coping,' pp. 102-103

findings.quote: while the acute stress response involves enhanced immunity, chronic stress suppresses immunity, increasing vulnerability to some infectious diseases.
findings.content: The acute stress response involves enhanced immunity, but chronic stress suppresses immunity, increasing vulnerability to infectious diseases. We get sick not from failing to activate the stress response but from activating it too often, too long, and for purely psychological reasons. The beneficial effects of stress (fight-or-flight for seconds to minutes) become damaging on the sustained timescale of chronic psychological stress.

findings.quote: Testosterone was administered to the middle-ranking male in each group (say, rank number 3 out of five), increasing their levels of aggression. Does this mean that these guys, stoked on 'roids, started challenging numbers 1 and 2 in the hierarchy? No. They became aggressive jerks to poor numbers 4 and 5. Testosterone did not create new social patterns of aggression; it exaggerated preexisting ones.
findings.content: Testosterone does not create aggression - it amplifies preexisting social patterns. In talapoin monkeys, testosterone given to middle-ranking males did not make them challenge higher-ranking individuals; it made them more aggressive to lower-ranking ones. In humans, testosterone does not raise baseline amygdala activity but boosts amygdala response to angry faces specifically. Testosterone makes subjects more punitive when provoked, enhancing 'vengeful reactive aggression' rather than creating new social patterns.

findings.quote: methylation differences emerged over the first week of life, were reversed with cross-fostering, persisted into adulthood.
findings.content: The cross-fostering experiment definitively proved that the epigenetic differences are caused by maternal behavior, not genetic inheritance. Pups born to low-LG mothers but raised by high-LG mothers developed the low-stress phenotype of their foster mothers, and vice versa. The pharmacological reversal via histone deacetylase inhibitor demonstrated that the epigenetic marks are modifiable even in adulthood, establishing that developmental calibration is potentially reversible - a finding with profound therapeutic implications.

findings.quote: Learned helplessness in the laboratory - combining the animal and human experimental results - produced eight of the nine symptoms [of depression], with the only exception being suicide and suicidal thoughts.
findings.content: Learned helplessness in the laboratory produces eight of the nine DSM symptoms of depression (excepting suicidal thoughts). The prelimbic medial prefrontal cortex detects contingency between behavior and outcomes and inhibits the dorsal raphe nucleus, restoring the capacity for active escape. When this detection circuit fails - due to chronic uncontrollable stress, developmental adversity, or prefrontal damage - the default passivity state persists as clinical depression.

findings.quote: More than half of respondents reported at least one, and one-fourth reported two or more categories of childhood exposures.
findings.content: The ACE dose-response gradient shows that childhood adversity is not a binary (traumatized/not) but a cumulative load: each additional category of exposure incrementally increases adult disease risk across behavioral, mental, and physical health domains. The clustering of risk behaviors (smoking, substance use, obesity, sexual risk-taking) suggests that these are not independent choices but downstream consequences of the same developmental calibration toward defensive/avoidant coping strategies.

findings.quote: The price of this accommodation to stress can be allostatic load, which is the wear and tear that results from chronic overactivity or underactivity of allostatic systems.
findings.content: McEwen's 1998 NEJM review: the physiologic response to stress, allostatic load, reflects wear and tear from not only life experiences but also genetic load, individual lifestyle habits (diet, exercise, substance abuse), and developmental experiences. Hormones associated with stress protect the body short-term through allostasis but in the long run cause disease. Four conditions produce allostatic load: (1) repeated stressors, (2) lack of adaptation to repeated stressors, (3) prolonged response due to delayed shutdown, and (4) inadequate response leading to compensatory hyperactivity of other systems.

findings.quote: More than half of respondents reported at least one, and one-fourth reported two or more categories of childhood exposures.
findings.content: The ACE Study identified seven categories of childhood adversity and found that more than half of respondents reported at least one, and one-fourth reported two or more categories. The graded dose-response relationship - where each additional ACE category incrementally increases risk - demonstrates that childhood adversity is cumulative rather than categorical. Persons with 4+ categories had 4-12 fold increased health risk, suggesting a threshold effect where the cascade becomes self-reinforcing.

findings.quote: In the same study, when the photographs were negative, the patterns of brain activation were equally revealing about the experience of loneliness, moment to moment. Whereas nonlonely participants paid comparable attention to negative images of people and objects, lonely individuals paid far more attention to the negative images depicting people. In both cases, the measure was activation of their visual cortex. When we observed the temporoparietal junction, an area involved in theory of mind and in perspective taking, the pattern of activation was the opposite. Lonely individuals appeared more likely than their nonlonely counterparts to respond to pictures of people in peril from their first-person perspective (as indicated by weaker activation of the temporoparietal junction). When we feel lonely, we tend to scan the horizon for any possibility of social danger, but with an eye toward protecting ourselves rather than with genuine concern for what others may be thinking or feeling.
findings.content: In the same Chicago Brain Imaging Center fMRI study, when participants viewed negative images, the patterns of brain activation were equally revealing. Nonlonely participants paid comparable attention to negative images of people and objects. Lonely individuals, however, paid far more attention to the negative images depicting people - measured by visual cortex activation. When observing the temporoparietal junction, an area involved in theory of mind and perspective taking, lonely individuals appeared more likely to respond to pictures of people in peril from their first-person perspective rather than with genuine concern for what others may be thinking or feeling.

findings.quote: loss of mother-figure, either by itself or in combination with other variables yet to be clearly identified, is capable of generating responses and processes that are of the greatest interest to psychopathology. Not only so, but these responses and processes, we concluded, are the very same as are known to be active in older individuals who are still disturbed by separations that they suffered in early life.
findings.content: Loss of the mother-figure generates responses and processes of the greatest interest to psychopathology. These responses are the very same as those active in older individuals still disturbed by early separations. On one hand: excessive demands on others, anxiety and anger when demands are unmet (dependent and hysterical personalities). On the other: blockage in the capacity to make deep relationships (affectionless and psychopathic personalities).

findings.quote: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) shows us that the emotional region of the brain that is activated when we experience rejection is, in fact, the same region - the dorsal anterior cingulate - that registers emotional responses to physical pain
findings.content: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) shows that the emotional region of the brain activated when we experience rejection is the same region - the dorsal anterior cingulate - that registers emotional responses to physical pain. The discovery that feelings of social rejection (isolation) and reactions to physical pain share the same hardware begins to suggest why, once loneliness becomes chronic, you cannot escape it merely by 'coming out of your shell,' losing weight, getting a fashion makeover, or meeting Mr. or Ms. Right.
findings.where: Chapter 1 'Lonely in a Social World,' pp. 8-9, citing Eisenberger, Lieberman, Williams (2003) 'Does rejection hurt? An fMRI study of social exclusion,' Science 302:290-292

findings.quote: These subcortical brain networks are quite similar in all mammals, but they are not identical in all details. This similarity extends even to certain species of birds that, for instance, also have separation-distress PANIC networks
findings.content: These subcortical brain networks are quite similar in all mammals, but they are not identical in all details. This similarity extends even to certain species of birds that, for instance, also have separation-distress PANIC networks. Across many species of warm-blooded vertebrates, a variety of basic emotional networks are anatomically situated in similar brain regions, and these networks serve remarkably similar functions.

findings.quote: Current neurobehavioral evidence indicates that there are at least four executive circuits of this type -- those which elaborate central states of expectancy, rage, fear, and panic.
findings.content: Four primary emotional executive circuits identified via electrical brain stimulation: expectancy (later renamed SEEKING), rage, fear, and panic. Each is a transhypothalamic command circuit that concurrently activates behavioral action patterns, physiological responses, and subjective states. These circuits developed early in mammalian brain evolution and the underlying control mechanisms remain similar across species.

findings.quote: The wire mother is biologically adequate but psychologically inept.
findings.content: Cloth mother serves as secure base for exploration. When frightened by novel stimuli, infants consistently fled to cloth mother regardless of food source. In open-field tests with cloth mother present, emotionality scores reduced by half. Without any mother, infants froze in crouched positions. Wire mother provided zero comfort function in any fear test.

findings.quote: Through prediction, your brain constructs the world you experience. It combines bits and pieces of your past and estimates how likely each bit applies in your current situation.
findings.content: The brain constructs the world you experience through prediction. Intrinsic brain activity - millions of nonstop predictions - is the brain's primary mode of operation. Past experience, organized as concepts, generates predictions that are tested against incoming sensory input. Events in the world merely tune these predictions rather than triggering responses. Evolution literally wired the brain for efficient prediction: 90 percent of connections entering primary visual cortex carry predictions from other brain regions, not sensory input from the world.

findings.quote: glucocorticoids decrease activation of the (cognitive) medial PFC during processing of emotional faces. Collectively, stress or glucocorticoid administration decreases accuracy when rapidly assessing emotions of faces.
findings.content: Chronic stress literally eats away at interoceptive and control networks. It causes the amygdala to expand while the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex atrophy. Glucocorticoids decrease activation of the cognitive medial PFC during emotional processing, decreasing accuracy when rapidly assessing emotions. During sustained stress, the systems that should regulate the stress response are themselves damaged by the stress response - a vicious cycle of worsening misregulation.

findings.quote: This domain of epigenetics was uncovered in a landmark 2004 study by Meaney and colleagues, one of the most cited papers published in the prestigious journal Nature Neuroscience. They had shown previously that offspring of more "attentive" rat mothers (those that frequently nurse, groom, and lick their pups) become adults with lower glucocorticoid levels, less anxiety, better learning, and delayed brain aging.
findings.content: Meaney's landmark 2004 study demonstrated that maternal care style in rats produces epigenetic changes in offspring's stress response genes. Offspring of more attentive mothers (frequent nursing, grooming, licking) become adults with lower glucocorticoid levels, less anxiety, better learning, and delayed brain aging. These changes are epigenetic - mothering style alters gene regulation in pups' brains. Remarkably, such pups as adults become more attentive mothers themselves, passing the trait epigenetically to the next generation.

findings.quote: Childhood abuse, for example, causes epigenetic changes in hundreds of genes in the human hippocampus. Moreover, Stephen Suomi of the National Institutes of Health and Szyf found that mothering style in monkeys has epigenetic effects on more than a thousand frontocortical genes.
findings.content: Childhood abuse causes epigenetic changes in hundreds of genes in the human hippocampus. Mothering style in monkeys has epigenetic effects on more than a thousand frontocortical genes. Hormonal responses to fetal and childhood experiences have epigenetic effects on genes related to BDNF, the vasopressin and oxytocin system, and estrogen sensitivity, with effects pertinent to adult cognition, personality, emotionality, and psychiatric health.

findings.quote: an epigenomic state of a gene can be established through behavioral programming, and it is potentially reversible.
findings.content: Maternal licking/grooming and arched-back nursing in rats alters offspring epigenome at the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) gene promoter in the hippocampus via DNA methylation and histone acetylation changes. Offspring of high-LG mothers have lower glucocorticoid levels, less anxiety, better learning, and delayed brain aging. Methylation differences emerged over the first week of life, were reversed with cross-fostering, and persisted into adulthood. Central infusion of a histone deacetylase inhibitor removed group differences - demonstrating that an epigenomic state established through behavioral programming is potentially reversible.

findings.quote: The troop's social culture was being transmitted.
findings.content: After a tuberculosis outbreak eliminated the most aggressive adult males from a baboon troop, the remaining troop - now with a 2:1 female-to-male ratio and disproportionately unaggressive and affiliative males - stayed close together, sat in contact, and groomed more than average. Levels of aggression were lower, and in an informative way: males still had a dominance hierarchy and fought with their rivals, but there was minimal displacement aggression onto innocent bystanders. Stress hormone levels were low; the neurochemistry of anxiety and benzodiazepines worked differently in these individuals. When male adolescents transferred in from other troops over the following years - having grown up in typical aggressive troops - they adopted the style of low aggression and high affiliation. The troop's social culture was being transmitted.
findings.where: Behave, Chapter 9, the Forest Troop narrative, pp. ~418-420 (ref Sapolsky & Share 2004)

findings.quote: Brain activations occurred in several regions of the reward system. Included were regions of the ventral tegmental area (VTA) associated with feelings of intense romantic love; the ventral pallidum, associated with feelings of deep attachment; the insular cortex and the anterior cingulate, associated with physical pain, anxiety, and the distress associated with physical pain; and the nucleus accumbens and orbitofrontal/prefrontal cortex, brain regions associated with assessing one's gains and losses - as well as craving and addiction. Most relevant to our story, activity in several of these brain regions has been correlated with the craving for cocaine and other drugs.
findings.content: When my colleagues redid the brain scanning experiment to look at rejection, we found that feelings of romantic rejection lit up activity in several brain regions linked with profound attachment, deep addiction, and physical pain. When you are rejected in love, many brain systems go to work, and rejection is one of the most painful experiences a human being can endure.
findings.where: Chapter 5 'Blueprint for Divorce' pp. 127-128, Fisher/Brown rejection fMRI study

findings.quote: During it the young child appears acutely distressed at having lost his mother and seeks to recapture her by the full exercise of his limited resources. He will often cry loudly, shake his cot, throw himself about, and look eagerly towards any sight or sound which might prove to be his missing mother.
findings.content: Bowlby's three-phase separation response in young children: protest (acute distress, crying, seeking the missing mother), despair (increasing hopelessness, withdrawal, deep mourning), and detachment (apparent recovery that masks emotional disengagement). The protest phase involves active attempts to recapture the mother; despair involves withdrawal and monotonous crying; detachment involves accepting care from others while showing striking absence of attachment behavior toward the mother on her return.

findings.quote: When we artificially activate brain emotion-behavior generating circuits, animals rapidly learn to turn off ESB that evokes fear- and anger-type responses, and they turn on brain stimulation that generates playful sounds, exploration, sexual eagerness and maternal care.
findings.content: Electrical brain stimulation (ESB) of specific subcortical regions produces coherent emotional behaviors in all mammals tested. Animals given control over ESB self-select: they turn off stimulation evoking fear/anger responses and turn on stimulation generating playful sounds, exploration, sexual eagerness, and maternal care. This reward/punishment valence demonstrates genuine affective experience, not mere behavioral reflexes.

findings.quote: the ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven emotional, or affective, systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy). Each of these systems controls distinct but specific types of behaviors associated with many overlapping physiological changes.
findings.content: The ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven emotional systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy). Each controls distinct behaviors with overlapping physiological changes and generates distinct types of affective consciousness. When stimulated in humans, people always experience intense emotional feelings. Capitalizations indicate that real physical and distinct networks for these emotions exist in mammalian brains.

findings.quote: primal emotional systems are made up of neuroanatomies and neurochemistries that are remarkably similar across all mammalian species. This suggests that these systems evolved a very long time ago and that at a basic emotional and motivational level, all mammals are more similar than they are different.
findings.content: Primal emotional systems are made up of neuroanatomies and neurochemistries remarkably similar across all mammalian species. This suggests these systems evolved a very long time ago and that at a basic emotional and motivational level, all mammals are more similar than different. Deep in the ancient affective recesses of our brains, we remain evolutionarily kin. The same neural paths and brain chemicals that arouse each of these seven systems are found within all mammals.

findings.quote: FEAR is an inborn capacity of the mammalian brain. However, FEAR, just like all other basic emotions, rapidly gets enmeshed with world events as it comes to be regulated by learning and encoded in our conscious minds.
findings.content: FEAR is an inborn capacity of the mammalian brain that rapidly gets enmeshed with world events through learning. Most basic emotions need not be expressed immediately after birth. Some - including CARE, LUST, and PLAY - come online long after others such as SEEKING, RAGE, and FEAR. The developmental timing reflects phylogenetic priority: the oldest and most survival-critical systems activate earliest.

Panksepp's textbook Affective Neuroscience establishes the methodology and evidence base for the seven subcortical affective systems. Across cross-species deep brain stimulation, lesion, and pharmacological studies, the same brain regions produce the same functional categories of affective response - SEEKING, FEAR, RAGE, LUST, CARE, PANIC, PLAY - across mammals, providing the empirical foundation for treating these as conserved motivational architecture rather than culturally constructed categories.

findings.quote: We found a graded relationship between the number of categories of childhood exposure and each of the adult health risk behaviors and diseases that were studied.
findings.content: The ACE Study (9,508 respondents) demonstrated a graded dose-response relationship between categories of childhood adversity (psychological abuse, physical abuse, sexual abuse, violence against mother, household substance abuse, mental illness, incarceration) and adult health outcomes. Persons with 4+ ACE categories had 4-12 fold increased risk for alcoholism, drug abuse, depression, and suicide attempts; 2-4 fold increased risk for smoking, poor health, STDs; 1.4-1.6 fold for inactivity and obesity. More than half of respondents reported at least one category. Adult diseases linked included ischemic heart disease, cancer, chronic lung disease, skeletal fractures, and liver disease.

findings.quote: people move their facial muscles in many different ways, not one consistent way, when feeling an instance of the same emotion category. Large meta-analyses conclude that a single emotion category involves different bodily responses, not a single, consistent response. Brain circuitry operates by the many-to-one principle of degeneracy: instances of a single emotion category, such as fear, are handled by different brain patterns at different times and in different people. Conversely, the same neurons can participate in creating different mental states (one-to-many).
findings.content: Barrett's comprehensive meta-analysis of brain-imaging, facial EMG, and autonomic nervous system studies finds no consistent physical fingerprint for any single emotion. Facial muscles move in many different ways for the same emotion category. Bodily responses vary across instances. Brain circuitry operates by degeneracy (many-to-one: different neural patterns produce the same emotion category) and core systems (one-to-many: the same neurons participate in different mental states). Variation, not uniformity, is the norm across all three measurement domains.

findings.quote: It has become increasingly clear during the past half century that primary-process affective mechanisms are concentrated in ancient subcortical midline brain regions that are anatomically and neurochemically, and hence, evolutionarily, similar in all mammalian species.
findings.content: Seven distinct emotional systems identified with specific neuroanatomy and neurochemistry: SEEKING (VTA/NAcc/lateral hypothalamus, DA+), RAGE (medial amygdala→BNST→hypothalamus→PAG, substance P+), FEAR (central amygdala→hypothalamus→dorsal PAG, glutamate+/CRF+), LUST (cortico-medial amygdala/BNST/preoptic, steroids+), CARE (anterior cingulate/BNST/preoptic/VTA, oxytocin+/prolactin+), PANIC (anterior cingulate/BNST/dorsomedial thalamus/PAG, opioids−/oxytocin−/CRF+), PLAY (dorsomedial diencephalon/parafascicular/PAG, opioids+/−). Each mapped in Fig. 2 with specific neurochemical modulators.
findings.where: Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews 35(9):1791-1804, p. 1795, Fig. 2. DOI: 10.1016/j.neubiorev.2011.08.003

findings.quote: Never have such profound emotional states been provoked by stimulating neocortical regions.
findings.content: All seven emotional systems survive radical neo-decortication (complete surgical removal of the cerebral cortex). Decorticate animals retain all emotional-instinctual urges intact, though their capacity to learn new instrumental behaviors is severely impaired. ESB of subcortical regions in humans produces intense affective experiences; neocortical stimulation never produces such emotional states.

findings.quote: These criteria have been fulfilled or approximated for a variety of brain systems that exist in all mammals studied so far.
findings.content: Three empirical criteria for determining existence of emotional feelings in animals, all fulfilled: (1) neural circuits must exist that activate coherent emotional behaviors, (2) artificial arousal of such systems must generate conditioned approach/escape/avoidance, (3) key neurochemistries and brain activation patterns must correlate with predicted affective changes in humans. These criteria have been fulfilled for multiple brain systems across all mammals studied.

Three convergent lines of evidence demonstrate subcortical affective states: (i) mammals are attracted to the same environmental rewards and drugs of abuse as humans; (ii) human emotional feelings depend on subcortical brain systems where evolutionarily homologous instinctual neural systems exist; (iii) artificial activations of deep brain emotional systems are liked and disliked by animals, as measured by approach and avoidance measures.

findings.quote: Most of the responses that cause human suffering are unnecessary in the individual instance but still perfectly normal because they have low costs but protect against huge possible losses. They are like false alarms from smoke detectors.
findings.content: Most of the responses that cause human suffering are unnecessary in the individual instance but still perfectly normal because they have low costs but protect against huge possible losses. They are like false alarms from smoke detectors. Systems that regulate protective responses such as vomiting and pain turn the response on whenever the benefits are greater than the costs, even if that means false alarms.
findings.where: Chapter 3, 'Why Are Minds So Vulnerable?' and Chapter 5, pp. 40-41 and pp. 73-74

findings.quote: The cost of not fleeing if the lion is present is 1,000 times greater than the cost of a panic attack, so the optimal strategy is to run like hell whenever the sound is loud enough to indicate a lion is present with a probability greater than 1/1,000.
findings.content: The cost of not fleeing if the lion is present is 1,000 times greater than the cost of a panic attack, so the optimal strategy is to run like hell whenever the sound is loud enough to indicate a lion is present with a probability greater than 1/1,000. This means that 999 times out of 1,000 you will flee unnecessarily. However, 1 time out of 1,000, fleeing will save your life.

findings.quote: the Smoke Detector Principle. Most of the responses that cause human suffering are unnecessary in the individual instance but still perfectly normal because they have low costs but protect against huge possible losses. They are like false alarms from smoke detectors. The occasional wail when you burn the toast is worth it to ensure that you are warned
findings.content: The Smoke Detector Principle: most defensive responses that cause human suffering are unnecessary in the individual instance but perfectly normal because they have low costs but protect against huge possible losses. They are like false alarms from smoke detectors - the occasional wail when you burn toast is worth it to ensure warning about every real fire. This explains why it is usually safe to use drugs to block vomiting and pain - most instances are false alarms.

findings.quote: systems that regulate protective responses such as vomiting and pain turn the response on whenever the benefits are greater than the costs, even if that means false alarms. The costs of such responses tend to be low compared to the benefits of avoiding danger. So when danger may or may not be present, the small cost of a response ensures protection against a much larger harm. That is why we put up with false alarms from smoke detectors. It is why we can safely use medications to block responses such as vomiting and pain. And it is why useless anxiety is so common.
findings.content: The Smoke Detector Principle explains why useless anxiety is so common. Systems that regulate protective responses turn the response on whenever the benefits are greater than the costs, even if that means false alarms. The costs of such responses tend to be low compared to the benefits of avoiding danger, so when danger may or may not be present, the small cost of a response ensures protection against a much larger harm.

findings.quote: Panic disorder is caused by false alarms in the emergency response system. The system has been honed to speed escape when life-threatening danger may be present. You are thirsty on the ancient African savanna and a watering hole is just ahead, but you hear a noise in the grass. It could be a lion, or it might just be a monkey. Should you flee?
findings.content: Panic disorder is caused by false alarms in the emergency response system. The system has been honed to speed escape when life-threatening danger may be present. On the ancient African savanna, a noise near a watering hole could be a lion or a monkey - the expected cost calculation (100 calories for fleeing vs. death for not fleeing when it IS a lion) means panic should be triggered whenever the probability of danger exceeds a tiny threshold. This cost asymmetry explains why panic attacks occur in objectively safe modern environments.

findings.quote: Out of 1000 episodes of flight at this response threshold, on the average, 999 will be false alarms and only 1 will be flight from an actual predator.
findings.content: The smoke detector principle formalized via signal detection theory. For all-or-none defenses, expression is optimal whenever p(Harm) > Cost_defense/Cost_harm. With a 1000:1 cost ratio (300 kcal flight vs 300,000 kcal predator attack), the optimal threshold produces 999 false alarms per 1 genuine escape. These false alarms are completely normal products of an optimal system, not dysfunction.
findings.where: Evolution and Human Behavior 26(1):88-105. DOI: 10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2004.08.002. Full text via UMich PDF.

findings.quote: I, and others, have called the brain system that detects and responds to threats the fear system. This was a mistake that has led to much confusion.
findings.content: LeDoux revises his terminology: calling the threat-detection system a fear system was a mistake that led to confusion, because people assume a fear system produces conscious fear. He now distinguishes defensive survival circuits (subcortical, nonconscious, conserved across vertebrates with invertebrate analogues) from conscious fear (a cognitive construction arising from multiple neural ingredients).

findings.quote: The feeling of fear occurs in the same way as the feeling of compassion or pride--through cognitive processing of neural raw materials.
findings.content: Fear as cognitive construction: conscious fear emerges from multiple neural ingredients (survival circuit activation, brain arousal, body feedback, memories, predictions) much as a soup's character emerges from raw materials. Some fears involve no survival circuit activation (social anxiety, existential concerns). Proposed terminology: replace fear conditioning with threat conditioning, fear system with defensive survival circuit, restrict fear exclusively to conscious experience.

findings.quote: Many of our current health problems result from the environments we have created to satisfy our desires. Most people in developed societies live better now physically than the kings and queens of just a century ago. We have a surfeit of delicious food, protection from the elements, time for leisure, and relief from pain. These accomplishments are spectacular, but they also cause most chronic disease.
findings.content: Many current health problems result from environments created to satisfy our desires. Most people in developed societies live better physically than kings and queens of a century ago - surfeit of delicious food, protection from elements, leisure time, relief from pain. These accomplishments are spectacular but they also cause most chronic disease. The mismatch between our evolved bodies and the environments we have created is a major source of illness.

findings.quote: these affective substrates are "archaeological treasures" - multi-faceted "jewels" of mind that embody our capacity for affective experience, a capacity that we still share with our animal cousins.
findings.content: These affective substrates are archaeological treasures - multi-faceted jewels of mind that embody our capacity for affective experience, a capacity we still share with our animal cousins. However, as humans, we have higher brain expansions that allow us to think deeply about our nature and our options to live more cerebrally, culturally, and creatively. We can bite our tongues when angry, but many choose not to.

findings.quote: You may suddenly hear with far greater clarity sounds that bear on the hypothesis that you are being stalked, but that ordinarily you would not perceive or attend to, such as creaks or rustling
findings.content: Fear example: when sensing a stalker, the emotion simultaneously (a) shifts perception to hear threat-relevant sounds with greater clarity, (b) reprioritizes goals so safety overrides all else, (c) triggers physiological preparation - dry mouth (digestion shutdown), blood to lower body, expanded visual field, increased breathing, (d) retrieves threat-relevant memories. Internal regulatory variables (IRVs) set thresholds, adjust weights, and calibrate responses across all these systems simultaneously.
findings.where: Handbook of Emotions 3rd ed (2008), pp. 114-137, fear example

findings.quote: Individuals who experience a panic attack react as if they had encountered a real danger, subsequently becoming not only more cautious but also more susceptible to additional attacks.
findings.content: Repeated danger exposure may adaptively lower response thresholds, creating vulnerability to runaway positive feedback. Panic disorder exemplifies this: individuals experiencing a panic attack react as if they encountered real danger, becoming more cautious and more susceptible to additional attacks. The clinical condition is an extreme of normal threshold-lowering, not a qualitatively different pathology.
findings.where: Evolution and Human Behavior 26(1):88-105, threshold dynamics section. Full text.

findings.quote: the hidden cost of chronic stress to the body over long time periods, which act as a predisposing factor for the effects of acute, stressful life events.
findings.content: Individual susceptibility to allostatic load is shaped by behavioral responses coupled to physiologic and pathophysiologic changes beginning early in life. The allostasis framework replaces the static homeostasis model with a dynamic model where the body actively adjusts to anticipated demands - but this adjustment has a cumulative cost when chronically activated. The predisposing-factor model explains why the same acute stressor produces different health outcomes in different individuals.

findings.quote: An evolutionary view explains why we have desires, why we can't satisfy them, and why it is so hard to set them aside: our brains were shaped to benefit our genes, not us.
findings.content: An evolutionary view explains why we have desires, why we cannot satisfy them, and why it is so hard to set them aside: our brains were shaped to benefit our genes, not us. Most suffering is emotional suffering. Anxiety and low mood exist for the same reason as pain and nausea - because they are useful in certain situations. They are often excessive for good evolutionary reasons.

findings.quote: The core problem for psychiatric diagnosis is the lack of a perspective on normal useful functions that physiology provides for the rest of medicine. Internal medicine doctors know the functions of the kidneys. They don't confuse protective defenses such as cough and pain with diseases such as pneumonia and cancer. Psychiatrists lack a similar framework for the utility of stress, sleep, anxiety, and mood, so psychiatric diagnostic categories remain confusing and crude.
findings.content: The core problem for psychiatric diagnosis is the lack of a perspective on normal useful functions that physiology provides for the rest of medicine. Internal medicine doctors know kidney functions and do not confuse protective defenses (cough, pain) with diseases (pneumonia, cancer). Psychiatrists lack a similar framework for the utility of stress, sleep, anxiety, and mood, so diagnostic categories remain confusing and crude. Anxiety and low mood are useful normal responses - it is time to give up the fantasy that each mental disorder has a specific cause.

findings.quote: Nearly everyone has wondered why human life is so full of suffering. Part of an answer is that natural selection shaped emotions such as anxiety, low mood, and grief because they are useful. More of an answer comes from recognizing that our suffering often benefits our genes.
findings.content: Natural selection shaped emotions such as anxiety, low mood, and grief because they are useful. More of an answer to why life is full of suffering comes from recognizing that our suffering often benefits our genes. Nearly everyone has wondered why human life is so full of suffering - an evolutionary perspective provides the first satisfying scientific explanation.

findings.quote: There are good reasons for bad feelings. Anxiety and depression are often excessive because they benefit genes at our expense, because of the Smoke Detector Principle, because we live in modern environments, and because regulation mechanisms are intrinsically vulnerable.
findings.content: Nesse's resolution: there are good reasons for bad feelings. Anxiety and depression are often excessive because (1) they benefit genes at our expense, (2) the Smoke Detector Principle, (3) we live in modern environments, and (4) regulation mechanisms are intrinsically vulnerable. Some disorders have specific brain causes; others are syndromes like kidney failure with many possible causes. Top-down and bottom-up causes interact to create tangled webs - this is not confusion, it is reality.

findings.quote: Simple pleasant and unpleasant feelings come from an ongoing process inside you called interoception. Interoception is your brain's representation of all sensations from your internal organs and tissues, the hormones in your blood, and your immune system. Think about what's happening within your body right this second. Your insides are in motion. Your heart sends blood rushing through your veins and arteries. Your lungs fill and empty. Your stomach digests food. This interoceptive activity produces the spectrum of basic feeling from pleasant to unpleasant, from calm to jittery, and even completely neutral.
findings.content: Interoception - the brain's representation of all sensations from internal organs, tissues, hormones, and the immune system - produces the spectrum of basic feeling from pleasant to unpleasant, calm to jittery. Interoception is a core ingredient of emotion, but these feelings are simpler than full-blown emotional experiences. The brain uses interoceptive predictions to regulate the body budget (allostasis) and creates meaning from these sensations via concepts.

findings.quote: stress doesn't come from the outside world. You construct it.
findings.content: Stress is constructed via the same brain mechanisms that construct emotion. In both cases the brain issues predictions about the body budget in relation to the outside world and makes meaning via concepts. The interoceptive network and the control network play the same roles in stress and emotion construction. The ascending and descending pathways between brain and body are identical. What differs is the end result - whether the brain categorizes sensations as stressful or emotional.

findings.quote: the cost of chronic exposure to fluctuating or heightened neural or neuroendocrine response resulting from repeated or chronic environmental challenge.
findings.content: Allostatic load is the cost of chronic exposure to fluctuating or heightened neural or neuroendocrine response resulting from repeated or chronic environmental challenge. Rather than maintaining constant internal conditions (homeostasis), physiologic systems fluctuate to meet demands from external forces - a state termed allostasis. The hidden cost of chronic stress accumulates over long time periods, acting as a predisposing factor for the effects of acute stressful life events.

findings.quote: there is good evidence, derived from observations of many species of bird and mammal, that an isolated animal is much more likely to be attacked and seized by a predator than is an animal that stays bunched together with others of its kind. Secondly, attachment behaviour is elicited particularly easily and intensely in animals which, by reason of age, size, or condition, are especially vulnerable to predators, for example the young, pregnant females, the sick. Thirdly, attachment behaviour is always elicited at high intensity in situations of alarm, which are commonly situations when a predator is either sensed or suspected. No other theory fits these facts.
findings.content: The biological function of attachment behavior is protection from predators. Three facts support this: (1) isolated animals are much more likely to be attacked by predators than animals that stay with others; (2) attachment behavior is most easily and intensely elicited in individuals especially vulnerable to predators - the young, pregnant females, the sick; (3) attachment behavior is always elicited at high intensity in situations of alarm when a predator is sensed or suspected. The paradoxical finding that punishment strengthens rather than weakens attachment is explained by this anti-predator function.

findings.quote: close study of IRMs reveals the remarkable fact that it is sometimes possible to offer stimulus situations that are even more effective than the natural situation. In other words, the natural situation is not always optimal.
findings.content: Close study of innate releasing mechanisms reveals the remarkable fact that it is sometimes possible to offer stimulus situations that are even more effective than the natural situation. In other words, the natural situation is not always optimal. This is the phenomenon of supernormal sign stimuli - an evolved response fires harder in reaction to an exaggerated artificial stimulus than to the natural cue it was shaped to detect.
findings.where: Chapter III, 'Behaviour as a Reaction to External Stimuli,' section 'Supernormal sign stimuli,' pp. 44-46

findings.content: Error Management Theory (EMT): when the costs of false-positive and false-negative errors were asymmetric over evolutionary history, selection favors psychological mechanisms that are predictably biased in the direction that minimizes the more costly error - not mechanisms that minimize total errors or achieve Bayesian optimality. This is a domain-specific alternative to the heuristics-and-biases program: biases are not cognitive flaws but adaptive design features. Haselton and Buss formalize: a mechanism will be biased toward the less costly error type whenever the cost asymmetry persisted recurrently in ancestral environments.

findings.quote: Allostatic load (AL) represents the 'wear and tear' the body experiences when repeated allostatic responses are activated during stressful situations (McEwen and Stellar, 1993)... While adaptive acutely, chronic over-activation of SAM- and HPA-axis products induce a 'domino effect' on interconnected biological systems that overcompensate and eventually collapse themselves, leaving the organism susceptible to stress-related diseases.
findings.content: Allostatic load represents the 'wear and tear' the body experiences when repeated allostatic responses are activated during stressful situations. While adaptive acutely, chronic over-activation of sympathetic-adrenal-medullary and HPA-axis products induce a 'domino effect' on interconnected biological systems that overcompensate and eventually collapse themselves, leaving the organism susceptible to stress-related diseases. Brain changes associated with chronic stress and allostatic load - synaptic and dendritic remodeling, suppressed neurogenesis, structural atrophy/hypertrophy - further diminish the body's ability to cognitively process and physiologically respond to stressors.

findings.quote: Many inputs now differ in quantity and intensity or no longer have the same fitness associations, thereby leading many mechanisms to produce maladaptive output.
findings.content: The mismatch framework has implications for public policy. Li et al. present specific examples: (1) despite modern sanitation benefits, immune systems evolved to be stimulated by bacterial exposure in infancy - overuse of antibacterial products may contribute to childhood asthma, allergies, and ear infections; (2) ecological conservation efforts have met limited success because conservation behavior is evolutionarily novel - humans evolved to consume local resources without concern when pollutant output was low and migration was feasible. Effective interventions should work with, rather than oppose, evolved tendencies such as self-interest, social status concerns, social imitation, and future discounting.
findings.where: Current Directions in Psychological Science 27(1):38-44, 2018. DOI: 10.1177/0963721417731378

findings.quote: My view is that some major illnesses considered distinct and "mental" are all rooted in a chronically unbalanced body budget and unbridled inflammation. We categorize and name them as different disorders, based on context, much like we categorize and name the same bodily changes as different emotions.
findings.content: Barrett proposes that major illnesses considered distinct and mental - chronic stress, chronic pain, anxiety, depression - are all rooted in a chronically unbalanced body budget and unbridled inflammation. Different disorders share symptoms, cause atrophy in the same brain regions, their sufferers exhibit low emotional granularity, and the same medications are prescribed across disorders. These illnesses do not have firm boundaries in nature; like emotions, they are constructed categories applied to the same highly variable biological processes.

findings.quote: SBT suggests the human brain expects access to social relationships that mitigate risk and diminish the level of effort needed to meet a variety of goals.
findings.content: Social Baseline Theory: the human brain expects access to social relationships that mitigate risk and diminish the level of effort needed to meet goals. Social and metabolic resources are treated almost interchangeably by the brain - isolation is processed as resource scarcity. Violations of the social proximity expectation increase cognitive and physiological effort as the brain perceives fewer available resources.

findings.quote: Humans evolved to be prone to obesity not because excess fat makes us healthy, but because it increases fertility. Along the same lines, our species' proclivities to be worried, anxious, and stressed cause much misery and unhappiness, but they are ancient adaptations to avoid or cope with danger.
findings.content: Humans evolved to be prone to obesity not because excess fat makes us healthy but because it increases fertility. Anxiety, worry, and stress cause misery and unhappiness but they are ancient adaptations to avoid or cope with danger. The mismatch hypothesis - that human bodies were adapted for very different conditions - is the core of evolutionary medicine.

findings.quote: psychological mechanisms are designed to be predictably biased when the costs of false-positive and false-negative errors were asymmetrical over evolutionary history.
findings.content: Error Management Theory (EMT): psychological mechanisms are designed to be predictably biased when the costs of false-positive and false-negative errors were asymmetrical over evolutionary history. Men's sexual overperception bias (overestimating women's sexual interest) and women's commitment underperception bias (underestimating men's commitment) are adaptive biases shaped by asymmetric error costs. EMT offers a systematic framework for predicting cognitive biases from ancestral cost asymmetries.

findings.quote: The major emotional operating systems are defined primarily by genetically coded neural circuits that generate well-organized behavior sequences that can be evoked by localized electrical stimulation of the brain. Representative behaviors generated by the various systems are indicated, and the approximate locations of the SEEKING, FEAR, and RAGE systems are depicted on a small frontal section through one side of the hypothalamus.
findings.content: Panksepp's historical contribution: in his 1982 paper he first distinguished four primary emotional command systems that are organized along discrete but interacting subcortical trajectories (mostly following the medial forebrain bundle). These are depicted in Figure 3.5 (original paper) with approximate anatomical locations for SEEKING, FEAR, and RAGE in the hypothalamus and their interconnections. The 1982 framework was the foundational statement of affective neuroscience as a research program distinct from behavioral or cognitive approaches. This is primary-source citation for the architectural claim that mammalian emotions are subcortically organized, not cortically derived.

findings.quote: emotional responses are dependent on the activation of the amygdala, and, as we discussed in chapter 3, the amygdala is likely crucial to ensuring playful reciprocity. The prefrontal cortex dampens the activity of the amygdala, which thus prevents emotional overreaction. Here is a potential mechanism by which experience with play fighting in the juvenile period refines the prefrontal circuits, and, in doing so, produces animals that are better able to regulate their subcortically generated emotions.
findings.content: Pellis's causal-mechanism proposal: play fighting in the juvenile period refines prefrontal circuits that dampen amygdala activity, which in turn prevents emotional overreaction in adult social situations. The amygdala is load-bearing for emotional-response generation (including the emotional content of play reciprocity), and the PFC dampens the amygdala - so play-induced PFC refinement is how juveniles develop adult emotional regulation.
findings.where: Chapter 4 'So, What Does Playing Buy You?' pp. ~93

findings.quote: For creatures shaped by evolution to feel safe in company and endangered when unwillingly alone, feelings of isolation and perceptions of threat reinforce each other to promote a higher and more persistent level of wariness. To prepare us to react efficiently when confronting threats to life and limb, nature provided us with the ability to be cognitively hypervigilant, along with a chain of physiological reactions known as the fight-or-flight response. But the neurological wiring we depend on today evolved in response to the kinds of hit-and-run stressors we faced millions of years ago. As a result, our stress response ('fight or flight') includes a prompt to immediate action that increases resistance in the cardiovascular system and floods the body with hormones that rev us up. If we were fending off wild dogs, those hormones could help save our lives. However, when our stressors consist of feeling isolated and unloved, the constant presence of these excitatory chemicals acts as a corrosive force that accelerates the aging process.
findings.content: For creatures shaped by evolution to feel safe in company and endangered when unwillingly alone, feelings of isolation and perceptions of threat reinforce each other to promote a higher and more persistent level of wariness. To prepare us to react efficiently when confronting threats to life and limb, nature provided us with the ability to be cognitively hypervigilant, along with a chain of physiological reactions known as the fight-or-flight response. But the neurological wiring we depend on today evolved in response to the kinds of hit-and-run stressors we faced millions of years ago. When our stressors consist of feeling isolated and unloved, the constant presence of these excitatory chemicals acts as a corrosive force.
findings.where: Chapter 2 'Variation, Regulation, and an Elastic Leash,' pp. 31-32

findings.quote: In contemporary society, as we've noted, most of our stressors do not come and go in the kind of short, life-or-death confrontations that drove the evolution of 'fight or flight.' We can have the same overbearing boss, the same long commute, the same worries about health care and retirement, and the same feelings of social isolation, hour after hour, year after year. Moreover, we now experience these persistent stressors over a life span that, on average, extends well beyond what was the norm during all but the last few centuries of our species' existence. The environment is entirely different now than it was in our environment of evolutionary adaptation
findings.content: Human stressors no longer come and go in the kind of short, life-or-death confrontations that drove the evolution of fight-or-flight. We can have the same overbearing boss, the same long commute, the same worries about health care and retirement, and the same feelings of social isolation, hour after hour, year after year. Moreover, we now experience these persistent stressors over a life span that, on average, extends well beyond what was the norm during all but the last few centuries of our species' existence. The environment is entirely different now than it was in our environment of evolutionary adaptation, but our sympathetic / parasympathetic architecture has not changed.
findings.where: Chapter 6 'The Wear and Tear of Loneliness,' pp. 103-104

findings.quote: In case it needs re-emphasis, we are not monkeys or even apes. We should not look to them, necessarily, to understand how people behave in the workplace, in the benefits office, on the local council, or the church committee. What these animal studies, from lab and field, give us are biologically plausible ways that social experience can be translated, via biological stress pathways, into disease.
findings.content: Animal studies, from lab and field, give us biologically plausible ways that social experience can be translated, via biological stress pathways, into disease. In case it needs re-emphasis, we are not monkeys or even apes - but the physiological stress response is similar in many different species. The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis that puts out cortisol operates similarly across mammals, and chronic activation of this system has systemic health consequences regardless of species.
findings.where: Chapter 4 'Stress in the Jungle? Stress in the Office?' pp. 115-116

findings.quote: Shame and humiliation are associated with attacks on, and losses of, social attractiveness.
findings.content: Social rank theory: humans evolved in social hierarchies where status determined access to resources and mates. Involuntary defeat strategy (IDS) is an evolved defensive response to status loss - when an organism loses rank and cannot escape, IDS produces behavioral inhibition, withdrawal, submissive signaling, and depressed mood. Depression in modern humans may reflect chronic activation of IDS in environments where status threats are persistent but escape or resolution is impossible.
findings.where: Br J Med Psychol 70(2):113-147, 1997. PMID: 9210990. Social rank and IDS sections.

findings.quote: People seek help mainly for symptoms, not diseases. Pain, fever, malaise, cough, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are protective responses. So are anxiety, jealousy, anger, and low mood. They are set off when something bad is happening. They are unpleasant but useful.
findings.content: Defensive responses such as pain, fever, cough, nausea, anxiety, jealousy, anger, and low mood are protective responses, not diseases. They are set off when something bad is happening. They are unpleasant but useful.

findings.quote: Organisms try to get sex, power, and resources and to avoid danger and loss. Pursuing these goals gives rise to a set of defined situations. Each one poses different adaptive challenges that shape a different emotional state. Opportunity arouses enthusiasm. Success arouses joy. Threat arouses anxiety. Loss arouses sadness.
findings.content: Four situations that arise in goal pursuit map to four emotions: opportunity arouses enthusiasm, success arouses joy, threat arouses anxiety, loss arouses sadness. Organisms try to get sex, power, and resources and to avoid danger and loss. Each situation poses different adaptive challenges that shape a different emotional state. The scheme can be expanded by adding emotions for alternative outcomes - disappointment when pursuit fails, relief when threat is avoided.

findings.quote: Why is this relevant to emotion? Because every brain region that's claimed to be a home of emotion in humans is a body-budgeting region within the interoceptive network. These regions, however, don't react in emotion. They don't react at all. They predict, intrinsically, to regulate your body budget. They issue predictions for sights, sounds, thoughts, memories, imagination, and, yes, emotions. The idea of an emotional brain region is an illusion caused by the outdated belief in a reactive brain. Neuroscientists understand this today, but the message hasn't trickled down to many psychologists, psychiatrists, sociologists, economists, and others who study emotion.
findings.content: Every brain region historically claimed as a home of emotion is actually a body-budgeting region within the interoceptive network. These regions do not react in emotion - they predict intrinsically to regulate the body budget, issuing predictions for sights, sounds, thoughts, memories, imagination, and emotions. The notion of a dedicated emotional brain region is an illusion caused by the outdated belief in a reactive brain.

findings.quote: Cumulative imbalance in the body budget - say, from growing up in adversity, where you don't feel safe or are deprived of basic necessities like nutritious food, quiet time to sleep, and so on - also changes the structure of your interoceptive network, rewiring your brain and reducing its ability to accurately regulate your body budget. All it takes are a couple of highly negative experiences for children to feel like they are living in a combat zone, reducing the size of their body-budgeting regions by the time they reach adulthood.
findings.content: Cumulative body-budget imbalance from growing up in adversity - without safety, nutritious food, or quiet time to sleep - changes the structure of the interoceptive network, rewiring the brain and reducing its ability to regulate the body budget. A couple of highly negative childhood experiences can reduce the size of body-budgeting regions by adulthood. Growing up in a harsh or chaotic family, with conflict or verbal criticism, increases inflammation in adolescent girls. Children bullied in childhood show low-grade inflammation persisting into adulthood, predisposing them to psychiatric and physical diseases.

findings.quote: every thought, memory, emotion, or perception that you construct in your life includes something about the state of your body. Your interoceptive network, which regulates your body budget, is launching these cascades. Every prediction you make, and every categorization your brain completes, is always in relation to the activity of your heart and lungs, your metabolism, your immune function, and the other systems that contribute to your body budget.
findings.content: Every thought, memory, emotion, or perception includes something about the state of the body. The interoceptive network, which regulates the body budget, launches the prediction cascades underlying all mental states. Every prediction and categorization occurs in relation to the activity of the heart, lungs, metabolism, immune function, and other body-budget systems. This means no mental state is purely cognitive or purely emotional - all are embodied through interoceptive prediction.

findings.quote: I will speak of these emotional systems in a variety of ways, using designations such as executive, command, and operating systems, to provide nuances of meaning that may be needed to conceptualize their overall functions. The use of the term executive implies that a neural system has a superordinate role in a cascade of hierarchical controls
findings.content: Panksepp's conceptual toolkit for emotional circuits: he calls them 'executive, command, and operating systems' - executive implies a superordinate role in hierarchical controls; command implies the circuit can INSTIGATE a full-blown emotional process (not just correlate with it); operating implies it coordinates and synchronizes multiple subsystems. Together these yield coherent psycho-behavioral and physiological responses that constitute an emotional 'organ system' - an anatomical network of interconnected neurons with endocrine, paracrine, and immune influences. This is the load-bearing architectural framing for why emotional circuits are mechanisms (Cor's M-framework) rather than mere sensorimotor reflexes.

findings.quote: Affective neuroscience has made a fresh start by proceeding from the bottom up, without denigrating our unique human abilities, and it is offering both a new vision of mental origins and new data to back up such assertions.
findings.content: The triangulation approach of affective neuroscience links the affective mind to animal brains by triangulating among (i) subjective mental states (most easily studied in humans), (ii) brain functions (more easily studied in animals), and (iii) natural instinctual emotional behaviors that all young mammals must exhibit early in life to survive. This bottom-up approach offers both a new vision of mental origins and new data.

findings.quote: In addition to the preceding primitive systems that are evident in all mammals soon after birth
findings.content: Panksepp's framework of 4 primary emotional command systems: expectancy/SEEKING, RAGE, FEAR, and separation-distress/PANIC. These are organized along discrete but interacting trajectories in the subcortical brain, largely following the medial forebrain bundle. These 4 systems are 'evident in all mammals soon after birth' - they are not cognitive achievements but mammalian hardware inherited from at least 150 million years of mammalian evolution. This is the central DA8 phylogenetic-priority claim: the affective substrate is ancient, pre-cortical, and conserved across all mammals.

findings.quote: the central concepts are those of behavioural systems and their control, of information, negative feedback, and a behavioural form of homeostasis. The more complex forms of instinctive behaviour are regarded as resulting from the execution of plans that, depending on the species, are more or less flexible.
findings.content: Bowlby's behavioral systems model: instinctive behavior operates through control systems using behavioral homeostasis. The central concepts are behavioral systems and their control, information, negative feedback, and homeostatic regulation. Complex instinctive behavior results from the execution of plans that, depending on species, are more or less flexible. Plan execution is initiated by receipt of information from sense organs and guided by continuous reception of feedback from results of action taken.

findings.quote: I remain convinced that it is useful, at least in the present state of our knowledge, to 'dissect' the master question into three stages.
