findings.content: Tinbergen's four questions framework: the complete study of behavior requires investigating (1) causation (mechanism - what internal and external stimuli trigger the behavior), (2) ontogeny (development - how the behavior develops during the organism's lifetime), (3) survival value (function - what adaptive advantage the behavior confers), and (4) evolution (phylogeny - how the behavior evolved across species). These four levels of analysis are complementary, not competing.

Electronic monitoring and algorithmic management in digital work environments reduce worker decision latitude, triggering M6 controllability failure (learned helplessness default). Combined with status-threat from visible performance metrics and always-on availability expectations activating M1 without resolution, this creates a chronic stress profile consistent with allostatic load accumulation.

findings.quote: Words seed your concepts, concepts drive your predictions, predictions regulate your body budget, and your body budget determines how you feel. Therefore, the more finely grained your vocabulary, the more precisely your predicting brain can calibrate your budget to your body's needs. In fact, people who exhibit higher emotional granularity go to the doctor less frequently, use medication less frequently, and spend fewer days hospitalized for illness.
findings.content: Emotional granularity - the ability to construct finer-grained emotional experiences - has direct health consequences. Words seed concepts, concepts drive predictions, predictions regulate the body budget, and the body budget determines how you feel. The more finely grained the vocabulary, the more precisely the predicting brain can calibrate the body budget to actual needs. People who exhibit higher emotional granularity go to the doctor less frequently, use medication less frequently, and spend fewer days hospitalized for illness.

findings.quote: Attacks from conspecifics (both infanticide and deaths due to lethal raids by bands of males from neighboring groups) are major sources of mortality.
findings.content: In chimpanzees, attacks from conspecifics - including infanticide and lethal raids by bands of males from neighboring groups - are major sources of mortality.

findings.quote: In every waking moment, your brain uses past experience, organized as concepts, to guide your actions and give your sensations meaning. When the concepts involved are emotion concepts, your brain constructs instances of emotion.
findings.content: Barrett's formal definition of the theory of constructed emotion: the brain uses past experience organized as concepts to guide actions and give sensations meaning. When emotion concepts are active, the brain constructs instances of emotion. Emotions are not triggered reactions but active constructions from interoceptive sensations, conceptual knowledge, and contextual predictions.

findings.quote: the ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven basic affective systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy)
findings.content: The ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven basic affective systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy). These designate specific functional networks of evolutionarily very ancient regions of our brains.
findings.where: Preface, 'Why Psychiatrists, Physicians, and Psychotherapists Should Understand the Seven Basic Affective Systems,' p. xi

findings.quote: Sexual gratification, arising from our capacity for LUST, feels good in a rather different way from the joys of rough-and-tumble PLAY or the tender bliss of caressing, nurturing, and CAREing for one's infant. FEAR is an entirely different kind of emotional 'pain' than frustrated RAGE; both differ from the PANICked misery of social isolation.
findings.content: Sexual gratification from LUST feels good in a different way from the joys of rough-and-tumble PLAY or the tender bliss of caressing and CARing for an infant. FEAR is an entirely different kind of emotional pain than frustrated RAGE; both differ from the panicked misery of social isolation (PANIC/GRIEF). These diverse affects provide guidance for living due to the survival-enhancing advantages each conferred over evolution. Affects are ancestral memories of how effectively we play the game of survival and reproduction.

findings.quote: The underlying circuits are genetically predetermined and designed to respond unconditionally to stimuli arising from major life-challenging circumstances. These circuits organize diverse behaviors by activating or inhibiting motor subroutines and concurrent autonomic-hormonal changes that have proved adaptive in the face of such life-challenging circumstances during the evolutionary history of the species. Emotive circuits change the sensitivities of sensory systems that are relevant for the behavioral sequences that have been aroused. Neural activity of emotive systems outlasts the precipitating circumstances. Emotive circuits can come under the conditional control of emotionally neutral environmental stimuli. Emotive circuits have reciprocal interactions with the brain mechanisms that elaborate higher decision-making processes and consciousness.
findings.content: Panksepp's six methodological criteria for identifying genuine emotional systems in the brain (Figure 3.3): (1) Underlying circuits are genetically predetermined to respond unconditionally to life-challenging stimuli; (2) they organize diverse behaviors by activating/inhibiting motor subroutines and autonomic-hormonal changes; (3) they change sensitivities of sensory systems relevant to the aroused behavioral sequences; (4) their neural activity outlasts precipitating circumstances; (5) they can come under conditional control of emotionally neutral stimuli; (6) they have reciprocal interactions with higher decision-making and consciousness circuits. Plus the seventh psychological criterion: they must generate affective feelings. This is Panksepp's load-bearing methodological framework for distinguishing emotional systems from general-purpose sensorimotor circuits.

findings.quote: Of course, as mentioned, there is a seventh psychological criterion: The emotional circuits must be able to generate affective feelings, but this is hard to incorporate into the conceptual diagram. I will eventually develop the idea that affect emerges from the many interactions of emotional systems depicted in Figure 3.3 with primal neural mechanisms that represent "the self" (see Chapter 16)
findings.content: Panksepp's central theoretical commitment - the seventh psychological criterion: emotional circuits must be able to generate affective feelings. This criterion is 'hard to incorporate into the conceptual diagram' but is the load-bearing claim that distinguishes affective neuroscience from behavioral neuroscience. Panksepp argues affect emerges from interactions of emotional systems with primal neural mechanisms that represent 'the self', particularly midbrain periaqueductal and deep tectal circuits interacting with frontal cortical systems. Arousal of the executive circuit for each emotion is a NECESSARY CONDITION for getting feeling states activated within the brain. Load-bearing for reading M1-M4/M9/M14 outputs as having affective content, not just behavioral output.

findings.quote: In addition to being the deep neural sources of psychic life, emotional circuits achieve their profound influence over the behavior and mental activity of an organism through the widespread effects on the rest of the nervous system. Emotive circuits change sensory, perceptual, and cognitive processing, and initiate a host of physiological changes that are naturally synchronized with the aroused behavioral tendencies characteristic of emotional experience.
findings.content: Panksepp's architectural claim about emotion-cognition interaction: emotional circuits achieve their profound influence over behavior and mental activity through widespread effects on the rest of the nervous system. Emotive circuits change sensory, perceptual, and cognitive processing, and initiate physiological changes synchronized with the aroused behavioral tendencies. This is NOT just a one-way emotion→behavior pathway - cognition is PENETRATED by emotional-circuit activity, meaning that 'cognitive' function cannot be cleanly separated from affective-circuit function. Load-bearing for Cor's framing that mechanism outputs (M1-M4, M9, M14) shape perception and attention upstream, not just behavior downstream.

Digital work exacerbates evolutionary mismatch through multiple simultaneous channels: sedentarism replacing embodied activity, always-on connectivity disrupting circadian boundaries, electronic surveillance replacing autonomy, remote/distributed work weakening face-to-face social bonds, and abstract screen-mediated tasks replacing tangible effort-outcome feedback. These mismatches are predicted to increase chronic work stress and related physical and mental health problems.

findings.quote: The SEEKING, or expectancy, system is characterized by a persistent exploratory inquisitiveness. This system engenders energetic forward locomotion - approach and engagement with the world - as an animal probes into the nooks and crannies of interesting places, objects, and events in ways that are characteristic of its species.
findings.content: The SEEKING system is characterized by persistent exploratory inquisitiveness. It engenders energetic forward locomotion - approach and engagement with the world - as animals probe nooks and crannies of interesting places, objects, and events. This system holds a special place among emotional systems because to some extent it plays a dynamic supporting role for all of the other emotions.

findings.quote: A very important neurochemical in this system is dopamine, especially the dopaminergic mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine circuits, which emanate from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) situated at the very back of the hypothalamus (Figure 3.6). These dopamine circuits tend to energize and coordinate the functions of many higher brain areas that mediate planning and foresight (such as the amygdala, nucleus accumbens, and frontal cortex - see next chapter) and promote states of eagerness and directed purpose in both humans and animals.
findings.content: Panksepp's specific neuroanatomical claim for SEEKING: dopamine is the key neurochemical, specifically the mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine circuits emanating from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) at the back of the hypothalamus. These dopamine circuits energize and coordinate higher brain areas mediating planning and foresight - amygdala, nucleus accumbens, frontal cortex - and promote states of eagerness and directed purpose in both humans and animals. Amphetamines and cocaine produce their psychic appeal by temporarily overarousing this emotional system; opiates, nicotine, and alcohol also derive hedonic appeal from interacting with it. This is the specific anatomical substrate that load-bears M2 and DA4 (proxy hijacking by stimulant drugs).

findings.quote: dopamine's contribution appears to be chiefly to cause 'wanting' for hedonic rewards, more than 'liking' or learning for those rewards.
findings.content: Dopamine's contribution to reward is chiefly to cause 'wanting' for hedonic rewards, more than 'liking' or learning. The wanting-liking dissociation means that dopamine attributes incentive salience to reward-related stimuli - making them attention-grabbing, attractive, and sought after - without necessarily making them pleasurable. This dissociation explains why addicts compulsively seek drugs they no longer enjoy.
findings.where: Abstract and Introduction (source lines 20-32); sourced from Berridge 2007 Debate paper on disk

findings.quote: Oystercatcher incubating 'supernormal' clutch of five eggs in preference to natural clutch of three.
findings.content: Supernormal stimuli: animals preferentially respond to exaggerated versions of natural sign stimuli. Oystercatchers incubate giant artificial eggs over their own normal-sized clutch. Herring gull chicks peck more vigorously at a red knitting needle with white stripes than at a realistic model of the parent's bill. The innate releasing mechanism responds to specific stimulus features, and artificial exaggeration of those features produces stronger responses than the natural stimulus.

findings.quote: The innate releasing mechanism usually seems to correspond more or less with the properties of the environmental object or situation at which the reaction is normally directed.
findings.content: The innate releasing mechanism corresponds to specific properties of environmental stimuli - sign stimuli. Animals respond to specific stimulus features (color, shape, movement pattern) rather than to the whole object. When artificial stimuli exaggerate these features beyond natural ranges, they produce supernormal responses - animals prefer the artificial exaggeration to the real thing. This demonstrates that the releasing mechanism is an open loop: it responds to features, not to the object as a whole.

findings.quote: These 'explosions' or 'vacuum activities' in a captive starling. It performed repeatedly the whole behaviour pattern of insect hunting, from watching the prey through catching, killing, and swallowing, without any discernible external stimulus.
findings.content: Vacuum activities: a captive starling performed the entire behavior pattern of insect hunting - watching, catching, killing, and swallowing - without any discernible external stimulus. Lorenz confirmed no insects were present. This demonstrates that motivational energy accumulates internally and can discharge behavior without any environmental trigger, when the threshold has been lowered sufficiently by deprivation.

Empirical basis for the dissociation (1998 review): Berridge and Robinson review converging evidence that (a) dopamine depletion leaves taste hedonic reactions (orofacial 'liking' responses to sweet tastes) intact, (b) normal new hedonic learning proceeds without intact dopamine neurotransmission, (c) pharmacological hedonic enhancement of palatability is preserved after dopamine depletion, yet (d) dopamine depletion abolishes the motivation to pursue the same rewards. They conclude: dopamine systems are necessary for 'wanting' incentives, but not for 'liking' them or for learning new 'likes' and 'dislikes.'

Hedonic 'liking' reactions are mediated by opioid systems in nucleus accumbens and ventral pallidum, not by dopamine. Dopamine codes incentive salience (wanting), not hedonic impact (liking). The hedonic reactions are homologous across mammals - humans share reaction details with hominids, moderately with monkeys, and lightly with rodents. This cross-species conservation of the liking system demonstrates its phylogenetic depth.
findings.where: Section on Liking (source lines 183-242); sourced from Berridge 2007 Debate paper on disk

findings.quote: recent evidence indicates that dopamine is neither necessary nor sufficient to mediate changes in hedonic 'liking' for sensory pleasures. Other recent evidence indicates that dopamine is not needed for new learning, and not sufficient to directly mediate learning by causing teaching or prediction signals. By contrast, growing evidence indicates that dopamine does contribute causally to incentive salience. Dopamine appears necessary for normal 'wanting', and dopamine activation can be sufficient to enhance cue-triggered incentive salience. Drugs of abuse that promote dopamine signals short circuit and sensitize dynamic mesolimbic mechanisms that evolved to attribute incentive salience to rewards.
findings.content: Dopamine is neither necessary nor sufficient to mediate changes in hedonic 'liking' for sensory pleasures. Other recent evidence indicates that dopamine is not needed for new learning, and not sufficient to directly mediate learning by causing teaching or prediction signals. By contrast, growing evidence indicates that dopamine does contribute causally to incentive salience. Dopamine appears necessary for normal 'wanting', and dopamine activation can be sufficient to enhance cue-triggered incentive salience. Drugs of abuse that promote dopamine signals short circuit and sensitize dynamic mesolimbic mechanisms that evolved to attribute incentive salience to rewards.

findings.quote: dopamine depletion caused a suppression of subjective ratings of wanting/desire to take more cocaine, but left subjective liking ratings for cocaine pleasure essentially unchanged (Leyton et al. 2005)... In several psychopharmacological studies, Brauer and colleagues (especially deWit) reported that dopamine blockade by neuroleptic antagonists may suppress wanting ratings or behavioral consumption of amphetamine or cigarettes, yet leave subjective liking ratings for the drugs untouched
findings.content: In normal human volunteers, temporary dietary manipulation to deplete brain dopamine levels (via ingestion of a deficient amino acid mixture) caused a dopamine-induced dissociation between subjective liking and wanting for intranasally administered cocaine. Dopamine depletion caused a suppression of subjective ratings of wanting/desire to take more cocaine, but left subjective liking ratings for cocaine pleasure essentially unchanged. Several psychopharmacological studies have similarly reported that dopamine blockade by neuroleptic antagonists may suppress wanting ratings or behavioral consumption of amphetamine or cigarettes, yet leave subjective liking ratings for the drugs untouched. Dopamine appears to correspond more closely to ratings of reward wanting than to reward liking.
findings.where: Section 'Analysis of hedonia hypothesis,' Leyton et al. 2005 and Brauer/de Wit studies, pp. 397-398

findings.quote: Phasic DA transmission is the short-lasting and impulse-dependent release that appears as a consequence of neural burst firing (Gonon, 1988; Suaud-Chagny et al., 1992). Following such bursts, high levels of DA molecules are released into the synaptic cleft at up to mM concentration (Garris et al., 1994), and then rapidly removed via a re-uptake system (Floresco et al. 2003). To the contrary, tonic DA levels are diffused in the extracellular space outside the synaptic clefts, but exist in very small concentrations (in the nM range), and change relatively slowly (Grace, 2000).
findings.content: The physiological basis for M2's mixed activation profile: dopamine transmission runs in two modes. Phasic release is short-lasting, impulse-dependent, cue and reward-prediction locked; tonic extracellular dopamine sits at low concentration and changes slowly, carrying a background level of appetitive engagement that varies with state (sleep-wake, arousal). For activation_class this grounds tonic_baseline as M2's primary class with event_triggered phasic spikes as secondary; the phasic incentive-salience side is already carried in C6 by Berridge.
findings.where: Section 2.5, Electric activity of DA cells

findings.quote: To keep playing - to stay in that machine zone where nothing else matters. It's like being in the eye of a storm, is how I'd describe it. Your vision is clear on the machine in front of you but the whole world is spinning around you, and you can't really hear anything.
findings.content: Machine gambling produces a 'zone' state - an absorptive dissociation where nothing else matters. Gamblers describe it as being 'in the eye of a storm' where vision narrows to the machine, the world spins around you, and you cannot hear anything. The primary reinforcer is not winning money but staying in the zone. The gambling industry explicitly designs for 'time-on-device' (TOD) as the target metric.

findings.quote: Modern slot machines are rarely the work of one company; they are symphonies of individual technologies that come together to create a single experience.
findings.content: Modern slot machines are engineered systems assembled from 1,200+ individual parts by teams of up to 300 people including mathematicians, graphic artists, marketers, and software engineers. They employ 'losses disguised as wins' (LDWs) - multiline outcomes where the total return is less than the wager but the machine celebrates with lights and sounds, producing the reinforcing arousal of a win on what is actually a net loss. Near-miss effects are engineered through clustering techniques that distort loss perception.

Schull's 15-year ethnography documents the "machine zone" - a dissociative state gamblers seek not to win money but to sustain. Mollie, a core informant, states: "I'm not playing to win... To keep playing - to stay in that machine zone where nothing else matters." She describes it as "being in the eye of a storm... You aren't really there - you're with the machine and that's all you're with." Clinical psychologist Robert Hunter confirms that modern video gambling "facilitates the dissociative process" - his patients describe "numbness or escape... climbing into the screen and getting lost." Gamblers are described as hanging "in a state of suspended animation," addicted not to the chance of winning but to "the world-dissolving state of subjective suspension and affective calm they derive from machine play." The industry itself tracks this as "time-on-device" (TOD), with developers noting "on these newer products, they can really get into that zone."
findings.where: Introduction: Mapping the Machine Zone, pp. 1-20

findings.content: Slot machine design systematically exploits the dissociation between wanting and liking through multiple reinforcement mechanisms. Virtual reel mapping creates "near miss" effects - clustering winning symbols adjacent to blanks on the payline so losses appear as almost-wins, which "have an invigorating or potentiating effect on any behavior that immediately follows" (Skinner). Multiline video slots produce "losses disguised as wins" (LDWs): a player betting 25 nickels wins back 15, receiving the full audiovisual celebration of winning - lights, music, graphics - while steadily losing. As one designer explained: "Positive reinforcement hides loss." This steady partial "winning" accommodates a "play-to-win-to-play" mode where time-on-device is the aim. The machines give players modulatory control over lines and coins, letting "rat people" design their own Skinner boxes - increasing reinforcement frequency while reducing unreinforced trials. The net effect: SEEKING/wanting circuits fire continuously on variable-ratio reinforcement while actual satisfaction (liking) never arrives.
findings.where: Ch. 3 Programming Chance (pp. 76-105), Ch. 4 Matching the Market (pp. 107-136)

findings.content: Casino architect Bill Friedman's comprehensive design system (13 trademarked "Friedman Casino Design Principles") systematically engineers the physical environment to induce and maintain the machine zone state. Core strategy: The Law of Space Elimination - eliminate "excess horizontal space, excessive visible depth, and excess vertical space" because gamblers "most avoid expanse." Best-performing slot machines are located in "insulated enclaves," tucked in "small alcoves, recesses, and corners." Gamblers confirm this: Mollie gravitates "toward the corners, where it felt safe"; Daniel wants "to be in my own little cave." The maze layout "rivets visitors' attention on the equipment immediately ahead" by truncating lines of sight - "walkers can only see a short distance ahead" - creating "structured chaos" that draws patrons deeper into the casino. Curving pathways eliminate sharp turns that require conscious commitment. Sequential chase lights (like airport runway lights) subliminally guide movement. Equipment is "crammed tightly together" with narrow aisles. The entire built environment functions as a behavioral funnel: from the property entrance that "should curve gently off the street" to the maze interior, each design element reduces the probability of conscious decision-making and increases the probability of sitting down at a machine.
findings.where: Ch 1: Interior Design for Interior States, pp. 39-48

findings.quote: when they took an L-DOPA dose, the DDS patients showed a sensitized over elevation in drug-stimulated dopamine neurotransmission in ventral striatum, including nucleus accumbens (Evans et al. 2006). Importantly for understanding dopamine's role, the excessive dopamine release measured by PET correlated strongly with subjective ratings of wanting for L-DOPA ('do you want to take more of what you consumed, right now?'). However, excessive dopamine release did not cause patients to give higher liking ratings to L-DOPA, and there was no correlation found between subjective liking ratings ('do you like the effects you feel right now?') and PET-measured dopamine release
findings.content: Parkinson's patients with 'dopamine dysregulation syndrome' (DDS) take far greater amounts of L-DOPA than prescribed in an apparently compulsive fashion and can develop other compulsive activities including gambling and obsessive pursuit of certain repetitive trivial activities ('punding'). PET neuroimaging of these DDS patients showed that after an L-DOPA dose, they exhibited a sensitized over-elevation in drug-stimulated dopamine neurotransmission in ventral striatum. Importantly, the excessive dopamine release measured by PET correlated strongly with subjective ratings of wanting for L-DOPA ('do you want to take more of what you consumed, right now?'), but did not cause patients to give higher liking ratings to L-DOPA - there was no correlation between subjective liking ratings and PET-measured dopamine release.
findings.where: Section 'Analysis of hedonia hypothesis,' Evans et al. 2006 PET study, pp. 396-397

findings.quote: that elusive point of absorption, beyond contingency
findings.content: The zone state is described as absorption 'beyond contingency' - a narrowly focused attention state where control dissolves into automaticity. Machine gamblers seek the zone not to win but to escape - from anxiety, grief, boredom, social pain. The machine provides a predictable, controllable micro-environment that the rest of life cannot match. This is proxy hijacking of M6 (controllability) as much as M2 (pursuit).

findings.quote: Depression may feel bad because brain separation-distress systems create psychological pain.
findings.content: PANIC/GRIEF circuitry maps directly onto brain targets for treatment-resistant depression: starts in the PAG, ascends through dorsomedial thalamus, and terminates in subcallosal anterior cingulate - the same regions targeted by deep brain stimulation (Mayberg et al., 2005). Key neurochemistry: declining opioids and oxytocin, elevated CRF, increased glutamate. Dynorphin mediates SEEKING shutdown as a distinct form of negative affect.

findings.quote: we found that oystercatchers preferred a clutch of five eggs to the normal clutch of three. Still more astonishing is the oystercatcher's preference for abnormally large eggs. If presented with an egg of normal oystercatcher size, one of herring gull's size, and one double the (linear) size of a herring gull's egg, the majority of choices fall upon the largest egg.
findings.content: Oystercatchers preferred a clutch of five eggs to the normal clutch of three. Still more astonishing is the oystercatcher's preference for abnormally large eggs: when presented with an egg of normal oystercatcher size, one of herring gull's size, and one double the linear size of a herring gull's egg, the majority of choices fall upon the largest egg. The bird reliably chooses the giant egg it cannot have evolved to recognize over the one it actually laid.
findings.where: Chapter III, 'Supernormal sign stimuli,' pp. 44-45, Figs. 42-43

findings.content: The gambling industry designs for 'extinction' - continued play until total asset depletion. Variable-ratio reward schedules maintain play because the next reward could come at any time. The mathematical structure of the game is invisible to the player, who experiences only the surface (lights, sounds, near-misses) while the underlying probability structure ensures net loss over time. The house edge is designed to be imperceptible on a per-spin basis.

findings.quote: Then, with neuroscientist Lucy Brown, psychologist Art Aron, and others, I put seventeen new lovers into the brain scanner: ten women and seven men who had been madly and happily in love for an average of 7.4 months. I will never forget the moment I first saw the results. I was standing in a darkened lab at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine. I felt like jumping in the sky. Before my eyes were scans showing blobs of activity in the ventral tegmental area, or VTA, a tiny factory near the base of the brain that makes dopamine and sends this natural stimulant to many brain regions. We found activity in many other brain regions, but the VTA was particularly important. This factory is part of the brain's reward system, the brain network that generates wanting, seeking, craving, energy, focus, and motivation.
findings.content: Fisher and colleagues put seventeen new lovers into the fMRI scanner - ten women and seven men who had been madly and happily in love for an average of 7.4 months. The scans showed blobs of activity in the ventral tegmental area (VTA), a tiny factory near the base of the brain that makes dopamine and sends this natural stimulant to many brain regions. This factory is part of the brain's reward system, the brain network that generates wanting, seeking, craving, energy, focus, and motivation. The VTA was particularly important. Men showed just as much activity in the VTA and other neural pathways for romantic passion as women did.
findings.where: Chapter 2 'Why Him? Why Her?' Romantic Attraction fMRI study, pp. 33-34, with Lucy Brown, Art Aron, and colleagues

findings.quote: This drive, this survival mechanism, is also an addiction. With a reanalysis of the data, we found activity in the nucleus accumbens (unpublished data), a brain region that is part of the reward system, is fueled by dopamine, and is associated with all of the addictions - including the cravings for heroin, cocaine, nicotine, alcohol, amphetamines, gambling, sex, and food.
findings.content: With a reanalysis of the Fisher/Brown/Aron fMRI data, activity was found in the nucleus accumbens - a brain region that is part of the reward system, is fueled by dopamine, and is associated with all of the addictions - including the cravings for heroin, cocaine, nicotine, alcohol, amphetamines, gambling, sex, and food. Romantic love is, in this architectural sense, a natural addiction, running through the same reward pathways that pathological addictions hijack.
findings.where: Chapter 2 'The Drive to Love... a Natural Addiction' pp. 35

findings.quote: To plot what industry insiders call the 'bliss point,' or the precise amount of sugar or fat or salt that will send consumers over the moon. At a laboratory in White Plains, New York, industry scientists who perform this alchemy walked me, step by step, through the process of engineering a new soda so that I could see the creation of bliss firsthand.
findings.content: The food industry engineers bliss points - the precise amount of sugar, fat, or salt that sends consumers over the moon. Industry scientists mathematically optimize the hedonic response curve for each product, finding the exact concentration that maximizes craving. This is not accidental food design but systematic exploitation of the reward system's response to ancestrally rare nutrient signals.

findings.quote: These were the three pillars of processed food, the creators of crave, and each of the CEOs needed them in huge quantities to turn their products into hits.
findings.content: Salt, sugar, and fat are the three pillars of processed food - the creators of crave. Each CEO needed them in huge quantities to turn products into hits. Officials discussed the power of foods to create cravings that overwhelm the best intentions of dieters. Industry-wide limits on mainline products (not just niche diet items) would be needed to diminish these cravings, but competitive pressure prevents any single company from unilaterally reducing palatability.

findings.quote: As indicated in Figure 14, nonlonely participants showed greater activity in the ventral striatum, one of the brain's 'reward centers,' when they saw a pleasant image of a person (a smiling farmer) than when they saw an equally pleasant picture of an object (a flower arrangement). For the nonlonely, a positive image of another human being obviously meant something special - it gave them a specific emotional boost as evidenced by changes in this specific area that registers pleasure. Lonely participants, however, when they viewed positive images of people, did not register the same boost: The activation of the ventral striatum in response to a happy face was in fact a bit weaker than when they saw the pleasant picture of the flowers. This finding aligns with self-reports in which lonely individuals said that they found positive social interactions to be less of an uplift than did their nonlonely counterparts.
findings.content: In a study at the University of Chicago Brain Imaging Center, volunteers viewed photographs of objects or people, selected to have positive or negative emotional impact. Nonlonely participants showed greater activity in the ventral striatum - one of the brain's reward centers - when they saw a pleasant image of a person (a smiling farmer) than when they saw an equally pleasant picture of an object (a flower arrangement). For the nonlonely, a positive image of another human being meant something special. Lonely participants, however, when viewing positive images of people, did not register the same boost: the activation of the ventral striatum in response to a happy face was in fact a bit weaker than when they saw the pleasant picture of the flowers.
findings.where: Chapter 9 'A Concerto for Two (or More) Voices,' Brain Imaging Center study, pp. 162-163

findings.quote: It is becoming harder to believe that general brain serotonergic and/or noradrenergic changes, which globally regulate aspects of forebrain arousal and dynamics, will specifically explain the morbid moods of depression.
findings.content: SSRIs have modest overall efficacy (STAR*D findings); serotonin and norepinephrine regulate general arousal, not the specific affect of depression. More targeted interventions include ultra-low-dose buprenorphine (which both activates mu-opioid receptors and blocks despair-promoting dynorphin/kappa receptors), oxytocin, CRF antagonists, and glutamate modulators (ketamine). Psychotherapeutic activation of CARE and PLAY systems remains almost completely untapped.

findings.quote: some of the infants who seemed most solidly attached to their mothers displayed little protest behaviour or separation anxiety, but rather showed the strength of their attachment to the mother through their readiness to use her as a secure base from which
findings.content: Ainsworth's secure base concept as reported by Bowlby: some infants who seemed most solidly attached to their mothers displayed little protest behavior or separation anxiety. Instead, they showed the strength of their attachment through their readiness to use the mother as a secure base from which to explore. This redefines secure attachment not as constant proximity-seeking but as confident exploration enabled by the availability of the attachment figure.

findings.quote: Current neurobehavioral evidence indicates that there are at least four executive circuits of this type -- those which elaborate central states of expectancy, rage, fear, and panic.
findings.content: Four primary emotional executive circuits identified via electrical brain stimulation: expectancy (later renamed SEEKING), rage, fear, and panic. Each is a transhypothalamic command circuit that concurrently activates behavioral action patterns, physiological responses, and subjective states. These circuits developed early in mammalian brain evolution and the underlying control mechanisms remain similar across species.

Positive affect has at least two distinct neural substrates: appetitive (anticipatory) positive affect mediated by ventral striatal dopamine systems (SEEKING), and consummatory positive affect (sensory pleasure) mediated by dopamine-independent opioid and GABA receptors in ventral striatum, amygdala, and orbital frontal cortex. Various neuropeptides mediate homeostatic satisfactions as a third category.

findings.quote: Through prediction, your brain constructs the world you experience. It combines bits and pieces of your past and estimates how likely each bit applies in your current situation.
findings.content: The brain constructs the world you experience through prediction. Intrinsic brain activity - millions of nonstop predictions - is the brain's primary mode of operation. Past experience, organized as concepts, generates predictions that are tested against incoming sensory input. Events in the world merely tune these predictions rather than triggering responses. Evolution literally wired the brain for efficient prediction: 90 percent of connections entering primary visual cortex carry predictions from other brain regions, not sensory input from the world.

findings.quote: When we artificially activate brain emotion-behavior generating circuits, animals rapidly learn to turn off ESB that evokes fear- and anger-type responses, and they turn on brain stimulation that generates playful sounds, exploration, sexual eagerness and maternal care.
findings.content: Electrical brain stimulation (ESB) of specific subcortical regions produces coherent emotional behaviors in all mammals tested. Animals given control over ESB self-select: they turn off stimulation evoking fear/anger responses and turn on stimulation generating playful sounds, exploration, sexual eagerness, and maternal care. This reward/punishment valence demonstrates genuine affective experience, not mere behavioral reflexes.

findings.quote: the ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven emotional, or affective, systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy). Each of these systems controls distinct but specific types of behaviors associated with many overlapping physiological changes.
findings.content: The ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven emotional systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy). Each controls distinct behaviors with overlapping physiological changes and generates distinct types of affective consciousness. When stimulated in humans, people always experience intense emotional feelings. Capitalizations indicate that real physical and distinct networks for these emotions exist in mammalian brains.

findings.quote: primal emotional systems are made up of neuroanatomies and neurochemistries that are remarkably similar across all mammalian species. This suggests that these systems evolved a very long time ago and that at a basic emotional and motivational level, all mammals are more similar than they are different.
findings.content: Primal emotional systems are made up of neuroanatomies and neurochemistries remarkably similar across all mammalian species. This suggests these systems evolved a very long time ago and that at a basic emotional and motivational level, all mammals are more similar than different. Deep in the ancient affective recesses of our brains, we remain evolutionarily kin. The same neural paths and brain chemicals that arouse each of these seven systems are found within all mammals.

Panksepp's textbook Affective Neuroscience establishes the methodology and evidence base for the seven subcortical affective systems. Across cross-species deep brain stimulation, lesion, and pharmacological studies, the same brain regions produce the same functional categories of affective response - SEEKING, FEAR, RAGE, LUST, CARE, PANIC, PLAY - across mammals, providing the empirical foundation for treating these as conserved motivational architecture rather than culturally constructed categories.

findings.quote: FEAR is an inborn capacity of the mammalian brain. However, FEAR, just like all other basic emotions, rapidly gets enmeshed with world events as it comes to be regulated by learning and encoded in our conscious minds.
findings.content: FEAR is an inborn capacity of the mammalian brain that rapidly gets enmeshed with world events through learning. Most basic emotions need not be expressed immediately after birth. Some - including CARE, LUST, and PLAY - come online long after others such as SEEKING, RAGE, and FEAR. The developmental timing reflects phylogenetic priority: the oldest and most survival-critical systems activate earliest.

findings.quote: people move their facial muscles in many different ways, not one consistent way, when feeling an instance of the same emotion category. Large meta-analyses conclude that a single emotion category involves different bodily responses, not a single, consistent response. Brain circuitry operates by the many-to-one principle of degeneracy: instances of a single emotion category, such as fear, are handled by different brain patterns at different times and in different people. Conversely, the same neurons can participate in creating different mental states (one-to-many).
findings.content: Barrett's comprehensive meta-analysis of brain-imaging, facial EMG, and autonomic nervous system studies finds no consistent physical fingerprint for any single emotion. Facial muscles move in many different ways for the same emotion category. Bodily responses vary across instances. Brain circuitry operates by degeneracy (many-to-one: different neural patterns produce the same emotion category) and core systems (one-to-many: the same neurons participate in different mental states). Variation, not uniformity, is the norm across all three measurement domains.

findings.quote: It has become increasingly clear during the past half century that primary-process affective mechanisms are concentrated in ancient subcortical midline brain regions that are anatomically and neurochemically, and hence, evolutionarily, similar in all mammalian species.
findings.content: Seven distinct emotional systems identified with specific neuroanatomy and neurochemistry: SEEKING (VTA/NAcc/lateral hypothalamus, DA+), RAGE (medial amygdala→BNST→hypothalamus→PAG, substance P+), FEAR (central amygdala→hypothalamus→dorsal PAG, glutamate+/CRF+), LUST (cortico-medial amygdala/BNST/preoptic, steroids+), CARE (anterior cingulate/BNST/preoptic/VTA, oxytocin+/prolactin+), PANIC (anterior cingulate/BNST/dorsomedial thalamus/PAG, opioids−/oxytocin−/CRF+), PLAY (dorsomedial diencephalon/parafascicular/PAG, opioids+/−). Each mapped in Fig. 2 with specific neurochemical modulators.
findings.where: Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews 35(9):1791-1804, p. 1795, Fig. 2. DOI: 10.1016/j.neubiorev.2011.08.003

findings.quote: Never have such profound emotional states been provoked by stimulating neocortical regions.
findings.content: All seven emotional systems survive radical neo-decortication (complete surgical removal of the cerebral cortex). Decorticate animals retain all emotional-instinctual urges intact, though their capacity to learn new instrumental behaviors is severely impaired. ESB of subcortical regions in humans produces intense affective experiences; neocortical stimulation never produces such emotional states.

findings.quote: These criteria have been fulfilled or approximated for a variety of brain systems that exist in all mammals studied so far.
findings.content: Three empirical criteria for determining existence of emotional feelings in animals, all fulfilled: (1) neural circuits must exist that activate coherent emotional behaviors, (2) artificial arousal of such systems must generate conditioned approach/escape/avoidance, (3) key neurochemistries and brain activation patterns must correlate with predicted affective changes in humans. These criteria have been fulfilled for multiple brain systems across all mammals studied.

Three convergent lines of evidence demonstrate subcortical affective states: (i) mammals are attracted to the same environmental rewards and drugs of abuse as humans; (ii) human emotional feelings depend on subcortical brain systems where evolutionarily homologous instinctual neural systems exist; (iii) artificial activations of deep brain emotional systems are liked and disliked by animals, as measured by approach and avoidance measures.

findings.quote: The SEEKING system (see Chapter 8): This emotional system is a coherently operating neuronal network that promotes a certain class of survival abilities. This system makes animals intensely interested in exploring their world and leads them to become excited when they are about to get what they desire. It eventually allows animals to find and eagerly anticipate the things they need for survival, including, of course, food, water, warmth, and their ultimate evolutionary survival need, sex. In other words, when fully aroused, it helps fill the mind with interest and motivates organisms to
findings.content: Panksepp's canonical definition of the SEEKING system: a coherently operating neuronal network that promotes survival by making animals intensely interested in exploring their world and excited when they are about to get what they desire. It drives animals to find and eagerly anticipate food, water, warmth, and sex. When fully aroused, it fills the mind with interest and motivates movement toward resources. In humans, this is 'one of the main brain systems that generates and sustains curiosity, even for intellectual pursuits'. Neuroanatomically the SEEKING system corresponds to the major self-stimulation system from midbrain to cortex, long misconceptualized as a 'reward or reinforcement system'. This is the foundational primary-source definition that load-bears M2 Pursuit/Exploration in Cor.
findings.where: Chapter 3 'The Varieties of Emotional Systems in the Brain' pp. ~53

findings.quote: When this brain system becomes underactive, as is common with aging, a form of depression results. When the system becomes spontaneously overactive, which can happen as a result of various kinds of stress, an animal's behavior becomes excessive and schizophrenic or manic symptoms may follow-especially the "functional" forms of psychosis that can be treated with traditional antipsychotic medications (which all reduce dopamine activity in the brain)
findings.content: Panksepp's clinical prediction from the SEEKING-system framework: when the SEEKING brain system becomes UNDERACTIVE (as is common with aging), a form of depression results. When it becomes spontaneously OVERACTIVE (from stress), animal behavior becomes excessive and schizophrenic or manic symptoms may follow - especially the 'functional' forms of psychosis treatable with traditional antipsychotic medications (all of which reduce dopamine activity). This predicts that depression-via-SEEKING-hypofunction is mechanistically distinct from depression-via-PANIC-overactivation (social loss), and provides a specific dopamine-centered prediction for M2 Pursuit/Exploration dysregulation. Load-bearing for reading modern anhedonic depression as a SEEKING-hypoactivation phenotype.

Incentive salience hypothesis (founding statement): Berridge and Robinson propose that mesolimbic dopamine does NOT mediate the hedonic impact of rewards ('liking'), does NOT mediate reward learning per se, but instead mediates the attribution of incentive salience - the process by which neural representations of reward-related stimuli become motivationally 'wanted.' Wanting (incentive salience) is a distinct, dissociable psychological process from liking (hedonic impact) and from learning (associative prediction). This three-way dissociation reframes the entire reward literature: dopamine is necessary for wanting but not for liking or for learning what to like.

findings.quote: The affective neuroethological perspective presented here, views the ML-DA system in terms of its ability to activate an instinctual emotional appetitive state (SEEKING) evolved to induce organisms to search for all varieties of life-supporting stimuli and to avoid harms.
findings.content: The Panksepp-school statement of what M2 is: the mesolimbic dopamine system activates an instinctual appetitive SEEKING state that induces organisms to search for all varieties of life-supporting stimuli. SEEKING is the general-purpose engagement disposition of the awake animal rather than a response to a specific deficit signal, which is why its activation profile is not homeostatic in the M13 sense: no single tissue variable builds pressure and terminates it.

findings.quote: We want so badly to be important, rich, loved, admired, attractive, and powerful. For what? The good feelings from succeeding are just about balanced by the bad feelings from failure. Our emotions benefit our genes far more than they do us.
findings.content: Our emotions benefit our genes far more than they do us. We want so badly to be important, rich, loved, admired, attractive, and powerful - but the good feelings from succeeding are just about balanced by the bad feelings from failure. The emotional system is calibrated not for individual happiness but for gene propagation, which explains why suffering is inherent rather than accidental.

findings.quote: depression is intimately related to 1) sustained overactivity of the separation-distress PANIC system that can, if prolonged, lead to a downward cascade of psychological despair (a theoretical view originally formulated by John Bowlby); and 2) the despair phase that follows the acute PANIC response which is characterized by abnormally low activity of the SEEKING system.
findings.content: Two-phase model of depression genesis: (1) sustained overactivity of the PANIC/GRIEF separation-distress system produces psychological pain, followed by (2) abnormally low SEEKING system activity during the despair phase. The initial agitated panic state transitions to shutdown when reunification attempts fail, paralleling Bowlby's protest-despair sequence.

findings.quote: depression is ordinarily, therefore, a normal, adaptive part of disengaging oneself from an incentive... Mood thus regulates the allocation of effort and resources - toward enterprises, strategies, and times likely to give a high payoff and away from unprofitable enterprises and times when efforts will likely be wasted or dangerous.
findings.content: The role of depression in disengaging motivation from an unreachable goal was specified explicitly in the incentive-disengagement theory of Klinger. If a commitment to pursue a goal encounters an obstacle, efforts increase and become aggressive. If the obstacle cannot be overcome, low mood helps to disengage the commitment and end the cycle. If the individual cannot disengage, low mood escalates. Klinger concludes, 'depression is ordinarily, therefore, a normal, adaptive part of disengaging oneself from an incentive.' Many other researchers also see a close relationship between depression and difficulty in disengaging from major commitments. Mood thus regulates the allocation of effort and resources - toward enterprises, strategies, and times likely to give a high payoff and away from unprofitable enterprises and times when efforts will likely be wasted or dangerous.
findings.where: Section 'Possible Functions of Low Mood and Depression,' pp. 15-16

findings.quote: The major emotional operating systems are defined primarily by genetically coded neural circuits that generate well-organized behavior sequences that can be evoked by localized electrical stimulation of the brain. Representative behaviors generated by the various systems are indicated, and the approximate locations of the SEEKING, FEAR, and RAGE systems are depicted on a small frontal section through one side of the hypothalamus.
findings.content: Panksepp's historical contribution: in his 1982 paper he first distinguished four primary emotional command systems that are organized along discrete but interacting subcortical trajectories (mostly following the medial forebrain bundle). These are depicted in Figure 3.5 (original paper) with approximate anatomical locations for SEEKING, FEAR, and RAGE in the hypothalamus and their interconnections. The 1982 framework was the foundational statement of affective neuroscience as a research program distinct from behavioral or cognitive approaches. This is primary-source citation for the architectural claim that mammalian emotions are subcortically organized, not cortically derived.

findings.quote: close study of IRMs reveals the remarkable fact that it is sometimes possible to offer stimulus situations that are even more effective than the natural situation. In other words, the natural situation is not always optimal.
findings.content: Close study of innate releasing mechanisms reveals the remarkable fact that it is sometimes possible to offer stimulus situations that are even more effective than the natural situation. In other words, the natural situation is not always optimal. This is the phenomenon of supernormal sign stimuli - an evolved response fires harder in reaction to an exaggerated artificial stimulus than to the natural cue it was shaped to detect.
findings.where: Chapter III, 'Behaviour as a Reaction to External Stimuli,' section 'Supernormal sign stimuli,' pp. 44-46

findings.quote: An evolutionary view explains why we have desires, why we can't satisfy them, and why it is so hard to set them aside: our brains were shaped to benefit our genes, not us.
findings.content: An evolutionary view explains why we have desires, why we cannot satisfy them, and why it is so hard to set them aside: our brains were shaped to benefit our genes, not us. Most suffering is emotional suffering. Anxiety and low mood exist for the same reason as pain and nausea - because they are useful in certain situations. They are often excessive for good evolutionary reasons.

findings.quote: In neurological terms, this change can be readily affected by a minor alteration to the reward systems of the hypothalamus, nucleus accumbens and amygdala. With a minimal change in the regulation of these juvenile interactions, it becomes reasonable to label them as play, albeit of a rudimentary form
findings.content: Pellis's identification of the neural substrates for play-motivated behavior: juvenile play interactions can be readily modified by alterations to the reward systems of the hypothalamus, nucleus accumbens, and amygdala. At the earlier evolutionary stages of play, these subcortical reward circuits are the primary regulators; at later stages (stage 4 emancipated play in rats), cortical mechanisms (PFC, motor cortex) add novel control layers on top. This grounds M4 at the subcortical-reward level and connects it to the DA8 phylogenetic-priority cascade (older circuits, newer cortical elaboration on top).

findings.quote: Organisms try to get sex, power, and resources and to avoid danger and loss. Pursuing these goals gives rise to a set of defined situations. Each one poses different adaptive challenges that shape a different emotional state. Opportunity arouses enthusiasm. Success arouses joy. Threat arouses anxiety. Loss arouses sadness.
findings.content: Four situations that arise in goal pursuit map to four emotions: opportunity arouses enthusiasm, success arouses joy, threat arouses anxiety, loss arouses sadness. Organisms try to get sex, power, and resources and to avoid danger and loss. Each situation poses different adaptive challenges that shape a different emotional state. The scheme can be expanded by adding emotions for alternative outcomes - disappointment when pursuit fails, relief when threat is avoided.

findings.quote: Why is this relevant to emotion? Because every brain region that's claimed to be a home of emotion in humans is a body-budgeting region within the interoceptive network. These regions, however, don't react in emotion. They don't react at all. They predict, intrinsically, to regulate your body budget. They issue predictions for sights, sounds, thoughts, memories, imagination, and, yes, emotions. The idea of an emotional brain region is an illusion caused by the outdated belief in a reactive brain. Neuroscientists understand this today, but the message hasn't trickled down to many psychologists, psychiatrists, sociologists, economists, and others who study emotion.
findings.content: Every brain region historically claimed as a home of emotion is actually a body-budgeting region within the interoceptive network. These regions do not react in emotion - they predict intrinsically to regulate the body budget, issuing predictions for sights, sounds, thoughts, memories, imagination, and emotions. The notion of a dedicated emotional brain region is an illusion caused by the outdated belief in a reactive brain.

findings.quote: In addition to the preceding primitive systems that are evident in all mammals soon after birth
findings.content: Panksepp's framework of 4 primary emotional command systems: expectancy/SEEKING, RAGE, FEAR, and separation-distress/PANIC. These are organized along discrete but interacting trajectories in the subcortical brain, largely following the medial forebrain bundle. These 4 systems are 'evident in all mammals soon after birth' - they are not cognitive achievements but mammalian hardware inherited from at least 150 million years of mammalian evolution. This is the central DA8 phylogenetic-priority claim: the affective substrate is ancient, pre-cortical, and conserved across all mammals.

findings.quote: every thought, memory, emotion, or perception that you construct in your life includes something about the state of your body. Your interoceptive network, which regulates your body budget, is launching these cascades. Every prediction you make, and every categorization your brain completes, is always in relation to the activity of your heart and lungs, your metabolism, your immune function, and the other systems that contribute to your body budget.
findings.content: Every thought, memory, emotion, or perception includes something about the state of the body. The interoceptive network, which regulates the body budget, launches the prediction cascades underlying all mental states. Every prediction and categorization occurs in relation to the activity of the heart, lungs, metabolism, immune function, and other body-budget systems. This means no mental state is purely cognitive or purely emotional - all are embodied through interoceptive prediction.

findings.quote: Affective neuroscience has made a fresh start by proceeding from the bottom up, without denigrating our unique human abilities, and it is offering both a new vision of mental origins and new data to back up such assertions.
findings.content: The triangulation approach of affective neuroscience links the affective mind to animal brains by triangulating among (i) subjective mental states (most easily studied in humans), (ii) brain functions (more easily studied in animals), and (iii) natural instinctual emotional behaviors that all young mammals must exhibit early in life to survive. This bottom-up approach offers both a new vision of mental origins and new data.

findings.quote: I will speak of these emotional systems in a variety of ways, using designations such as executive, command, and operating systems, to provide nuances of meaning that may be needed to conceptualize their overall functions. The use of the term executive implies that a neural system has a superordinate role in a cascade of hierarchical controls
findings.content: Panksepp's conceptual toolkit for emotional circuits: he calls them 'executive, command, and operating systems' - executive implies a superordinate role in hierarchical controls; command implies the circuit can INSTIGATE a full-blown emotional process (not just correlate with it); operating implies it coordinates and synchronizes multiple subsystems. Together these yield coherent psycho-behavioral and physiological responses that constitute an emotional 'organ system' - an anatomical network of interconnected neurons with endocrine, paracrine, and immune influences. This is the load-bearing architectural framing for why emotional circuits are mechanisms (Cor's M-framework) rather than mere sensorimotor reflexes.

findings.quote: Thus, when mother is called away a child's attachment behaviour is likely to be elicited and his exploratory behaviour inhibited; conversely, when a child explores too far, a mother's care behaviour is likely to be elicited and whatever else she is doing to be inhibited. In a happy couple these four classes of behaviour occur and progress together in harmony. But risk of conflict is ever-present.
findings.content: Attachment behavior as one of four interacting classes in mother-child interaction: (a) the child's attachment behavior, (b) the child's exploratory behavior and play (antithetic to attachment), (c) the mother's caretaking behavior, and (d) the mother's behavior antithetic to care. When the mother is called away, the child's attachment behavior is elicited and exploratory behavior inhibited; when the child explores too far, the mother's care behavior is elicited. In a happy couple these four classes occur in harmony, but risk of conflict is ever-present.

findings.quote: I remain convinced that it is useful, at least in the present state of our knowledge, to 'dissect' the master question into three stages.
findings.content: Tinbergen's four questions framework: the complete study of behavior requires investigating (1) causation (mechanism - what internal and external stimuli trigger the behavior), (2) ontogeny (development - how the behavior develops during the organism's lifetime), (3) survival value (function - what adaptive advantage the behavior confers), and (4) evolution (phylogeny - how the behavior evolved across species). These four levels of analysis are complementary, not competing.

Some features of digital work may be more matched with ancestral work conditions than traditional industrial/office work: flexible scheduling restoring autonomy over time allocation, broader access to skill-learning and collaboration networks, and potential for reduced commuting allowing more time for non-work regulatory needs. Digital work is a mixed mismatch profile, not a uniformly mismatched one.

The two theoretical mechanisms Miller invokes for how courtship traits evolved: (1) Zahavi's handicap principle - costly ornaments reliably signal fitness because low-fitness pretenders cannot afford the costly display, forcing honesty through wastefulness; (2) Fisher's runaway selection - mate preferences become genetically linked to ornaments, creating positive-feedback escalation of trait complexity. Mental traits function as either direct fitness indexes (intelligence correlates intrinsically with fitness) or as handicaps (costly displays revealing hidden quality). Psychological biases including "novelty-seeking and pleasure-seeking" shape ornament design.

Consumer goods function substantially as fitness-indicator proxies: signaling intelligence, conscientiousness, openness, stability, and mate value rather than delivering the underlying benefits (mate access, belonging, status-resolution) that the signaling machinery evolved to obtain. Luxury consumption, branded goods, and status markers are industrialized exploitation of mate-choice and status-monitoring mechanisms. Consumers chase proxies that activate these systems without resolving the conditions the systems were selected to track.

findings.quote: In every waking moment, your brain uses past experience, organized as concepts, to guide your actions and give your sensations meaning. When the concepts involved are emotion concepts, your brain constructs instances of emotion.
findings.content: Barrett's formal definition of the theory of constructed emotion: the brain uses past experience organized as concepts to guide actions and give sensations meaning. When emotion concepts are active, the brain constructs instances of emotion. Emotions are not triggered reactions but active constructions from interoceptive sensations, conceptual knowledge, and contextual predictions.

findings.quote: the ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven basic affective systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy)
findings.content: The ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven basic affective systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy). These designate specific functional networks of evolutionarily very ancient regions of our brains.
findings.where: Preface, 'Why Psychiatrists, Physicians, and Psychotherapists Should Understand the Seven Basic Affective Systems,' p. xi

findings.quote: The underlying circuits are genetically predetermined and designed to respond unconditionally to stimuli arising from major life-challenging circumstances. These circuits organize diverse behaviors by activating or inhibiting motor subroutines and concurrent autonomic-hormonal changes that have proved adaptive in the face of such life-challenging circumstances during the evolutionary history of the species. Emotive circuits change the sensitivities of sensory systems that are relevant for the behavioral sequences that have been aroused. Neural activity of emotive systems outlasts the precipitating circumstances. Emotive circuits can come under the conditional control of emotionally neutral environmental stimuli. Emotive circuits have reciprocal interactions with the brain mechanisms that elaborate higher decision-making processes and consciousness.
findings.content: Panksepp's six methodological criteria for identifying genuine emotional systems in the brain (Figure 3.3): (1) Underlying circuits are genetically predetermined to respond unconditionally to life-challenging stimuli; (2) they organize diverse behaviors by activating/inhibiting motor subroutines and autonomic-hormonal changes; (3) they change sensitivities of sensory systems relevant to the aroused behavioral sequences; (4) their neural activity outlasts precipitating circumstances; (5) they can come under conditional control of emotionally neutral stimuli; (6) they have reciprocal interactions with higher decision-making and consciousness circuits. Plus the seventh psychological criterion: they must generate affective feelings. This is Panksepp's load-bearing methodological framework for distinguishing emotional systems from general-purpose sensorimotor circuits.

findings.quote: Of course, as mentioned, there is a seventh psychological criterion: The emotional circuits must be able to generate affective feelings, but this is hard to incorporate into the conceptual diagram. I will eventually develop the idea that affect emerges from the many interactions of emotional systems depicted in Figure 3.3 with primal neural mechanisms that represent "the self" (see Chapter 16)
findings.content: Panksepp's central theoretical commitment - the seventh psychological criterion: emotional circuits must be able to generate affective feelings. This criterion is 'hard to incorporate into the conceptual diagram' but is the load-bearing claim that distinguishes affective neuroscience from behavioral neuroscience. Panksepp argues affect emerges from interactions of emotional systems with primal neural mechanisms that represent 'the self', particularly midbrain periaqueductal and deep tectal circuits interacting with frontal cortical systems. Arousal of the executive circuit for each emotion is a NECESSARY CONDITION for getting feeling states activated within the brain. Load-bearing for reading M1-M4/M9/M14 outputs as having affective content, not just behavioral output.

findings.quote: In addition to being the deep neural sources of psychic life, emotional circuits achieve their profound influence over the behavior and mental activity of an organism through the widespread effects on the rest of the nervous system. Emotive circuits change sensory, perceptual, and cognitive processing, and initiate a host of physiological changes that are naturally synchronized with the aroused behavioral tendencies characteristic of emotional experience.
findings.content: Panksepp's architectural claim about emotion-cognition interaction: emotional circuits achieve their profound influence over behavior and mental activity through widespread effects on the rest of the nervous system. Emotive circuits change sensory, perceptual, and cognitive processing, and initiate physiological changes synchronized with the aroused behavioral tendencies. This is NOT just a one-way emotion→behavior pathway - cognition is PENETRATED by emotional-circuit activity, meaning that 'cognitive' function cannot be cleanly separated from affective-circuit function. Load-bearing for Cor's framing that mechanism outputs (M1-M4, M9, M14) shape perception and attention upstream, not just behavior downstream.

Ancestral work was characteristically small-group, embodied, skill-based, and autonomy-rich. Psychological adaptations for work - cognitive mechanisms for toolmaking, resource acquisition, learning, and cooperative production - evolved in the context of small networks of hunter-gatherers where effort-outcome links were visible and physical.

findings.quote: the brain encodes threats directed at familiar others very similarly to how it encodes threats directed at the self - but no such similarity obtains for strangers. Representing relational partners as extensions or aspects of the self could effectively yield bioenergetic resources by influencing how the brain budgets the resources immediately at its disposal. If the relational partner can be counted on to meet all or part of an environmental demand, one’s own resources can either be conserved or devoted to other problems as if personal bioenergetic resources were literally increased. This could explain how the brain construes resources available to relational partners as resources available to the self. Indeed, it suggests that attachment may reflect a neural (and conceptual) conflation of self and other.
findings.content: Social Baseline Theory suggests that the brain encodes what we subjectively experience as the self in ways that literally include close others. The brain encodes threats directed at familiar others very similarly to how it encodes threats directed at the self - but no such similarity obtains for strangers. Representing relational partners as extensions or aspects of the self could effectively yield bioenergetic resources by influencing how the brain budgets the resources immediately at its disposal. If the relational partner can be counted on to meet all or part of an environmental demand, one's own resources can either be conserved or devoted to other problems as if personal bioenergetic resources were literally increased. This suggests that attachment may reflect a neural (and conceptual) conflation of self and other.
findings.where: Section 'Risk, effort, and the expanded self,' p. 89

findings.quote: The innermost group consists of about three to five people.
findings.content: Friendship circles nest in a sequence scaling by factors of approximately three: innermost 5 (close confidants who provide emotional and physical support), then 15 (sympathy group, roughly jury size), 50 (typical hunter-gatherer overnight camp), 150 (Dunbar number, clan/tribal size), with additional layers at 500 and 1500. Each layer represents a qualitatively different type of social relationship with different obligations and investment requirements.

The Strange Situation paradigm: 8 episodes (~21 min) of separation and reunion in a novel room. Three attachment classifications identified: Type B (Secure, ~65-70%) - uses mother as secure base, distressed at separation, seeks contact at reunion, quickly soothed. Type A (Avoidant, ~21%) - conspicuous avoidance at reunion, ignores mother, minimal contact-maintaining. Type C (Ambivalent/Resistant, ~14%) - clingy before separation, intensely distressed during, simultaneously seeks and resists contact at reunion.
findings.where: Patterns of Attachment (1978). DOI: 10.4324/9781315802428. Book, not freely available.

findings.content: The sensitivity hypothesis: maternal sensitivity to infant signals throughout the first year predicts attachment classification. Securely attached infants had consistently responsive mothers. Avoidant infants had rejecting mothers with aversion to close bodily contact. Ambivalent infants had inconsistently responsive mothers. Five behavioral dimensions scored on 1-7 scale: proximity seeking, contact maintaining, avoidance, resistance, search behavior.
findings.where: Patterns of Attachment (1978), sensitivity and scoring chapters

findings.quote: Each layer increases relationship numbers by an approximate multiple of 3 (5-15-50-150) but decreasing levels of intimacy (strong, medium, and weak ties) and frequency of interaction.
findings.content: Personal social networks consist of hierarchically inclusive nested layers of approximately 5/15/50/150 individuals, each layer roughly 3x the previous. Support group (~5): individuals from whom one would seek personal advice in severe distress. Sympathy group (~15): people whose sudden death would be greatly upsetting, contacted at least monthly. Affinity group (~50): casual but close friends. Active network (~150): total recognized and annually interacted with.
findings.where: British Journal of Psychology 103(2):149-168. DOI: 10.1111/j.2044-8295.2011.02061.x. PMID: 22506741. Abstract-limited.

findings.quote: attachment style is related in theoretically meaningful ways to mental models of self and social relationships and to relationship experiences with parents.
findings.content: Attachment style is related to mental models of self and relationships and to childhood relationship memories. Secure adults recall parents as respectful and accepting. Anxious adults remember intermittently available parents. Avoidant adults recall critical and distant parents. Continuity of style is due in part to Bowlby's internal working models - cognitive representations of self and others formed in early relationships that persist and shape adult relational patterns.

findings.quote: Mothers of the securely attached (Group B) babies were, throughout the first year, more sensitively responsive to infant signals than were the mothers of the two anxiously attached groups.
findings.content: Feeding does not determine attachment. No evidence that methods of feeding significantly affected infant development. Instead, sensitive maternal responsiveness to infant signals determines attachment security. Securely attached infants develop working models of mother as accessible and responsive - therein lies security. Insecurely attached infants whose signals were disregarded have no basis for believing mother is responsive, consequently they are anxious.
findings.where: American Psychologist 34(10):932-937, sensitivity and working models section

findings.content: Approximately 40% of available social time is devoted to the innermost 5 people (support clique), and another 20% to the next 10 (completing the sympathy group of 15). Two-thirds of total social time goes to just 15 people, despite having ~150 in the active network.
findings.where: British Journal of Psychology 103(2):149-168, citing Roberts et al and other empirical sources

findings.quote: the association was strongest for complex measures of social integration (OR = 1.91; 95% CI 1.63 to 2.23) and lowest for binary indicators of residential status (living alone versus with others) (OR = 1.19; 95% CI 0.99 to 1.44).
findings.content: Moderator analysis: the association between social relationships and mortality was strongest for complex measures of social integration (OR = 1.91), i.e., multidimensional indices capturing quality and diversity of relationships, and weakest for binary indicators of residential status (living alone vs. with others, OR = 1.19). This gradient indicates that mere co-presence is insufficient; what matters is the structural richness of the social network, not just whether someone shares a roof. The finding rules out the simple hypothesis that mere co-presence buffers stress, and points to relationship quality and network structure as the operative variables.

findings.quote: The overall effect was not moderated by participant sex, length of follow-up, initial health status of participants, or cause of death.
findings.content: Social relationships predict mortality regardless of age, sex, initial health status, cause of death, or geographic region. The effect is not mediated by any single health behavior - it operates across all-cause mortality. Living alone (binary measure) shows the weakest effect (OR=1.19) while complex social integration measures show the strongest (OR=1.91), suggesting that relationship quality and network structure matter more than simple social contact.

Meta-analytic finding: across 148 independent studies pooling 308,849 participants followed for an average of 7.5 years, individuals with stronger social relationships had a 50% increased likelihood of survival compared to individuals with weaker social relationships (random-effects weighted OR = 1.50, 95% CI 1.42-1.59). The association held consistently across age, sex, initial health status, cause of death, and follow-up period. This is the largest, best-controlled quantification of the social-relationships-and-mortality link available.

findings.quote: when we found loneliness in one member of a pair of these identical twins, our prediction of loneliness in the second member of the pair was right approximately forty-eight percent of the time. To understand the significance of that predictive ability, consider that whether an individual is lonely or not lonely is a fifty-fifty proposition, like a coin toss. But our forty-eight percent predictive accuracy was not based on a one-shot flip of the coin. This was a case of being able to predict the outcome forty-eight percent of the time throughout the whole series of several thousand twin pairs. The odds of being right by chance half the time in a series of thousands of fifty-fifty propositions are virtually nil. So what our ability to predict indicated was the influence of heredity. It so happens that a heritability coefficient around .48 also holds true for most of the other genetically influenced major personality characteristics such as neuroticism, agreeableness, and anxiety.
findings.content: Between 1991 and 2003, Dorret Boomsma of the Free University Amsterdam tracked thousands of identical twins in the Netherlands Twin Register on items measuring loneliness.
