When one member of an identical twin pair was lonely, loneliness in the second member could be predicted approximately 48% of the time - a heritability coefficient around .48 that holds true for most major personality characteristics including neuroticism, agreeableness, and anxiety. The genes set the course, but the environment still strongly influences the final destination.
findings.where: Chapter 2 'Variation, Regulation, and an Elastic Leash,' pp. 23-24

findings.quote: Fostering the growth of secure attachment facilitates rather than hampers the growth of healthy self-reliance.
findings.content: Secure attachment facilitates rather than hampers independence. Babies responding positively to close bodily contact also respond positively to being put down and move into exploratory play. Longitudinal follow-up: secure infants became more cooperative, more competent with peers, more curious, more self-directed, and more ego-resilient. Avoidant infants remained more aggressive and noncompliant. Ambivalent infants were more easily frustrated and less persistent.

Protest-despair-detachment: three-phase response to separation from attachment figure. Protest = active attempts to recover the figure (crying, searching, resistance to comforting by others). Despair = withdrawal, hopelessness, reduced activity. Detachment = apparent indifference if caregiver does not return. Based on Robertson's hospital observations and Bowlby's theoretical framework.
findings.where: Attachment and Loss Vol 2 (1973), Part I: Security, Anxiety, and Distress

findings.content: Anger as functional attachment behavior: anger in response to separation is not aggression but protest - a signal to communicate distress and motivate the attachment figure to return. Secure attachment promotes independence and self-reliance, not dependence. Anxious attachment (insecure base) creates heightened susceptibility to fear and anxiety through unreliable caregiver availability.
findings.where: Attachment and Loss Vol 2 (1973), Ch. 16 (Anger, Anxiety, Attachment), Ch. 20 (Secure Attachment and Self-reliance)

findings.quote: In our Ohio State studies we found that the greater the degree of loneliness of the student volunteers, the higher their TPR, even when their overall blood pressure remained normal. This was the case even when we added a bit of stress by asking the students to get up and speak in public, and also when we beeped them during the course of a normal day. In these situations, stress caused blood pressure, TPR, and cardiac output to go up for everyone. But because the lonely group started out with higher TPR, their TPR under stress was higher still.
findings.content: In our Ohio State studies we found that the greater the degree of loneliness of the student volunteers, the higher their total peripheral resistance (TPR), even when their overall blood pressure remained normal. Active coping raises blood pressure primarily by revving up cardiac output. Coping passively - which is what we do when we feel isolated - raises blood pressure primarily by constricting the small arteries, also known as increasing TPR. Higher TPR forces the heart muscle to work harder to distribute the same amount of liquid through the blood vessels.
findings.where: Chapter 6 'The Wear and Tear of Loneliness,' Pathway 4, pp. 103-104

findings.quote: recent analyses suggest that it may have been the particular demands of the more intense forms of pairbonding that was the critical factor that triggered this evolutionary development
findings.content: Across five vertebrate taxa (carnivores, ungulates, bats, birds, primates), pair-bonded species consistently have larger relative brain sizes than non-pair-bonded species. Fisher combined probability test: chi-squared(10)=48.04, p<<0.001. The effect holds even excluding primates: chi-squared(8)=46.42, p<0.001.
findings.where: Science 317(5843):1344-1347, DOI: 10.1126/science.1145463. PMID: 17823343. Companion data in Shultz & Dunbar 2007 Proc B (PMC2274976).

findings.quote: Primate sociality is based on bonded relationships of a kind that are found only in pairbonds in other taxa.
findings.content: Primates are the sole exception to the pair-bonding rule: only in primates does group size (not pair-bonding) predict brain size. Strong positive correlation between group size and brain size in primates (lambda=0.80, F(1,40)=8.14, p<0.01). No such relationship in carnivores (p=0.80) or artiodactyls (p=0.58).
findings.where: Science 317(5843):1344-1347 and Shultz & Dunbar 2007 Proc B (PMC2274976), PGLS analysis

findings.quote: These results undermine conventional notions of what constitutes social complexity. Indeed, we doubt that many would have seriously suggested that pairbonded social systems are more complex (and by implication, more cognitively demanding) than large polygamous or promiscuously mating groups.
findings.content: Anthropoid primates differ significantly from all other taxa in proportion of species with bonded social structure (chi-squared(2)=8.49, p=0.01). Strepsirhine primates do NOT differ from ungulates and carnivores (chi-squared(2)=1.89, p=0.39). The bonding generalization is specific to anthropoids, not all primates.
findings.where: Shultz & Dunbar 2007 Proc B (PMC2274976), bonded relationships analysis

findings.quote: The guiding evolutionary concept was that neural systems that elaborate social attachments have evolutionary relations with those that mediate the affective qualities of physical pain, including modulation by the same chemistries such as endogenous opioids.
findings.content: PANIC/separation-distress system evolved from physical pain mechanisms. Social attachments are mediated by the same neurochemistry as physical pain, particularly endogenous opioids. The PAG is the brain area from which emotional distress is most readily evoked in both humans and animals with the lowest ESB levels. Social exclusion and depression activate anterior cingulate regions known to regulate pain.

findings.quote: Neocortex ratio is thus the single most powerful predictor of group size in these species.
findings.content: Stepwise regression on 24 anthropoid primate species with 9 brain volume indices confirms neocortex ratio as the single most powerful predictor of group size. Independent contrasts analysis: r²=0.395, F(1,22)=15.39, P=0.001. No other brain index makes a significant contribution after neocortex ratio is included.
findings.where: Evolutionary Anthropology 6(5):178-190, Table 2 and stepwise regression section. DOI: 10.1002/(SICI)1520-6505(1998)6:5<178::AID-EVAN5>3.0.CO;2-8

findings.quote: brain evolution has not been a history of simple expansion in total volume. Rather, brain evolution has been mosaic in character, with both the rate and the extent of evolution having varied between components of the system.
findings.content: Relative neocortex volume correlates with group size but NOT range area, while relative hippocampus size shows the reverse pattern (correlates with range but NOT group size). This double dissociation demonstrates that brain evolution is mosaic: specific brain components serve specific functions, not general intelligence.
findings.where: Evolutionary Anthropology 6(5):178-190, hippocampus section, citing Barton & Purvis

findings.quote: there is no intrinsic reason to suppose that memory per se is the issue. The social brain hypothesis is about the ability to manipulate information, not simply to remember it.
findings.content: The social brain constraint is about ability to manipulate social information, not simply to remember individuals. Apes show grade-shifted cognitive demands per relationship compared to monkeys: apes are good psychologists (they read minds via theory of mind), while monkeys are good ethologists (they read behavior).
findings.where: Evolutionary Anthropology 6(5):178-190, discussion of cognitive mechanisms

findings.quote: Group size is found to be a function of relative neocortical volume, but the ecological variables are not. This is interpreted as evidence in favour of the social intellect theory and against the ecological theories.
findings.content: Neocortex ratio (neocortex volume / rest-of-brain volume) predicts mean group size across 38 primate genera with r²=0.764 (t34=10.35, P<0.001). The regression equation log10(N) = 0.093 + 3.389·log10(CR) yields a predicted human group size of ~148, matching ethnographic data. Human neocortex ratio = 4.10.
findings.where: Journal of Human Evolution 22(6):469-493, Table 1 and regression analysis

findings.quote: even if it were true that energetic considerations constrain brain size, a proper functional explanation must still be given to explain why brains grow to the size they do.
findings.content: Ecological variables fail to predict neocortex ratio. Percentage fruit in diet is unrelated. Range size and day journey length correlate in raw form but collapse to near zero when body mass is partialled out (residual r²=0.017 for range, r²<0.001 for day journey). Extractive foraging also fails once anthropoids are analyzed separately.
findings.where: Journal of Human Evolution 22(6):469-493, ecological analysis section

findings.quote: the number of neocortical neurons limits the organism's information-processing capacity and that this then limits the number of relationships that an individual can monitor simultaneously.
findings.content: The number of neocortical neurons limits information-processing capacity, which constrains the number of relationships an individual can monitor simultaneously. The constraint operates on relationship structure and quality, not raw number of dyads.

findings.quote: the data suggest that the information overload occurs in terms of the structure of relationships within tightly bonded grooming cliques rather than in terms of the total number of dyads within the group as a whole.
findings.content: Female group size (r²=0.568) is a worse predictor of neocortex ratio than total group size (r²=0.764), indicating the cognitive constraint operates on total group membership, not just the reproductively relevant female core.
findings.where: Journal of Human Evolution 22(6):469-493, female group size analysis

findings.quote: this interval of delay depresses the intensity of the affectional response below that of the infant monkeys that were surrogate-mothered from birth onward.
findings.content: Late-adopted controls (surrogates introduced at day 250) reached ~9 hours daily contact within 10 days but behavioral intensity remained lower than birth-reared animals. This demonstrates a sensitive period for attachment formation - delay depresses the intensity of affectional response.

In birds, lifelong pair-bonds (not annual re-pairing) predict larger brains. Bi-parental care does not drive the effect. The cognitive demand is specifically about maintaining long-term bonded relationships, not mate choice or parental coordination per se.
findings.where: Science 317(5843):1344-1347 and Shultz & Dunbar 2007 Proc B, bird analysis

findings.quote: In primates, there is a quantitative relationship between brain size and social group size (group size is a monotonic function of brain size)... In other mammals and birds, the relationship is a qualitative one: Large brains are associated with categorical differences in mating system.
findings.content: The social brain hypothesis takes two distinct forms across taxa. In primates: a quantitative relationship where group size is a monotonic function of brain size. In all other mammals and birds: a qualitative relationship where pair-bonded species have categorically larger brains than non-pair-bonded species.
findings.where: Annals of Human Biology 36(5):562-572, abstract and introduction. DOI: 10.1080/03014460902960289. PMID: 19575315

findings.quote: SBT suggests that proximity to social resources decreases the cost of climbing both the literal and figurative hills we face, because the brain construes social resources as bioenergetic resources, much like oxygen or glucose. Indeed, evidence suggests that hills literally appear less steep when standing next to a friend. Moreover, socially isolated individuals consume more sugar, even after adjusting for body mass index, weight related self-image, depression, physical activity, educational level, age and income. To the human brain, social and metabolic resources are treated almost interchangeably.
findings.content: Social Baseline Theory suggests that proximity to social resources decreases the cost of climbing both the literal and figurative hills we face, because the brain construes social resources as bioenergetic resources, much like oxygen or glucose. Evidence suggests that hills literally appear less steep when standing next to a friend. Moreover, socially isolated individuals consume more sugar, even after adjusting for body mass index, weight-related self-image, depression, physical activity, educational level, age, and income. To the human brain, social and metabolic resources are treated almost interchangeably.
findings.where: Section 'Social relationships decrease the predicted cost of the environment,' p. 88

findings.quote: Although the brain is highly responsive to perceived threat, even simple handholding can substantially attenuate threat responses.
findings.content: SBT describes two mechanisms for social regulation: risk distribution (safety in numbers) and load sharing (distribution of effort toward shared goals). During supportive handholding, the threat-responsive brain returns to a baseline state of relative calm - not through activation of regulatory circuitry but through decreased perceived demand. The brain encodes relational partners as extensions of the self, effectively pooling bioenergetic resources.

findings.quote: Monkey grooming is not about removing fleas. Rather, it is about the intimacy of massage. The physical stimulation of the skin triggers the release of endorphins in the brain.
findings.content: Primate grooming is not about removing fleas - it is about the intimacy of massage. Physical stimulation of the skin triggers endorphin release in the brain. Low-level pain associated with generalized stresses is dealt with by the endorphin system, creating a sense of wellbeing and relaxed contentedness. Grooming is the mechanism through which primate social bonds are maintained.

findings.quote: Laughter - and I mean deep belly laughter, not the polite titters that tinkled among T.S. Eliot's teacups - is an extremely effective releaser of endorphins, probably because the physical effort of laughter's heaving chest is quite hard work for the muscles.
findings.content: Laughter - deep belly laughter, not polite titters - is an extremely effective releaser of endorphins, probably because the physical effort is hard work for the muscles. Communal laughter creates a sense of bondedness that goes beyond tension release. Language evolved as a form of grooming at distance - 'I'd rather be here with you than over there with Jennifer.'

findings.quote: especially the endogenous opioid peptides, are already known to modify feeling states in humans and corresponding behavioral changes in animals.
findings.content: Panksepp's original discovery linking endogenous opioids to separation distress: brain opioids (especially beta-endorphin and enkephalins) modulate social feelings and separation distress, AND opioids promote social bonding. Oxytocin and opioids work together to inhibit separation distress. This is Panksepp's foundational finding that attachment pain shares neural substrates with physical pain - the 'social pain' hypothesis at the molecular level. Load-bearing for M3 Social Bonding, DA8 Phylogenetic Priority (opioid system is ancient), and for reading depression/grief as dysregulation of an opioid-modulated affective circuit rather than a purely cognitive state.
findings.where: Chapter 6 'Neurochemical Maps of the Brain' pp. ~101

findings.quote: we now have considerable evidence that opioids participate
findings.content: Panksepp's more specific primary-source claim: brain opioids promote the development of food and social attachments, and the inhibition of separation distress. In young animals, opioid agonists reduce separation-distress vocalizations; opioid antagonists increase them. This is the neurochemical bridge from physical pain (classically opioid-modulated) to social pain (separation distress), grounding the architectural claim that social rejection activates the same molecular systems as physical injury. Load-bearing for the M3 cascade connecting social bonds to physical-pain circuitry and for the DA8 phylogenetic-priority claim that attachment evolved by repurposing older pain-modulation systems.

Although the brain is highly responsive to perceived threat, even simple handholding can substantially attenuate threat responses. These effects are potentiated by higher relationship quality, intimacy, and higher perceived mutuality. Critically, the likeliest mechanisms linking social support to diminished threat responding - regulatory circuits within the prefrontal cortex - are not more activated by support provision as originally hypothesized, but less so. During supportive handholding in particular, the threat responsive brain appears to return to a baseline state of relative calm, suggesting the difference is attributable less to the activation of regulatory circuitry and more to a decrease in perceived demand associated with the threat, a decrease proportional to the increase in resources brought to bear by the relational partner.
findings.where: Section 'Risk, effort, and the expanded self,' pp. 88-89

findings.quote: Please recall the prairie vole. These individuals form lifelong pair-bonds soon after puberty and raise several litters as a team. And this pairing has been directly correlated with neurochemical activities in the brain. When prairie voles first engage in sex, copulation triggers activity in oxytocin receptors (in the nucleus accumbens) among females and vasopressin receptors (in the ventral pallidum) among males. This stimulates dopamine release in several brain regions - producing feelings of wanting, seeking, focus, energy, pleasure, and motivation - driving these furry little creatures to prefer a particular mate, initiate a pair-bond, and express enduring attachment behaviors. But specific variations in a particular gene in the vasopressin system contribute to variability in the strength of a male prairie vole's pair-bond, including the degree to which a male expresses sexual fidelity to his partner.
findings.content: When prairie voles first engage in sex, copulation triggers activity in oxytocin receptors (in the nucleus accumbens) among females and vasopressin receptors (in the ventral pallidum) among males. This stimulates dopamine release in several brain regions - producing feelings of wanting, seeking, focus, energy, pleasure, and motivation - driving these furry little creatures to prefer a particular mate, initiate a pair-bond, and express enduring attachment behaviors. Specific variations in a particular gene in the vasopressin system contribute to variability in the strength of a male prairie vole's pair-bond, including the degree to which a male expresses sexual fidelity to his partner.
findings.where: Chapter 4 'Why Adultery?' Biology of Adultery section, pp. 92-93

findings.quote: In our studies, the lonely, both young and old, perceived the hassles and stresses of everyday life to be more severe than did their nonlonely counterparts, even though the objective stressors they encountered were essentially the same. Compounding the problem, the lonely found the small social uplifts of everyday life to be less intense and less gratifying.
findings.content: In our studies, the lonely, both young and old, perceived the hassles and stresses of everyday life to be more severe than did their nonlonely counterparts, even though the objective stressors they encountered were essentially the same. The lonely also found the small social uplifts of everyday life to be less intense and less gratifying. The presence of and interaction with other people in their lives did not cause them to rate the severity of everyday stressors any less intensely.
findings.where: Chapter 6 'The Wear and Tear of Loneliness,' Pathway 3 'Perceived Stress and Coping,' pp. 102-103

findings.quote: This article explores the possibility that romantic love is an attachment process--a biosocial process by which affectional bonds are formed between adult lovers, just as affectional bonds are formed earlier in life between human infants and their parents.
findings.content: Adult romantic love is an attachment process: affectional bonds form between adult lovers just as between infants and parents. Three adult attachment styles parallel Ainsworth's infant categories. Distribution: ~56% secure, ~25% avoidant, ~19% anxious-ambivalent (N=620 in Study 1), closely matching infant distributions (~62/23/15%). Secure adults describe relationships as happy, friendly, trusting. Avoidant adults fear closeness and doubt romantic love exists. Anxious adults experience love as obsessive with constant abandonment worry.

Oxytocin (OT) operates through three distinct but neurobiologically consistent mechanisms to support human affiliative bonds. (a) Parent-infant bonding: maternal OT levels measured in the first trimester predicted postpartum behavior (gaze, positive affect, motherese, affectionate touch); OT was stable within individuals across pregnancy; fathers showed comparable baseline OT to mothers and active paternal care activated the OT system. OT administration to fathers increased their touch behavior AND independently increased infant salivary OT, RSA, social gaze, and toy exploration - demonstrating cross-dyadic transmission. (b) Pair bonding: new romantic partners showed significantly higher plasma OT than singles, even higher than new parents; OT correlated with interactive synchrony (social focus, positive affect, affectionate touch) and was stable over six months. (c) Group affiliation: OT was linked to children's best-friend relationship quality and broader social engagement. Across all bond types, OT levels showed "biological synchrony" between partners - mother-father OT was inter-correlated, parent-infant OT was inter-related, and romantic partners' OT levels were concordant.

In a study of 112 parents and their 4-6 month olds, active parental touch triggered measurable OT responses. Mothers providing high levels of affectionate touch (>66% of interaction time) showed increased salivary OT from pre- to post-interaction, while mothers providing minimal touch (<33%) showed no such increase. Fathers who provided high levels of stimulatory contact (moving child's limbs, throwing infant in air) similarly increased their OT levels, but those engaging in minimal stimulatory touch did not. Risk alleles on the OXTR rs2254298 and CD38 rs3796863 SNPs were associated with both lower plasma OT and reduced parental affectionate touch, paralleling findings of high vs. low licking-and-grooming rat dams.

Cross-generational transmission of the oxytocin system operates through parenting behavior rather than genetics alone. In a study of parents and 6-month-old infants, parent-infant OT levels were inter-related at both baseline and following contact, and the degree of OT increase was correlated between parent and child. Critically, parent-infant behavioral synchrony moderated the intergenerational effect: when synchrony was high, parent-child OT concordance was strong; when synchrony was low, no association emerged. Adults' retrospective accounts of warm parental care in childhood predicted higher current plasma OT. Risk alleles on OXTR and CD38 predicted lower OT, less affectionate touch, and shorter episodes of gaze synchrony. Mothers and fathers who reported more positive care in their own childhood provided more affectionate touch to their infants.

Bio-behavioral synchrony is the mechanism by which organisms become members of a social group. Among mammalian species, dyad-specific maternal-infant bonds are built on repeatedly experienced patterns of sensory, motor, and behavioral cues. Human mothers provide approximately 70% of their social behaviors during the 7% of the time newborns spend in alert-scanning state, creating temporal contingencies between infant state and maternal social behavior from the first post-birth hours. These social contingencies are supported by physiological periodicities maturing in the fetus during the third trimester: the biological clock and cardiac pacemaker. As soon as the human infant is born, it can experience a temporal match between its own state and the response of the social environment. This early temporal concordance is a critical human addition to the physiological provisions embedded in maternal proximity in other mammals.

findings.quote: Thus, Warneken et al. (2006, 2007) had infants of this age engage in a joint activity with an adult, such as obtaining a toy by each operating one side of an apparatus. Then, the adult simply stopped playing her role for no reason. The children were not happy about this and did various things to attempt to reengage their partner. (They did not do this if her stopping was for a good reason; e.g., she had to attend to something else [Warneken et al., 2012].) Interesting, when this same situation was arranged for human-raised chimpanzees, they simply ignored the recalcitrant partner and tried to find ways to achieve the goal on their own.
findings.content: Children vs chimps reengagement experiment: Warneken et al. had 14-18 month old human infants engage in joint activity with an adult (operating an apparatus). When the adult stopped playing her role for no reason, children were unhappy and attempted to reengage the partner. When the SAME situation was arranged for human-raised chimpanzees, chimps ignored the partner and tried to complete the goal alone. This dissociation - even at prelinguistic ages, humans expect partners in joint activity to be committed enough to reengage, chimps do not - is a central behavioral marker of joint intentionality.

findings.quote: Importantly, when children of this same age have it in their common ground with a collaborative partner that each is counting on the other to come through (we are interdependent), they both feel obligated to the other (see Gilbert, 1989, 1990). Thus, Gräfenhain et al. (2009) had preschoolers explicitly agree to play a game with one adult, and then another adult attempted to lure them away to a more exciting game. Although two-year-old children mostly just bolted to the new game straightaway, from three years of age children paused before departing and "took leave," either verbally or by handing the adult the tool they had been using together. The children seemed to recognize that joint goals involve joint commitments, the breaking of which requires some kind of acknowledgment or even apology. No study of this type has ever been done with chimpanzees, but there are no published reports of one chimpanzee taking leave from, making excuses to, or apologizing to another for breaking a joint commitment.
findings.content: Taking leave: Gräfenhain 2009 had preschoolers explicitly agree to play a game with one adult; then another adult attempted to lure them to a more exciting game. Two-year-olds mostly bolted to the new game, but from age 3 children paused before departing and 'took leave' - verbally or by handing the adult the shared tool. Children recognized that joint goals involve joint commitments, the breaking of which requires acknowledgment. No published reports of chimpanzees taking leave from, making excuses to, or apologizing to another for breaking a joint commitment exist. This is specific evidence for commitment-as-moral-obligation in joint intentionality.

findings.quote: A quick survey of available ethnography indicates how widespread shared care is among foraging peoples.
findings.content: Ethnographic survey of shared care among foraging peoples: !Kung San babies have available the mother's entire social world with intense face-to-face interactions from girls. Trobriand Islanders routinely share infants who are suckled by lactating allomothers. Hadza babies under four are held by mothers 69% of the time and by allomothers the rest. These mothers trust others and allow them to take infants shortly after birth.

findings.quote: But primates are unusual. Instead of decamping after they mate, fathers in most species in the order Primates remain year-round in the same social group as the mothers of their offspring.
findings.content: Primates are unusual: instead of decamping after mating, fathers in most primate species remain in the same social group year-round. In New World monkeys like titi and night monkeys, fathers are primary attachment figures - infants are more attached to fathers than mothers. This establishes paternal care as an ancestral primate capacity, not a modern cultural invention.

findings.quote: if a mouse is injected with BCG, the vaccine against tuberculosis, it passes through a short-term phase of sickness behaviour in the first few days after vaccination but then remains socially isolated from other mice and takes less pleasure in life for many weeks. It looks very much as if the mouse has become chronically depressed as a result of being inflamed.
findings.content: Chronic sickness behavior in mice: BCG vaccination produces a short-term acute sickness-behavior phase (first few days), followed by SOCIAL ISOLATION and REDUCED PLEASURE in drinking sweetened water (anhedonia) that lasts for weeks. The anhedonia (via sucrose-preference testing) maps to a core symptom of major depressive disorder. This is the strongest animal-model evidence that persistent inflammation produces a persistent depression-like state rather than just acute illness behavior, and that the behavioral change reflects a genuine motivational/hedonic change rather than passive sickness.

findings.quote: individuals with adequate social relationships have a 50% greater likelihood of survival compared to those with poor or insufficient social relationships.
findings.content: Meta-analysis of 148 studies (308,849 participants, 7.5 year average follow-up): individuals with stronger social relationships had a 50% greater likelihood of survival (OR=1.50, 95% CI 1.42-1.59). This effect is comparable to smoking cessation and exceeds the influence of obesity and physical inactivity on mortality. Complex social integration measures showed the strongest effect (OR=1.91). The association held across age, sex, initial health status, cause of death, follow-up period, and geographic region.
findings.where: PLoS Medicine, DOI: 10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316, PMID: 20668659 (open access full text)

findings.quote: More than half of respondents reported at least one, and one-fourth reported two or more categories of childhood exposures.
findings.content: The ACE Study identified seven categories of childhood adversity and found that more than half of respondents reported at least one, and one-fourth reported two or more categories. The graded dose-response relationship - where each additional ACE category incrementally increases risk - demonstrates that childhood adversity is cumulative rather than categorical. Persons with 4+ categories had 4-12 fold increased health risk, suggesting a threshold effect where the cascade becomes self-reinforcing.

findings.quote: F93-96 females did not seem to treat transfer males in a contingent manner
findings.content: Cultural transmission mechanism: resident females were the key. Transfer males arrived as aggressive as those joining control troops. But Forest Troop females had shorter latency to groom/present to newcomers and were unconditionally more affiliative - not contingent on newcomer behavior. The pattern was NOT an artifact of sex ratio: five other troops with similar ratios resembled controls, not Forest Troop.
findings.where: PLoS Biology 2(4):e106, transmission analysis. Full text.

findings.content: 10-year longitudinal RCT (N=146): Kangaroo Care (14 days skin-to-skin) vs incubator care in preterm infants. KC increased autonomic functioning (RSA), maternal attachment, reduced maternal anxiety. Enhanced child cognitive development and executive functions from 6 months to 10 years. By age 10: better sleep organization, more mature EEG patterns, better cognitive control. 14 days of contact correction produced a decade of measurable developmental advantage.

findings.quote: Thus, critically, the troop's unique culture was being adopted by new males joining the troop.
findings.content: Forest Troop natural experiment: bovine tuberculosis selectively killed the most aggressive males (46% of adult males who competed at a garbage dump), leaving atypically unaggressive survivors with a >2:1 female-to-male ratio. A decade later (1993-96), when NO original males remained, the low-aggression culture persisted: relaxed dominance hierarchy, reduced male-to-female aggression, more male-female grooming, closer proximity to females/infants.
findings.where: PLoS Biology 2(4):e106. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pbio.0020106. PMC387274. Full text.

findings.quote: Across the three intervals, the mean proportion of repeated campmates was 12.1%.
findings.content: Across 6 years / 4 waves, Hadza camps continuously dissolve and reconstitute: only ~12% of campmates repeat year-over-year (implying ~88% annual turnover), yet cooperative assortment persists.

findings.quote: Depression may feel bad because brain separation-distress systems create psychological pain.
findings.content: PANIC/GRIEF circuitry maps directly onto brain targets for treatment-resistant depression: starts in the PAG, ascends through dorsomedial thalamus, and terminates in subcallosal anterior cingulate - the same regions targeted by deep brain stimulation (Mayberg et al., 2005). Key neurochemistry: declining opioids and oxytocin, elevated CRF, increased glutamate. Dynorphin mediates SEEKING shutdown as a distinct form of negative affect.

findings.quote: some of the infants who seemed most solidly attached to their mothers displayed little protest behaviour or separation anxiety, but rather showed the strength of their attachment to the mother through their readiness to use her as a secure base from which
findings.content: Ainsworth's secure base concept as reported by Bowlby: some infants who seemed most solidly attached to their mothers displayed little protest behavior or separation anxiety. Instead, they showed the strength of their attachment through their readiness to use the mother as a secure base from which to explore. This redefines secure attachment not as constant proximity-seeking but as confident exploration enabled by the availability of the attachment figure.

findings.quote: loss of mother-figure, either by itself or in combination with other variables yet to be clearly identified, is capable of generating responses and processes that are of the greatest interest to psychopathology. Not only so, but these responses and processes, we concluded, are the very same as are known to be active in older individuals who are still disturbed by separations that they suffered in early life.
findings.content: Loss of the mother-figure generates responses and processes of the greatest interest to psychopathology. These responses are the very same as those active in older individuals still disturbed by early separations. On one hand: excessive demands on others, anxiety and anger when demands are unmet (dependent and hysterical personalities). On the other: blockage in the capacity to make deep relationships (affectionless and psychopathic personalities).

findings.quote: close examination reveals that the different signalling components of attachment behaviour are far from being interchangeable; rather, each is found to be distinctive and to be complementary to each of the others.
findings.content: Signalling components of attachment behavior - including crying - are distinctive and complementary, not interchangeable. Crying takes several different forms elicited by different conditions: crying from hunger builds slowly and becomes rhythmical; crying from pain is loud from the start with a sudden long initial cry. Different signal types elicit different components of maternal behavior, demonstrating that attachment signaling is a differentiated communication system.

findings.quote: in another of our brain scanning experiments, led this time by psychologist Bianca Acevedo, we put seventeen long-married women and men into the fMRI scanner, ten women and seven men. Their average length of marriage was twenty-one years; most had grown children; and all had told us that they were still in love with their spouse. The results were astonishing: the VTA and other basic brain regions associated with early-stage intense romantic love were just as active among these long-term lovers as among our newly-in-love younger men and women. With one exception: Our newly-in-love participants showed activity in a specific brain region associated with anxiety, whereas in our long-term lovers this angst was replaced by new activity in brain regions linked with calm and pain suppression.
findings.content: In Acevedo et al.'s fMRI brain scanning experiment, seventeen long-married women and men were scanned while viewing photos of their spouse. Average length of marriage was twenty-one years; most had grown children; all said they were still in love with their spouse. The results were astonishing: the VTA and other basic brain regions associated with early-stage intense romantic love were just as active among these long-term lovers as among newly-in-love younger men and women. One exception: newly-in-love participants showed activity in a brain region associated with anxiety, whereas in long-term lovers this angst was replaced by new activity in brain regions linked with calm and pain suppression.
findings.where: Chapter 2 'The Trajectory of Love' pp. 38-39, Acevedo, Aron, Fisher, Brown long-term marriage fMRI study

findings.quote: Our studies showed that loneliness on a given day predicted a higher rise in cortisol the next morning. In addition, when we drew blood from our older adults and analyzed their white cells, we found that loneliness somehow penetrated the deepest recesses of the cell to alter the way genes were being expressed. Loneliness predicted changes in DNA transcription that, in turn, made changes in the cell's sensitivity to circulating cortisol, dampening the ability to shut off the inflammatory response.
findings.content: Our studies showed that loneliness on a given day predicted a higher rise in cortisol the next morning. When we drew blood from our older adults and analyzed their white cells, we found that loneliness somehow penetrated the deepest recesses of the cell to alter the way genes were being expressed. Loneliness predicted changes in DNA transcription that, in turn, made changes in the cell's sensitivity to circulating cortisol, dampening the ability to shut off the inflammatory response.
findings.where: Chapter 6 'The Wear and Tear of Loneliness,' pp. 105-106, citing Cole, Hawkley, Arevalo, Sung, Rose & Cacioppo 'Social regulation of gene expression in human leukocytes'

findings.quote: As indicated in Figure 14, nonlonely participants showed greater activity in the ventral striatum, one of the brain's 'reward centers,' when they saw a pleasant image of a person (a smiling farmer) than when they saw an equally pleasant picture of an object (a flower arrangement). For the nonlonely, a positive image of another human being obviously meant something special - it gave them a specific emotional boost as evidenced by changes in this specific area that registers pleasure. Lonely participants, however, when they viewed positive images of people, did not register the same boost: The activation of the ventral striatum in response to a happy face was in fact a bit weaker than when they saw the pleasant picture of the flowers. This finding aligns with self-reports in which lonely individuals said that they found positive social interactions to be less of an uplift than did their nonlonely counterparts.
findings.content: In a study at the University of Chicago Brain Imaging Center, volunteers viewed photographs of objects or people, selected to have positive or negative emotional impact. Nonlonely participants showed greater activity in the ventral striatum - one of the brain's reward centers - when they saw a pleasant image of a person (a smiling farmer) than when they saw an equally pleasant picture of an object (a flower arrangement). For the nonlonely, a positive image of another human being meant something special. Lonely participants, however, when viewing positive images of people, did not register the same boost: the activation of the ventral striatum in response to a happy face was in fact a bit weaker than when they saw the pleasant picture of the flowers.
findings.where: Chapter 9 'A Concerto for Two (or More) Voices,' Brain Imaging Center study, pp. 162-163

findings.quote: In the same study, when the photographs were negative, the patterns of brain activation were equally revealing about the experience of loneliness, moment to moment. Whereas nonlonely participants paid comparable attention to negative images of people and objects, lonely individuals paid far more attention to the negative images depicting people. In both cases, the measure was activation of their visual cortex. When we observed the temporoparietal junction, an area involved in theory of mind and in perspective taking, the pattern of activation was the opposite. Lonely individuals appeared more likely than their nonlonely counterparts to respond to pictures of people in peril from their first-person perspective (as indicated by weaker activation of the temporoparietal junction). When we feel lonely, we tend to scan the horizon for any possibility of social danger, but with an eye toward protecting ourselves rather than with genuine concern for what others may be thinking or feeling.
findings.content: In the same Chicago Brain Imaging Center fMRI study, when participants viewed negative images, the patterns of brain activation were equally revealing. Nonlonely participants paid comparable attention to negative images of people and objects. Lonely individuals, however, paid far more attention to the negative images depicting people - measured by visual cortex activation. When observing the temporoparietal junction, an area involved in theory of mind and perspective taking, lonely individuals appeared more likely to respond to pictures of people in peril from their first-person perspective rather than with genuine concern for what others may be thinking or feeling.

findings.quote: exams could have a dramatic dampening effect on the immune response, leaving the students more vulnerable to infections. Further studies showed that lonely students were far more adversely affected than those who felt socially contented.
findings.content: In laboratory stressor studies, loneliness and the immune response interact: lonely students were far more adversely affected by examination stress than those who felt socially contented. Chronic low-grade inflammation promoted by persistent loneliness connects to cardiovascular disease and to the allostatic-load cascade.
findings.where: Chapter 6 'The Wear and Tear of Loneliness,' p. 104

findings.quote: Tana was raised in a Romanian orphanage. At age seven, relief workers found her all skin and bones and only half the height of a normal child her age.
findings.content: Touch deprivation in Romanian orphanages produced devastating consequences: children were skeletal, half normal height, unable to walk or run. After months of regular nutrition and massage therapy, orphanage children recovered physically - illustrating that touch is not merely pleasant but a biological necessity for normal development. Touch deprivation produces growth hormone suppression and immune dysfunction.

findings.quote: Women with physical contact before stress exhibited significantly lower cortisol and heart rate responses to stress but no different plasma oxytocin levels.
findings.content: Physical contact from a partner before stress significantly lowers cortisol and heart rate responses. A ten-minute neck and shoulder massage produced greater stress buffering than verbal social support or no partner interaction. Touch-based social regulation operates through direct physiological pathways (cortisol suppression, cardiovascular calming) not just psychological comfort.

findings.quote: It is becoming harder to believe that general brain serotonergic and/or noradrenergic changes, which globally regulate aspects of forebrain arousal and dynamics, will specifically explain the morbid moods of depression.
findings.content: SSRIs have modest overall efficacy (STAR*D findings); serotonin and norepinephrine regulate general arousal, not the specific affect of depression. More targeted interventions include ultra-low-dose buprenorphine (which both activates mu-opioid receptors and blocks despair-promoting dynorphin/kappa receptors), oxytocin, CRF antagonists, and glutamate modulators (ketamine). Psychotherapeutic activation of CARE and PLAY systems remains almost completely untapped.

findings.quote: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) shows us that the emotional region of the brain that is activated when we experience rejection is, in fact, the same region - the dorsal anterior cingulate - that registers emotional responses to physical pain
findings.content: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) shows that the emotional region of the brain activated when we experience rejection is the same region - the dorsal anterior cingulate - that registers emotional responses to physical pain. The discovery that feelings of social rejection (isolation) and reactions to physical pain share the same hardware begins to suggest why, once loneliness becomes chronic, you cannot escape it merely by 'coming out of your shell,' losing weight, getting a fashion makeover, or meeting Mr. or Ms. Right.
findings.where: Chapter 1 'Lonely in a Social World,' pp. 8-9, citing Eisenberger, Lieberman, Williams (2003) 'Does rejection hurt? An fMRI study of social exclusion,' Science 302:290-292

findings.quote: These subcortical brain networks are quite similar in all mammals, but they are not identical in all details. This similarity extends even to certain species of birds that, for instance, also have separation-distress PANIC networks
findings.content: These subcortical brain networks are quite similar in all mammals, but they are not identical in all details. This similarity extends even to certain species of birds that, for instance, also have separation-distress PANIC networks. Across many species of warm-blooded vertebrates, a variety of basic emotional networks are anatomically situated in similar brain regions, and these networks serve remarkably similar functions.

findings.quote: large groups are created by welding together sets of smaller grooming cliques
findings.content: The regression slope of 3.389 (greater than 1) indicates large groups are created by combining smaller grooming cliques, not by uniformly expanding the social network. The cognitive limit lies in maintaining clique-internal relationship quality, not total relationship count.
findings.where: Journal of Human Evolution 22(6):469-493, discussion of slope

findings.quote: contact comfort is a variable of overwhelming importance in the development of affectional response, whereas lactation is a variable of negligible importance.
findings.content: Contact comfort overwhelms lactation as determinant of infant attachment. Infant rhesus monkeys spent 17-18 hours/day on cloth-covered surrogate mother vs ~1 hour on wire mother, regardless of which mother provided milk. No measurable difference between cloth-fed and wire-fed groups in cloth preference. 8 newborn monkeys in dual-surrogate condition tested over 165+ consecutive days.
findings.where: American Psychologist 13:673-685. Full text at psychclassics.yorku.ca/Harlow/love.htm

findings.quote: The wire mother is biologically adequate but psychologically inept.
findings.content: Cloth mother serves as secure base for exploration. When frightened by novel stimuli, infants consistently fled to cloth mother regardless of food source. In open-field tests with cloth mother present, emotionality scores reduced by half. Without any mother, infants froze in crouched positions. Wire mother provided zero comfort function in any fear test.

Cross-fostering pups of low-licking/grooming (low-LG) rat mothers to high-LG mothers REVERSED the epigenetic programming at the glucocorticoid receptor gene promoter in hippocampus. Offspring of low-LG mothers who were cross-fostered to high-LG mothers showed: (1) reversed DNA methylation patterns matching biological high-LG offspring, (2) normalized histone acetylation, (3) restored NGFI-A transcription factor binding, (4) increased GR expression, and (5) attenuated HPA stress responses. These changes emerged over the first week of life and persisted into adulthood. Additionally, central infusion of a histone deacetylase inhibitor in adult offspring of low-LG mothers removed all group differences, demonstrating that the epigenomic state is causally responsible for the phenotypic differences.

Total social isolation from birth produces devastating behavioral deficits scaling with duration. 3-month isolates slowly recovered with minimal long-term damage (one died of emotional anorexia). 6-month isolates showed severe deficits in virtually every aspect of social behavior - no contact play, only limited recovery. 12-month isolates were almost obliterated socially - zero activity play, persistent fear, no positive social behavior.

Upon release from isolation, monkeys entered a state of emotional shock characterized by autistic self-clutching and rocking, blank staring, cage circling, and self-mutilation. When placed with normal peers, isolated monkeys sat huddled in corners and were bullied. Recovery possible with younger therapist monkeys who engaged in clinging and simple play without aggression.
findings.where: PNAS 54(1):90-97, post-isolation behavior and recovery sections

findings.quote: the various human groups that can be identified in any society seem to cluster rather tightly around a series of values (5, 12, 35, 150, 500, and 2,000) with virtually no overlap in the variance around these characteristic values.
findings.content: Human social groups cluster at characteristic values of approximately 5, 12, 35, 150, 500, and 2,000 with virtually no overlap in variance between layers. These represent stable points in the degrees of familiarity and correspond to support clique, sympathy group, band, clan/village, mega-band, and tribe respectively.

findings.quote: A large body of observational data from the Wisconsin laboratories indicates that heterosexual behaviour is greatly influenced by early experience, and the failure of infants to form effective infant-infant affectional relations delays or destroys adequate adult heterosexual behaviour
findings.content: Harlow's deprivation experiments with rhesus monkeys: infants reared in social environments differing greatly from the environment of evolutionary adaptedness show severe disruption. Failure to form effective infant-infant affectional relations delays or destroys adequate adult heterosexual behavior. Even monkeys with adequate peer play but no maternal experience show considerable individual differences in adult social and sexual competence.

findings.quote: This domain of epigenetics was uncovered in a landmark 2004 study by Meaney and colleagues, one of the most cited papers published in the prestigious journal Nature Neuroscience. They had shown previously that offspring of more "attentive" rat mothers (those that frequently nurse, groom, and lick their pups) become adults with lower glucocorticoid levels, less anxiety, better learning, and delayed brain aging.
findings.content: Meaney's landmark 2004 study demonstrated that maternal care style in rats produces epigenetic changes in offspring's stress response genes. Offspring of more attentive mothers (frequent nursing, grooming, licking) become adults with lower glucocorticoid levels, less anxiety, better learning, and delayed brain aging. These changes are epigenetic - mothering style alters gene regulation in pups' brains. Remarkably, such pups as adults become more attentive mothers themselves, passing the trait epigenetically to the next generation.

findings.quote: Childhood abuse, for example, causes epigenetic changes in hundreds of genes in the human hippocampus. Moreover, Stephen Suomi of the National Institutes of Health and Szyf found that mothering style in monkeys has epigenetic effects on more than a thousand frontocortical genes.
findings.content: Childhood abuse causes epigenetic changes in hundreds of genes in the human hippocampus. Mothering style in monkeys has epigenetic effects on more than a thousand frontocortical genes. Hormonal responses to fetal and childhood experiences have epigenetic effects on genes related to BDNF, the vasopressin and oxytocin system, and estrogen sensitivity, with effects pertinent to adult cognition, personality, emotionality, and psychiatric health.

findings.quote: an epigenomic state of a gene can be established through behavioral programming, and it is potentially reversible.
findings.content: Maternal licking/grooming and arched-back nursing in rats alters offspring epigenome at the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) gene promoter in the hippocampus via DNA methylation and histone acetylation changes. Offspring of high-LG mothers have lower glucocorticoid levels, less anxiety, better learning, and delayed brain aging. Methylation differences emerged over the first week of life, were reversed with cross-fostering, and persisted into adulthood. Central infusion of a histone deacetylase inhibitor removed group differences - demonstrating that an epigenomic state established through behavioral programming is potentially reversible.

findings.quote: oxytocin, which mediates various pro-social processes, including maternal behavior and the inhibition of separation distress (Chapters 12 to 14), can yield a tripeptide called PLG (proline-leucine-glycine), which mediates none of the above but has antidepressant effects.
findings.content: Panksepp's early summary of oxytocin's pro-social functions: oxytocin mediates various pro-social processes including female sexual response, orgasm, maternal behavior, social memory, and the INHIBITION of separation distress. It is a single neuropeptide that operates across the sexual-maternal-social-bonding domains - exactly the molecular overlap that allows evolution to construct the 'social contract' by repurposing reproductive circuits for broader bonding. This is primary-source evidence for the M14/M9/M3 architectural overlap in Cor's specification.

findings.quote: If a rat is experimentally injected with infectious bacteria, it behaves a bit like I did after the dentist. It withdraws from social contact with other animals, it doesn't move so much, its sleeping and eating cycles are disturbed. In short, infection reliably causes a syndrome in animals - called sickness behaviour - that is roughly recognisable as akin to the human experience of depression. In fact, you don't even need to infect a rat to see this sickness behaviour. It is enough to inject the rat with cytokines, proving that it is not the germ itself that causes sickness behaviour but the immune response to infection. Inflammation directly causes depression-like behaviours in animals - that is beyond doubt.
findings.content: Dantzer's foundational finding (Bullmore synthesizes): injecting a rat with infectious bacteria produces sickness behavior - social withdrawal, reduced movement, disturbed sleep-wake cycles, reduced eating. Injecting cytokines alone (without bacteria) reproduces the syndrome, demonstrating it is the IMMUNE RESPONSE that causes sickness behavior, not the pathogen itself. Inflammation directly causes depression-like behaviors in animals. This is load-bearing for M8's cascade - the immune system drives behavioral change via cytokine signaling regardless of pathogen presence.
findings.where: Chapter 1 'Daring to Think Differently' pp. early chapters

findings.quote: At discharge or 40 to 41 weeks' postmenstrual age: "KMC was associated with a statistically significant reduction in the risk of mortality (risk ratio [RR] 0.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.39 to 0.92; eight trials, 1736 infants)." At latest follow-up: "KMC was associated with a significantly decreased risk of mortality (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.95; 12 trials, 2293 infants; moderate-quality evidence)."
findings.content: Cochrane meta-analysis of kangaroo mother care (KMC) vs conventional care in low-birthweight infants. In STABILIZED LBW infants, KMC significantly reduced the risk of mortality at discharge or 40-41 weeks postmenstrual age (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.39-0.92; 8 trials, 1736 infants) and at latest follow-up (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48-0.95; 12 trials, 2293 infants; moderate-quality evidence). RR 0.60 is the source of the frequently cited ~40% KMC mortality reduction (1 - 0.60). KMC also reduced nosocomial infection and hypothermia and improved growth and breastfeeding. This is corpus grounding for the claim that continuous skin-to-skin (C-tactile) contact is a mortality-level regulatory input for the preterm/LBW infant, not a comfort measure - the basis of R1 and of empirical demonstration ED9.

findings.quote: The troop's social culture was being transmitted.
findings.content: After a tuberculosis outbreak eliminated the most aggressive adult males from a baboon troop, the remaining troop - now with a 2:1 female-to-male ratio and disproportionately unaggressive and affiliative males - stayed close together, sat in contact, and groomed more than average. Levels of aggression were lower, and in an informative way: males still had a dominance hierarchy and fought with their rivals, but there was minimal displacement aggression onto innocent bystanders. Stress hormone levels were low; the neurochemistry of anxiety and benzodiazepines worked differently in these individuals. When male adolescents transferred in from other troops over the following years - having grown up in typical aggressive troops - they adopted the style of low aggression and high affiliation. The troop's social culture was being transmitted.
findings.where: Behave, Chapter 9, the Forest Troop narrative, pp. ~418-420 (ref Sapolsky & Share 2004)

findings.quote: During it the young child appears acutely distressed at having lost his mother and seeks to recapture her by the full exercise of his limited resources. He will often cry loudly, shake his cot, throw himself about, and look eagerly towards any sight or sound which might prove to be his missing mother.
findings.content: Bowlby's three-phase separation response in young children: protest (acute distress, crying, seeking the missing mother), despair (increasing hopelessness, withdrawal, deep mourning), and detachment (apparent recovery that masks emotional disengagement). The protest phase involves active attempts to recapture the mother; despair involves withdrawal and monotonous crying; detachment involves accepting care from others while showing striking absence of attachment behavior toward the mother on her return.

findings.quote: Brain activations occurred in several regions of the reward system. Included were regions of the ventral tegmental area (VTA) associated with feelings of intense romantic love; the ventral pallidum, associated with feelings of deep attachment; the insular cortex and the anterior cingulate, associated with physical pain, anxiety, and the distress associated with physical pain; and the nucleus accumbens and orbitofrontal/prefrontal cortex, brain regions associated with assessing one's gains and losses - as well as craving and addiction. Most relevant to our story, activity in several of these brain regions has been correlated with the craving for cocaine and other drugs.
findings.content: When my colleagues redid the brain scanning experiment to look at rejection, we found that feelings of romantic rejection lit up activity in several brain regions linked with profound attachment, deep addiction, and physical pain. When you are rejected in love, many brain systems go to work, and rejection is one of the most painful experiences a human being can endure.
findings.where: Chapter 5 'Blueprint for Divorce' pp. 127-128, Fisher/Brown rejection fMRI study

findings.quote: The babies who were massaged gained 47 percent more weight than those not massaged, a clearly significant weight gain.
findings.content: Moderate-pressure massage therapy causes preterm infants to gain more weight, leave tube feeding earlier, perform better on neurological examinations, and be discharged earlier at lower hospital cost. The mechanism involves stimulation of pressure receptors leading to increased vagal activity. Increased serotonin and decreased substance P may mediate the pain-alleviating effects of touch.

findings.quote: Several decades ago, Harry Harlow, at the University of Wisconsin, performed a classic experiment on touching monkeys. He built one surrogate mother out of terry cloth and a second surrogate mother out of wire mesh. For some of the monkey infants, the terry-cloth mother provided milk, and the wire mother did not. For others, the condition was reversed. The monkey infants preferred the cloth mother without the milk over the wire mother with milk, suggesting that they needed the touch stimulation as much as, if not more than, the nourishment.
findings.content: Field's synthesis of Harlow's foundational primate touch-deprivation work: infant rhesus monkeys preferred a terry-cloth surrogate mother without milk over a wire-mesh mother with milk, suggesting that touch stimulation is at least as important as nourishment. Harlow's experiments showed that infants without any surrogate developed self-clasping behavior, failed to develop normal grooming or reproduction, and had broken immune systems. Suomi's follow-up showed that Plexiglas separation (vision, hearing, smell preserved but no touch) was sufficient to produce these deficits - touch itself was the critical missing stimulation, not the other sensory modalities. This is the primary-source chain Field uses to ground touch as a distinct regulatory input in R1's architecture.
findings.where: Field, Touch (2014) Chapter 3 'Touch in Early Development', pp. ~47

findings.quote: the ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven emotional, or affective, systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy). Each of these systems controls distinct but specific types of behaviors associated with many overlapping physiological changes.
findings.content: The ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven emotional systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy). Each controls distinct behaviors with overlapping physiological changes and generates distinct types of affective consciousness. When stimulated in humans, people always experience intense emotional feelings. Capitalizations indicate that real physical and distinct networks for these emotions exist in mammalian brains.

findings.quote: primal emotional systems are made up of neuroanatomies and neurochemistries that are remarkably similar across all mammalian species. This suggests that these systems evolved a very long time ago and that at a basic emotional and motivational level, all mammals are more similar than they are different.
findings.content: Primal emotional systems are made up of neuroanatomies and neurochemistries remarkably similar across all mammalian species. This suggests these systems evolved a very long time ago and that at a basic emotional and motivational level, all mammals are more similar than different. Deep in the ancient affective recesses of our brains, we remain evolutionarily kin. The same neural paths and brain chemicals that arouse each of these seven systems are found within all mammals.

Panksepp's textbook Affective Neuroscience establishes the methodology and evidence base for the seven subcortical affective systems. Across cross-species deep brain stimulation, lesion, and pharmacological studies, the same brain regions produce the same functional categories of affective response - SEEKING, FEAR, RAGE, LUST, CARE, PANIC, PLAY - across mammals, providing the empirical foundation for treating these as conserved motivational architecture rather than culturally constructed categories.

findings.quote: We found a graded relationship between the number of categories of childhood exposure and each of the adult health risk behaviors and diseases that were studied.
findings.content: The ACE Study (9,508 respondents) demonstrated a graded dose-response relationship between categories of childhood adversity (psychological abuse, physical abuse, sexual abuse, violence against mother, household substance abuse, mental illness, incarceration) and adult health outcomes. Persons with 4+ ACE categories had 4-12 fold increased risk for alcoholism, drug abuse, depression, and suicide attempts; 2-4 fold increased risk for smoking, poor health, STDs; 1.4-1.6 fold for inactivity and obesity. More than half of respondents reported at least one category. Adult diseases linked included ischemic heart disease, cancer, chronic lung disease, skeletal fractures, and liver disease.

findings.quote: people move their facial muscles in many different ways, not one consistent way, when feeling an instance of the same emotion category. Large meta-analyses conclude that a single emotion category involves different bodily responses, not a single, consistent response. Brain circuitry operates by the many-to-one principle of degeneracy: instances of a single emotion category, such as fear, are handled by different brain patterns at different times and in different people. Conversely, the same neurons can participate in creating different mental states (one-to-many).
findings.content: Barrett's comprehensive meta-analysis of brain-imaging, facial EMG, and autonomic nervous system studies finds no consistent physical fingerprint for any single emotion. Facial muscles move in many different ways for the same emotion category. Bodily responses vary across instances. Brain circuitry operates by degeneracy (many-to-one: different neural patterns produce the same emotion category) and core systems (one-to-many: the same neurons participate in different mental states). Variation, not uniformity, is the norm across all three measurement domains.

findings.quote: It has become increasingly clear during the past half century that primary-process affective mechanisms are concentrated in ancient subcortical midline brain regions that are anatomically and neurochemically, and hence, evolutionarily, similar in all mammalian species.
findings.content: Seven distinct emotional systems identified with specific neuroanatomy and neurochemistry: SEEKING (VTA/NAcc/lateral hypothalamus, DA+), RAGE (medial amygdala→BNST→hypothalamus→PAG, substance P+), FEAR (central amygdala→hypothalamus→dorsal PAG, glutamate+/CRF+), LUST (cortico-medial amygdala/BNST/preoptic, steroids+), CARE (anterior cingulate/BNST/preoptic/VTA, oxytocin+/prolactin+), PANIC (anterior cingulate/BNST/dorsomedial thalamus/PAG, opioids−/oxytocin−/CRF+), PLAY (dorsomedial diencephalon/parafascicular/PAG, opioids+/−). Each mapped in Fig. 2 with specific neurochemical modulators.
findings.where: Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews 35(9):1791-1804, p. 1795, Fig. 2. DOI: 10.1016/j.neubiorev.2011.08.003

findings.quote: Never have such profound emotional states been provoked by stimulating neocortical regions.
findings.content: All seven emotional systems survive radical neo-decortication (complete surgical removal of the cerebral cortex). Decorticate animals retain all emotional-instinctual urges intact, though their capacity to learn new instrumental behaviors is severely impaired. ESB of subcortical regions in humans produces intense affective experiences; neocortical stimulation never produces such emotional states.

findings.quote: These criteria have been fulfilled or approximated for a variety of brain systems that exist in all mammals studied so far.
findings.content: Three empirical criteria for determining existence of emotional feelings in animals, all fulfilled: (1) neural circuits must exist that activate coherent emotional behaviors, (2) artificial arousal of such systems must generate conditioned approach/escape/avoidance, (3) key neurochemistries and brain activation patterns must correlate with predicted affective changes in humans. These criteria have been fulfilled for multiple brain systems across all mammals studied.

Three convergent lines of evidence demonstrate subcortical affective states: (i) mammals are attracted to the same environmental rewards and drugs of abuse as humans; (ii) human emotional feelings depend on subcortical brain systems where evolutionarily homologous instinctual neural systems exist; (iii) artificial activations of deep brain emotional systems are liked and disliked by animals, as measured by approach and avoidance measures.

findings.quote: for the twenty-odd tribal societies where census data are available, these clan groups turn out to have a mean size of 153
findings.content: Extrapolating from the relationship between neocortex size and group size for monkeys and apes gives a group size of about 150 - the limit on the number of social relationships that humans can have. For the twenty-odd tribal societies where census data are available, clan groups turn out to have a mean size of 153. The sizes of all but one of the village- and clan-like groupings for these societies fall between one hundred and 230. Once you start to look, groups of about this size turn up everywhere - in military units, in business organizations, in Christmas-card networks.

findings.quote: Extrapolating from the relationship for monkeys and apes gives a group size of about 150 - the limit on the number of social relationships that humans can have, a figure that is now graced by the title Dunbar's Number.
findings.content: The social brain hypothesis: there is a strong correlation between group size (social world complexity) and neocortex size in primates. Extrapolating gives a human group size of about 150 - the limit on the number of social relationships humans can maintain, now known as Dunbar's Number. The need to live in larger groups drove the evolution of large brains in primates.

findings.quote: But inspection of brain activity in several studies - elaborated on below - now suggests the brain responds to being alone as if sensory stimuli have been added, not taken away. That is, the brain looks more "at rest" when social resources are obviously available. This presents a puzzle potentially resolvable by considering proximity to a familiar other the brain's true "baseline" state, and being alone as more like an experimental treatment - a context that adds perceived work for the brain to do.
findings.content: Social Baseline Theory suggests the human brain expects access to social relationships that mitigate risk and diminish the level of effort needed to meet a variety of goals. The default and intrinsically social ecology the brain expects to function within is one of proximity to trusted others. Inspection of brain activity now suggests the brain responds to being alone as if sensory stimuli have been added, not taken away. That is, the brain looks more 'at rest' when social resources are obviously available. Proximity to a familiar other is the brain's true 'baseline' state, and being alone is more like an experimental treatment - a context that adds perceived work for the brain to do.

findings.quote: The pain of depression -- arising mostly from social loss and social defeat -- may be the price we mammals pay for the evolutionary advantages of social bonds that enrich our lives and promote procreation and survival.
findings.content: The pain of depression arises from the evolutionary price of social bonds: PANIC/GRIEF evolved from general pain mechanisms (birds possess a homologous system). This psychic-pain system promotes social cohesion, forges bonds between infants and caretakers, and fortifies friendships and sexual relationships. Depression is the cost mammals pay for the survival advantages of social bonds.

findings.quote: organisations of fewer than 150 people work fine on a person-to-person basis, but once they grow larger than this they need a formal hierarchy if they are to work efficiently
findings.content: A rule of thumb commonly used in business organisation theory is that organisations of fewer than 150 people work fine on a person-to-person basis, but once they grow larger than this they need a formal hierarchy if they are to work efficiently. Sociologists have known since the 1950s that there is a critical threshold in the region of 150 to two hundred, with larger companies suffering a disproportionate amount of absenteeism and sickness.

findings.quote: Facebook, MySpace and Bebo. Darwin and his contemporaries could not have conceived of such things, even in their wildest dreams.
findings.content: Social media breaks through time and geography constraints but creates perverse competition in friend counts. Most users know little about connections beyond approximately 200. The limits of online friendship reveal the constraint that Dunbar's number reflects - not communication bandwidth but cognitive capacity for maintaining genuine relationships. Digital tools extend reach but cannot expand the social brain's processing limit.

findings.quote: the everyday relationships of anthropoid primates involve a form of 'bondedness' that is only found elsewhere in reproductive pairbonds.
findings.content: Anthropoid primates co-opted pair-bond bonding mechanisms for group-level social relationships. The everyday relationships of anthropoid primates involve a form of bondedness found only in reproductive pair-bonds in other taxa. This unique generalization created qualitatively different primate sociality.

findings.quote: for separation distress to highlight striking species
findings.content: Panksepp notes important species differences in separation-distress systems - they exhibit striking interspecies variability even though the basic circuit is conserved. This calibration variability is important for understanding human-unique attachment patterns: the PANIC system is mammal-universal but its specific tuning (sensitivity thresholds, recovery dynamics, cross-modal signaling) varies with species ecology. For humans, separation distress is tuned for the long juvenile dependency period and for loss of specific attachment figures rather than general social absence. This grounds DA7 Developmental Calibration at the PANIC-circuit level.

findings.quote: the current environment deviates in greater or less degree from the environment of evolutionary adaptedness and so does not conform to that required for function to be fulfilled
findings.content: For a biological system, the environment of adaptedness is the environment within which the system gradually became evolved - its environment of evolutionary adaptedness. A behavioural system can be in functionally effective order, namely capable of achieving functional consequences, yet the current environment may deviate in greater or less degree from the environment of evolutionary adaptedness and so does not conform to that required for function to be fulfilled.
findings.where: Chapter 4, 'Man's Environment of Evolutionary Adaptedness,' p. 50, and Chapter 9, p. 128

findings.quote: In Chapter 3 it was emphasised that in the higher vertebrates most behavioural systems are to some extent environmentally labile, namely, the form they take in an adult turns in some degree on the kind of environment in which that adult is reared. The advantage of this is that the form ultimately to be taken by the system is in some degree left open so that it can, during development, become adapted to the particular environment in which the individual finds himself. Such flexibility, however, is not without its price. Provided the environment met with during development lies within certain limits, the ultimate form of a behavioural system may be well adapted, namely be such that, when activated, it commonly achieves a functional consequence. But when the environment in which development takes place falls outside those limits the form taken by the system may be ill adapted, namely be such that, when activated, it fails often or always to achieve a functional consequence.
findings.content: In the higher vertebrates most behavioural systems are to some extent environmentally labile - the form they take in an adult turns in some degree on the kind of environment in which that adult is reared. The advantage of this is that the form ultimately to be taken by the system is in some degree left open so that it can, during development, become adapted to the particular environment in which the individual finds himself. Provided the environment met with during development lies within certain limits, the ultimate form of a behavioural system may be well adapted. But when the environment in which development takes place falls outside those limits the form taken by the system may be ill adapted.

findings.quote: The theory of secondary drive holds that a liking to be with other members of the species is a result of being fed by them.
findings.content: Bowlby's critique of secondary drive theory: the theory that attachment to the mother is secondary to feeding (that the child learns to like the mother because she feeds it) is rejected. Bowlby argues attachment is a primary motivational system independent of feeding, as demonstrated by Harlow's rhesus monkey experiments and by the observation that punishment paradoxically strengthens rather than weakens attachment.

findings.quote: the antithesis 'innate versus acquired' is unreal. Just as area is a product of length multiplied by width so every biological character, whether it be morphological, physiological, or behavioural, is a product of the interaction of genetic endowment with environment. Terms like innate and acquired must therefore be cast into limbo and a new terminology employed.
findings.content: The innate-acquired antithesis is unreal. Every biological character - morphological, physiological, or behavioral - is a product of the interaction of genetic endowment with environment. Bowlby adopts Hinde's terminology: characters little influenced by environmental variation are 'environmentally stable'; those much influenced are 'environmentally labile.' Attachment behavior has both stable and labile components - the basic behavioral system is species-typical but its organization is shaped by developmental experience.

findings.quote: the young child's hunger for his mother's love and presence is as great as his hunger for food, and that in consequence her absence inevitably generates 'a powerful sense of loss and anger'.
