findings.content: The young child's hunger for the mother's love and presence is as great as hunger for food, and her absence inevitably generates a powerful sense of loss and anger. This framing establishes attachment as a primary motivational need on par with nutrition - not secondary to it - and positions separation distress as a necessary consequence of the attachment system's design rather than a sign of weakness or pathology.

findings.quote: Those which I believe we can identify at present are sucking, clinging, and following, in all of which the baby is the principal active partner, and crying and smiling in which his behaviour serves to activate maternal behaviour.
findings.content: Attachment is primary, not secondary to feeding. Bowlby proposed five component instinctual responses - sucking, clinging, following (baby is active partner) and crying, smiling (activate maternal behavior) - all primary and initially independent, becoming integrated and focused on one mother figure during the second six months of life. This broke with Freudian secondary drive theory.

findings.quote: Children will cling even to mothers who are continually cross and sometimes cruel to them. The attachment of the small child to his mother seems to a large degree independent of her personal qualities.
findings.content: Children attach to cruel mothers: the attachment of the small child to the mother seems largely independent of her personal qualities. This observation is incompatible with secondary drive (feeding-based reinforcement) models. Bowlby drew on ethology (Lorenz's imprinting, Harlow's contact comfort) and proposed monotropy: the tendency for instinctual responses to be directed toward a particular individual, not promiscuously.

findings.quote: The social brain hypothesis has suggested that natural social network sizes may have a characteristic size in humans. This is determined in part by cognitive constraints and in part by the time costs of servicing relationships.
findings.content: Mean Facebook friend count matches Dunbar's number prediction. Sample 1 (N=2000, nationally stratified UK): mean=155.2 friends (z=0.20, p=0.842 vs prediction of 150, 95% CI=100-200). Sample 2 (N=1375, nationally stratified UK professionals): mean=182.8 (z=1.29, p=0.198). Only 14.2% and 13.4% respectively had more than 300 friends.
findings.where: Royal Society Open Science 3(1):150292. DOI: 10.1098/rsos.150292. PMID: 26909163. PMC4736918. Full open-access text.

findings.quote: We can only interact coherently with a very small number of other people (about three, in fact) at any one time.
findings.content: Online inner social layers replicate offline sizes exactly. Support clique (crisis contacts): mean=4.1, not significantly different from offline values of 3.8+/-2.29 (z=0.13, p=0.897) or generic value of 5 (z=0.39, p=0.694). Sympathy group (close friends): mean=13.6, not different from 11.3+/-6.19 (z=0.37, p=0.711) or 15 (z=0.23, p=0.818).
findings.where: Royal Society Open Science 3(1):150292, inner layer analysis

findings.quote: On average, respondents in Sample 1 considered that only 27.6% of their Facebook friends could be considered 'genuine' (i.e. close) friends, with a strong modal value between 0 and 10%.
findings.content: Only 27.6% of Facebook friends are considered genuine (close) friends, with a strong modal value between 0 and 10%. Large online networks add only loose acquaintances, not close friends. People with unusually large networks do not increase close friendships but add weakly-defined acquaintances.
findings.where: Royal Society Open Science 3(1):150292, genuine friends analysis

findings.quote: it may be that face-to-face meetings are required from time to time to prevent friendships, in particular, sliding down through the network layers and eventually slipping over the edge of the 150 layer into the category of acquaintances.
findings.content: Face-to-face contact is required to prevent friendships from decaying through the network layers and eventually becoming mere acquaintances. Social media may slow the natural rate of decay but cannot substitute for in-person interaction. This directly confirms that the bonding system requires physical co-presence that technology cannot replace.

findings.quote: social media may function mainly to prevent friendships decaying over time in the absence of opportunities for face-to-face contact.
findings.content: Age strongly predicts total network size (r=-0.972, p=0.006) with 18-24 year olds averaging 282 friends, but inner layers show minimal age variation (support clique: r=-0.837, p=0.077; sympathy group: r=-0.042, p=0.947). The cognitive/time constraint on intimate relationships is stable across ages even as total network size varies.
findings.where: Royal Society Open Science 3(1):150292, age effects analysis

findings.quote: At each layer, the benefits are asymptotic but the costs of maintaining a relationship at that level (most obviously, the time that has to be invested in servicing it) are roughly linear with the number of relationships.
findings.content: At each social layer, the benefits of adding more relationships are asymptotic (diminishing returns), while the costs of maintenance - primarily time - are roughly linear with relationship count. The intersection of these curves creates natural breakpoints that generate the layered structure. This is a cost-benefit explanation for why Dunbar layers exist.
findings.where: British Journal of Psychology 103(2):149-168. DOI: 10.1111/j.2044-8295.2011.02061.x. Abstract-limited.

findings.quote: anthropoid primates may have generalized the bonding processes that characterize monogamous pairbonds to other non-reproductive relationships ('friendships'), thereby giving rise to the quantitative relationship between group size and brain size that we find in this taxon.
findings.content: Anthropoid primates generalized the bonding processes that characterize monogamous pair-bonds to non-reproductive relationships (friendships), creating a unique quantitative brain-group size relationship not seen in any other taxon. This explains why primate sociality is qualitatively different from all other mammals.
findings.where: Annals of Human Biology 36(5):562-572, central argument. DOI: 10.1080/03014460902960289

findings.quote: the demands of behavioural coordination that are the more likely
findings.content: The primary cognitive cost of pair-bonding is behavioral coordination and synchrony (scheduling, conflict resolution, spatial proximity maintenance), not mate choice optimization. This coordination demand requires perspective-taking capacities that may have provided the substrate for theory of mind.
findings.where: Annals of Human Biology 36(5):562-572, Table I and discussion. DOI: 10.1080/03014460902960289

findings.content: The phase shift from qualitative (pair-bonding) to quantitative (group-size) social brain processing likely occurred in the Eocene, coinciding with dietary shifts from insectivory to frugivory that may have created ecological conditions favoring larger social groups in early primates.
findings.where: Annals of Human Biology 36(5):562-572, evolutionary timing section. DOI: 10.1080/03014460902960289

findings.quote: The attachments created within AI companions promise intimacy and connection, yet structurally foreclose the possibility of genuine reciprocal relationships in which the user’s human autonomy is respected.
findings.content: Muldoon & Parke's 'cruel companionship' thesis: AI companions activate the human social-bonding response - the evolved tendency to treat a responsive interlocutor as a social being - while structurally foreclosing the genuine reciprocal relationship that would resolve it. Being incapable of genuine understanding, mutual vulnerability, or embodied presence, the companion fires the bonding cue but supplies none of the resolving function, leaving users 'trapped in a cycle of emotional engagement with an app that cannot fulfil their human needs.' Theoretical (political-economy / cultural-studies), not empirical.
findings.where: §'Cruel companionship', pp. 9-10 (canonical quote); cue-activation claim at §'The rise of AI companions', pp. 4-5

findings.quote: Social pain, also known as loneliness, evolved for a similar reason: because it protected the individual from the danger of remaining isolated. Our forebears depended on social bonds for safety and for the successful replication of their genes in the form of offspring who themselves survived long enough to reproduce. Feelings of loneliness told them when those protective bonds were endangered or deficient. In the same way that physical pain serves as a prompt to change behavior - the pain of burning skin tells you to pull your finger away from the frying pan - loneliness developed as a stimulus to get humans to pay more attention to their social connections, and to reach out toward others, to renew frayed or broken bonds.
findings.content: Social pain, also known as loneliness, evolved because it protected the individual from the danger of remaining isolated. Our forebears depended on social bonds for safety and for the successful replication of their genes. Feelings of loneliness told them when those protective bonds were endangered or deficient. In the same way that physical pain serves as a prompt to change behavior - the pain of burning skin tells you to pull your finger away from the frying pan - loneliness developed as a stimulus to get humans to pay more attention to their social connections, and to reach out toward others, to renew frayed or broken bonds.
findings.where: Chapter 1 'Lonely in a Social World,' p. 7

findings.quote: In English, we have a word for pain and a word for thirst, but no single, specific terms that mean the opposite. We merely reference the absence of these aversive conditions, which makes sense, because their absence is considered part of the normal state. Our research suggests that 'not lonely' - there is no better, more specific term for it - is also, like 'not thirsty' or 'not in pain,' very much part of the normal state. Health and well-being for a member of our species requires, among other things, being satisfied and secure in our bonds with other people, a condition of 'not being lonely' that, for want of a better word, we call social connection.
findings.content: In English, we have a word for pain and a word for thirst, but no single, specific terms that mean the opposite. We merely reference the absence of these aversive conditions, which makes sense, because their absence is considered part of the normal state. 'Not lonely' - there is no better, more specific term for it - is also, like 'not thirsty' or 'not in pain,' very much part of the normal state. Health and well-being for a member of our species requires, among other things, being satisfied and secure in our bonds with other people, a condition of 'not being lonely' that, for want of a better word, we call social connection.
findings.where: Chapter 1 'Lonely in a Social World,' p. 8

findings.quote: Although both are aversive, uncomfortable states, loneliness and depression are in many ways opposites. Loneliness, like hunger, is a warning to do something to alter an uncomfortable and possibly dangerous condition. Depression makes us apathetic. Whereas loneliness urges us to move forward, depression holds us back.
findings.content: Cacioppo frames loneliness as a functional evolved signal rather than a defect: loneliness, like hunger, is an aversive warning whose adaptive function is to prompt corrective action (return to social bonds). Depression is a distinct state that suppresses action rather than motivating it - the two states operate in functional opposition but can both be present at chronic intensity. Cacioppo elsewhere in the chapter (pp. ~85, lines 3360-3362) proposes that depression itself may have an adaptive social role as the complementary pole of this push-pull regulation system.
findings.where: Chapter 5 'The Universal and the Particular,' pp. 83-85

findings.quote: The standard operating procedure - staying within the tightly prescribed boundaries - is called homeostasis. The process of making special adjustments of those boundaries according to the broader needs of the organism is called allostasis. Homeostasis is like the first chair violinist: vitally important, but wedded to playing the musical score faithfully as it is written. Allostasis is more like a conductor, responsible for the entire orchestra, who brings a particular interpretation to the performance, and who may, within certain broader limits, alter the tempo or volume or other dynamics of the score as written by the composer. Both ways of proceeding are necessary and desirable, but every time a body system responds to a stressor, whether the response is homeostatic or allostatic, there is a physiological cost to making the adjustment. The more complex the allostatic adjustment, the greater the number of bodily systems - endocrine, cardiovascular, immune - that become involved. The more systems, the larger the needed adjustments, and the more frequently these adjustments are required, the higher the physiological cost of bringing your body back to normal. The total cost of all these adjustments, the rigidly constrained and the more broadly orchestrated, is called the allostatic load.
findings.content: The body's ability to maintain stability through change - allostasis - has a physiological cost, and the total cost of all these adjustments is called the allostatic load. The stress of having only limited power in a hierarchy, or the stress of feeling isolated in your community, your school, or your marriage, increases wear and tear throughout the system. Loneliness causes ill health through a grinding process of wear and tear that proceeds along five intersecting pathways: health behaviors, exposure to stressors, perceived stress and coping, physiological response to stress, and rest/restoration/repair.
findings.where: Chapter 6 'The Wear and Tear of Loneliness,' pp. 98-99, citing McEwen allostasis framework

findings.quote: As E. O. Wilson's image of the elastic leash suggests, heritability in human behavior means that the genes set the course, but that the environment still strongly influences the final destination. The influence of genes on a purely physical characteristic such as eye color is generally 100 percent, as is the influence of genes on certain conditions such as Huntington's disease. In those cases, genes are in fact destiny; the environment is never going to change the outcome. With the genetic bias toward a greater need for feelings of connection, however, a genetic contribution of forty-eight percent allows for a fifty-two percent contribution from the world we encounter. Mediating between the genes and the environment is the organism - which is to say, you and me. And here is where social cognition - our subjective perceptions - plays such an important role in determining the net outcome.
findings.content: A genetic thermostat for connection sets different individuals at different points along a social-need spectrum, but the thermostat is highly elastic - genes set the course, but the environment still strongly influences the final destination. The elastic-leash framing (E. O. Wilson) captures this: heritability in human behavior means genes bias outcomes without fully determining them. The organism mediates between genes and environment, and subjective social perception plays a determining role in the net outcome.
findings.where: Chapter 2 'Variation, Regulation, and an Elastic Leash,' pp. 24-25

findings.quote: As we have just seen, loneliness is a perpetrator that uses five different modus operandi to undermine our health. Once we see loneliness on the list of serious risk factors for illness and early death, right alongside smoking, obesity, and lack of exercise, that context should heighten our motivation to improve our level of social satisfaction, both as individuals and as a society. But in a broader sense, the power we can now assign to loneliness, and conversely the power we can now assign to social connection, illuminates human nature itself, underscoring the 'obligatorily gregarious' aspect of our species that is too often overlooked. Our sociality is central to who we are.
findings.content: Loneliness is a perpetrator that uses five different modus operandi to damage health: (1) health behaviors; (2) exposure to stressors; (3) perceived stress and coping; (4) physiological response to stress; and (5) rest, restoration, and repair. Using loneliness as a window on sociality provides a unified account of why chronic social disconnection produces the pattern of morbidity and mortality observed in the epidemiological literature.
findings.where: Chapter 7 'Sympathetic Threads,' pp. 126-127 recap of the five-pathways framework introduced in Chapter 6

findings.quote: The Hadza live in temporary camps that average about 30 individuals.
findings.content: Hadza camp size centers near 30 individuals, composed of several unrelated nuclear families.

findings.quote: Every 4-8 weeks entire camps shift location usually in response to resource availability.
findings.content: Camp membership is fission-fusion: entire camps relocate on a weeks timescale, so the group as a unit does not persist.

findings.quote: Because of the structural complexity of postagricultural societies, I considered only traditional hunter-gatherer and small-scale horticultural societies. Although census data on such societies are limited, those that are available suggest that there is indeed a consistent group size in the region of 150 individuals (Fig. 7).
findings.content: Ethnographic data from hunter-gatherer and horticultural societies validates the ~150 predicted by the primate neocortex regression (95% CI 100-230). The clan/village organizational level consistently clusters at this value, supporting the social brain hypothesis prediction for human-scale groups.

findings.quote: Moreover, infants and mothers are induced to awaken by an arousal exhibited by the other (within seconds) therein creating interconnected, mutually dependent, synchronous arousals [1, 2].
findings.content: Cosleeping mother and infant induce arousals in one another within seconds, creating interconnected, mutually-dependent, synchronous arousals (nighttime physiological co-regulation).

findings.quote: the behavior can be seen to be intimately linked to underlying EEGs, breathing patterns, changes in sleep architecture, body temperature and linked simultaneously to maternal physiological and behavioral events [5].
findings.content: Across the sleep period, cosleeping infant behavior is intimately linked to underlying EEG, breathing patterns, sleep architecture, and body temperature, coupled simultaneously to maternal physiological and behavioral events.

findings.quote: as bedsharing safety is determined specifically by how it is practiced and by whom and what adverse factors could be associated
findings.content: McKenna himself stresses that bedsharing safety depends entirely on how it is practiced and on adverse co-factors - the live SIDS/safety contestation that keeps co-sleeping from being a clean "ancestral good".

findings.quote: Throughout most of human history, people grew up enmeshed in dense family networks that knitted together distant cousins and in-laws. In these regulated-relational worlds, people's survival, identity, security, marriages, and success depended on the health and prosperity of kin-based networks, which often formed discrete institutions known as clans, lineages, houses, or tribes.
findings.content: Throughout most of human history, people grew up enmeshed in dense family networks of distant cousins and in-laws. Survival, identity, security, marriages, and success depended on kin-based networks (clans, lineages, houses, tribes). People were endowed with inherited obligations, responsibilities, and privileges in relation to others in a dense social web. This social interdependence bred emotional interdependence, leading people to strongly identify with in-groups and make sharp in-group/out-group distinctions.

findings.quote: The banning of sororate and levirate marriages were among the first actions taken as the Church began to restructure European families.
findings.content: The Church's Marriage and Family Program (MFP) restructured European families by banning cousin marriage, levirate and sororate marriage, adoption, and polygyny. Starting as early as 315 CE with the Synod of Neocaesarea banning men from marrying a dead brother's wife, these prohibitions systematically dismantled the kin-based institutions that had organized human social life for millennia.

findings.quote: Likewise, emotions are social reality. A physical event like a change in heart rate, blood pressure, or respiration becomes an emotional experience only when we, with emotion concepts that we have learned from our culture, imbue the sensations with additional functions by social agreement.
findings.content: Emotions are social reality - not physical reality. A physical event like a change in heart rate or blood pressure becomes an emotional experience only when emotion concepts, learned from culture, imbue the sensations with additional functions by social agreement. Barrett draws an analogy to cupcakes and muffins: chemically identical baked goods distinguished only by the cultural category applied. Words and concepts from culture shape brain wiring and physical changes during emotion.

findings.quote: So consider what happens if you're in a stressful social situation, like when a clique of coworkers suddenly stops inviting you to join them at lunch, or when friends read your text messages but don't answer. As per normal, your brain predicts you need fuel that your body doesn't require, temporarily impacting your budget. But what if the social situation doesn't resolve quickly? What if this social rejection is your life every day? Your body stays on alert, flush with cortisol and cytokines. Now your brain starts treating your body as if it were sick or damaged, and chronic inflammation sets in.
findings.content: Social rejection as chronic body-budget crisis: when social exclusion becomes a daily reality (coworkers stop inviting you to lunch, friends read your texts but do not answer), the brain continuously predicts fuel needs the body does not require. Cortisol and cytokines stay elevated. The brain treats the body as if it were sick or damaged, and chronic inflammation sets in. Inflammation in the brain affects predictions that manage the body budget, driving the budget into overdraft and creating a vicious cycle of worsening misregulation.

findings.quote: In the theory of constructed emotion, however, the dividing line between brain and world is permeable, perhaps nonexistent. Your brain's core systems combine in various ways to construct your perceptions, memories, thoughts, feelings, and other mental states.
findings.content: In the theory of constructed emotion, the dividing line between brain and world is permeable, perhaps nonexistent. The brain models the world through prediction and simulation; interoceptive predictions produce feelings of affect, influence every action, and determine what the organism cares about. At the same time, the outside world wires the brain: as an infant, sensory input seeds the earliest concepts; as language develops, the brain hardwires itself to the social world. Culture is not amorphous - it helped wire the brain, and behavior in turn wires the brains of the next generation.

findings.quote: SBT suggests the human brain expects access to social relationships that mitigate risk and diminish the level of effort needed to meet a variety of goals.
findings.content: Social Baseline Theory: the human brain expects access to social relationships that mitigate risk and diminish the level of effort needed to meet goals. Social and metabolic resources are treated almost interchangeably by the brain - isolation is processed as resource scarcity. Violations of the social proximity expectation increase cognitive and physiological effort as the brain perceives fewer available resources.

findings.quote: depression is intimately related to 1) sustained overactivity of the separation-distress PANIC system that can, if prolonged, lead to a downward cascade of psychological despair (a theoretical view originally formulated by John Bowlby); and 2) the despair phase that follows the acute PANIC response which is characterized by abnormally low activity of the SEEKING system.
findings.content: Two-phase model of depression genesis: (1) sustained overactivity of the PANIC/GRIEF separation-distress system produces psychological pain, followed by (2) abnormally low SEEKING system activity during the despair phase. The initial agitated panic state transitions to shutdown when reunification attempts fail, paralleling Bowlby's protest-despair sequence.

findings.quote: The suggestion that female-female bonding, based on knowledge of the relationships of other individuals, was more important fits much better with views about the structure of nonhuman primate societies where relationships between females are all-important.
findings.content: Language evolved in the context of social bonding between females. Female-female bonding based on knowledge of others' relationships was more important than male-male bonding in driving language evolution. This fits with primate societies where relationships between females are all-important for group cohesion and infant survival.

findings.quote: It was most likely a form of chorusing, a kind of communal singing without the words. Its function, I think, was to generate the same kind of surge of endorphins as that produced during grooming.
findings.content: Communal singing and music evolved as a bonding mechanism to generate endorphin surges when time constraints on social grooming became prohibitive in larger groups. Music was most likely a form of chorusing - communal singing without words - that preceded language. Its function was to generate the same endorphin surge as grooming but for multiple individuals simultaneously, solving the time-budget problem of maintaining bonds in groups beyond 50.

findings.quote: Kinship provides a surprisingly deep and sometimes unrecognised framework for our social life, not just in traditional small-scale societies, but for us today as well.
findings.content: Kinship provides a deep and often unrecognized framework for social cooperation, not just in traditional small-scale societies but in modern WEIRD contexts as well. Extended family networks function as migration facilitators, employment networks, and mutual-aid systems - illustrating that kin-based cooperation remains active even in supposedly individualistic societies.

findings.quote: these early hominin mothers relied on groupmates to help protect, care for, and provision their unusually slow-maturing children
findings.content: Mothers and Others is about the emergence of a particular mode of childrearing known as 'cooperative breeding' and its psychological implications for apes in the line leading to Homo sapiens. Cooperative breeding refers to any species with alloparental assistance in both the care and provisioning of young. Unlike mothers among other African apes, who nurtured infants on their own, these early hominin mothers relied on groupmates to help protect, care for, and provision their unusually slow-maturing children and keep them on the survivable side of starvation.

findings.quote: Of all the attachments mammalian babies form, none is more powerful than that between baby primates and their mothers. The emotional ties that bind ape mothers to their infants and infants to their mothers are unusually long-lasting.
findings.content: Of all attachments mammalian babies form, none is more powerful than that between baby primates and their mothers. The emotional ties binding ape mothers to infants and infants to mothers are unusually long-lasting. But in cooperatively breeding humans, this dyadic bond is embedded in a wider network of allomaternal attachments that share the regulatory burden.

findings.quote: Bowlby demonstrated that babies are genetically programmed to seek and form an attachment to a trusted figure. Secure attachment to one or more trusted caretakers is an essential aspect of emotional development in humans, just as it is in all other primates.
findings.content: Hrdy on attachment theory: Bowlby's insights that babies are genetically programmed to seek and form attachment to a trusted figure, and that secure attachment to one or more trusted caretakers is essential for emotional development, rank among the greatest contributions of evolutionary-minded psychologists. BUT Bowlby's original framing (exclusive maternal attachment) produces dilemmas for mothers wanting self-confident children AND lives/careers of their own. Hrdy's refinement: 'one or more trusted caretakers' - plural attachment figures, not a single dyadic bond. This is load-bearing for how M9 Care/Alloparenting integrates with M3 Social Bonding in Cor's architecture.

findings.quote: The PANIC system (see Chapter 14): To be a mammal is to be born socially dependent. Brain evolution has provided safeguards to assure that parents (usually the mother) take care of the offspring, and the offspring have powerful emotional systems to indicate that they are in need of care (as reflected in crying or, as scientists prefer to say, separation calls). The nature of these distress systems in the brains of caretakers and those they care for has only recently been clarified; they provide a neural substrate for understanding many other social emotional processes.
findings.content: Panksepp's definition of the PANIC separation-distress system, one of his most distinctive theoretical contributions: to be a mammal is to be born socially dependent. Brain evolution has provided safeguards to ensure parents take care of offspring AND offspring have powerful emotional systems to indicate they need care - reflected in crying (scientifically: separation calls). The nature of these distress systems in the brains of caretakers and those they care for provides a neural substrate for understanding many other social emotional processes. This is load-bearing for M3 Social Bonding and M9 Care/Alloparenting - Panksepp is the primary source for reading attachment distress as a specific affective circuit rather than a learned association.

findings.quote: This environment I propose to term the system's 'environment of adaptedness'. Only within its environment of adaptedness can it be expected that a system will work efficiently. In any other environment it cannot be expected to do so. In some such cases a system may in fact work reasonably well; in others it does not work at all; and in others again it gives rise to behaviour that is at best unusual and at worst positively unfavourable to survival.
findings.content: Bowlby's concept of the environment of adaptedness: every behavioral system has a particular environment to which it is adapted. Only within this environment can the system work efficiently. In any other environment it may work reasonably well, give rise to unusual behavior, or produce outcomes positively unfavourable to survival. Each species and each system within a species has its own environment of adaptedness, defined in terms of specific variables.

findings.quote: What an animal requires is something more like a working model of its environment. The use to which a model in the brain is put is to transmit, store, and manipulate information that helps in making predictions as to how what are here termed set-goals can be achieved.
findings.content: Bowlby's internal working model concept: the brain provides not merely a static map but a working model of the environment. This model transmits, stores, and manipulates information to generate predictions about how set-goals can be achieved. The working model concept explains how the child builds and updates mental representations of the attachment figure's availability and responsiveness, which then guide future attachment behavior.

findings.quote: there is good evidence, derived from observations of many species of bird and mammal, that an isolated animal is much more likely to be attacked and seized by a predator than is an animal that stays bunched together with others of its kind. Secondly, attachment behaviour is elicited particularly easily and intensely in animals which, by reason of age, size, or condition, are especially vulnerable to predators, for example the young, pregnant females, the sick. Thirdly, attachment behaviour is always elicited at high intensity in situations of alarm, which are commonly situations when a predator is either sensed or suspected. No other theory fits these facts.
findings.content: The biological function of attachment behavior is protection from predators. Three facts support this: (1) isolated animals are much more likely to be attacked by predators than animals that stay with others; (2) attachment behavior is most easily and intensely elicited in individuals especially vulnerable to predators - the young, pregnant females, the sick; (3) attachment behavior is always elicited at high intensity in situations of alarm when a predator is sensed or suspected. The paradoxical finding that punishment strengthens rather than weakens attachment is explained by this anti-predator function.

findings.quote: Because the bias of a child to attach himself especially to one figure seems to be well established and also to have far-reaching implications for psychopathology, I believe it merits a special term. In the earlier paper I referred to it as 'monotropy'.
findings.content: Bowlby coins the term monotropy for the child's bias to attach especially to one figure, noting this bias is well-established and has far-reaching implications for psychopathology. While children form multiple attachments, there is a strong tendency to direct attachment behavior principally toward one person - the principal attachment figure.

findings.quote: The existence of sensitive periods in early life during which the form to be taken by an adult's instinctive behaviour is in great part determined is yet another characteristic of instinctive behaviour to which Freud drew attention. In the psychoanalytic tradition it is represented in the concepts of fixation and of stage in libidinal organisation.
findings.content: Sensitive periods in attachment development: Bowlby draws attention to the existence of sensitive periods in early life during which the form of adult instinctive behavior is largely determined. In the psychoanalytic tradition this is represented in the concepts of fixation and stage in libidinal organization. The sensitive period concept explains why early attachment experiences have disproportionate influence on later relationship patterns.

findings.quote: psychologically, these trade-offs are related to the level of trust in a relationship, and that this is itself a function of the time invested in the relationship.
findings.content: Trust is the proximal psychological mechanism mediating social layer structure. Trade-offs at each layer are related to the level of trust in a relationship, and trust is itself a function of time invested. Trust operates as a cognitive heuristic that calibrates relationship investment to expected reciprocity at each layer.

findings.quote: an essential part of the ground plan of the human species--as well as that of many other species
findings.content: Attachment is an essential part of the biological ground plan of the human species. Hunter-gatherer societies show much more mother-infant contact than Western societies. Humans evolved as a species in which infants are carried and fed at frequent intervals. When attachment behavior is intensely activated, it is close bodily contact that is specifically required - not proximity alone.
findings.where: American Psychologist 34(10):932-937. DOI: 10.1037//0003-066x.34.10.932. Full text via Smith College.

findings.quote: Shame is rooted in a genetically evolved psychological package that is associated with social devaluation in the eyes of others.
findings.content: Shame is rooted in a genetically evolved psychological package associated with social devaluation in the eyes of others. In regulated-relational societies, shame can be experienced vicariously - a crime by one person brings shame to parents, siblings, and distant relations. The reverberation of shame through kin networks creates collective accountability. WEIRD societies shifted from shame-based to guilt-based moral psychology as kin networks dissolved.

findings.quote: By selectively attending to particular kinds of ideas and individuals under particular circumstances, our cultural learning abilities adaptively rewire our brains and biology to better calibrate them for navigating our culturally constructed worlds.
findings.content: Cultural learning rewires brains and biology. When learners watch others, they actively calibrate neurocircuitry in ways that move perceptions, preferences, behaviors, and judgments closer to those of chosen models. By selectively filtering and recombining beliefs, practices, techniques, and motivations acquired from others, cultural learning abilities adaptively rewire brains to better calibrate them for navigating culturally constructed worlds.

findings.quote: Nearly everyone has wondered why human life is so full of suffering. Part of an answer is that natural selection shaped emotions such as anxiety, low mood, and grief because they are useful. More of an answer comes from recognizing that our suffering often benefits our genes.
findings.content: Natural selection shaped emotions such as anxiety, low mood, and grief because they are useful. More of an answer to why life is full of suffering comes from recognizing that our suffering often benefits our genes. Nearly everyone has wondered why human life is so full of suffering - an evolutionary perspective provides the first satisfying scientific explanation.

findings.quote: A small group of philosophers of action (e.g., Bratman, 1992; Searle, 1995; Gilbert, 1989; Tuomela, 2007) have investigated how humans put their heads together with others in acts of so-called shared intentionality, or "we" intentionality. When individuals participate with others in collaborative activities, together they form joint goals and joint attention, which then create individual roles and individual perspectives that must be coordinated within them (Moll and Tomasello, 2007).
findings.content: Tomasello's central thesis: what makes human thinking unique is its fundamentally cooperative nature. Humans put their heads together with others in acts of shared intentionality - 'we' intentionality - creating joint goals and joint attention that constitute a plural agent. This capacity enables everything from collaborative hunting to cultural institutions. Great apes, despite knowing much about others as intentional agents, do NOT engage in shared intentionality and do NOT form human-like culture. Shared intentionality is the specific human-unique adaptation.

findings.quote: as a specific form of human collaborative activity and shared intentionality, human cooperative communication involves a set of special intentional and inferential processes - first identified by Grice (1957, 1975) and since elaborated and amended by Sperber and Wilson (1996), Clark (1996), Levinson (2000), and Tomasello (2008). Human communicators conceptualize situations and entities via external communicative vehicles for other persons; these other persons then attempt to determine why the communicator thinks that these situations and entities will be relevant for them.
findings.content: Cooperative communication as second-personal process: humans communicators conceptualize situations via external communicative vehicles for other persons; recipients then attempt to determine why the communicator thinks these will be relevant for them. This dialogic process involves not just shared-intentionality motivations but complex recursive inferences about others' intentions toward my intentional states. This form of communication - unique to humans, characteristic even of prelinguistic infant gestures - presupposes a shared conceptual framework (common conceptual ground) AND appreciation of the partner's individual intentions within it. Grounds M11 cooperation AND M3 social bonding through the communication channel.

findings.quote: Dunbar (1998), for example, documented that primate brain size correlates most strongly not with primates' physical ecology but, rather, with their social group size (as a proxy for social complexity).
findings.content: Tomasello cites Dunbar 1998: primate brain size correlates most strongly not with physical ecology but with social group size (as proxy for social complexity). Primates' social cognition is aimed mainly at competition (Machiavellian intelligence) - tracking dominance and affiliative relationships that affect competition for food and mates. This frames Dunbar's cognitive constraint as operating specifically through competitive social tracking.
findings.where: A Natural History of Human Thinking (2014), pp. 76-77 (lines 2987-2996 in text file)

findings.quote: group size is only a very gross indicator of social complexity (Dunbar focuses on the greater numbers of social relationships and reputations to be kept track of), and brain size is only a very gross indicator of cognitive capacities, so the social brain hypothesis gives us only a very general indication of the actual processes involved on either side of the correlation.
findings.content: Tomasello discusses the social brain hypothesis as supporting evidence for the evolution of human cooperation. Gowlett et al. (2012) traced brain-group size correlation across human evolution and found an especially big jump at ~400kya (Homo heidelbergensis), coinciding with Tomasello's hypothesized joint intentionality transition. However, Tomasello notes the hypothesis provides only a very general indication: group size is a gross indicator of social complexity and brain size a gross indicator of cognitive capacities.
findings.where: A Natural History of Human Thinking (2014), pp. 133-134 (lines 5168-5185 in text file)

findings.quote: We have underestimated just how important shared care and provisioning of offspring by group members other than parents have been in shaping prosocial impulses.
findings.content: We have underestimated how important shared care and provisioning by group members other than parents have been in shaping prosocial impulses. Without shared care and provisioning, all intergroup strategizing and strife would have been evolutionarily speaking signifying nothing. Cooperative breeding - where there is shared care and provisioning of young - is the key innovation that made human-level prosociality possible.

findings.quote: 'Cooperative breeding' refers to any species with alloparental assistance in both the care and provisioning of young.
findings.content: Cooperative breeding refers to any species with alloparental assistance in both care and provisioning of young. Unlike mothers among other African apes who nurtured infants alone, early hominin mothers relied on groupmates to protect, care for, and provision their slow-maturing children. This mode of child-rearing had profound psychological implications for the ape line leading to Homo sapiens.

findings.quote: When politicians lament the 'decline of the family,' they have in mind departures from the nuclear family: a man, his wife, and their biological children. However, the template for this kind of family dates back only a century or so, at most to Victorian times.
findings.content: The idealized nuclear family (breadwinner father, homemaker mother, biological children) dates back only about a century, to Victorian times at most. In American contexts, it became the template only in the 1950s. This family structure is a historical aberration - for the vast majority of human history, children were raised in extended kin networks with multiple allomaternal caregivers. The 'decline of the family' that politicians lament is actually a departure from an extremely brief historical norm.

findings.quote: Humans' large neocortex is an obvious possibility. Not only do human mothers need more help getting big-brained babies through narrow birth canals but they are better able to evaluate the costs and benefits of their own behavior.
findings.content: Hrdy cites Dunbar & Shultz (2007) on the correlation between large brain size and long juvenile/adolescent life phases. The neocortex discussion in Mothers and Others frames brain evolution through alloparenting: humans' large neocortex enables evaluation of allomaternal trustworthiness, while also creating the extended dependency that necessitates cooperative breeding. This connects Dunbar's social brain to Hrdy's cooperative breeding hypothesis as complementary explanations.
findings.where: Mothers and Others (2009), endnotes ch. 8 note 4 (line 13045), main text pp. 39-40 (lines 1580-1614, 1795-1801, 2940-2943)

findings.quote: Among humans living in foraging societies, a helpful mate and/or alloparents were usually essential for a mother to rear any infant at all. In a surprisingly broad range of creatures, indispensable alloparents provide many of the same forms of care a mother might, protecting and provisioning, even suckling another female's infant in cases where the alloparent is
findings.content: Hrdy's core allomothering thesis: Among humans living in foraging societies, a helpful mate and/or alloparents were usually essential for a mother to rear any infant at all. Indispensable alloparents provide many of the same forms of care a mother might - protecting, provisioning, even suckling another female's infant. This is load-bearing for M9 Care/Alloparenting: human infants are NOT raised dyadically, and the mother-as-sole-caregiver framing misses the evolutionary architecture entirely.

findings.quote: Regarding human reciprocal altruism, it is shown that the details of the psychological system that regulates this altruism can be explained by the model. Specifically, friendship, dislike, moralistic aggression, gratitude, sympathy, trust, suspicion, trustworthiness, aspects of guilt, and some forms of dishonesty and hypocrisy can be explained as important adaptations to regulate the altruistic system.
findings.content: Gratitude, sympathy, trust, suspicion, and guilt are not arbitrary emotions but specific adaptations for regulating reciprocal altruism. Gratitude motivates reciprocation; sympathy motivates initial altruistic acts toward those in need; trust calibrates willingness to cooperate; suspicion monitors potential cheaters; guilt motivates relationship repair after defection. Each emotion functions as a regulatory mechanism within the reciprocal altruism system.
findings.where: Q Rev Biol 46(1):35-57, 1971. DOI: 10.1086/406755. Human reciprocal altruism section.

findings.content: Henrich cites Dunbar 1998 on the social brain hypothesis in the context of arguing that human intelligence is collective rather than individual. Endnote references place Dunbar alongside Byrne and Whiten (1992) and Humphrey (1976) as proponents of the Machiavellian intelligence view that Henrich then challenges: cultural evolution, not individual social cognition, is what makes humans smart. Group size matters for Henrich primarily as a driver of cumulative cultural complexity, not through Dunbar's cognitive constraint mechanism.
findings.where: The Secret of Our Success (2016), endnotes 7 and 19 (lines 12444, 12498), main text ch. 2 and ch. 12

findings.quote: In much the same way as an infected animal, a wounded or sick human, like me after root canal work, shows a characteristic pattern of behaviour. Ill or invalid human beings withdraw from social contact, reduce their physical activity, eat less, and are less hedonic. They are also quietly anxious and have disturbed sleep. This is a very engrained and consistent pattern of behaviour, written into our DNA by genes that must have evolved millions of years before H sapiens. As we have seen, this sickness behaviour is strongly driven by innate inflammatory mechanisms.
findings.content: Bullmore's evolutionary framing of sickness behavior: in ancestral environments with high infant/adult mortality from infection, genes that made the innate inflammatory response more aggressive would be selected. Those same genes drive the characteristic sickness-behavior syndrome (social withdrawal, reduced activity, loss of appetite, disturbed sleep, anxiety) - not as a defect but as an evolved protective response. Sickness behavior is 'genetically programmed convalescence' that conserves metabolic resources for immune function.
findings.where: Chapter 5 'Why?' - evolutionary framing of sickness behavior

findings.quote: The contemporary psychological investigation of human attachment began with a British psychiatrist, John Bowlby, and an American psychologist, Mary Ainsworth, who proposed that, to promote the survival of their young, primates have evolved an innate attachment system designed to motivate infants to seek comfort and safety from their primary caregiver, generally mother. Since then extensive research has been done on the behaviors, feelings, and biological mechanisms associated with this attachment system in human adults and other creatures. Moreover, researchers have proposed that these attachment circuits remain active throughout the life course - serving as a foundation for emotional commitment between pair-bonded partners for the purpose of raising offspring.
findings.content: The contemporary psychological investigation of human attachment began with Bowlby and Ainsworth, who proposed that, to promote the survival of their young, primates have evolved an innate attachment system designed to motivate infants to seek comfort and safety from their primary caregiver. Extensive research has shown that these attachment circuits remain active throughout the life course - serving as a foundation for emotional commitment between pair-bonded partners for the purpose of raising offspring. The adult pair-bond attachment system is an extension of, not a replacement for, the infant-caregiver attachment system.

findings.quote: For creatures shaped by evolution to feel safe in company and endangered when unwillingly alone, feelings of isolation and perceptions of threat reinforce each other to promote a higher and more persistent level of wariness. To prepare us to react efficiently when confronting threats to life and limb, nature provided us with the ability to be cognitively hypervigilant, along with a chain of physiological reactions known as the fight-or-flight response. But the neurological wiring we depend on today evolved in response to the kinds of hit-and-run stressors we faced millions of years ago. As a result, our stress response ('fight or flight') includes a prompt to immediate action that increases resistance in the cardiovascular system and floods the body with hormones that rev us up. If we were fending off wild dogs, those hormones could help save our lives. However, when our stressors consist of feeling isolated and unloved, the constant presence of these excitatory chemicals acts as a corrosive force that accelerates the aging process.
findings.content: For creatures shaped by evolution to feel safe in company and endangered when unwillingly alone, feelings of isolation and perceptions of threat reinforce each other to promote a higher and more persistent level of wariness. To prepare us to react efficiently when confronting threats to life and limb, nature provided us with the ability to be cognitively hypervigilant, along with a chain of physiological reactions known as the fight-or-flight response. But the neurological wiring we depend on today evolved in response to the kinds of hit-and-run stressors we faced millions of years ago. When our stressors consist of feeling isolated and unloved, the constant presence of these excitatory chemicals acts as a corrosive force.
findings.where: Chapter 2 'Variation, Regulation, and an Elastic Leash,' pp. 31-32

findings.quote: In contemporary society, as we've noted, most of our stressors do not come and go in the kind of short, life-or-death confrontations that drove the evolution of 'fight or flight.' We can have the same overbearing boss, the same long commute, the same worries about health care and retirement, and the same feelings of social isolation, hour after hour, year after year. Moreover, we now experience these persistent stressors over a life span that, on average, extends well beyond what was the norm during all but the last few centuries of our species' existence. The environment is entirely different now than it was in our environment of evolutionary adaptation
findings.content: Human stressors no longer come and go in the kind of short, life-or-death confrontations that drove the evolution of fight-or-flight. We can have the same overbearing boss, the same long commute, the same worries about health care and retirement, and the same feelings of social isolation, hour after hour, year after year. Moreover, we now experience these persistent stressors over a life span that, on average, extends well beyond what was the norm during all but the last few centuries of our species' existence. The environment is entirely different now than it was in our environment of evolutionary adaptation, but our sympathetic / parasympathetic architecture has not changed.
findings.where: Chapter 6 'The Wear and Tear of Loneliness,' pp. 103-104

findings.quote: where depression and loneliness converge is in a diminished sense of personal control, which leads to passive coping. This induced passivity is one of the reasons that, despite the pain and urgency that loneliness imposes, it does not always lead to effective action. Loss of executive control leads to lack of persistence, and frustration leads to what the psychologist Martin Seligman has termed 'learned helplessness.'
findings.content: Loneliness and depression share a diminished sense of personal control, which leads to passive coping. This induced passivity is one of the reasons that, despite the pain and urgency that loneliness imposes, it does not always lead to effective action. Loss of executive control leads to lack of persistence, and frustration leads to what Martin Seligman has termed 'learned helplessness.'
findings.where: Chapter 5 'The Universal and the Particular,' p. 83

findings.content: Bullmore's key hypothesis on the function of sickness-behavior social withdrawal: it serves a tribe-level protective function in ancestral human groups. Extended-family tribes of few hundred genetically related individuals were vulnerable to contagious disease wiping out the whole gene pool. Isolation of the sick individual - quarantine - reduces the risk of uninfected tribal members becoming infected. The patient's inflamed behavior puts HIM at anxiety-provoking risk of predation at the margins, for the sake of the tribe as a whole. Sickness behavior was naturally selected as much for tribal-DNA survival as individual-DNA survival.

findings.quote: Relatedness within camps is low with primary kin comprising, on average, 1.43 and 1.93 of men and women's campmates respectively.
findings.content: Direct relatedness measure: primary kin are a small minority of a camp.

findings.quote: Among the Ache and Hadza, frequent visiting and long lifespans mean that adults typically interact with more than three hundred same-sex adults during their lifetimes. This implies a social universe of about a thousand individuals, when opposite-sex adults and children are included.
findings.content: Among Ache and Hadza foragers, lifetime same-sex interaction exceeds 300 adults, implying a lifetime "social universe" of about a thousand individuals once opposite-sex adults and children are included.

findings.quote: Precontact Northern Ache men, for example, are expected to have hunted with 206 men, conversed with 290 men, and watch tool making by 302 different men in a lifetime (Table S16 in File S1). Eastern Hadza men are expected to converse with 427 other Hadza men, hunt with 303 men, and watch tool making by 395 different men in a lifetime. In contrast, chimpanzees living in typical communities of 11 adult males are expected to interact with a mean of only 21 other adult males in a lifetime
findings.content: Per-activity lifetime interaction counts for Ache/Hadza men (hundreds of partners) vs ~21 for male chimpanzees: lifetime human social universe is an order of magnitude larger.

findings.quote: Additionally, close companions often interact with a somewhat different set of individuals, so that the total number of indirect interactants that each individual hears about repeatedly in detailed stories, and could expect to possibly meet some time during their lifetime is clearly more than 1,000. This is a much higher number of individually known social interactants than reported for any other primate, and possibly more than any other species on earth. It is also much greater than the predicted 150 significant social interactants (known as “Dunbar's number”) that was extrapolated from primate brain by social group size regressions
findings.content: The lifetime pool of individually-known interactants is clearly >1,000 - which Hill et al. explicitly note is far above the ~150 figure (the Dunbar number) that was extrapolated from primate brain / social-group-size regressions.

findings.quote: An "ego" (the naming person) is 44.2 times (95% C.I. 37.6 to 51.4) more likely to name an "alter" (the named person) in the campmate network, and 14.3 times (95% C.I. 12.2 to 16.4) more likely to name an alter in the gift network, if the alter reciprocated the social tie by also naming the ego as a friend
findings.content: Hadza campmate/gift networks show strong dyadic reciprocity even though nominations are private and controlling for kin ties.

findings.quote: in both the campmate and gift networks, social ties are significantly more likely when two people are similar in age, height, weight, body fat, and handgrip strength.
findings.content: Homophily in Hadza social ties runs on age and physical/condition traits (the "shuffle" is similarity-driven, not random).

findings.quote: social distance appears to be as important as genetic relatedness and physical proximity in explaining assortativity in cooperation
findings.content: Cooperative assortment in Hadza networks: similarity in cooperation extends to two degrees, and social distance rivals genetic relatedness in explaining it (kinship is not the sole glue).

findings.quote: first-order relatives make up less than 10% of residential camps
findings.content: Within-camp relatedness is low: most co-residents are not first-order kin.

findings.quote: Like vasopressin, oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus. Unlike vasopressin, oxytocin is released in all female mammals (including women) during the birthing process. It initiates contractions of the uterus and stimulates the mammary glands to produce milk. But oxytocin also stimulates bonding between a mother and her infant. And more and more data now indicate that oxytocin can also produce feelings of attachment to a preferred mating partner. You have undoubtedly felt the power of these 'cuddle chemicals,' as vasopressin and oxytocin are sometimes called. At orgasm, the activities of oxytocin spike in men and women. These 'satisfaction hormones' undoubtedly contribute to your sense of fusion, closeness, and attachment after sweet sex with a beloved.
findings.content: Like vasopressin, oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus. Unlike vasopressin, oxytocin is released in all female mammals (including women) during the birthing process. It initiates contractions of the uterus and stimulates the mammary glands to produce milk. But oxytocin also stimulates bonding between a mother and her infant. And more and more data now indicate that oxytocin can also produce feelings of attachment to a preferred mating partner. At orgasm, the activities of oxytocin spike in men and women. These satisfaction hormones undoubtedly contribute to your sense of fusion, closeness, and attachment after sweet sex with a beloved.

findings.quote: Our analyses on complementary datasets using different methods yield wildly different numbers. Bayesian and generalized least-squares phylogenetic methods generate approximations of average group sizes between 69-109 and 16-42, respectively. However, enormous 95% confidence intervals (4-520 and 2-336, respectively) imply that specifying any one number is futile. A cognitive limit on human group size cannot be derived in this manner.
findings.content: Redoing the neocortex-ratio-to-group-size regression that produced 'Dunbar's number' with modern phylogenetic comparative methods (Bayesian and generalized least-squares) on complementary primate datasets yields wildly unstable human estimates: point estimates of 69-109 (Bayesian) and 16-42 (GLS), with 95 percent confidence intervals of 4-520 and 2-336 respectively. No single number is statistically supportable; a cognitive limit on human group size cannot be derived this way. CHALLENGE to the precise ~150 figure as a cognitive ceiling, cited to Dunbar 1992's neocortex-ratio extrapolation (ext 483).

findings.quote: This evolving proto-WEIRD psychology gradually laid the groundwork for the rise of impersonal markets, urbanization, constitutional governments, democratic politics, individualistic religions, scientific societies, and relentless innovation.
findings.content: One sect of Christianity drove the spread of social norms that dramatically altered marriage, families, inheritance, and ownership in parts of Europe over centuries. This transformation of family life initiated psychological changes that spurred new forms of urbanization and fueled impersonal commerce. An evolving proto-WEIRD psychology laid the groundwork for impersonal markets, constitutional governments, democratic politics, individualistic religions, scientific societies, and relentless innovation.

findings.quote: Why is this relevant to emotion? Because every brain region that's claimed to be a home of emotion in humans is a body-budgeting region within the interoceptive network. These regions, however, don't react in emotion. They don't react at all. They predict, intrinsically, to regulate your body budget. They issue predictions for sights, sounds, thoughts, memories, imagination, and, yes, emotions. The idea of an emotional brain region is an illusion caused by the outdated belief in a reactive brain. Neuroscientists understand this today, but the message hasn't trickled down to many psychologists, psychiatrists, sociologists, economists, and others who study emotion.
findings.content: Every brain region historically claimed as a home of emotion is actually a body-budgeting region within the interoceptive network. These regions do not react in emotion - they predict intrinsically to regulate the body budget, issuing predictions for sights, sounds, thoughts, memories, imagination, and emotions. The notion of a dedicated emotional brain region is an illusion caused by the outdated belief in a reactive brain.

findings.quote: Chimpanzees perform best on tests requiring a rudimentary theory of mind when they are in competitive situations.
findings.content: Chimpanzees perform best on tests requiring rudimentary theory of mind when they are in competitive situations. But human children develop robust theory of mind in cooperative contexts - because in a cooperatively breeding species, infants who could read the intentions of multiple caregivers had a survival advantage. Human mind-reading evolved not for competition but for navigating the cooperative breeding network.

findings.quote: We now realize that maternal behavior circuits remain closely intermeshed with those that control sexuality, and this suggests how evolution gradually constructed the basic neural substrates for the social contract (i.e., the possibilities for love and bonding) in the mammalian brain.
findings.content: Panksepp's architectural claim about the evolution of social bonding: maternal behavior circuits remain closely intermeshed with those that control sexuality. This suggests how evolution gradually constructed the basic neural substrates for the 'social contract' - 'the possibilities for love and bonding' - in the mammalian brain. Maternal nurturance probably arose gradually from preexisting circuits that initially mediated reproductive behaviors. This is THE foundational architectural claim for why Cor's M3 Social Bonding, M9 Care/Alloparenting, and M14 Reproductive Motivation share substrate - they were built by evolution as extensions and overlays of the same neurochemical machinery, not as independent systems.

findings.quote: the central concepts are those of behavioural systems and their control, of information, negative feedback, and a behavioural form of homeostasis. The more complex forms of instinctive behaviour are regarded as resulting from the execution of plans that, depending on the species, are more or less flexible.
findings.content: Bowlby's behavioral systems model: instinctive behavior operates through control systems using behavioral homeostasis. The central concepts are behavioral systems and their control, information, negative feedback, and homeostatic regulation. Complex instinctive behavior results from the execution of plans that, depending on species, are more or less flexible. Plan execution is initiated by receipt of information from sense organs and guided by continuous reception of feedback from results of action taken.

findings.quote: Thus, when mother is called away a child's attachment behaviour is likely to be elicited and his exploratory behaviour inhibited; conversely, when a child explores too far, a mother's care behaviour is likely to be elicited and whatever else she is doing to be inhibited. In a happy couple these four classes of behaviour occur and progress together in harmony. But risk of conflict is ever-present.
findings.content: Attachment behavior as one of four interacting classes in mother-child interaction: (a) the child's attachment behavior, (b) the child's exploratory behavior and play (antithetic to attachment), (c) the mother's caretaking behavior, and (d) the mother's behavior antithetic to care. When the mother is called away, the child's attachment behavior is elicited and exploratory behavior inhibited; when the child explores too far, the mother's care behavior is elicited. In a happy couple these four classes occur in harmony, but risk of conflict is ever-present.

findings.quote: Low control at work is an important contributor to disease, but there are ways of depriving people of control other than subjecting them to difficult conditions at work. The Rick and Maria story makes plain that low control over life circumstances is not confined to work. Low control in these other spheres, too, may be important for health.
findings.content: Marmot explicitly generalises the workplace-control finding to non-workplace spheres of life: low control in domestic, economic, and other spheres is also a causal exposure for disease, not an ancillary correlate of workplace conditions. The Whitehall II extension (asking civil servants about perceived control at home and in life in general) is what he uses to ground this generalisation empirically.

findings.quote: Human psychological mechanisms are adaptations that evolved to process environmental inputs, turning them into behavioral outputs that, on average, increase survival or reproductive prospects. Modern contexts, however, differ vastly from the environments that existed as human psychological mechanisms evolved.
findings.content: Evolutionary mismatch occurs when human psychological mechanisms, adapted to process ancestral environmental inputs, encounter modern contexts that differ vastly from those environments. Many inputs now differ in quantity, intensity, or no longer have the same fitness associations, leading mechanisms to produce maladaptive output. Li et al. classify mismatch along four dimensions: source (natural vs human-induced), type (forced vs hijacked), cause (input changes vs output-consequence changes), and consequences (effects on reproductive fitness crossed with effects on individual well-being). Tables 1-3 provide worked examples for each dimension.
findings.where: Current Directions in Psychological Science 27(1):38-44, 2018. DOI: 10.1177/0963721417731378

findings.quote: Cumulative imbalance in the body budget - say, from growing up in adversity, where you don't feel safe or are deprived of basic necessities like nutritious food, quiet time to sleep, and so on - also changes the structure of your interoceptive network, rewiring your brain and reducing its ability to accurately regulate your body budget. All it takes are a couple of highly negative experiences for children to feel like they are living in a combat zone, reducing the size of their body-budgeting regions by the time they reach adulthood.
findings.content: Cumulative body-budget imbalance from growing up in adversity - without safety, nutritious food, or quiet time to sleep - changes the structure of the interoceptive network, rewiring the brain and reducing its ability to regulate the body budget. A couple of highly negative childhood experiences can reduce the size of body-budgeting regions by adulthood. Growing up in a harsh or chaotic family, with conflict or verbal criticism, increases inflammation in adolescent girls. Children bullied in childhood show low-grade inflammation persisting into adulthood, predisposing them to psychiatric and physical diseases.

findings.quote: The skin is the first and the largest sense organ to develop prenatally. The fetus is suspended in amniotic fluid and receives active stimulation from the fluid and the mother and others as they touch her abdomen. The fetus becomes increasingly active as this happens. The fetus also touches itself by thumb sucking and grasping the umbilical cord. The fetus gets a continuous massage for the entire nine months from both the amniotic fluid and the mother's insides. In addition, a pregnant woman naturally massages her baby in the womb. Touch alters oxytocin (an estrogen-dependent chemical), which relaxes the individual, promotes touch, encourages bonding, triggers milk letdown during breastfeeding, and sets off the uterine contractions that accompany childbirth.
findings.content: Field's phylogenetic framing of touch as the first sense organ. The skin is the largest sense organ because it is the largest organ in the body - the 'first and largest sense organ to develop prenatally'. The fetus receives continuous touch stimulation in utero from amniotic fluid, maternal internal movement, and external touch to the mother's abdomen. Touch alters oxytocin, which relaxes the individual, promotes touch (positive feedback), encourages bonding, triggers milk letdown during breastfeeding, and initiates uterine contractions during childbirth. This is the architectural grounding for R1 Touch as a phylogenetically ancient regulatory input distinct from vision and hearing, with downstream effects on M9 Care/Alloparenting and M3 Social Bonding via oxytocin.
findings.where: Field, Touch (2014) Chapter 3 'Touch in Early Development', pp. ~49

findings.quote: Affective neuroscience has made a fresh start by proceeding from the bottom up, without denigrating our unique human abilities, and it is offering both a new vision of mental origins and new data to back up such assertions.
findings.content: The triangulation approach of affective neuroscience links the affective mind to animal brains by triangulating among (i) subjective mental states (most easily studied in humans), (ii) brain functions (more easily studied in animals), and (iii) natural instinctual emotional behaviors that all young mammals must exhibit early in life to survive. This bottom-up approach offers both a new vision of mental origins and new data.

findings.quote: I will speak of these emotional systems in a variety of ways, using designations such as executive, command, and operating systems, to provide nuances of meaning that may be needed to conceptualize their overall functions. The use of the term executive implies that a neural system has a superordinate role in a cascade of hierarchical controls
findings.content: Panksepp's conceptual toolkit for emotional circuits: he calls them 'executive, command, and operating systems' - executive implies a superordinate role in hierarchical controls; command implies the circuit can INSTIGATE a full-blown emotional process (not just correlate with it); operating implies it coordinates and synchronizes multiple subsystems. Together these yield coherent psycho-behavioral and physiological responses that constitute an emotional 'organ system' - an anatomical network of interconnected neurons with endocrine, paracrine, and immune influences. This is the load-bearing architectural framing for why emotional circuits are mechanisms (Cor's M-framework) rather than mere sensorimotor reflexes.

findings.quote: In addition to the preceding primitive systems that are evident in all mammals soon after birth
findings.content: Panksepp's framework of 4 primary emotional command systems: expectancy/SEEKING, RAGE, FEAR, and separation-distress/PANIC. These are organized along discrete but interacting trajectories in the subcortical brain, largely following the medial forebrain bundle. These 4 systems are 'evident in all mammals soon after birth' - they are not cognitive achievements but mammalian hardware inherited from at least 150 million years of mammalian evolution. This is the central DA8 phylogenetic-priority claim: the affective substrate is ancient, pre-cortical, and conserved across all mammals.

findings.quote: I remain convinced that it is useful, at least in the present state of our knowledge, to 'dissect' the master question into three stages.
findings.content: Tinbergen's four questions framework: the complete study of behavior requires investigating (1) causation (mechanism - what internal and external stimuli trigger the behavior), (2) ontogeny (development - how the behavior develops during the organism's lifetime), (3) survival value (function - what adaptive advantage the behavior confers), and (4) evolution (phylogeny - how the behavior evolved across species). These four levels of analysis are complementary, not competing.

findings.quote: In every waking moment, your brain uses past experience, organized as concepts, to guide your actions and give your sensations meaning. When the concepts involved are emotion concepts, your brain constructs instances of emotion.
findings.content: Barrett's formal definition of the theory of constructed emotion: the brain uses past experience organized as concepts to guide actions and give sensations meaning. When emotion concepts are active, the brain constructs instances of emotion. Emotions are not triggered reactions but active constructions from interoceptive sensations, conceptual knowledge, and contextual predictions.

findings.quote: the ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven basic affective systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy)
findings.content: The ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven basic affective systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy). These designate specific functional networks of evolutionarily very ancient regions of our brains.
findings.where: Preface, 'Why Psychiatrists, Physicians, and Psychotherapists Should Understand the Seven Basic Affective Systems,' p. xi

findings.quote: Sexual gratification, arising from our capacity for LUST, feels good in a rather different way from the joys of rough-and-tumble PLAY or the tender bliss of caressing, nurturing, and CAREing for one's infant. FEAR is an entirely different kind of emotional 'pain' than frustrated RAGE; both differ from the PANICked misery of social isolation.
findings.content: Sexual gratification from LUST feels good in a different way from the joys of rough-and-tumble PLAY or the tender bliss of caressing and CARing for an infant. FEAR is an entirely different kind of emotional pain than frustrated RAGE; both differ from the panicked misery of social isolation (PANIC/GRIEF). These diverse affects provide guidance for living due to the survival-enhancing advantages each conferred over evolution. Affects are ancestral memories of how effectively we play the game of survival and reproduction.

findings.quote: The underlying circuits are genetically predetermined and designed to respond unconditionally to stimuli arising from major life-challenging circumstances. These circuits organize diverse behaviors by activating or inhibiting motor subroutines and concurrent autonomic-hormonal changes that have proved adaptive in the face of such life-challenging circumstances during the evolutionary history of the species. Emotive circuits change the sensitivities of sensory systems that are relevant for the behavioral sequences that have been aroused. Neural activity of emotive systems outlasts the precipitating circumstances. Emotive circuits can come under the conditional control of emotionally neutral environmental stimuli. Emotive circuits have reciprocal interactions with the brain mechanisms that elaborate higher decision-making processes and consciousness.
findings.content: Panksepp's six methodological criteria for identifying genuine emotional systems in the brain (Figure 3.3): (1) Underlying circuits are genetically predetermined to respond unconditionally to life-challenging stimuli; (2) they organize diverse behaviors by activating/inhibiting motor subroutines and autonomic-hormonal changes; (3) they change sensitivities of sensory systems relevant to the aroused behavioral sequences; (4) their neural activity outlasts precipitating circumstances; (5) they can come under conditional control of emotionally neutral stimuli; (6) they have reciprocal interactions with higher decision-making and consciousness circuits. Plus the seventh psychological criterion: they must generate affective feelings. This is Panksepp's load-bearing methodological framework for distinguishing emotional systems from general-purpose sensorimotor circuits.

findings.quote: Of course, as mentioned, there is a seventh psychological criterion: The emotional circuits must be able to generate affective feelings, but this is hard to incorporate into the conceptual diagram. I will eventually develop the idea that affect emerges from the many interactions of emotional systems depicted in Figure 3.3 with primal neural mechanisms that represent "the self" (see Chapter 16)
findings.content: Panksepp's central theoretical commitment - the seventh psychological criterion: emotional circuits must be able to generate affective feelings. This criterion is 'hard to incorporate into the conceptual diagram' but is the load-bearing claim that distinguishes affective neuroscience from behavioral neuroscience.
