This central adiposity may be the result of a complex series of reactions involving cortisol metabolism; central obesity occurs in Cushing's Syndrome, a disorder characterised by over-secretion of cortisol.
findings.where: Chapter 4 'Stress in the Jungle? Stress in the Office?' pp. 121-122, citing Whitehall II metabolic markers

findings.quote: We used measures of effort/reward imbalance in the workplace in our studies in Poland, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Hungary. This study confirmed the importance for poor health of low control at work and generally. In addition, people whose work was characterised by a high degree of imbalance between effort and reward had a 60 per cent greater chance of being in poor health than those with an appropriate balance.
findings.content: People whose work was characterised by a high degree of imbalance between efforts put in and rewards received had higher risk of disease, independently of low control at work. Two distinct psychosocial features - low control and effort/reward imbalance - both contribute to the work-health gradient in Whitehall II.
findings.where: Chapter 7 'Health and Work' p. 190-191, Whitehall II effort/reward analysis, citing Siegrist model

findings.quote: people move their facial muscles in many different ways, not one consistent way, when feeling an instance of the same emotion category. Large meta-analyses conclude that a single emotion category involves different bodily responses, not a single, consistent response. Brain circuitry operates by the many-to-one principle of degeneracy: instances of a single emotion category, such as fear, are handled by different brain patterns at different times and in different people. Conversely, the same neurons can participate in creating different mental states (one-to-many).
findings.content: Barrett's comprehensive meta-analysis of brain-imaging, facial EMG, and autonomic nervous system studies finds no consistent physical fingerprint for any single emotion. Facial muscles move in many different ways for the same emotion category. Bodily responses vary across instances. Brain circuitry operates by degeneracy (many-to-one: different neural patterns produce the same emotion category) and core systems (one-to-many: the same neurons participate in different mental states). Variation, not uniformity, is the norm across all three measurement domains.

findings.quote: There is nothing normal or useful about psychotic depression or mania. Both are serious diseases that result from broken mood regulation mechanisms.
findings.content: There is nothing normal or useful about psychotic depression or mania. Both are serious diseases that result from broken mood regulation mechanisms. Nesse explicitly distinguishes these from normal-but-excessive low mood - the mood regulation system itself is damaged, not just producing adaptive but unwanted signals.

findings.quote: The growing body of adaptive information available in the minds of other people also drove genetic evolution to create a second form of human status, called prestige, which now operates alongside the dominance status we inherited from our ape ancestors.
findings.content: Over our evolutionary history, the growing body of adaptive information available in the minds of other people drove genetic evolution to create a second form of human status, called prestige, which now operates alongside the dominance status we inherited from our ape ancestors. The evolution of prestige came with new emotions, motivations, and bodily displays that are distinct from those associated with dominance. Prestige explains why people unconsciously mimic more successful individuals in conversations, why star athletes like LeBron James can sell car insurance, how someone can be famous for being famous, and why the most prestigious participants should donate first at charity events but speak last in decision-making bodies.

findings.quote: I proposed that leveling mechanisms may be necessary because, as with chimpanzees, underlying dominance and submission tendencies facilitate competition among individuals and constitute a powerful force for hierarchy in group life.
findings.content: Leveling mechanisms may be necessary because underlying dominance and submission tendencies facilitate competition among individuals and constitute a powerful force for hierarchy in group life. Humans have innate dominance tendencies that must be actively suppressed through egalitarian leveling. The tension between the impulse to dominate and the egalitarian ethos is a fundamental feature of human political psychology.

findings.quote: The finding that Dominance and Prestige can coexist within social groups as viable rank-promoting strategies suggests that human social hierarchies are multidimensional.
findings.content: Two experimental studies of hierarchy formation among previously unacquainted people showed that Dominance (using force and intimidation to induce fear) and Prestige (sharing expertise and know-how to gain freely conferred respect) are near-orthogonal (mean correlation close to zero) yet each independently secures real rank: greater perceived influence, greater actual influence over group decisions, and more visual attention from others. Dominance produced influence even where dominant individuals were rated less likable, so influence is separable from liking. Establishes M5's earned-prestige-versus-coerced-dominance distinction as a measurable feature of live human groups rather than a purely theoretical claim, and shows coerced dominance is a partial resolver of rank rather than a non-resolver.

findings.quote: humans have innate needs to be seen as attractive to others. These needs form the basis for shame and mediate evaluations of social standing (status), social acceptance and social bonds.
findings.content: Humans have innate needs to be seen as attractive to others, forming the basis for shame. Shame and humiliation derive from attacks on social attractiveness. Internal shame experience derives from submissive defense strategies signaling awareness of lost social standing to limit damage from higher-ranking individuals.

findings.quote: The internal experiences of shame are derived from submissive strategies where one seeks to signal to others awareness of loss of social standing and limit possible damage.
findings.content: Shame derives from an evolved submissive defense where the organism signals awareness of lost social standing to limit damage from higher-ranking individuals. The signal function of shame is appeasement: by displaying shame (gaze aversion, postural collapse, blushing), the organism communicates acceptance of lower rank and reduces the probability of continued attack. This is adaptive in hierarchical contexts but becomes pathological when chronically activated by modern status comparison (social media, workplace evaluation, academic competition).
findings.where: Br J Med Psychol 70(2):113-147, 1997. PMID: 9210990. Shame mechanism section.

findings.quote: The sociometer system would serve its purpose if it simply assured that the person maintained sufficient social connections with a relatively small set of personally significant people
findings.content: The sociometer is calibrated to a small, bounded set of personally significant others rather than to an unbounded audience, and it responds primarily to exclusion (a deprivation state) rather than to ever-greater inclusion: in Studies 3 and 4, exclusion for personal reasons lowered state self-esteem while inclusion produced no matching rise, and random exclusion did not lower it. Directly supports M5's resolution condition that the monitored reference group is bounded and personally known, and M5's mismatch prediction that global mediated audiences over-drive a monitor built for a small group.

findings.quote: Measures of prestige and dominance were largely independent, and although both predicted leader status, prestige was more important.
findings.content: Among the Chabu (recently settled Ethiopian hunter-gatherers), peer-rated prestige and dominance were largely independent, and although both predicted elected leader status, prestige was clearly more important (dominance's effect was weaker and sensitive to the statistical prior). Most leadership traits covaried strongly, indicating a general leadership/respect factor, and women as well as men held elected leadership. Supports M5's earned-prestige-preferred clause in a non-WEIRD small-scale society and confirms the biased-social-learning (Mentor-salience) prediction of the Henrich & Gil-White model.

findings.quote: Prestigious but not dominant men marry wives who first give birth at earlier ages, which multivariate analysis suggests is the strongest pathway between status and fitness in this population.
findings.content: Among Tsimane forager-horticulturalists (Bolivia), both dominance (men more likely to win a dyadic physical confrontation) and prestige (men with more community-wide influence) associate with higher fertility, via different pathways: dominant men have higher intra-marital fertility for their age, while prestigious men show both higher intra-marital fertility and lower offspring mortality. Prestige is the strongest single pathway from status to fitness in this population. Both routes elicit allies' support and competitors' deference but do not buy extra provisioning. Non-WEIRD cross-cultural replication that the dominance/prestige distinction is real and carries genuine fitness consequences, grounding the inclusive-fitness (P1) basis of M5.

findings.quote: The status syndrome is not about disease for the poor and good health for everyone else. It 1s a gradient. Marx's concept of alienation may well be relevant to our discussion of control, but it is a graded phenomenon: you can have degrees of it.
findings.content: Marmot's core framing of the status syndrome as a graded phenomenon rather than a poor-vs-non-poor binary. He reinforces this elsewhere (source lines 361-365, pp. ~4-5) with 'Wherever we are in the hierarchy, our health is likely to be better than those below us and worse than those above us. The socially excluded are at the end of a health spectrum, but it is the social gradient in health, the status syndrome, that is the challenge.' The diseases of the status syndrome are those of rich societies that have dealt with absolute deprivation: heart disease, diabetes, mental illness.

findings.quote: Shame is rooted in a genetically evolved psychological package that is associated with social devaluation in the eyes of others.
findings.content: Shame is rooted in a genetically evolved psychological package associated with social devaluation in the eyes of others. In regulated-relational societies, shame can be experienced vicariously - a crime by one person brings shame to parents, siblings, and distant relations. The reverberation of shame through kin networks creates collective accountability. WEIRD societies shifted from shame-based to guilt-based moral psychology as kin networks dissolved.

findings.quote: While attributing specific functions to specific mood states is a mistake, the capacity for mood can be said to have a general function: mood reallocates investments of time, effort, resources, and risk taking to maximize Darwinian fitness in situations of varying propitiousness. High and low moods adjust cognition and behavior to cope with propitious and unpropitious situations.
findings.content: Mood reallocates investments of time, effort, resources, and risk taking to maximize Darwinian fitness in situations of varying propitiousness. High and low moods adjust cognition and behavior to cope with propitious and unpropitious situations. Attributing specific functions to specific mood states is a mistake - the capacity for mood has a general function as a resource-allocation system.

findings.quote: We want so badly to be important, rich, loved, admired, attractive, and powerful. For what? The good feelings from succeeding are just about balanced by the bad feelings from failure. Our emotions benefit our genes far more than they do us.
findings.content: Our emotions benefit our genes far more than they do us. We want so badly to be important, rich, loved, admired, attractive, and powerful - but the good feelings from succeeding are just about balanced by the bad feelings from failure. The emotional system is calibrated not for individual happiness but for gene propagation, which explains why suffering is inherent rather than accidental.

findings.quote: Sometimes low mood should be respected as normal and useful to help adjust a person's motivation and life directions. However, often the situation can't be changed. The loss of a friend, continuing abuse, inability to get a job, trying every night to help a child get off drugs, finding no relief from chronic pain - those are good reasons, but the resulting bad feelings are harmful even if they are normal.
findings.content: Low mood can be (1) normal and useful for adjusting motivation, (2) normal but harmful because the situation cannot be changed (loss, abuse, chronic pain), (3) normal but useless because of the Smoke Detector Principle, (4) normal but useless because we live in environments so different from those we evolved in, or (5) caused by abnormalities in the mood regulation system. Clinicians should take the same medical approach to low mood as to physical pain: find the cause and fix it, but always relieve suffering.

findings.quote: Likewise, emotions are social reality. A physical event like a change in heart rate, blood pressure, or respiration becomes an emotional experience only when we, with emotion concepts that we have learned from our culture, imbue the sensations with additional functions by social agreement.
findings.content: Emotions are social reality - not physical reality. A physical event like a change in heart rate or blood pressure becomes an emotional experience only when emotion concepts, learned from culture, imbue the sensations with additional functions by social agreement. Barrett draws an analogy to cupcakes and muffins: chemically identical baked goods distinguished only by the cultural category applied. Words and concepts from culture shape brain wiring and physical changes during emotion.

findings.quote: cultural evolution initiated a process of self-domestication, driving genetic evolution to make us prosocial, docile, rule followers who expect a world governed by social norms monitored and enforced by communities.
findings.content: Cultural evolution initiated a process of self-domestication, driving genetic evolution to make us prosocial, docile, rule followers who expect a world governed by social norms monitored and enforced by communities. Norms influence a vast range of human action, including ancient and fundamentally important domains such as kin relations, mating, food sharing, parenting, and reciprocity. Over our evolutionary history, norm violations such as ignoring a food taboo, botching a ritual, or failing to give one's in-laws their due from one's hunting successes meant reputational damage, gossip, and a consequent loss of marriage opportunities and allies. Repeated norm violations sometimes provoked ostracism or even execution at the hands of one's community.

findings.quote: cultural evolution initiated a process of self-domestication, driving genetic evolution to make us prosocial, docile, rule followers who expect a world governed by social norms monitored and enforced by communities.
findings.content: Cultural evolution initiated a process of self-domestication, driving genetic evolution to make humans prosocial, docile, rule-following organisms who expect a world governed by social norms monitored and enforced by communities. Cultural products like fire, cooking, tools, clothing, and language became the main selective pressures that genetically shaped human minds and bodies - culture-gene coevolution creating a new kind of animal.

findings.quote: This is an example of biased cultural transmission, which occurs when people tend to acquire some cultural variants rather than others.
findings.content: Biased cultural transmission: people tend to acquire some cultural variants rather than others. Biases may be innate preferences or cultural preferences acquired in earlier social learning. Conformist bias (When in Rome, do as the Romans do) makes evolutionary sense because adaptive behavior tends to become more common than maladaptive behavior. Prestige bias: people grant prestige to those perceived as having superior cultural variants, compensating them for the privilege of imitation.

findings.quote: You are engaged in maladaptive behavior right now.
findings.content: Modern middle-class reproductive restraint is a striking maladaptation: professional status-seeking consumes resources (time, money, effort) needed for reproduction. Evolved psychology for status competition in Pleistocene tribal contexts now causes fitness loss in modern economies. People prioritize career advancement, education, and consumption over reproduction - the very success of cultural transmission mechanisms (prestige bias, conformist bias) producing behaviors that reduce genetic fitness.

findings.quote: egalitarianism involves a very special type of hierarchy, a curious type that is based on antihierarchical feelings
findings.content: My thesis is that egalitarianism does not result from the mere absence of hierarchy. Rather, egalitarianism involves a very special type of hierarchy, a curious type that is based on antihierarchical feelings. If a stable egalitarian hierarchy is to be achieved, the basic flow of power in society must be reversed definitively. Our political nature favors the formation of orthodox hierarchies - hierarchies like those of chimpanzees or gorillas, or humans living in chiefdoms or states. It is politically ambitious individuals, those with special learned or innate propensities to dominate, who are likely to become upstarts in egalitarian bands or tribes.
findings.where: Chapter 1, 'The Question of Egalitarian Society,' pp. 8-9

findings.quote: In effect, it is the rank and file who are on top, and the would-be alphas who remain under their thumbs. The fact that the occasional successful intimidator can rise to tyrannize these egalitarians for a time does not negate the characterization, for the group's next move is to dominate the dominator by removing him.
findings.content: Reverse dominance hierarchy: the rank and file are on top, and would-be alphas remain under their thumbs. When an occasional intimidator rises to tyrannize, the group's next move is to dominate the dominator by removing him. This is the fundamental political structure of human forager bands - not the absence of hierarchy but the active suppression of dominance by coalitions of subordinates.

findings.quote: In humans, it seems safe to assume that the larger the brain, the greater the degree of political intelligence and the higher the probability that subordinate coalitions could definitively suppress alpha-type behavior. Humans were ready to form moral communities and reverse their dominance hierarchies 100,000 years ago, and probably considerably earlier.
findings.content: The earliest human precursor was likely an African ape that formed political coalitions enabling the rank and file to whittle away at alpha powers. By the Late Paleolithic, humans possessed an egalitarian ethos and political order similar to present-day hunting bands. The larger the brain, the greater the political intelligence and the higher the probability that subordinate coalitions could suppress alpha-type behavior. Humans were ready to form moral communities and reverse their dominance hierarchies 100,000 years ago, probably earlier.

findings.quote: For example, in shame the focus is on the self, while in humiliation the focus is on the harm done by others.
findings.content: Shame, humiliation, and guilt differ as evolved social strategies: shame focuses on the self (submissive appeasement), humiliation focuses on harm done by others (agonistic challenge), guilt focuses on specific actions and consequences for others (relationship repair). These map onto different adaptive responses to different types of social evaluation threat.

findings.quote: Shame and humiliation are associated with attacks on, and losses of, social attractiveness.
findings.content: Social rank theory: humans evolved in social hierarchies where status determined access to resources and mates. Involuntary defeat strategy (IDS) is an evolved defensive response to status loss - when an organism loses rank and cannot escape, IDS produces behavioral inhibition, withdrawal, submissive signaling, and depressed mood. Depression in modern humans may reflect chronic activation of IDS in environments where status threats are persistent but escape or resolution is impossible.
findings.where: Br J Med Psychol 70(2):113-147, 1997. PMID: 9210990. Social rank and IDS sections.

findings.quote: Individualism is best thought of as a psychological cluster that allows people to better navigate WEIRD social worlds by calibrating their perceptions, attention, judgments, and emotions.
findings.content: Individualism is a psychological cluster that calibrates perceptions, attention, judgments, and emotions for navigating WEIRD social worlds. Most populations reveal psychological packages that similarly fit their societies' institutions, technologies, environments, and languages. The psychology-institution fit is bidirectional - institutions shape psychology through cultural learning, and psychology shapes which institutions can emerge and persist.

findings.quote: Often, especially in formerly non-state societies, the newly transplanted institutions created a misfit with people's cultural psychology, leading to poorly functioning governments, economies, and civil societies.
findings.content: Impersonal institutions (representative governments, universities, social safety nets) evolved in Europe and have been exported to numerous populations. Often, especially in formerly non-state societies, newly transplanted institutions create a misfit with people's cultural psychology, leading to poorly functioning governments, economies, and civil societies. The institutional-psychological mismatch produces systemic dysfunction.

findings.quote: The core problem for psychiatric diagnosis is the lack of a perspective on normal useful functions that physiology provides for the rest of medicine. Internal medicine doctors know the functions of the kidneys. They don't confuse protective defenses such as cough and pain with diseases such as pneumonia and cancer. Psychiatrists lack a similar framework for the utility of stress, sleep, anxiety, and mood, so psychiatric diagnostic categories remain confusing and crude.
findings.content: The core problem for psychiatric diagnosis is the lack of a perspective on normal useful functions that physiology provides for the rest of medicine. Internal medicine doctors know kidney functions and do not confuse protective defenses (cough, pain) with diseases (pneumonia, cancer). Psychiatrists lack a similar framework for the utility of stress, sleep, anxiety, and mood, so diagnostic categories remain confusing and crude. Anxiety and low mood are useful normal responses - it is time to give up the fantasy that each mental disorder has a specific cause.

findings.quote: There are good reasons for bad feelings. Anxiety and depression are often excessive because they benefit genes at our expense, because of the Smoke Detector Principle, because we live in modern environments, and because regulation mechanisms are intrinsically vulnerable.
findings.content: Nesse's resolution: there are good reasons for bad feelings. Anxiety and depression are often excessive because (1) they benefit genes at our expense, (2) the Smoke Detector Principle, (3) we live in modern environments, and (4) regulation mechanisms are intrinsically vulnerable. Some disorders have specific brain causes; others are syndromes like kidney failure with many possible causes. Top-down and bottom-up causes interact to create tangled webs - this is not confusion, it is reality.

findings.quote: Low moods prevent us from wasting effort in pursuit of unreachable goals, but they often escalate into pathological depression.
findings.content: Low mood prevents us from wasting effort in pursuit of unreachable goals, but it often escalates into pathological depression. The signal is functionally adaptive - it indicates that current strategies are failing and effort should be redirected - but the signal itself can become the problem when the mood regulation system cannot disengage.

findings.quote: Many inputs now differ in quantity and intensity or no longer have the same fitness associations, thereby leading many mechanisms to produce maladaptive output.
findings.content: The mismatch framework has implications for public policy. Li et al. present specific examples: (1) despite modern sanitation benefits, immune systems evolved to be stimulated by bacterial exposure in infancy - overuse of antibacterial products may contribute to childhood asthma, allergies, and ear infections; (2) ecological conservation efforts have met limited success because conservation behavior is evolutionarily novel - humans evolved to consume local resources without concern when pollutant output was low and migration was feasible. Effective interventions should work with, rather than oppose, evolved tendencies such as self-interest, social status concerns, social imitation, and future discounting.
findings.where: Current Directions in Psychological Science 27(1):38-44, 2018. DOI: 10.1177/0963721417731378

findings.quote: In the theory of constructed emotion, however, the dividing line between brain and world is permeable, perhaps nonexistent. Your brain's core systems combine in various ways to construct your perceptions, memories, thoughts, feelings, and other mental states.
findings.content: In the theory of constructed emotion, the dividing line between brain and world is permeable, perhaps nonexistent. The brain models the world through prediction and simulation; interoceptive predictions produce feelings of affect, influence every action, and determine what the organism cares about. At the same time, the outside world wires the brain: as an infant, sensory input seeds the earliest concepts; as language develops, the brain hardwires itself to the social world. Culture is not amorphous - it helped wire the brain, and behavior in turn wires the brains of the next generation.

findings.quote: The secret of our species' success resides not in the power of our individual minds, but in the collective brains of our communities.
findings.content: The secret of our species' success resides not in the power of individual minds but in the collective brains of communities. Humans became simultaneously the most cooperative and the most warlike of primates - large-scale societies enabling both technological innovation and intergroup conflict. The collective brain hypothesis explains why larger, more interconnected populations innovate faster.

findings.quote: In the hypothesis of Tomasello et al. (2012), obligate collaborative foraging became an evolutionarily stable strategy for early humans because of two interrelated processes: interdependence and social selection. The first and most basic point is that humans began a lifestyle in which individuals could not procure their daily sustenance alone but instead were interdependent with others in their foraging activities - which meant that individuals needed to develop the skills and motivations to forage collaboratively or else starve. There was thus direct and immediate selective pressure for skills and motivations for joint collaborative activity (joint intentionality). The second point is that as a natural outcome of this interdependence, individuals began to make evaluative judgments about others as potential collaborative partners: they began to be socially selective, since choosing a poor partner meant less food. Cheaters and laggards were thus selected against, and bullies lost their power to bully.
findings.content: Obligate collaborative foraging as evolutionarily stable strategy: interdependence + social selection. Early humans began a lifestyle in which individuals could not procure daily food alone - they were interdependent. This created direct selective pressure for joint-intentionality skills. As a natural outcome, individuals made evaluative judgments about potential collaborative partners - social selection against cheaters and laggards, and against bullies. Critically, individuals had to worry about BOTH evaluating others AND how others were evaluating them (self-image concern) - a uniquely human cognitive preoccupation.

findings.quote: Dunbar (1998), for example, documented that primate brain size correlates most strongly not with primates' physical ecology but, rather, with their social group size (as a proxy for social complexity).
findings.content: Tomasello cites Dunbar 1998: primate brain size correlates most strongly not with physical ecology but with social group size (as proxy for social complexity). Primates' social cognition is aimed mainly at competition (Machiavellian intelligence) - tracking dominance and affiliative relationships that affect competition for food and mates. This frames Dunbar's cognitive constraint as operating specifically through competitive social tracking.
findings.where: A Natural History of Human Thinking (2014), pp. 76-77 (lines 2987-2996 in text file)

findings.quote: Moralistic punishment is more effective in supporting large-scale cooperation than reciprocity for two reasons.
findings.content: Moralistic punishment is more effective than reciprocity at supporting large-scale cooperation. Punishment takes forms including reduced status, fewer friends, and fewer mating opportunities. In groups where a norm is common, people who violate it are punished. When newcomers arrive, they rapidly learn local norms and maintain them despite different evolved psychology. Cultural group selection - tribes with cooperation-promoting norms outcompete those without.

findings.quote: The tribal social instincts result from the gene-culture co-evolution of tribal-scale societies by the process described above. Consequently, humans are able to make common cause with a sizable, culturally defined set of distantly related individuals, a form of social organization that is absent in other primates.
findings.content: Tribal social instincts result from gene-culture coevolution of tribal-scale societies. Humans are able to make common cause with a sizable, culturally defined set of distantly related individuals - a form of social organization absent in other primates. These instincts equip humans with the psychological machinery for in-group cooperation, out-group vigilance, and norm-governed behavior in groups of 50-500.

findings.quote: Tribal instincts cause people to use symbolic markers to define the boundaries of in-groups and establish, for example, who is eligible for empathy, who should excite suspicion, and, in some horrible cases, who should be killed.
findings.content: Symbolic markers of group boundaries motivate important behavior. Tribal instincts cause people to use symbolic markers to define who is eligible for empathy, who should excite suspicion, and in some cases who should be killed. Small differences in arrow styles, dress, or dialect become psychologically salient signals of group membership. People essentialist ethnic groups as species-like categories.

findings.quote: In the section that follows, we describe what seem to us to be the main work-around mechanisms, and the conflicts, compromises, and modes of failure that each entails.
findings.content: Complex societies employ institutional work-arounds to simulate tribal-scale relationships: hierarchical command backed by force, segmentary hierarchy, and symbolic in-group marking. Each work-around creates predictable conflicts and failure modes - elite exploitation from hierarchical command, subgroup factionalism from segmentary structure, and fundamentalism from symbolic marking. These are not design flaws but inherent consequences of scaling tribal instincts beyond their natural range.

findings.quote: Stigmatized roles such as 'cheater' or 'selfish bully' are labeled (and sanctioned) to make the system work in spite of predictable conflicts. This moralistic approach works reasonably well in curbing individual selfishness or tendencies to dominate, precisely because the group knows how to become aggressive in dealing with those it labels as deviants.
findings.content: Moral enforcement of sharing: the meat-sharing habit of nomadic foragers is transformed by language and morality so that definitive rules exist. Stigmatized roles such as 'cheater' or 'selfish bully' are labeled and sanctioned to make the system work despite predictable conflicts. An armed group can be exceedingly dangerous to any deviant - even the most powerful hunter - and hunters are always armed.

Trivers identifies conditions maximizing the chance reciprocal altruism will be selected for: (1) many altruistic situations in the lifetime of the altruists, (2) a given altruist repeatedly interacts with the same small set of individuals, and (3) pairs of altruists are exposed symmetrically to altruistic situations - each able to render roughly equivalent benefits at roughly equivalent costs. He elaborates these into biological parameters: long lifetime, low dispersal rate, mutual dependence, parental care, dominance hierarchy structure (less dominance facilitates reciprocity), and aid in combat. Selection discriminates against cheaters when cheating has later adverse effects that outweigh the benefit of not reciprocating - the altruist curtails future altruistic gestures to the cheater.
findings.where: Q Rev Biol 46(1):35-57, 1971. DOI: 10.1086/406755. Key conditions section.

findings.quote: The answer that I shall lay out in this book, is that for people above a threshold of material well-being, another kind of well-being 1s central. Autonomy - how much control you have over your life - and the opportunities you have for full social engagement and participation are crucial for health, well-being and longevity. It is inequality in these that plays a big part in producing the social gradient in health. Degrees of control and participation underlie the status syndrome.
findings.content: Among people above a threshold of material well-being, the higher their status in the pecking order the healthier they are likely to be. In other words, health follows a social gradient. I call this the status syndrome. For people above a threshold of material well-being, another kind of well-being is central. Autonomy - how much control you have over your life - and the opportunities you have for full social engagement and participation are crucial for health, well-being and longevity. It is inequality in these that plays a big part in producing the social gradient in health. Degrees of control and participation underlie the status syndrome.

findings.quote: In case it needs re-emphasis, we are not monkeys or even apes. We should not look to them, necessarily, to understand how people behave in the workplace, in the benefits office, on the local council, or the church committee. What these animal studies, from lab and field, give us are biologically plausible ways that social experience can be translated, via biological stress pathways, into disease.
findings.content: Animal studies, from lab and field, give us biologically plausible ways that social experience can be translated, via biological stress pathways, into disease. In case it needs re-emphasis, we are not monkeys or even apes - but the physiological stress response is similar in many different species. The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis that puts out cortisol operates similarly across mammals, and chronic activation of this system has systemic health consequences regardless of species.
findings.where: Chapter 4 'Stress in the Jungle? Stress in the Office?' pp. 115-116

findings.quote: There is little doubt, however, that purely psychological stimuli can arouse the physiological stress response, whether or not we experience an emotion such as fear.
findings.content: The chronic-stress-pathway translation from social experience to disease in humans. Marmot's synthesis draws on Sapolsky's fight-or-flight account (source lines 4763-4793, pp. ~115-116) - the sympathetic-adrenal-medullary and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axes, with immune function inhibited as 'another feature of the stress response' (line 4783) - and adds the critical observation that these biological stress pathways can be triggered by purely psychological stimuli, whether or not the person consciously experiences fear. Chronic activation of these pathways in the low-status, low-control condition translates perceived social experience into elevated cortisol, insulin resistance, central adiposity, dyslipidemia, immune suppression, and cardiovascular disease.
findings.where: Chapter 4 pp. 116-118, synthesizing the HPA/cortisol stress-disease pathway

findings.quote: The discovery of how important control and participation are for health leads in a different direction: to the circumstances in which we live and work. In other words, this is health research that leads us to focus, not on access to the latest medical technology, but on the way we think about the sort of lives we want for ourselves, and the sort of society in which we want to lead them.
findings.content: Much of the evidence for the importance of control in health comes from the observation that where people are unable to direct the circumstances of their own lives, health suffers. The social gradient in health affects everyone - it is not simply a question of 'them and us'. Understanding the social gradient requires focusing not on access to the latest medical technology, but on the way we think about the sort of lives we want for ourselves, and the sort of society in which we want to lead them.
findings.where: Introduction, p. 4, and Chapter 5 opening framing

findings.quote: It does not pretend to be a complete account of human mental evolution, because it addresses only those psychological adaptations manifest in sexual courtship.
findings.content: Miller's sexual-selection argument is explicitly scope-limited. He says it does NOT explain: adaptations shared with other primates (foraging, predator avoidance, parenting), the nature of consciousness, the dynamics of cultural change, or traits better explained by natural selection, kin selection, or reciprocal altruism. The argument applies to self-ornamentation, display, status, ideology, fashion, and aesthetics - to psychological adaptations manifest in sexual courtship. Miller also flags: minimal sexual dimorphism in human mental traits puzzles the classic "choosy-female, displaying-male" model and requires mutual-choice sexual selection models; sexual selection theory itself remains "very much under development"; empirical support is "patchy"; the theory risks over-emphasizing courtship functions of language and creative intelligence while neglecting their other fitness benefits.

Many distinctively human cognitive and behavioral traits - language fluency, art, music, humor, creativity, generosity, moral judgment - evolved as fitness indicators under sexual selection (mate-choice pressure), not solely as survival adaptations under natural selection. Sexual selection broadens the set of selection pressures shaping the human motivational and cognitive architecture beyond survival to include mate-choice display and discrimination.

findings.quote: Our analyses on complementary datasets using different methods yield wildly different numbers. Bayesian and generalized least-squares phylogenetic methods generate approximations of average group sizes between 69-109 and 16-42, respectively. However, enormous 95% confidence intervals (4-520 and 2-336, respectively) imply that specifying any one number is futile. A cognitive limit on human group size cannot be derived in this manner.
findings.content: Redoing the neocortex-ratio-to-group-size regression that produced 'Dunbar's number' with modern phylogenetic comparative methods (Bayesian and generalized least-squares) on complementary primate datasets yields wildly unstable human estimates: point estimates of 69-109 (Bayesian) and 16-42 (GLS), with 95 percent confidence intervals of 4-520 and 2-336 respectively. No single number is statistically supportable; a cognitive limit on human group size cannot be derived this way. CHALLENGE to the precise ~150 figure as a cognitive ceiling, cited to Dunbar 1992's neocortex-ratio extrapolation (ext 483).

findings.quote: Organisms try to get sex, power, and resources and to avoid danger and loss. Pursuing these goals gives rise to a set of defined situations. Each one poses different adaptive challenges that shape a different emotional state. Opportunity arouses enthusiasm. Success arouses joy. Threat arouses anxiety. Loss arouses sadness.
findings.content: Four situations that arise in goal pursuit map to four emotions: opportunity arouses enthusiasm, success arouses joy, threat arouses anxiety, loss arouses sadness. Organisms try to get sex, power, and resources and to avoid danger and loss. Each situation poses different adaptive challenges that shape a different emotional state. The scheme can be expanded by adding emotions for alternative outcomes - disappointment when pursuit fails, relief when threat is avoided.

findings.quote: Low control at work is an important contributor to disease, but there are ways of depriving people of control other than subjecting them to difficult conditions at work. The Rick and Maria story makes plain that low control over life circumstances is not confined to work. Low control in these other spheres, too, may be important for health.
findings.content: Marmot explicitly generalises the workplace-control finding to non-workplace spheres of life: low control in domestic, economic, and other spheres is also a causal exposure for disease, not an ancillary correlate of workplace conditions. The Whitehall II extension (asking civil servants about perceived control at home and in life in general) is what he uses to ground this generalisation empirically.

findings.quote: This evolving proto-WEIRD psychology gradually laid the groundwork for the rise of impersonal markets, urbanization, constitutional governments, democratic politics, individualistic religions, scientific societies, and relentless innovation.
findings.content: One sect of Christianity drove the spread of social norms that dramatically altered marriage, families, inheritance, and ownership in parts of Europe over centuries. This transformation of family life initiated psychological changes that spurred new forms of urbanization and fueled impersonal commerce. An evolving proto-WEIRD psychology laid the groundwork for impersonal markets, constitutional governments, democratic politics, individualistic religions, scientific societies, and relentless innovation.

findings.quote: People seek help mainly for symptoms, not diseases. Pain, fever, malaise, cough, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are protective responses. So are anxiety, jealousy, anger, and low mood. They are set off when something bad is happening. They are unpleasant but useful.
findings.content: Defensive responses such as pain, fever, cough, nausea, anxiety, jealousy, anger, and low mood are protective responses, not diseases. They are set off when something bad is happening. They are unpleasant but useful.

findings.quote: Human psychological mechanisms are adaptations that evolved to process environmental inputs, turning them into behavioral outputs that, on average, increase survival or reproductive prospects. Modern contexts, however, differ vastly from the environments that existed as human psychological mechanisms evolved.
findings.content: Evolutionary mismatch occurs when human psychological mechanisms, adapted to process ancestral environmental inputs, encounter modern contexts that differ vastly from those environments. Many inputs now differ in quantity, intensity, or no longer have the same fitness associations, leading mechanisms to produce maladaptive output. Li et al. classify mismatch along four dimensions: source (natural vs human-induced), type (forced vs hijacked), cause (input changes vs output-consequence changes), and consequences (effects on reproductive fitness crossed with effects on individual well-being). Tables 1-3 provide worked examples for each dimension.
findings.where: Current Directions in Psychological Science 27(1):38-44, 2018. DOI: 10.1177/0963721417731378

findings.quote: This is an elaboration of, but entirely consistent with, my hypothesis that what is important 1s control and opportunities to participate fully in society. The effort/reward model implies that lack of reward means lack of full participation. In the Siegrist model, lack of appropriate reward for effort expended causes emotional distress and activates biological stress pathways, with consequences for disease.
findings.content: Marmot integrates Siegrist's effort/reward model into his control/participation hypothesis by treating 'reward' (esteem, recognition, appropriate return for effort) as a mode of full social participation. Lack of appropriate reward therefore maps onto the same autonomy/participation pathway that drives the health gradient; it is not a third distinct factor but an extension of the participation axis through the workplace reciprocity channel.
findings.where: Chapter 5 'Who's in Charge?' pp. 131-132 synthesizing Karasek + Siegrist

findings.content: Electronic monitoring and algorithmic management in digital work environments reduce worker decision latitude, triggering M6 controllability failure (learned helplessness default). Combined with status-threat from visible performance metrics and always-on availability expectations activating M1 without resolution, this creates a chronic stress profile consistent with allostatic load accumulation.

Miller frames consumer signaling specifically around the "Central Six" personality dimensions: general intelligence plus the Big Five (openness, conscientiousness, agreeableness, stability, extraversion). These are the traits consumers attempt to display via purchases, and personality research on the Big Five is presented as directly applicable to consumer behavior. This gives a specific mapping: consumer goods = signaling vehicles for Central Six traits = proxies for mate-choice and friend-selection mechanisms that evolved to read these traits in conspecifics.

The two theoretical mechanisms Miller invokes for how courtship traits evolved: (1) Zahavi's handicap principle - costly ornaments reliably signal fitness because low-fitness pretenders cannot afford the costly display, forcing honesty through wastefulness; (2) Fisher's runaway selection - mate preferences become genetically linked to ornaments, creating positive-feedback escalation of trait complexity. Mental traits function as either direct fitness indexes (intelligence correlates intrinsically with fitness) or as handicaps (costly displays revealing hidden quality). Psychological biases including "novelty-seeking and pleasure-seeking" shape ornament design.

findings.quote: Words seed your concepts, concepts drive your predictions, predictions regulate your body budget, and your body budget determines how you feel. Therefore, the more finely grained your vocabulary, the more precisely your predicting brain can calibrate your budget to your body's needs. In fact, people who exhibit higher emotional granularity go to the doctor less frequently, use medication less frequently, and spend fewer days hospitalized for illness.
findings.content: Emotional granularity - the ability to construct finer-grained emotional experiences - has direct health consequences. Words seed concepts, concepts drive predictions, predictions regulate the body budget, and the body budget determines how you feel. The more finely grained the vocabulary, the more precisely the predicting brain can calibrate the body budget to actual needs. People who exhibit higher emotional granularity go to the doctor less frequently, use medication less frequently, and spend fewer days hospitalized for illness.

Consumer goods function substantially as fitness-indicator proxies: signaling intelligence, conscientiousness, openness, stability, and mate value rather than delivering the underlying benefits (mate access, belonging, status-resolution) that the signaling machinery evolved to obtain. Luxury consumption, branded goods, and status markers are industrialized exploitation of mate-choice and status-monitoring mechanisms. Consumers chase proxies that activate these systems without resolving the conditions the systems were selected to track.

findings.quote: In every waking moment, your brain uses past experience, organized as concepts, to guide your actions and give your sensations meaning. When the concepts involved are emotion concepts, your brain constructs instances of emotion.
findings.content: Barrett's formal definition of the theory of constructed emotion: the brain uses past experience organized as concepts to guide actions and give sensations meaning. When emotion concepts are active, the brain constructs instances of emotion. Emotions are not triggered reactions but active constructions from interoceptive sensations, conceptual knowledge, and contextual predictions.

findings.quote: The mechanism of learned helplessness is now very well-charted biologically, and the original theory got it backward. Passivity in response to shock is not learned. It is the default, unlearned response to prolonged aversive events and it is mediated by the serotonergic activity of the dorsal raphe nucleus, which in turn inhibits escape.
findings.content: The mechanism of learned helplessness has been biologically well-charted and the original theory got it backward. Passivity in response to prolonged aversive events is not learned - it is the default, unlearned response mediated by serotonergic activity of the dorsal raphe nucleus, which inhibits escape. What is actually learned is the detection of control: the prelimbic region of medial prefrontal cortex detects response-outcome contingency and inhibits the dorsal raphe, enabling active coping.

Passivity is the default, not learned. The original learned helplessness theory got it backward. Passivity in response to prolonged aversive events is the unlearned default response, not a learned expectation of uncontrollability. The neural evidence shows that aversive shock per se activates serotonergic (5-HT) neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus regardless of controllability. Both escapable and inescapable shock produce equal excitatory input to the DRN. There is nothing in the brain selectively turned on by lack of control - only something that turns things off when control is present.

Dorsal raphe nucleus 5-HT activation is both necessary and sufficient for passivity/anxiety. Three experimental strategies converge: (1) blocking DRN activation during inescapable shock (via lesion or pharmacological agents) prevents passivity - subjects behave as nonshocked controls; (2) preventing desensitization of 5-HT1A autoreceptors during inescapable shock also eliminates passivity; (3) blocking 5-HT receptors in target regions (amygdala, PAG) during testing eliminates passivity and fear. For sufficiency: directly activating DRN via microinjected GABA antagonist picrotoxin or benzodiazepine antagonist beta-carboline produces the full behavioral syndrome of inescapable shock without any shock at all.

Control is detected via vmPFC-DMS circuit, then vmPFC inhibits dorsal raphe. Two separable prelimbic cortex functions identified: (1) DETECT - a prelimbic-dorsomedial striatum (DMS) circuit detects contingency between response and outcome (the presence of control); (2) ACT - separate prelimbic neurons project to DRN and inhibit 5-HT neurons via GABAergic interneurons. Retrograde tracing confirmed these are distinct neuronal populations - no colocalization. Inactivating the vmPFC-to-DRN pathway during escapable shock makes the animal react as if shock were inescapable despite perfect escape performance. Activating this pathway during inescapable shock makes the animal react as if shock were escapable.

Experience of control produces lasting immunization via plasticity in vmPFC-DRN pathway. Prior escapable shock prevents passivity/anxiety from later inescapable shock even in completely different situations (trans-situational). This 'immunization' requires new protein synthesis in the prelimbic cortex - blocking protein synthesis after escapable shock eliminates immunization but not the immediate protective effect of control. The escapable shock experience induces plasticity proteins (e.g., phosphorylated ERK) in prelimbic neurons projecting to DRN, increasing their excitability. After immunization, even inescapable shock now activates the prelimbic-DRN inhibitory pathway as if the shock were escapable - the circuit now EXPECTs control.

findings.quote: It turns out the answer is both. We asked managers to rate jobs for their degree of control, and we asked civil servants themselves to tell us how much control they had. The correlation between them was surprisingly low. It seemed that subjective perception and external ratings of control were capturing something different about the job. Yet these two measures, the one more or less independent of the other, both predicted heart disease.
findings.content: Marmot addresses the subjective-vs-objective control measurement problem in Whitehall II by asking both managers (to rate jobs for degree of control) and civil servants (to self-report perceived control). The correlation between the two measures was surprisingly low - they captured different things about the job - yet both independently predicted heart disease. The methodological framing ('In the Whitehall II study, we wrestled with this problem in relation to low control at work') is at source lines 5271-5273, pp. ~128, and leads through a colour anecdote to the finding at 5291-5297.
findings.where: Chapter 5 'Who's in Charge?' pp. 128-129, Whitehall II methodology

findings.quote: In another study subjects waited an unknown length of time to receive a shock. This lack of predictability and control was so aversive that many chose to receive a stronger shock immediately. And in the others the period of anticipatory dread increasingly activated the amygdala.
findings.content: Lack of predictability and control over stressors is so aversive that subjects chose to receive a stronger shock immediately rather than wait an unknown time for a weaker one. The period of anticipatory dread increasingly activated the amygdala.

findings.quote: the worst stress-related health typically occurs in middle management, with its killer combo of high work demands but little autonomy - responsibility without control.
findings.content: Subordinate organisms are typically the most stressed and unhealthy. Lab rodents, primates from rhesus monkeys to lemurs, hamsters, guinea pigs, wolves, rabbits, pigs, fish, and sugar gliders all show that subordinate individuals have elevated resting glucocorticoids - chronic activation of the stress response even in the absence of acute stressors. The worst stress-related health in humans occurs in middle management, with its killer combination of high work demands but little autonomy - responsibility without control.

findings.quote: Acute and chronic stress cause an imbalance of neural circuitry subserving cognition, decision making, anxiety and mood that can increase or decrease expression of those behaviors and behavioral states. In the short term, such as for increased fearful vigilance and anxiety in a threatening environment, these changes may be adaptive; but, if the danger passes and the behavioral state persists along with the changes in neural circuitry, such maladaptation may need intervention
findings.content: Acute and chronic stress cause an imbalance of neural circuitry subserving cognition, decision making, anxiety and mood that can increase or decrease expression of those behaviors and behavioral states. In the short term, such as for increased fearful vigilance and anxiety in a threatening environment, these changes may be adaptive; but, if the danger passes and the behavioral state persists along with the changes in neural circuitry, such maladaptation may need intervention with a combination of pharmacological and behavioral therapies. Chronic restraint stress causes dendritic shortening in medial prefrontal cortex but produces dendritic growth in neurons of the basolateral amygdala - opposite structural effects in interconnected regions, reflecting different functional roles under sustained stress.
findings.where: Introduction and Section 2.4, 'Prefrontal cortex and amygdala,' pp. 3-4

findings.quote: Learned helplessness in the laboratory - combining the animal and human experimental results - produced eight of the nine symptoms [of depression], with the only exception being suicide and suicidal thoughts.
findings.content: Learned helplessness in the laboratory produces eight of the nine DSM symptoms of depression (excepting suicidal thoughts). The prelimbic medial prefrontal cortex detects contingency between behavior and outcomes and inhibits the dorsal raphe nucleus, restoring the capacity for active escape. When this detection circuit fails - due to chronic uncontrollable stress, developmental adversity, or prefrontal damage - the default passivity state persists as clinical depression.

findings.quote: More than half of respondents reported at least one, and one-fourth reported two or more categories of childhood exposures.
findings.content: The ACE dose-response gradient shows that childhood adversity is not a binary (traumatized/not) but a cumulative load: each additional category of exposure incrementally increases adult disease risk across behavioral, mental, and physical health domains. The clustering of risk behaviors (smoking, substance use, obesity, sexual risk-taking) suggests that these are not independent choices but downstream consequences of the same developmental calibration toward defensive/avoidant coping strategies.

findings.quote: A large body of evidence now exists that supports the demand/control model: people whose jobs are characterised by high demands and low control have a higher risk of developing coronary heart disease than others in jobs with more control. Our own Whitehall II study in the British civil service showed stronger support for the effects of low control on heart disease than for the adverse effects of high demand. Other studies in the US and Sweden, however, do show that a combination of high demand and low control is harmful to health. We also found a strong relation between low control at work and depressive symptoms.
findings.content: A large body of evidence supports the demand/control model: people whose jobs are characterised by high demands and low control have a higher risk of developing coronary heart disease than others in jobs with more control. The Whitehall II study showed stronger support for the effects of low control on heart disease than for the adverse effects of high demand alone. Other studies in the US and Sweden show that a combination of high demand and low control is harmful to health. A strong relation was also found between low control at work and depressive symptoms.
findings.where: Chapter 5 'Who's in Charge?' pp. 127-128, citing Karasek demand/control model and Whitehall II heart-disease outcomes

findings.quote: People at the same level in the occupational hierarchy with differing amounts of control had markedly different rates of disease - low control consistently led to more disease.
findings.content: People at the same level in the occupational hierarchy with differing amounts of control had markedly different rates of disease - low control consistently led to more disease. In Whitehall II, within-grade variation in control predicted heart disease: it was not simply grade per se doing the work, but the low control that tended to accompany lower grades.
findings.where: Chapter 5 'Who's in Charge?' p. 128, Whitehall II analysis

findings.quote: In Whitehall II, we found lower control in lower grades whether we consider people's self-reports or managers' 'objective' assessment of how much control each job entails. In Whitehall II, this gradient in control over work appears to have strong implications for the gradient in heart disease and mental illness. Statistically, low control was an important contributor to the higher rate of heart disease in the lower grades.
findings.content: In Whitehall II, lower control appeared in lower grades whether we consider people's self-reports or managers' 'objective' assessment of how much control each job entails. Statistically, low control was an important contributor to the higher rate of heart disease in the lower grades. The nature of the hierarchy is less control the lower you go.
findings.where: Chapter 5 'Who's in Charge?' p. 129, Whitehall II structural finding

findings.quote: that elusive point of absorption, beyond contingency
findings.content: The zone state is described as absorption 'beyond contingency' - a narrowly focused attention state where control dissolves into automaticity. Machine gamblers seek the zone not to win but to escape - from anxiety, grief, boredom, social pain. The machine provides a predictable, controllable micro-environment that the rest of life cannot match. This is proxy hijacking of M6 (controllability) as much as M2 (pursuit).

findings.quote: Through prediction, your brain constructs the world you experience. It combines bits and pieces of your past and estimates how likely each bit applies in your current situation.
findings.content: The brain constructs the world you experience through prediction. Intrinsic brain activity - millions of nonstop predictions - is the brain's primary mode of operation. Past experience, organized as concepts, generates predictions that are tested against incoming sensory input. Events in the world merely tune these predictions rather than triggering responses. Evolution literally wired the brain for efficient prediction: 90 percent of connections entering primary visual cortex carry predictions from other brain regions, not sensory input from the world.

findings.quote: If a rat is experimentally injected with infectious bacteria, it behaves a bit like I did after the dentist. It withdraws from social contact with other animals, it doesn't move so much, its sleeping and eating cycles are disturbed. In short, infection reliably causes a syndrome in animals - called sickness behaviour - that is roughly recognisable as akin to the human experience of depression. In fact, you don't even need to infect a rat to see this sickness behaviour. It is enough to inject the rat with cytokines, proving that it is not the germ itself that causes sickness behaviour but the immune response to infection. Inflammation directly causes depression-like behaviours in animals - that is beyond doubt.
findings.content: Dantzer's foundational finding (Bullmore synthesizes): injecting a rat with infectious bacteria produces sickness behavior - social withdrawal, reduced movement, disturbed sleep-wake cycles, reduced eating. Injecting cytokines alone (without bacteria) reproduces the syndrome, demonstrating it is the IMMUNE RESPONSE that causes sickness behavior, not the pathogen itself. Inflammation directly causes depression-like behaviors in animals. This is load-bearing for M8's cascade - the immune system drives behavioral change via cytokine signaling regardless of pathogen presence.
findings.where: Chapter 1 'Daring to Think Differently' pp. early chapters

findings.quote: We used measures of effort/reward imbalance in the workplace in our studies in Poland, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Hungary. This study confirmed the importance for poor health of low control at work and generally. In addition, people whose work was characterised by a high degree of imbalance between effort and reward had a 60 per cent greater chance of being in poor health than those with an appropriate balance.
findings.content: People whose work was characterised by a high degree of imbalance between efforts put in and rewards received had higher risk of disease, independently of low control at work. Two distinct psychosocial features - low control and effort/reward imbalance - both contribute to the work-health gradient in Whitehall II.
findings.where: Chapter 7 'Health and Work' p. 190-191, Whitehall II effort/reward analysis, citing Siegrist model

findings.quote: We found a graded relationship between the number of categories of childhood exposure and each of the adult health risk behaviors and diseases that were studied.
findings.content: The ACE Study (9,508 respondents) demonstrated a graded dose-response relationship between categories of childhood adversity (psychological abuse, physical abuse, sexual abuse, violence against mother, household substance abuse, mental illness, incarceration) and adult health outcomes. Persons with 4+ ACE categories had 4-12 fold increased risk for alcoholism, drug abuse, depression, and suicide attempts; 2-4 fold increased risk for smoking, poor health, STDs; 1.4-1.6 fold for inactivity and obesity. More than half of respondents reported at least one category. Adult diseases linked included ischemic heart disease, cancer, chronic lung disease, skeletal fractures, and liver disease.

THE INVERSION: The original learned helplessness theory got it backward. Passivity is NOT learned - it is the default, unlearned neural response to prolonged aversive stimulation, mediated by serotonergic activation of the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN). What IS learned is control, via the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) inhibiting the DRN. The neural circuit operates in three stages: (1) PASSIVITY/ANXIETY - aversive shock activates DRN 5-HT neurons, which release serotonin in the periaqueductal gray (inhibiting escape behavior) and amygdala (potentiating fear/anxiety); DRN sensitization via 5-HT1A autoreceptor desensitization persists for days. (2) DETECT/ACT - the prelimbic region of vmPFC detects controllability via a circuit with the dorsal medial striatum, then a separate prelimbic population projects to and inhibits DRN 5-HT neurons via GABAergic interneurons. (3) EXPECT - after learning control, plasticity changes in the PL-DRN pathway create an expectation circuit that responds to future aversive events as if controllable. In vivo microdialysis showed inescapable shock produces sustained 5-HT elevation in DRN, while escapable shock causes 5-HT to drop precipitously as the animal learns the escape response. DRN activation is both necessary (blockade prevents helplessness) and sufficient (direct DRN activation reproduces all behavioral sequelae).

Learned helplessness maps onto 8 of 9 DSM depression symptoms. Combining animal and human experimental results, learned helplessness produced: sad mood, loss of interest, weight loss, sleep problems, psychomotor problems, fatigue, worthlessness, and indecisiveness/poor concentration. Only suicide/suicidal thoughts not produced - unsurprising given mild laboratory aversive events. The converse also held: depressed people who had not received inescapable events behaved in the laboratory as if they had - showing passivity in shuttlebox and giving up on cognitive problems. The passivity/anxiety symptoms of learned helplessness map directly onto depression symptoms.

findings.quote: While attributing specific functions to specific mood states is a mistake, the capacity for mood can be said to have a general function: mood reallocates investments of time, effort, resources, and risk taking to maximize Darwinian fitness in situations of varying propitiousness. High and low moods adjust cognition and behavior to cope with propitious and unpropitious situations.
findings.content: Mood reallocates investments of time, effort, resources, and risk taking to maximize Darwinian fitness in situations of varying propitiousness. High and low moods adjust cognition and behavior to cope with propitious and unpropitious situations. Attributing specific functions to specific mood states is a mistake - the capacity for mood has a general function as a resource-allocation system.

findings.quote: Sometimes low mood should be respected as normal and useful to help adjust a person's motivation and life directions. However, often the situation can't be changed. The loss of a friend, continuing abuse, inability to get a job, trying every night to help a child get off drugs, finding no relief from chronic pain - those are good reasons, but the resulting bad feelings are harmful even if they are normal.
findings.content: Low mood can be (1) normal and useful for adjusting motivation, (2) normal but harmful because the situation cannot be changed (loss, abuse, chronic pain), (3) normal but useless because of the Smoke Detector Principle, (4) normal but useless because we live in environments so different from those we evolved in, or (5) caused by abnormalities in the mood regulation system. Clinicians should take the same medical approach to low mood as to physical pain: find the cause and fix it, but always relieve suffering.

findings.quote: Low moods prevent us from wasting effort in pursuit of unreachable goals, but they often escalate into pathological depression.
findings.content: Low mood prevents us from wasting effort in pursuit of unreachable goals, but it often escalates into pathological depression. The signal is functionally adaptive - it indicates that current strategies are failing and effort should be redirected - but the signal itself can become the problem when the mood regulation system cannot disengage.

findings.quote: depression is ordinarily, therefore, a normal, adaptive part of disengaging oneself from an incentive... Mood thus regulates the allocation of effort and resources - toward enterprises, strategies, and times likely to give a high payoff and away from unprofitable enterprises and times when efforts will likely be wasted or dangerous.
findings.content: The role of depression in disengaging motivation from an unreachable goal was specified explicitly in the incentive-disengagement theory of Klinger. If a commitment to pursue a goal encounters an obstacle, efforts increase and become aggressive. If the obstacle cannot be overcome, low mood helps to disengage the commitment and end the cycle. If the individual cannot disengage, low mood escalates. Klinger concludes, 'depression is ordinarily, therefore, a normal, adaptive part of disengaging oneself from an incentive.' Many other researchers also see a close relationship between depression and difficulty in disengaging from major commitments. Mood thus regulates the allocation of effort and resources - toward enterprises, strategies, and times likely to give a high payoff and away from unprofitable enterprises and times when efforts will likely be wasted or dangerous.
findings.where: Section 'Possible Functions of Low Mood and Depression,' pp. 15-16

findings.quote: stress doesn't come from the outside world. You construct it.
findings.content: Stress is constructed via the same brain mechanisms that construct emotion. In both cases the brain issues predictions about the body budget in relation to the outside world and makes meaning via concepts. The interoceptive network and the control network play the same roles in stress and emotion construction. The ascending and descending pathways between brain and body are identical. What differs is the end result - whether the brain categorizes sensations as stressful or emotional.

findings.quote: where depression and loneliness converge is in a diminished sense of personal control, which leads to passive coping. This induced passivity is one of the reasons that, despite the pain and urgency that loneliness imposes, it does not always lead to effective action. Loss of executive control leads to lack of persistence, and frustration leads to what the psychologist Martin Seligman has termed 'learned helplessness.'
findings.content: Loneliness and depression share a diminished sense of personal control, which leads to passive coping. This induced passivity is one of the reasons that, despite the pain and urgency that loneliness imposes, it does not always lead to effective action. Loss of executive control leads to lack of persistence, and frustration leads to what Martin Seligman has termed 'learned helplessness.'
findings.where: Chapter 5 'The Universal and the Particular,' p. 83

findings.quote: The answer that I shall lay out in this book, is that for people above a threshold of material well-being, another kind of well-being 1s central. Autonomy - how much control you have over your life - and the opportunities you have for full social engagement and participation are crucial for health, well-being and longevity. It is inequality in these that plays a big part in producing the social gradient in health. Degrees of control and participation underlie the status syndrome.
findings.content: Among people above a threshold of material well-being, the higher their status in the pecking order the healthier they are likely to be. In other words, health follows a social gradient. I call this the status syndrome. For people above a threshold of material well-being, another kind of well-being is central. Autonomy - how much control you have over your life - and the opportunities you have for full social engagement and participation are crucial for health, well-being and longevity. It is inequality in these that plays a big part in producing the social gradient in health. Degrees of control and participation underlie the status syndrome.

findings.quote: The discovery of how important control and participation are for health leads in a different direction: to the circumstances in which we live and work. In other words, this is health research that leads us to focus, not on access to the latest medical technology, but on the way we think about the sort of lives we want for ourselves, and the sort of society in which we want to lead them.
findings.content: Much of the evidence for the importance of control in health comes from the observation that where people are unable to direct the circumstances of their own lives, health suffers. The social gradient in health affects everyone - it is not simply a question of 'them and us'. Understanding the social gradient requires focusing not on access to the latest medical technology, but on the way we think about the sort of lives we want for ourselves, and the sort of society in which we want to lead them.
findings.where: Introduction, p. 4, and Chapter 5 opening framing

findings.quote: Low control at work is an important contributor to disease, but there are ways of depriving people of control other than subjecting them to difficult conditions at work. The Rick and Maria story makes plain that low control over life circumstances is not confined to work. Low control in these other spheres, too, may be important for health.
findings.content: Marmot explicitly generalises the workplace-control finding to non-workplace spheres of life: low control in domestic, economic, and other spheres is also a causal exposure for disease, not an ancillary correlate of workplace conditions. The Whitehall II extension (asking civil servants about perceived control at home and in life in general) is what he uses to ground this generalisation empirically.

findings.quote: the central concepts are those of behavioural systems and their control, of information, negative feedback, and a behavioural form of homeostasis. The more complex forms of instinctive behaviour are regarded as resulting from the execution of plans that, depending on the species, are more or less flexible.
findings.content: Bowlby's behavioral systems model: instinctive behavior operates through control systems using behavioral homeostasis. The central concepts are behavioral systems and their control, information, negative feedback, and homeostatic regulation. Complex instinctive behavior results from the execution of plans that, depending on species, are more or less flexible. Plan execution is initiated by receipt of information from sense organs and guided by continuous reception of feedback from results of action taken.

findings.quote: This is an elaboration of, but entirely consistent with, my hypothesis that what is important 1s control and opportunities to participate fully in society. The effort/reward model implies that lack of reward means lack of full participation. In the Siegrist model, lack of appropriate reward for effort expended causes emotional distress and activates biological stress pathways, with consequences for disease.
findings.content: Marmot integrates Siegrist's effort/reward model into his control/participation hypothesis by treating 'reward' (esteem, recognition, appropriate return for effort) as a mode of full social participation. Lack of appropriate reward therefore maps onto the same autonomy/participation pathway that drives the health gradient; it is not a third distinct factor but an extension of the participation axis through the workplace reciprocity channel.
findings.where: Chapter 5 'Who's in Charge?' pp. 131-132 synthesizing Karasek + Siegrist

findings.content: Some features of digital work may be more matched with ancestral work conditions than traditional industrial/office work: flexible scheduling restoring autonomy over time allocation, broader access to skill-learning and collaboration networks, and potential for reduced commuting allowing more time for non-work regulatory needs. Digital work is a mixed mismatch profile, not a uniformly mismatched one.

Electronic monitoring and algorithmic management in digital work environments reduce worker decision latitude, triggering M6 controllability failure (learned helplessness default). Combined with status-threat from visible performance metrics and always-on availability expectations activating M1 without resolution, this creates a chronic stress profile consistent with allostatic load accumulation.

findings.quote: Words seed your concepts, concepts drive your predictions, predictions regulate your body budget, and your body budget determines how you feel. Therefore, the more finely grained your vocabulary, the more precisely your predicting brain can calibrate your budget to your body's needs. In fact, people who exhibit higher emotional granularity go to the doctor less frequently, use medication less frequently, and spend fewer days hospitalized for illness.
findings.content: Emotional granularity - the ability to construct finer-grained emotional experiences - has direct health consequences. Words seed concepts, concepts drive predictions, predictions regulate the body budget, and the body budget determines how you feel. The more finely grained the vocabulary, the more precisely the predicting brain can calibrate the body budget to actual needs. People who exhibit higher emotional granularity go to the doctor less frequently, use medication less frequently, and spend fewer days hospitalized for illness.
