Offspring of low-LG mothers who were cross-fostered to high-LG mothers showed: (1) reversed DNA methylation patterns matching biological high-LG offspring, (2) normalized histone acetylation, (3) restored NGFI-A transcription factor binding, (4) increased GR expression, and (5) attenuated HPA stress responses. These changes emerged over the first week of life and persisted into adulthood. Additionally, central infusion of a histone deacetylase inhibitor in adult offspring of low-LG mothers removed all group differences, demonstrating that the epigenomic state is causally responsible for the phenotypic differences.

findings.quote: This domain of epigenetics was uncovered in a landmark 2004 study by Meaney and colleagues, one of the most cited papers published in the prestigious journal Nature Neuroscience. They had shown previously that offspring of more "attentive" rat mothers (those that frequently nurse, groom, and lick their pups) become adults with lower glucocorticoid levels, less anxiety, better learning, and delayed brain aging.
findings.content: Meaney's landmark 2004 study demonstrated that maternal care style in rats produces epigenetic changes in offspring's stress response genes. Offspring of more attentive mothers (frequent nursing, grooming, licking) become adults with lower glucocorticoid levels, less anxiety, better learning, and delayed brain aging. These changes are epigenetic - mothering style alters gene regulation in pups' brains. Remarkably, such pups as adults become more attentive mothers themselves, passing the trait epigenetically to the next generation.

findings.quote: an epigenomic state of a gene can be established through behavioral programming, and it is potentially reversible.
findings.content: Maternal licking/grooming and arched-back nursing in rats alters offspring epigenome at the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) gene promoter in the hippocampus via DNA methylation and histone acetylation changes. Offspring of high-LG mothers have lower glucocorticoid levels, less anxiety, better learning, and delayed brain aging. Methylation differences emerged over the first week of life, were reversed with cross-fostering, and persisted into adulthood. Central infusion of a histone deacetylase inhibitor removed group differences - demonstrating that an epigenomic state established through behavioral programming is potentially reversible.

findings.quote: oxytocin, which mediates various pro-social processes, including maternal behavior and the inhibition of separation distress (Chapters 12 to 14), can yield a tripeptide called PLG (proline-leucine-glycine), which mediates none of the above but has antidepressant effects.
findings.content: Panksepp's early summary of oxytocin's pro-social functions: oxytocin mediates various pro-social processes including female sexual response, orgasm, maternal behavior, social memory, and the INHIBITION of separation distress. It is a single neuropeptide that operates across the sexual-maternal-social-bonding domains - exactly the molecular overlap that allows evolution to construct the 'social contract' by repurposing reproductive circuits for broader bonding. This is primary-source evidence for the M14/M9/M3 architectural overlap in Cor's specification.

findings.quote: Childhood abuse, for example, causes epigenetic changes in hundreds of genes in the human hippocampus. Moreover, Stephen Suomi of the National Institutes of Health and Szyf found that mothering style in monkeys has epigenetic effects on more than a thousand frontocortical genes.
findings.content: Childhood abuse causes epigenetic changes in hundreds of genes in the human hippocampus. Mothering style in monkeys has epigenetic effects on more than a thousand frontocortical genes. Hormonal responses to fetal and childhood experiences have epigenetic effects on genes related to BDNF, the vasopressin and oxytocin system, and estrogen sensitivity, with effects pertinent to adult cognition, personality, emotionality, and psychiatric health.

findings.quote: At discharge or 40 to 41 weeks' postmenstrual age: "KMC was associated with a statistically significant reduction in the risk of mortality (risk ratio [RR] 0.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.39 to 0.92; eight trials, 1736 infants)." At latest follow-up: "KMC was associated with a significantly decreased risk of mortality (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.95; 12 trials, 2293 infants; moderate-quality evidence)."
findings.content: Cochrane meta-analysis of kangaroo mother care (KMC) vs conventional care in low-birthweight infants. In STABILIZED LBW infants, KMC significantly reduced the risk of mortality at discharge or 40-41 weeks postmenstrual age (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.39-0.92; 8 trials, 1736 infants) and at latest follow-up (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48-0.95; 12 trials, 2293 infants; moderate-quality evidence). RR 0.60 is the source of the frequently cited ~40% KMC mortality reduction (1 - 0.60). KMC also reduced nosocomial infection and hypothermia and improved growth and breastfeeding. This is corpus grounding for the claim that continuous skin-to-skin (C-tactile) contact is a mortality-level regulatory input for the preterm/LBW infant, not a comfort measure - the basis of R1 and of empirical demonstration ED9.

findings.quote: During it the young child appears acutely distressed at having lost his mother and seeks to recapture her by the full exercise of his limited resources. He will often cry loudly, shake his cot, throw himself about, and look eagerly towards any sight or sound which might prove to be his missing mother.
findings.content: Bowlby's three-phase separation response in young children: protest (acute distress, crying, seeking the missing mother), despair (increasing hopelessness, withdrawal, deep mourning), and detachment (apparent recovery that masks emotional disengagement). The protest phase involves active attempts to recapture the mother; despair involves withdrawal and monotonous crying; detachment involves accepting care from others while showing striking absence of attachment behavior toward the mother on her return.

findings.quote: Several decades ago, Harry Harlow, at the University of Wisconsin, performed a classic experiment on touching monkeys. He built one surrogate mother out of terry cloth and a second surrogate mother out of wire mesh. For some of the monkey infants, the terry-cloth mother provided milk, and the wire mother did not. For others, the condition was reversed. The monkey infants preferred the cloth mother without the milk over the wire mother with milk, suggesting that they needed the touch stimulation as much as, if not more than, the nourishment.
findings.content: Field's synthesis of Harlow's foundational primate touch-deprivation work: infant rhesus monkeys preferred a terry-cloth surrogate mother without milk over a wire-mesh mother with milk, suggesting that touch stimulation is at least as important as nourishment. Harlow's experiments showed that infants without any surrogate developed self-clasping behavior, failed to develop normal grooming or reproduction, and had broken immune systems. Suomi's follow-up showed that Plexiglas separation (vision, hearing, smell preserved but no touch) was sufficient to produce these deficits - touch itself was the critical missing stimulation, not the other sensory modalities. This is the primary-source chain Field uses to ground touch as a distinct regulatory input in R1's architecture.
findings.where: Field, Touch (2014) Chapter 3 'Touch in Early Development', pp. ~47

findings.quote: the ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven emotional, or affective, systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy). Each of these systems controls distinct but specific types of behaviors associated with many overlapping physiological changes.
findings.content: The ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven emotional systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy). Each controls distinct behaviors with overlapping physiological changes and generates distinct types of affective consciousness. When stimulated in humans, people always experience intense emotional feelings. Capitalizations indicate that real physical and distinct networks for these emotions exist in mammalian brains.

findings.quote: primal emotional systems are made up of neuroanatomies and neurochemistries that are remarkably similar across all mammalian species. This suggests that these systems evolved a very long time ago and that at a basic emotional and motivational level, all mammals are more similar than they are different.
findings.content: Primal emotional systems are made up of neuroanatomies and neurochemistries remarkably similar across all mammalian species. This suggests these systems evolved a very long time ago and that at a basic emotional and motivational level, all mammals are more similar than different. Deep in the ancient affective recesses of our brains, we remain evolutionarily kin. The same neural paths and brain chemicals that arouse each of these seven systems are found within all mammals.

Panksepp's textbook Affective Neuroscience establishes the methodology and evidence base for the seven subcortical affective systems. Across cross-species deep brain stimulation, lesion, and pharmacological studies, the same brain regions produce the same functional categories of affective response - SEEKING, FEAR, RAGE, LUST, CARE, PANIC, PLAY - across mammals, providing the empirical foundation for treating these as conserved motivational architecture rather than culturally constructed categories.

findings.quote: FEAR is an inborn capacity of the mammalian brain. However, FEAR, just like all other basic emotions, rapidly gets enmeshed with world events as it comes to be regulated by learning and encoded in our conscious minds.
findings.content: FEAR is an inborn capacity of the mammalian brain that rapidly gets enmeshed with world events through learning. Most basic emotions need not be expressed immediately after birth. Some - including CARE, LUST, and PLAY - come online long after others such as SEEKING, RAGE, and FEAR. The developmental timing reflects phylogenetic priority: the oldest and most survival-critical systems activate earliest.

findings.quote: We found a graded relationship between the number of categories of childhood exposure and each of the adult health risk behaviors and diseases that were studied.
findings.content: The ACE Study (9,508 respondents) demonstrated a graded dose-response relationship between categories of childhood adversity (psychological abuse, physical abuse, sexual abuse, violence against mother, household substance abuse, mental illness, incarceration) and adult health outcomes. Persons with 4+ ACE categories had 4-12 fold increased risk for alcoholism, drug abuse, depression, and suicide attempts; 2-4 fold increased risk for smoking, poor health, STDs; 1.4-1.6 fold for inactivity and obesity. More than half of respondents reported at least one category. Adult diseases linked included ischemic heart disease, cancer, chronic lung disease, skeletal fractures, and liver disease.

findings.quote: It takes on the order of 13 million calories to rear a modern human from birth to maturity
findings.content: It takes on the order of 13 million calories to rear a modern human from birth to maturity, and the young of these early hominins would also have been very costly. Unlike other ape youngsters, they would have depended on nutritional subsidies from caregivers long after they were weaned. Years before a mother's previous children were self-sufficient, she would give birth to another infant, and the care these dependent youngsters required would be far in excess of what a foraging mother by herself could regularly supply.

findings.quote: One widely accepted tenet of life history theory is that, across species, those with bigger babies relative to the mother's body size will also tend to exhibit longer intervals between births because the more babies cost the mother to produce, the longer she will need to recoup before reproducing again. Yet humans - like marmosets - provide a paradoxical exception to this rule.
findings.content: Humans produce the largest, slowest-maturing, most costly babies of any primate yet breed the fastest (every 3-4 years vs. 6-8 years for other apes). This paradox requires approximately 13 million calories per child from birth to independence. The only way this is possible is through alloparental provisioning - mothers cannot meet these costs alone. Life-history theory predicts longer birth intervals for costlier offspring; cooperative breeding is what breaks this constraint.

findings.quote: Ornithologists used to call such assistants "helpers"; primatologists called them "aunts" (after the British "auntie," to designate a female relative or trusted family friend). In 1975, Edward O.Wilson decided it was time for a more dignified designation: allo- (from the Greek for "other than") plus parent.
findings.content: Hrdy's 'allomother' term precision: E.O. Wilson coined 'alloparent' in 1975 to replace imprecise 'helpers' (ornithologists) and 'aunts' (primatologists). Hrdy refines further to 'allomothers' - all caretakers OTHER than the mother (whose identity is usually known for sure). The precision matters: in cooperative-breeding species, alloparents play critical roles, allowing mothers to breed at a faster rate than would otherwise be possible. Humans fit this pattern.

findings.quote: alloparenting is particularly well developed and played a special role in the evolution of our own large-brained, slow-growing, and extraordinarily inventive species.
findings.content: Hrdy's alloparenting role in human evolution: alloparenting is particularly well developed and played a special role in the evolution of our own large-brained, slow-growing, and extraordinarily inventive species. This links the cross-species cooperative-breeding finding to the specific human case: our unusually extended juvenile period and large brains require more caloric provisioning than a single mother can provide, making allomothering not a cultural addition but a species architecture.

findings.quote: My melding of vocation with family has been supported by a steadfast partner, resilient children, and the generous hearts of alloparents - all the individuals other than me and my husband who helped us rear our children. As I would learn, mothers have worked for as long as our species has existed, and they have depended on others to help them rear their children.
findings.content: Hrdy's autobiographical framing: she describes her own reliance on alloparents to melding vocation with family, and grew up herself being reared by a succession of governesses. Her experience - that mothers have worked for as long as our species has existed and depended on others to help rear their children - is the implicit empirical anchor for the broader thesis. This is not mere anecdote but frames the book's central argument that maternal self-sacrifice as a norm is a modern-Western construction, not an evolutionary given.

findings.quote: Among all fathers, time spent in direct childcare was linked with the degree of amygdala-STS connectivity.
findings.content: fMRI study of 89 first-time parents in three groups: primary-caregiving mothers, secondary-caregiving fathers, and primary-caregiving fathers raising infants without maternal involvement. All parents activated a shared global parental caregiving network integrating emotional processing and mentalizing circuits. Primary-caregiving fathers showed amygdala activation comparable to primary-caregiving mothers alongside father-typical superior temporal sulcus activation, and amygdala-STS connectivity scaled with time spent in direct childcare across all fathers. The care network is shared across sexes and its recruitment tracks caregiving experience.
findings.where: PNAS 111(27):9792-9797. Abstract + Results, full text via PMC4103311.

findings.quote: these early hominin mothers relied on groupmates to help protect, care for, and provision their unusually slow-maturing children
findings.content: Mothers and Others is about the emergence of a particular mode of childrearing known as 'cooperative breeding' and its psychological implications for apes in the line leading to Homo sapiens. Cooperative breeding refers to any species with alloparental assistance in both the care and provisioning of young. Unlike mothers among other African apes, who nurtured infants on their own, these early hominin mothers relied on groupmates to help protect, care for, and provision their unusually slow-maturing children and keep them on the survivable side of starvation.

findings.quote: We have underestimated just how important shared care and provisioning of offspring by group members other than parents have been in shaping prosocial impulses.
findings.content: We have underestimated how important shared care and provisioning by group members other than parents have been in shaping prosocial impulses. Without shared care and provisioning, all intergroup strategizing and strife would have been evolutionarily speaking signifying nothing. Cooperative breeding - where there is shared care and provisioning of young - is the key innovation that made human-level prosociality possible.

findings.quote: 'Cooperative breeding' refers to any species with alloparental assistance in both the care and provisioning of young.
findings.content: Cooperative breeding refers to any species with alloparental assistance in both care and provisioning of young. Unlike mothers among other African apes who nurtured infants alone, early hominin mothers relied on groupmates to protect, care for, and provision their slow-maturing children. This mode of child-rearing had profound psychological implications for the ape line leading to Homo sapiens.

findings.quote: Of all the attachments mammalian babies form, none is more powerful than that between baby primates and their mothers. The emotional ties that bind ape mothers to their infants and infants to their mothers are unusually long-lasting.
findings.content: Of all attachments mammalian babies form, none is more powerful than that between baby primates and their mothers. The emotional ties binding ape mothers to infants and infants to mothers are unusually long-lasting. But in cooperatively breeding humans, this dyadic bond is embedded in a wider network of allomaternal attachments that share the regulatory burden.

findings.quote: for their pronounced ambivalence toward newborns and their extremely contingent maternal commitment. Infants have adapted, as we will see later, with special traits for attracting the attention of potential caretakers.
findings.content: Humans display pronounced ambivalence toward newborns and extremely contingent maternal commitment. Unlike the steady investment other great ape mothers show, human mothers assess whether conditions support successful rearing before committing fully. Infants have adapted with special traits - cuteness, prolonged eye contact, social smiling - for attracting attention from potential caretakers. Maternal commitment is conditional on perceived alloparental support.

findings.quote: When politicians lament the 'decline of the family,' they have in mind departures from the nuclear family: a man, his wife, and their biological children. However, the template for this kind of family dates back only a century or so, at most to Victorian times.
findings.content: The idealized nuclear family (breadwinner father, homemaker mother, biological children) dates back only about a century, to Victorian times at most. In American contexts, it became the template only in the 1950s. This family structure is a historical aberration - for the vast majority of human history, children were raised in extended kin networks with multiple allomaternal caregivers. The 'decline of the family' that politicians lament is actually a departure from an extremely brief historical norm.

findings.quote: Among humans living in foraging societies, a helpful mate and/or alloparents were usually essential for a mother to rear any infant at all. In a surprisingly broad range of creatures, indispensable alloparents provide many of the same forms of care a mother might, protecting and provisioning, even suckling another female's infant in cases where the alloparent is
findings.content: Hrdy's core allomothering thesis: Among humans living in foraging societies, a helpful mate and/or alloparents were usually essential for a mother to rear any infant at all. Indispensable alloparents provide many of the same forms of care a mother might - protecting, provisioning, even suckling another female's infant. This is load-bearing for M9 Care/Alloparenting: human infants are NOT raised dyadically, and the mother-as-sole-caregiver framing misses the evolutionary architecture entirely.

findings.quote: Clearly, for cooperatively breeding mammals, a female's physical capacity to conceive and bear viable young is only a small part of the equation. She must also be able to carry through with the enterprise - rearing offspring to independence.
findings.content: Hrdy on contingent maternal commitment: For cooperatively breeding mammals, a female's physical capacity to conceive and bear viable young is only a small part of the equation. She must also be able to CARRY THROUGH with the enterprise - rearing offspring to independence. This is the foundational argument that maternal investment is context-dependent, not unconditional - mothers evaluate whether circumstances (including alloparent availability, food resources, and infant health) permit successful rearing, and adjust their investment accordingly. Load-bearing for M9 Care/Alloparenting and for reading maternal ambivalence as adaptive rather than pathological.

findings.quote: a woman's maternal emotions (those concerned with producing and nurturing offspring and keeping them alive) continued to be viewed as separate from and even antithetical to the rest of her - her sexuality and, particularly, her ambition. Yet the compartmentalized way we have learned to think about these emotions has nothing to do with how they evolved.
findings.content: Hrdy on the compartmentalization error: maternal emotions (producing/nurturing/keeping offspring alive) have been viewed as separate from and even antithetical to the rest of a woman - her sexuality and her ambition. This compartmentalized framing has nothing to do with how these emotions evolved. In the ancestral environment, the same female was simultaneously pursuing reproductive goals AND maternal goals AND resource goals AND social-position goals, with all of them integrated rather than competing. The modern fragmentation is cultural, not evolutionary.

findings.quote: there is a great deal of neuropeptide specificity in the coding of behavior, and it is esthetically pleasing to note that we often observe a correspondence between the peripheral functions of these neuropeptides and their role within the brain (Table 6.1). For instance, in the periphery, insulin controls metabolic dispersion of nutrients, while in the brain it helps mediate satiety (see Chapter 9). Likewise, in the periphery, the hormone angiotensin promotes water retention in the kidney, while in the brain it promotes thirst. Thus, many neuropeptide languages highlight the tendency of evolution to reutilize existing elements for new tasks that are harmonious with previous functions.
findings.content: Panksepp's observation of evolutionary economy in neuropeptide coding: there is extensive correspondence between the peripheral and central functions of neuropeptides - insulin controls peripheral glucose dispersion AND central satiety; angiotensin controls peripheral water retention AND central thirst; oxytocin controls peripheral birthing and milk letdown AND central maternal acceptance and readiness. Many peptides highlight evolution's tendency to REUTILIZE existing elements for new tasks harmonious with previous functions. This exaptation pattern is load-bearing for the DA8 architectural claim that newer mechanisms (social bonding) are built from older ones (reproductive physiology).

findings.quote: Species following the model should tend to evolve behaviour such that each organism appears to be attempting to maximize its inclusive fitness.
findings.content: Hamilton's genetical mathematical model allows for interactions between relatives on one another's fitness. Using Wright's Coefficient of Relationship as the measure of replica genes in a relative, Hamilton found inclusive fitness - a quantity incorporating the maximizing property of Darwinian fitness. Species following the model tend to evolve behaviour where each organism appears to maximize its inclusive fitness, implying limited restraint on selfish competitive behaviour and possibility of limited self-sacrifices.

findings.quote: To express the matter more vividly, in the world of our model organisms, whose behaviour is determined strictly by genotype, we expect to find that no one is prepared to sacrifice his life for any single person but that everyone will sacrifice it when he can thereby save more than two brothers, or four half-brothers, or eight first cousins . . .
findings.content: Hamilton's rule, in its modern canonical form, states that a social behaviour is favoured by natural selection when rB > C, where r is the coefficient of relatedness between actor and recipient, B is the fitness benefit to the recipient, and C is the fitness cost to the actor. Hamilton's original 1964 paper introduced this principle using a gain-ratio inequality (his condition for an altruistic action to be favoured was -k > 1/r, with k the ratio of gain and r Wright's coefficient of relationship); the compact "rB > C" algebraic notation is a later popularization. The principle explains when organisms will sacrifice personal fitness to benefit relatives and predicts that the altruism threshold decreases with increasing relatedness - in Hamilton's own example, an organism should sacrifice its life to save "more than two brothers, or four half-brothers, or eight first cousins" (siblings r=0.5, cousins r=0.125).
findings.where: Journal of Theoretical Biology 7(1):1-16 and 7(1):17-52, 1964. PMID: 5875341/5875340

findings.quote: Humans' large neocortex is an obvious possibility. Not only do human mothers need more help getting big-brained babies through narrow birth canals but they are better able to evaluate the costs and benefits of their own behavior.
findings.content: Hrdy cites Dunbar & Shultz (2007) on the correlation between large brain size and long juvenile/adolescent life phases. The neocortex discussion in Mothers and Others frames brain evolution through alloparenting: humans' large neocortex enables evaluation of allomaternal trustworthiness, while also creating the extended dependency that necessitates cooperative breeding. This connects Dunbar's social brain to Hrdy's cooperative breeding hypothesis as complementary explanations.
findings.where: Mothers and Others (2009), endnotes ch. 8 note 4 (line 13045), main text pp. 39-40 (lines 1580-1614, 1795-1801, 2940-2943)

findings.quote: Bowlby demonstrated that babies are genetically programmed to seek and form an attachment to a trusted figure. Secure attachment to one or more trusted caretakers is an essential aspect of emotional development in humans, just as it is in all other primates.
findings.content: Hrdy on attachment theory: Bowlby's insights that babies are genetically programmed to seek and form attachment to a trusted figure, and that secure attachment to one or more trusted caretakers is essential for emotional development, rank among the greatest contributions of evolutionary-minded psychologists. BUT Bowlby's original framing (exclusive maternal attachment) produces dilemmas for mothers wanting self-confident children AND lives/careers of their own. Hrdy's refinement: 'one or more trusted caretakers' - plural attachment figures, not a single dyadic bond. This is load-bearing for how M9 Care/Alloparenting integrates with M3 Social Bonding in Cor's architecture.

findings.quote: Even in normally gentle and herbivorous primates like langurs and gorillas, other members of the same species can be a threat to infant survival every bit as hazardous as lurking predators. This was a new kind of selective pressure on mothers, one not previously dreamed of.
findings.content: Infanticide by males as selective pressure: Even in normally gentle primates like langurs and gorillas, other members of the same species can be a threat to infant survival every bit as hazardous as lurking predators. This creates selective pressure on mothers. Hrdy's specific hypothesis: female langurs' apparently promiscuous mating with invading males (even when pregnant/not ovulating) casts wide the web of possible paternity - males almost never attack infants they might have fathered. Males use past mating relations as a cue to attack or tolerate an infant. This is load-bearing for M14 Reproductive Motivation and for reading female sexuality in light of infanticide risk.

findings.quote: The PANIC system (see Chapter 14): To be a mammal is to be born socially dependent. Brain evolution has provided safeguards to assure that parents (usually the mother) take care of the offspring, and the offspring have powerful emotional systems to indicate that they are in need of care (as reflected in crying or, as scientists prefer to say, separation calls). The nature of these distress systems in the brains of caretakers and those they care for has only recently been clarified; they provide a neural substrate for understanding many other social emotional processes.
findings.content: Panksepp's definition of the PANIC separation-distress system, one of his most distinctive theoretical contributions: to be a mammal is to be born socially dependent. Brain evolution has provided safeguards to ensure parents take care of offspring AND offspring have powerful emotional systems to indicate they need care - reflected in crying (scientifically: separation calls). The nature of these distress systems in the brains of caretakers and those they care for provides a neural substrate for understanding many other social emotional processes. This is load-bearing for M3 Social Bonding and M9 Care/Alloparenting - Panksepp is the primary source for reading attachment distress as a specific affective circuit rather than a learned association.

findings.quote: This environment I propose to term the system's 'environment of adaptedness'. Only within its environment of adaptedness can it be expected that a system will work efficiently. In any other environment it cannot be expected to do so. In some such cases a system may in fact work reasonably well; in others it does not work at all; and in others again it gives rise to behaviour that is at best unusual and at worst positively unfavourable to survival.
findings.content: Bowlby's concept of the environment of adaptedness: every behavioral system has a particular environment to which it is adapted. Only within this environment can the system work efficiently. In any other environment it may work reasonably well, give rise to unusual behavior, or produce outcomes positively unfavourable to survival. Each species and each system within a species has its own environment of adaptedness, defined in terms of specific variables.

findings.quote: What an animal requires is something more like a working model of its environment. The use to which a model in the brain is put is to transmit, store, and manipulate information that helps in making predictions as to how what are here termed set-goals can be achieved.
findings.content: Bowlby's internal working model concept: the brain provides not merely a static map but a working model of the environment. This model transmits, stores, and manipulates information to generate predictions about how set-goals can be achieved. The working model concept explains how the child builds and updates mental representations of the attachment figure's availability and responsiveness, which then guide future attachment behavior.

findings.quote: Because the bias of a child to attach himself especially to one figure seems to be well established and also to have far-reaching implications for psychopathology, I believe it merits a special term. In the earlier paper I referred to it as 'monotropy'.
findings.content: Bowlby coins the term monotropy for the child's bias to attach especially to one figure, noting this bias is well-established and has far-reaching implications for psychopathology. While children form multiple attachments, there is a strong tendency to direct attachment behavior principally toward one person - the principal attachment figure.

findings.quote: The existence of sensitive periods in early life during which the form to be taken by an adult's instinctive behaviour is in great part determined is yet another characteristic of instinctive behaviour to which Freud drew attention. In the psychoanalytic tradition it is represented in the concepts of fixation and of stage in libidinal organisation.
findings.content: Sensitive periods in attachment development: Bowlby draws attention to the existence of sensitive periods in early life during which the form of adult instinctive behavior is largely determined. In the psychoanalytic tradition this is represented in the concepts of fixation and stage in libidinal organization. The sensitive period concept explains why early attachment experiences have disproportionate influence on later relationship patterns.

findings.quote: In order to elucidate the links between exercise and aging, I propose a corollary to the grandmother hypothesis, which I call the active grandparent hypothesis. According to this idea, human longevity was not only selected for but also made possible by having to work moderately during old age to help as many children, grandchildren, and other younger relatives as possible to survive and thrive. That is, while there might have been selection for genes (as yet unidentified) that help humans live past the age of fifty, there was also selection for genes that repair and maintain our bodies when we are physically active. As a result, many of the mechanisms that slow aging and extend life are turned on by physical activity, especially as we get older. Human health and longevity are thus extended both by and for physical activity.
findings.content: Lieberman's own theoretical contribution - the active grandparent hypothesis - proposes that human longevity was not only selected for but also made possible by physical activity in older age. The core mechanism: humans evolved unique longevity BECAUSE grandparents who stayed physically active (walking, digging, carrying, provisioning grandchildren) increased their inclusive fitness through kin-selection effects, AND natural selection favored genes that repair and maintain the body in response to physical activity stress. Human longevity is thus extended BOTH by and FOR physical activity. This is the central evolutionary argument for M10's cascade - the repair/maintenance mechanisms that slow aging are turned on by movement, especially as we age, because natural selection never had a version of our species in which old people were inactive.

findings.quote: Like vasopressin, oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus. Unlike vasopressin, oxytocin is released in all female mammals (including women) during the birthing process. It initiates contractions of the uterus and stimulates the mammary glands to produce milk. But oxytocin also stimulates bonding between a mother and her infant. And more and more data now indicate that oxytocin can also produce feelings of attachment to a preferred mating partner. You have undoubtedly felt the power of these 'cuddle chemicals,' as vasopressin and oxytocin are sometimes called. At orgasm, the activities of oxytocin spike in men and women. These 'satisfaction hormones' undoubtedly contribute to your sense of fusion, closeness, and attachment after sweet sex with a beloved.
findings.content: Like vasopressin, oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus. Unlike vasopressin, oxytocin is released in all female mammals (including women) during the birthing process. It initiates contractions of the uterus and stimulates the mammary glands to produce milk. But oxytocin also stimulates bonding between a mother and her infant. And more and more data now indicate that oxytocin can also produce feelings of attachment to a preferred mating partner. At orgasm, the activities of oxytocin spike in men and women. These satisfaction hormones undoubtedly contribute to your sense of fusion, closeness, and attachment after sweet sex with a beloved.

findings.quote: Chimpanzees perform best on tests requiring a rudimentary theory of mind when they are in competitive situations.
findings.content: Chimpanzees perform best on tests requiring rudimentary theory of mind when they are in competitive situations. But human children develop robust theory of mind in cooperative contexts - because in a cooperatively breeding species, infants who could read the intentions of multiple caregivers had a survival advantage. Human mind-reading evolved not for competition but for navigating the cooperative breeding network.

findings.quote: Thus, when mother is called away a child's attachment behaviour is likely to be elicited and his exploratory behaviour inhibited; conversely, when a child explores too far, a mother's care behaviour is likely to be elicited and whatever else she is doing to be inhibited. In a happy couple these four classes of behaviour occur and progress together in harmony. But risk of conflict is ever-present.
findings.content: Attachment behavior as one of four interacting classes in mother-child interaction: (a) the child's attachment behavior, (b) the child's exploratory behavior and play (antithetic to attachment), (c) the mother's caretaking behavior, and (d) the mother's behavior antithetic to care. When the mother is called away, the child's attachment behavior is elicited and exploratory behavior inhibited; when the child explores too far, the mother's care behavior is elicited. In a happy couple these four classes occur in harmony, but risk of conflict is ever-present.

findings.quote: The skin is the first and the largest sense organ to develop prenatally. The fetus is suspended in amniotic fluid and receives active stimulation from the fluid and the mother and others as they touch her abdomen. The fetus becomes increasingly active as this happens. The fetus also touches itself by thumb sucking and grasping the umbilical cord. The fetus gets a continuous massage for the entire nine months from both the amniotic fluid and the mother's insides. In addition, a pregnant woman naturally massages her baby in the womb. Touch alters oxytocin (an estrogen-dependent chemical), which relaxes the individual, promotes touch, encourages bonding, triggers milk letdown during breastfeeding, and sets off the uterine contractions that accompany childbirth.
findings.content: Field's phylogenetic framing of touch as the first sense organ. The skin is the largest sense organ because it is the largest organ in the body - the 'first and largest sense organ to develop prenatally'. The fetus receives continuous touch stimulation in utero from amniotic fluid, maternal internal movement, and external touch to the mother's abdomen. Touch alters oxytocin, which relaxes the individual, promotes touch (positive feedback), encourages bonding, triggers milk letdown during breastfeeding, and initiates uterine contractions during childbirth. This is the architectural grounding for R1 Touch as a phylogenetically ancient regulatory input distinct from vision and hearing, with downstream effects on M9 Care/Alloparenting and M3 Social Bonding via oxytocin.
findings.where: Field, Touch (2014) Chapter 3 'Touch in Early Development', pp. ~49

findings.quote: In addition to the preceding primitive systems that are evident in all mammals soon after birth, we also have more sophisticated special-purpose socioemotional systems that are engaged at appropriate times in the lives of all mammals-for instance, those that mediate sexual LUST (see Chapter 12), maternal CARE (see Chapter 13), and roughhousing PLAY (see Chapter 15). Each of these is built around neural complexities that are only provisionally understood. Sexual urges are mediated by specific brain circuits and chemistries that are quite distinct for males and females but appear to share some components such as the physiological and psychological effects of oxytocin, which also promotes maternal motivation.
findings.content: Panksepp's identification of three additional special-purpose socioemotional systems beyond the 4 primitive ones: sexual LUST (Ch 12), maternal CARE (Ch 13), and roughhousing PLAY (Ch 15). Sexual urges are mediated by distinct brain circuits and chemistries for males and females but share components such as oxytocin, which also promotes maternal motivation. Maternal behavior circuits remain closely intermeshed with sexuality circuits, suggesting how evolution gradually constructed the basic neural substrates for 'the social contract' - the possibilities for love and bonding - in the mammalian brain. This is load-bearing for M14 Reproductive Motivation, M9 Care/Alloparenting, M4 Social Calibration/Play, and the architectural claim that social bonding evolved as an extension of pre-existing reproductive circuits.

findings.quote: We now realize that maternal behavior circuits remain closely intermeshed with those that control sexuality, and this suggests how evolution gradually constructed the basic neural substrates for the social contract (i.e., the possibilities for love and bonding) in the mammalian brain.
findings.content: Panksepp's architectural claim about the evolution of social bonding: maternal behavior circuits remain closely intermeshed with those that control sexuality. This suggests how evolution gradually constructed the basic neural substrates for the 'social contract' - 'the possibilities for love and bonding' - in the mammalian brain. Maternal nurturance probably arose gradually from preexisting circuits that initially mediated reproductive behaviors. This is THE foundational architectural claim for why Cor's M3 Social Bonding, M9 Care/Alloparenting, and M14 Reproductive Motivation share substrate - they were built by evolution as extensions and overlays of the same neurochemical machinery, not as independent systems.

findings.quote: Attacks from conspecifics (both infanticide and deaths due to lethal raids by bands of males from neighboring groups) are major sources of mortality.
findings.content: In chimpanzees, attacks from conspecifics - including infanticide and lethal raids by bands of males from neighboring groups - are major sources of mortality.

findings.quote: the ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven basic affective systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy)
findings.content: The ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven basic affective systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy). These designate specific functional networks of evolutionarily very ancient regions of our brains.
findings.where: Preface, 'Why Psychiatrists, Physicians, and Psychotherapists Should Understand the Seven Basic Affective Systems,' p. xi

findings.quote: Sexual gratification, arising from our capacity for LUST, feels good in a rather different way from the joys of rough-and-tumble PLAY or the tender bliss of caressing, nurturing, and CAREing for one's infant. FEAR is an entirely different kind of emotional 'pain' than frustrated RAGE; both differ from the PANICked misery of social isolation.
findings.content: Sexual gratification from LUST feels good in a different way from the joys of rough-and-tumble PLAY or the tender bliss of caressing and CARing for an infant. FEAR is an entirely different kind of emotional pain than frustrated RAGE; both differ from the panicked misery of social isolation (PANIC/GRIEF). These diverse affects provide guidance for living due to the survival-enhancing advantages each conferred over evolution. Affects are ancestral memories of how effectively we play the game of survival and reproduction.

findings.quote: The underlying circuits are genetically predetermined and designed to respond unconditionally to stimuli arising from major life-challenging circumstances. These circuits organize diverse behaviors by activating or inhibiting motor subroutines and concurrent autonomic-hormonal changes that have proved adaptive in the face of such life-challenging circumstances during the evolutionary history of the species. Emotive circuits change the sensitivities of sensory systems that are relevant for the behavioral sequences that have been aroused. Neural activity of emotive systems outlasts the precipitating circumstances. Emotive circuits can come under the conditional control of emotionally neutral environmental stimuli. Emotive circuits have reciprocal interactions with the brain mechanisms that elaborate higher decision-making processes and consciousness.
findings.content: Panksepp's six methodological criteria for identifying genuine emotional systems in the brain (Figure 3.3): (1) Underlying circuits are genetically predetermined to respond unconditionally to life-challenging stimuli; (2) they organize diverse behaviors by activating/inhibiting motor subroutines and autonomic-hormonal changes; (3) they change sensitivities of sensory systems relevant to the aroused behavioral sequences; (4) their neural activity outlasts precipitating circumstances; (5) they can come under conditional control of emotionally neutral stimuli; (6) they have reciprocal interactions with higher decision-making and consciousness circuits. Plus the seventh psychological criterion: they must generate affective feelings. This is Panksepp's load-bearing methodological framework for distinguishing emotional systems from general-purpose sensorimotor circuits.

findings.quote: Sidney Jourard, a University of Florida psychologist, visited cafés in different parts of the world and recorded the number of times two people who were sharing coffee touched each other. In London, the tally was 0; in Gainesville, Florida, 2; in Paris 110; and in San Juan, Puerto Rico, more than 180. Most sociologists would agree that societies like those in the Mediterranean countries (e.g., Spain, France, Italy, Greece, Turkey, Egypt) are contact societies, whereas the more northern societies in countries such as Holland, Great Britain, and the United States are not.
findings.content: Jourard's cross-cultural café-touch observations, reported by Field: in cafés where two people shared coffee, the number of physical contacts in one hour varied from 0 (London) to 2 (Gainesville Florida) to 110 (Paris) to more than 180 (San Juan Puerto Rico). This documents the dramatic cross-cultural variation in touch frequency and grounds the 'touch hunger' framing that Field extends to industrialized screen-mediated life. The cross-cultural data also ground R1's architectural claim that the touch input has a wide tolerance range but a floor below which developmental and regulatory deficits appear.
findings.where: Field, Touch (2014) Chapter 2 'Touch as Communication', pp. ~24-25

findings.quote: a baby monkey raised on a bare wire-mesh cage floor survives with difficulty, if at all, during the first five days of life.
findings.content: Infant monkeys raised on bare wire-mesh cage floors survived with difficulty during the first 5 days of life. Adding a wire-mesh cone improved survival. Covering the cone with terry cloth produced husky, healthy, happy babies. This demonstrates that tactile comfort is not merely a preference but a survival-critical input.

findings.quote: Monkey grooming is not about removing fleas. Rather, it is about the intimacy of massage. The physical stimulation of the skin triggers the release of endorphins in the brain.
findings.content: Primate grooming is not about removing fleas - it is about the intimacy of massage. Physical stimulation of the skin triggers endorphin release in the brain. Low-level pain associated with generalized stresses is dealt with by the endorphin system, creating a sense of wellbeing and relaxed contentedness. Grooming is the mechanism through which primate social bonds are maintained.

Oxytocin (OT) operates through three distinct but neurobiologically consistent mechanisms to support human affiliative bonds. (a) Parent-infant bonding: maternal OT levels measured in the first trimester predicted postpartum behavior (gaze, positive affect, motherese, affectionate touch); OT was stable within individuals across pregnancy; fathers showed comparable baseline OT to mothers and active paternal care activated the OT system. OT administration to fathers increased their touch behavior AND independently increased infant salivary OT, RSA, social gaze, and toy exploration - demonstrating cross-dyadic transmission. (b) Pair bonding: new romantic partners showed significantly higher plasma OT than singles, even higher than new parents; OT correlated with interactive synchrony (social focus, positive affect, affectionate touch) and was stable over six months. (c) Group affiliation: OT was linked to children's best-friend relationship quality and broader social engagement. Across all bond types, OT levels showed "biological synchrony" between partners - mother-father OT was inter-correlated, parent-infant OT was inter-related, and romantic partners' OT levels were concordant.

In a study of 112 parents and their 4-6 month olds, active parental touch triggered measurable OT responses. Mothers providing high levels of affectionate touch (>66% of interaction time) showed increased salivary OT from pre- to post-interaction, while mothers providing minimal touch (<33%) showed no such increase. Fathers who provided high levels of stimulatory contact (moving child's limbs, throwing infant in air) similarly increased their OT levels, but those engaging in minimal stimulatory touch did not. Risk alleles on the OXTR rs2254298 and CD38 rs3796863 SNPs were associated with both lower plasma OT and reduced parental affectionate touch, paralleling findings of high vs. low licking-and-grooming rat dams.

Bio-behavioral synchrony is the mechanism by which organisms become members of a social group. Among mammalian species, dyad-specific maternal-infant bonds are built on repeatedly experienced patterns of sensory, motor, and behavioral cues. Human mothers provide approximately 70% of their social behaviors during the 7% of the time newborns spend in alert-scanning state, creating temporal contingencies between infant state and maternal social behavior from the first post-birth hours. These social contingencies are supported by physiological periodicities maturing in the fetus during the third trimester: the biological clock and cardiac pacemaker. As soon as the human infant is born, it can experience a temporal match between its own state and the response of the social environment. This early temporal concordance is a critical human addition to the physiological provisions embedded in maternal proximity in other mammals.

10-year longitudinal RCT (N=146): Kangaroo Care (14 days skin-to-skin) vs incubator care in preterm infants. KC increased autonomic functioning (RSA), maternal attachment, reduced maternal anxiety. Enhanced child cognitive development and executive functions from 6 months to 10 years. By age 10: better sleep organization, more mature EEG patterns, better cognitive control. 14 days of contact correction produced a decade of measurable developmental advantage.

findings.quote: We have since found that moderate pressure is key to the massage therapy effects. We massage babies from head to foot (all but their chests and stomachs; they do not want to be touched there, most likely because that is where all the tubes have been inserted). The babies who were massaged gained 47 percent more weight than those not massaged, a significant weight gain.
findings.content: Field's foundational premature-infant massage finding: infants massaged from head to foot (excluding chest and stomach where IVs were inserted) gained 47 percent more weight than unmassaged infants. This established touch as a quantifiable developmental input with direct physiological consequences on growth. The initial study motivated the establishment of the Touch Research Institute at the University of Miami School of Medicine in 1992 and launched a research program of over 100 touch/massage studies. Critically, earlier attempts by other researchers had failed to show growth effects because they used light-touch (tickling-like) stimulation; Field's group discovered that moderate pressure is necessary for the physiological response.

findings.quote: Tana was raised in a Romanian orphanage. At age seven, relief workers found her all skin and bones and only half the height of a normal child her age.
findings.content: Touch deprivation in Romanian orphanages produced devastating consequences: children were skeletal, half normal height, unable to walk or run. After months of regular nutrition and massage therapy, orphanage children recovered physically - illustrating that touch is not merely pleasant but a biological necessity for normal development. Touch deprivation produces growth hormone suppression and immune dysfunction.

findings.quote: I examine the physiological and biochemical effects of touch and massage therapy, including decreased heart rate, blood pressure, and cortisol and increased oxytocin.
findings.content: Touch and massage therapy produce measurable neurobiological effects: decreased heart rate, blood pressure, and cortisol; increased oxytocin. Brain imaging shows activation of orbitofrontal cortex and caudate cortex during affective touch. The physiological pathway involves stimulation of pressure receptors leading to vagal activation, which in turn modulates the HPA axis and immune function.

findings.quote: Women with physical contact before stress exhibited significantly lower cortisol and heart rate responses to stress but no different plasma oxytocin levels.
findings.content: Physical contact from a partner before stress significantly lowers cortisol and heart rate responses. A ten-minute neck and shoulder massage produced greater stress buffering than verbal social support or no partner interaction. Touch-based social regulation operates through direct physiological pathways (cortisol suppression, cardiovascular calming) not just psychological comfort.

findings.quote: We compared 'grandparent' volunteers massaging infants (figure 2.2), with 'grandparent' volunteers being massaged themselves. Both experiences had positive effects, including such lifestyle changes as participants having more social contacts, drinking less coffee, and making fewer trips to the doctor's office.
findings.content: Elderly volunteers who massaged infants showed positive health effects: more social contacts, less coffee consumption, fewer doctor visits. Being massaged and giving massage both produced benefits. This reciprocal caregiving-through-touch model demonstrates that touch regulation is bidirectional - the giver of touch benefits physiologically as well as the receiver.

findings.quote: contact comfort is a variable of overwhelming importance in the development of affectional response, whereas lactation is a variable of negligible importance.
findings.content: Contact comfort overwhelms lactation as determinant of infant attachment. Infant rhesus monkeys spent 17-18 hours/day on cloth-covered surrogate mother vs ~1 hour on wire mother, regardless of which mother provided milk. No measurable difference between cloth-fed and wire-fed groups in cloth preference. 8 newborn monkeys in dual-surrogate condition tested over 165+ consecutive days.
findings.where: American Psychologist 13:673-685. Full text at psychclassics.yorku.ca/Harlow/love.htm

findings.quote: At discharge or 40 to 41 weeks' postmenstrual age: "KMC was associated with a statistically significant reduction in the risk of mortality (risk ratio [RR] 0.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.39 to 0.92; eight trials, 1736 infants)." At latest follow-up: "KMC was associated with a significantly decreased risk of mortality (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.95; 12 trials, 2293 infants; moderate-quality evidence)."
findings.content: Cochrane meta-analysis of kangaroo mother care (KMC) vs conventional care in low-birthweight infants. In STABILIZED LBW infants, KMC significantly reduced the risk of mortality at discharge or 40-41 weeks postmenstrual age (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.39-0.92; 8 trials, 1736 infants) and at latest follow-up (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48-0.95; 12 trials, 2293 infants; moderate-quality evidence). RR 0.60 is the source of the frequently cited ~40% KMC mortality reduction (1 - 0.60). KMC also reduced nosocomial infection and hypothermia and improved growth and breastfeeding. This is corpus grounding for the claim that continuous skin-to-skin (C-tactile) contact is a mortality-level regulatory input for the preterm/LBW infant, not a comfort measure - the basis of R1 and of empirical demonstration ED9.

findings.quote: The babies who were massaged gained 47 percent more weight than those not massaged, a clearly significant weight gain.
findings.content: Moderate-pressure massage therapy causes preterm infants to gain more weight, leave tube feeding earlier, perform better on neurological examinations, and be discharged earlier at lower hospital cost. The mechanism involves stimulation of pressure receptors leading to increased vagal activity. Increased serotonin and decreased substance P may mediate the pain-alleviating effects of touch.

findings.quote: Several decades ago, Harry Harlow, at the University of Wisconsin, performed a classic experiment on touching monkeys. He built one surrogate mother out of terry cloth and a second surrogate mother out of wire mesh. For some of the monkey infants, the terry-cloth mother provided milk, and the wire mother did not. For others, the condition was reversed. The monkey infants preferred the cloth mother without the milk over the wire mother with milk, suggesting that they needed the touch stimulation as much as, if not more than, the nourishment.
findings.content: Field's synthesis of Harlow's foundational primate touch-deprivation work: infant rhesus monkeys preferred a terry-cloth surrogate mother without milk over a wire-mesh mother with milk, suggesting that touch stimulation is at least as important as nourishment. Harlow's experiments showed that infants without any surrogate developed self-clasping behavior, failed to develop normal grooming or reproduction, and had broken immune systems. Suomi's follow-up showed that Plexiglas separation (vision, hearing, smell preserved but no touch) was sufficient to produce these deficits - touch itself was the critical missing stimulation, not the other sensory modalities. This is the primary-source chain Field uses to ground touch as a distinct regulatory input in R1's architecture.
findings.where: Field, Touch (2014) Chapter 3 'Touch in Early Development', pp. ~47

findings.quote: Many human cultures know the primary value of touch. In some primitive cultures, for example, people live skin-to-skin with virtually everyone.
findings.content: Many human cultures live skin-to-skin with virtually everyone, maintaining continuous physical contact as the primary mode of social interaction. Modern Western cultures are historically unusual in the degree of touch avoidance and personal-space norms. The reduction of casual physical contact in WEIRD societies represents a mismatch with the ancestral pattern of continuous tactile social regulation.

findings.quote: Moreover, infants and mothers are induced to awaken by an arousal exhibited by the other (within seconds) therein creating interconnected, mutually dependent, synchronous arousals [1, 2].
findings.content: Cosleeping mother and infant induce arousals in one another within seconds, creating interconnected, mutually-dependent, synchronous arousals (nighttime physiological co-regulation).

findings.quote: the behavior can be seen to be intimately linked to underlying EEGs, breathing patterns, changes in sleep architecture, body temperature and linked simultaneously to maternal physiological and behavioral events [5].
findings.content: Across the sleep period, cosleeping infant behavior is intimately linked to underlying EEG, breathing patterns, sleep architecture, and body temperature, coupled simultaneously to maternal physiological and behavioral events.

findings.quote: as bedsharing safety is determined specifically by how it is practiced and by whom and what adverse factors could be associated
findings.content: McKenna himself stresses that bedsharing safety depends entirely on how it is practiced and on adverse co-factors - the live SIDS/safety contestation that keeps co-sleeping from being a clean "ancestral good".

findings.quote: an essential part of the ground plan of the human species--as well as that of many other species
findings.content: Attachment is an essential part of the biological ground plan of the human species. Hunter-gatherer societies show much more mother-infant contact than Western societies. Humans evolved as a species in which infants are carried and fed at frequent intervals. When attachment behavior is intensely activated, it is close bodily contact that is specifically required - not proximity alone.
findings.where: American Psychologist 34(10):932-937. DOI: 10.1037//0003-066x.34.10.932. Full text via Smith College.

findings.quote: The skin is the first and the largest sense organ to develop prenatally. The fetus is suspended in amniotic fluid and receives active stimulation from the fluid and the mother and others as they touch her abdomen. The fetus becomes increasingly active as this happens. The fetus also touches itself by thumb sucking and grasping the umbilical cord. The fetus gets a continuous massage for the entire nine months from both the amniotic fluid and the mother's insides. In addition, a pregnant woman naturally massages her baby in the womb. Touch alters oxytocin (an estrogen-dependent chemical), which relaxes the individual, promotes touch, encourages bonding, triggers milk letdown during breastfeeding, and sets off the uterine contractions that accompany childbirth.
findings.content: Field's phylogenetic framing of touch as the first sense organ. The skin is the largest sense organ because it is the largest organ in the body - the 'first and largest sense organ to develop prenatally'. The fetus receives continuous touch stimulation in utero from amniotic fluid, maternal internal movement, and external touch to the mother's abdomen. Touch alters oxytocin, which relaxes the individual, promotes touch (positive feedback), encourages bonding, triggers milk letdown during breastfeeding, and initiates uterine contractions during childbirth. This is the architectural grounding for R1 Touch as a phylogenetically ancient regulatory input distinct from vision and hearing, with downstream effects on M9 Care/Alloparenting and M3 Social Bonding via oxytocin.
findings.where: Field, Touch (2014) Chapter 3 'Touch in Early Development', pp. ~49

findings.quote: For thousands of generations, the health span and life span of a typical hunter-gatherer who did not die in infancy probably looked something like the top graph in figure 28. The graph is based on medical surveys of hunter-gatherers, who mostly die from respiratory and infectious diseases, violence, and accidents and have a relatively low incidence of long-term chronic noninfectious conditions. These and other data indicate that about two-thirds of older hunter-gatherers remain at high functional capacity with limited morbidity until just before death, which most often occurs in the seventh decade. Accordingly, their health span and life span are very similar.
findings.content: Medical surveys of hunter-gatherers show ~2/3 of older hunter-gatherers remain at high functional capacity with limited morbidity until just before death, which most often occurs in the seventh decade. Their health span and life span are very similar - they die mostly from respiratory and infectious diseases, violence, and accidents rather than from chronic noninfectious diseases. This is the empirical contrast case for the industrial extension-of-morbidity pattern and is load-bearing for M10's cascade framing: sedentarism contributes to the gap between life span and health span that defines the industrialized mortality profile.

findings.quote: In a famous 1986 study, Eric Ravussin and colleagues asked 177 people to spend twenty-four hours (one at a time) in an enclosed ten-by-twelve-foot chamber that measured precisely how many calories they spent. To the researchers' surprise, the individuals who fidgeted spent between one hundred and eight hundred calories more per day than those who sat inertly. Other studies have found that simply fidgeting while seated can expend as much as twenty calories an hour as well as promote beneficial levels of blood flow to restless arms and legs. One study even found a 30 percent lower rate of all-cause mortality among people who fidget after adjusting for other forms of physical activity, smoking, diet, and alcohol consumption.
findings.content: The Ravussin 1986 chamber-calorimeter study: 177 people each spent 24 hours in a sealed chamber measuring precise caloric expenditure. Fidgeters spent between 100 and 800 calories MORE per day than those who sat inertly. Subsequent work: fidgeting can expend ~20 calories per hour while seated. One study found a 30% lower rate of all-cause mortality among fidgeters after adjusting for other physical activity, smoking, diet, and alcohol. This is a counterintuitive but load-bearing data point for M10's cascade framing - low-intensity involuntary movement throughout the day has measurable metabolic and mortality effects, reinforcing the embedded-movement reading of the mechanism.

Cross-sectional analysis of 1,237,194 US adults: exercisers had 43.2% fewer days of poor mental health per month (1.49 fewer days) than matched non-exercisers. All exercise types associated with reduced mental health burden. Optimal dose: 3-5 sessions/week, 45 minutes each. Exercise effect on mental health LARGER than effects of education or income.

findings.quote: One of the most venerable long-term studies on how exercise affects aging is the Cooper Center Longitudinal Study in Dallas, started in 1970 by the man who coined the term 'aerobics,' Dr. Kenneth Cooper. One of its analyses tracked more than ten thousand men and three thousand women older than thirty-five to test if physically fit exercisers lived longer and healthier lives. They generally did. After adjusting for age (because an older person is more likely to pass away in a given year than a younger person), Cooper found that the most physically fit men and women had mortality rates about one-third to one-fourth of those who were least fit. Further, a subsample of those who were initially out of shape but started to exercise and increased their fitness halved their age-adjusted mortality rate compared to those who remained inactive and unfit.
findings.content: The Cooper Center Longitudinal Study (Kenneth Cooper, Dallas, 1970-) tracked 10,000+ men and 3,000+ women over age 35 to test the effect of cardiovascular fitness on mortality and chronic disease. Findings: the most physically fit had mortality rates about one-third to one-fourth of the least fit after age adjustment. A subsample initially out of shape who increased their fitness halved their age-adjusted mortality rate. Among 18,000+ middle-aged individuals tracked for chronic disease, the most fit were about half as likely to develop diabetes and Alzheimer's, and if they got sick, did so later. This is a primary empirical grounding for M10's cascade effects on health span.

findings.quote: In a celebrated study, the Stanford medical professor James Fries showed that preventive medicine could help people stay healthier for longer through a compression of morbidity. Fries initially based his argument on a massive study that measured life span, disability, and three risk factors for disease (high body weight, smoking, and lack of exercise) among more than twenty-three hundred alumni from the University of Pennsylvania. Predictably, the alums with two or more risk factors died 3.6 to 3.9 years earlier than those with one or no risk factors; perhaps more impressively, they lengthened their period of disability prior to death by 5.8 to 8.3 years. Simply put, an unhealthy lifestyle affects morbidity twice as much as mortality.
findings.content: Fries's compression-of-morbidity model: preventive behavior (exercise, not smoking, normal weight) shortens the period of disability before death. From a University of Pennsylvania cohort of 2,300+ alumni, people with two or more risk factors died 3.6-3.9 years earlier AND lengthened their disability period by 5.8-8.3 years. Unhealthy lifestyle affects morbidity roughly twice as much as mortality. This is load-bearing for the M10 health-span-vs-life-span distinction: physical activity's effects are primarily on compression of morbidity, not on raw life extension.

findings.quote: One effort to do this is the Stanford Runners Study conducted by, once again, James Fries. In 1984, he and his students began studying more than five hundred members of amateur running clubs along with more than four hundred healthy but physically inactive controls. Back then, the subjects were over the age of fifty and healthy: few smoked, none drank heavily, and none were obese. Then, for the next twenty-one years, Fries and his colleagues patiently kept track of each subject's physical activity habits, administered a yearly disability questionnaire that measures functions like the ability to walk, dress, and do routine activities, and recorded the year and cause of every death that occurred.
findings.content: The Stanford Runners Study (Fries 1984-2005, 21-year follow-up): 500+ amateur runners over age 50 vs 400+ healthy sedentary controls matched on smoking and obesity status. After 21 years, non-runners were ~3x more likely to die in a given year, ~2x more likely to die of heart disease and cancer, ~3x more likely to die of neurological disease, and >10x more likely to die of infections. Runners' disability scores were roughly half of non-runners' by study end - equivalent to being ~15 years younger by this measure. This isolates physical activity's effect on morbidity from the confounds of smoking and obesity, and is load-bearing for the M10/DC1 compression-of-morbidity cascade.

findings.quote: Among the many studies of the Hadza, one asked forty-six Hadza adults to wear lightweight heart rate monitors for several days. According to these sensors, the average adult Hadza spends a grand total of three hours and forty minutes a day doing light activities and two hours and fourteen minutes a day doing moderate or vigorous activities. Although these few hours of hustling and bustling per day make them about twelve times more active than the average American or European, by no stretch of the imagination could one characterize their workloads as backbreaking. On average, the women walk five miles a day and dig for several hours, whereas the men walk between seven and ten miles a day. And when they aren't being very active, they typically rest or do light work.
findings.content: Quantitative data from Hadza heart rate monitor study: average adult Hadza spends ~3h40m/day on light activities and ~2h14m/day on moderate-vigorous activities. Hadza men walk 7-10 miles/day, women walk 5 miles/day and dig for several hours. This is roughly 12x more active than the average American or European - but the absolute level is modest, not 'backbreaking'. The finding grounds M10's claim that hunter-gatherer physical activity is embedded rather than exercise-shaped, and is far less than Western intuitions assume.
findings.where: Chapter 1 'Are We Born to Rest or Run?' pp. ~17

findings.quote: Although there is much variation, PALs of hunter-gatherers average 1.9 for men and 1.8 for women, slightly below PAL scores for subsistence farmers, which average 2.1 for men and 1.9 for women. To put these values into context, hunter-gatherer PALs are about the same as those of factory workers and farmers in the developed world (1.8), and about 15 percent higher than PALs of people with desk jobs in developed countries (1.6). In other words, typical hunter-gatherers are about as physically active as Americans or Europeans who include about an hour of exercise in their daily routine. In case you are wondering, most mammals in the wild have PALs of 3.3 or more, nearly twice as high as hunter-gatherers. Thus, comparatively speaking, humans who must hunt and gather all the food they eat and make everything they own by hand are substantially less active than average free-ranging mammals.
findings.content: Physical Activity Level (PAL) data across populations reveals the surprising result that typical hunter-gatherers are only about 15% more active than industrialized people with desk jobs - equivalent to adding one hour of walking per day to a sedentary Westerner's routine. Hunter-gatherer PALs average 1.9 (men) / 1.8 (women) vs 1.6 for desk workers. Wild mammals average PAL 3.3+, nearly twice hunter-gatherer levels. This is Lieberman's central empirical claim against 'we evolved to exercise' intuitions: humans are at the less-active end of the mammalian spectrum, and the Western sedentary gap is smaller than folk imagination assumes.
findings.where: Chapter 1 'Are We Born to Rest or Run?' pp. ~19-20

findings.content: Ancestral human diet was characterized by: higher protein (34% vs 12% of calories), dramatically lower refined carbohydrate and sugar, higher fiber (100-150g/day vs 20g), lower sodium, higher potassium, higher micronutrient density, and near-zero processed food. Modern Western diet diverges from these parameters in almost every measurable dimension simultaneously.

findings.quote: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammation of the arterial walls that results from how you shuttle cholesterol and triglycerides (fats) around your body.
findings.content: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammation of the arterial walls resulting from how the body shuttles cholesterol and triglycerides. The process is driven by the mismatch between ancestral diet/activity patterns (which kept LDL cholesterol low and HDL high) and modern sedentary high-calorie environments that invert this ratio. Chronic arterial inflammation is a paradigm case of allostatic load from metabolic mismatch.

findings.quote: Here, we test the hypothesis that the ways in which urban populations rest, rather than the amount of time spent resting, represents an inactivity mismatch with an evolutionarily relevant hunting and gathering lifestyle, and propose that this mismatch may contribute to the negative health impacts of sedentary behavior today.
findings.content: The Inactivity Mismatch Hypothesis (Raichlen, Pontzer et al. 2020): Hadza adults spend similar amounts of time in nonambulatory rest as industrialized adults (~9.9 hours/day), but they rest in postures - squatting, kneeling, ground-sitting - that maintain higher lower-limb muscle activity than Western chair-sitting. Measured via thigh-worn accelerometers plus electromyography in the field. The hypothesis: human physiology evolved in a context of high muscle activity across the waking day BOTH through physical activity AND through resting postures with sustained low-level muscle contraction. Modern chair-sitting is the mismatch - not the total amount of rest, but the specific posture during rest.
findings.where: Raichlen, Pontzer et al. 2020 PNAS 117(13):7115-7121, Introduction

findings.quote: In addition to ground-sitting postures, Hadza individuals also spend a large percentage of their nonambulatory time in squatting (∼18%) and kneeling postures (∼12.5%) that differ from ground sitting by individuals maintaining an elevated buttocks. [...] For soleus, the assisted squat posture (squatting with heels in ground contact and with the buttocks resting on a small rock) elicited significantly higher muscle activity compared with chair sitting.
findings.content: The empirical result: Hadza adults spend roughly as much time in nonambulatory rest as industrialized adults (~9.9 hours/day for Hadza vs ~8.8 hours/day for Australian adults in comparison data), with similar average sedentary bout duration (~15 min) and similar numbers of transitions between sitting and standing per day (~50 vs ~38 for European adults). But Hadza nonambulatory time occurs heavily in squatting (~18%) and kneeling (~12.5%) postures that elicit significantly higher muscle activity than chair-sitting. The Hadza data refute the naive 'hunter-gatherers never sit' assumption and reframe the mismatch as about HOW humans rest, not HOW MUCH.
findings.where: Raichlen et al. 2020 PNAS, Results section

findings.quote: A wave of obesity and chronic, preventable illnesses and disabilities is sweeping across the globe. These preventable diseases include certain cancers, type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis, heart disease, strokes, kidney disease, some allergies, dementia, depression, anxiety, insomnia, and other illnesses.
findings.content: A wave of preventable chronic illnesses is sweeping across the globe: certain cancers, type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis, heart disease, strokes, kidney disease, allergies, dementia, depression, anxiety, insomnia. Billions also suffer from lower back pain, fallen arches, plantar fasciitis, myopia, arthritis, constipation, and acid reflux. These are mismatch diseases - conditions whose prevalence surged when human environments departed from the conditions under which human bodies evolved.

The Danish 2-week sedentary-forced experiment: healthy young men paid to sit for a fortnight and take no more than 1500 steps per day (about a mile) gained 7% more organ (visceral) fat and began to exhibit classic signs of chronic inflammation including reduced ability to take up blood sugar after a meal. The mechanism is clear: inactivity + adequate calories → organ fat accumulation → inflammatory cytokines → metabolic dysregulation. This is load-bearing for the M10/M8/DC1 cascade - sedentarism drives the allostatic-load pathway through the organ-fat-inflammation channel.

findings.quote: Walk or run 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) a day (barefoot, of course), climb a few trees, chase squirrels in the park, throw rocks, eschew chairs, and sleep on a board instead of a mattress.
findings.content: Modern sedentary lifestyle is directly mismatched with ancestral activity patterns. Walking or running 10+ kilometers daily, climbing trees, throwing, eschewing chairs, and sleeping on hard surfaces were normal for most of human evolutionary history.
