The primal-lifestyle movement correctly identifies the mismatch but often oversimplifies the solution. The key insight is that the chair-based, shoe-bound, indoor modern lifestyle is a novel environment that human bodies are poorly adapted to navigate.

findings.quote: My opinion is that while many animals are driven by deep instincts to move, sometimes causing pleasure, exercise as we define it - discretionary, planned physical activity for the sake of physical improvement - is a uniquely human behavior. In fact, I think it is fair to make two generalizations about human exercise. First, while youngsters have always played and sports are a human universal, exercise outside the context of sports was extremely rare until relatively recently. Second, as recent technological and social developments have diminished industrialized people's need to be physically active, a growing chorus of experts has never ceased to raise the alarm that we aren't exercising enough.
findings.content: Lieberman's theoretical framing of exercise as a uniquely modern human behavior rather than an evolved adaptation. He distinguishes play (common across mammals, driven by deep instincts) from exercise (discretionary, planned physical activity for physical improvement - rare outside sports until recently). This is load-bearing for M10's framing that 'normal' movement is embedded in life rather than set aside as exercise, and for DA4's reading of exercise as a proxy category that only emerged when daily physical activity was extracted by technological laborsaving.
findings.where: Chapter 1 'Are We Born to Rest or Run?' pp. ~21-22

findings.quote: We have also medicalized exercise. By this I mean we pathologize a lack of physical activity, and we prescribe particular doses and types of exercise to help prevent and treat disease. The U.S. government recommends I engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate or 75 minutes of vigorous exercise a week and weight train at least twice a week. Epidemiologists have calculated that this level of activity will reduce my risk of dying prematurely by 50 percent and lower my chances of getting heart disease, Alzheimer's, and certain cancers by roughly 30 to 50 percent. Insurance companies offer me incentives to exercise, and entire professions have sprung up to motivate me to exercise in the first place, help me work out, and fix me up once I get injured.
findings.content: Lieberman's description of the medicalization, commercialization, and industrialization of exercise as modern substitutes for the daily physical activity that industrialization extracted. He frames this explicitly as pathologizing inactivity and prescribing dose-response exercise. This is a clean DA4 Proxy Hijacking case: the embedded daily-movement target has been replaced by a market proxy (gym membership, specialized clothing, activity trackers, prescribed minutes) that only partially captures the original function.
findings.where: Chapter 1 'Are We Born to Rest or Run?' pp. ~24

findings.quote: Among the many hyperbolic statements written about sitting, maybe the most extreme is that sitting is the new smoking. While cigarettes are novel, addictive, expensive, smelly, toxic, and the world's number one killer, sitting is as old as the hills and utterly natural. More truthfully, the problem isn't sitting itself, but hours upon hours of inactive sitting combined with little to no exercise. If our ancestors from generations ago behaved like today's hunter-gatherers and farmers, then they likely sat for five to ten hours a day, as much as some but not all contemporary Americans and Europeans. But they also got plenty of physical activity when not sitting, and when these chairless ancestors plunked themselves down, they didn't rest in supportive chairs with seat backs; instead, they squirmed as they squatted, kneeled, or sat on the ground, using about the same degree of muscle activity in their thighs, calves, and backs as when they stood. When the Hadza sit, squat, or kneel, they typically do so for only fifteen minutes at a time.
findings.content: Lieberman explicitly debunks the 'sitting is the new smoking' meme as hyperbolic. The problem is not sitting itself - hunter-gatherers sit for 5-10 hours per day, as much as many Western office workers - but rather hours of inactive sitting without intervening physical activity. Hunter-gatherer sitting is typically shorter bouts (15 min at a time for Hadza), combined with light chores, child care, and frequent standing. The claim reframes M10 as a cascade about muscle-engagement distribution throughout the day rather than a blanket condemnation of rest.

findings.quote: Many things surprised me when I first walked into a Hadza camp mid-morning on a torrid, sunny day in 2013, but I remember being especially struck by how everyone was apparently doing nothing. Hadza camps consist of a few temporary grass huts that blend in with the surrounding bushes. I didn't realize I had walked into a camp until I found myself amid about fifteen Hadza men, women, and children who were sitting on the ground as shown in figure 2. The women and children were relaxing on one side, and the men on another. One fellow was straightening some arrows, and a few children were toddling about, but no one was engaged in any hard work. To be sure, the Hadza weren't lounging on sofas, watching TV, munching potato chips, and sipping soda, but they were doing what so many health experts warn us to avoid: sitting.
findings.content: Lieberman's first-person observation of a Hadza hunter-gatherer camp in 2013 contradicts the standard Western assumption about hunter-gatherer activity levels. Upon arrival he found Hadza men, women, and children sitting on the ground, doing light chores, with no one engaged in hard work. This became the load-bearing empirical touchstone for M10's resolution-conditions framing: 'normal' human physical activity is embedded in daily life rather than set aside as 'exercise', and includes substantial rest and sitting.
findings.where: Chapter 1 'Are We Born to Rest or Run?' pp. ~15-17

findings.quote: When Herman Pontzer and his colleagues measured daily energy expenditures in the Hadza, they were surprised to find that the highly active Hadza spend about the same total number of calories per day as sedentary industrialized people with the same lean body weight. In addition, when Pontzer and colleagues collected energetic data from adults in many countries including the United States, Ghana, Jamaica, and South Africa, they observed that more active people spent only slightly more calories per day than more sedentary people who weighed the same. In addition, individuals who were more physically active didn't have total energy budgets as high as their exertions would predict. How could someone who spent five hundred extra calories a day exercising not have a total energy budget that is five hundred calories higher? The proposed explanation is that people's total energy budgets are constrained: if I use five hundred extra calories walking, I'll spend less energy on my resting metabolism to help pay for my exertions.
findings.content: The Pontzer constrained energy expenditure hypothesis: highly active Hadza spend about the same total daily energy as sedentary industrialized people with the same lean body weight. Across countries (US, Ghana, Jamaica, South Africa), more active people spend only slightly more calories per day than sedentary people of the same weight. The proposed mechanism is metabolic compensation - when one burns extra calories exercising, resting metabolism is reduced to keep total energy budget roughly constant. This is load-bearing for M13 Energy Regulation and for DA4 (exercise-as-weight-loss is a weak proxy for metabolic health).

findings.quote: We get sick from chronic diseases by doing what we evolved to do but under conditions for which our bodies are poorly adapted, and we then pass on those same conditions to our children, who also then get sick.
findings.content: Humans get sick from chronic diseases by doing what they evolved to do but under conditions their bodies are poorly adapted to, then pass those conditions to their children in a vicious cycle. Lieberman calls this dysevolution - an intergenerational feedback loop where mismatch diseases persist because modern environments prevent natural selection from eliminating the underlying susceptibilities.

findings.quote: diabetes is a growing problem because human bodies, like those of captive primates, were adapted primarily for very different conditions that render us inadequately adapted to cope with modern diets and physical inactivity.
findings.content: Type 2 diabetes is a mismatch disease: human bodies, like captive primates, were adapted for very different conditions and are inadequately adapted to cope with modern diets and physical inactivity. The answer does not lie solely in cellular and genetic mechanisms but in the evolutionary mismatch between ancestral and modern environments.

findings.quote: In order to elucidate the links between exercise and aging, I propose a corollary to the grandmother hypothesis, which I call the active grandparent hypothesis. According to this idea, human longevity was not only selected for but also made possible by having to work moderately during old age to help as many children, grandchildren, and other younger relatives as possible to survive and thrive. That is, while there might have been selection for genes (as yet unidentified) that help humans live past the age of fifty, there was also selection for genes that repair and maintain our bodies when we are physically active. As a result, many of the mechanisms that slow aging and extend life are turned on by physical activity, especially as we get older. Human health and longevity are thus extended both by and for physical activity.
findings.content: Lieberman's own theoretical contribution - the active grandparent hypothesis - proposes that human longevity was not only selected for but also made possible by physical activity in older age. The core mechanism: humans evolved unique longevity BECAUSE grandparents who stayed physically active (walking, digging, carrying, provisioning grandchildren) increased their inclusive fitness through kin-selection effects, AND natural selection favored genes that repair and maintain the body in response to physical activity stress. Human longevity is thus extended BOTH by and FOR physical activity. This is the central evolutionary argument for M10's cascade - the repair/maintenance mechanisms that slow aging are turned on by movement, especially as we age, because natural selection never had a version of our species in which old people were inactive.

findings.quote: My last book, The Story of the Human Body, made the case that many of the diseases that kill us slowly today are mismatch diseases caused by our bodies being imperfectly or inadequately adapted to modern environmental conditions like smoking, obesity, and physical inactivity. Although these diseases are commonly classified as diseases of aging because they tend to arise when we are middle-aged, they are not caused by age, nor should they be considered inevitable consequences of aging. Plenty of people live to old age without getting these diseases, which rarely if ever afflict elderly hunter-gatherers and many aged people who live in subsistence societies.
findings.content: Lieberman's explicit mismatch framing of the epidemiological transition and 'diseases of aging'. Many chronic noninfectious diseases that kill us slowly today (heart disease, type 2 diabetes, Alzheimer's, chronic respiratory disease, osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, autoimmune diseases) are mismatch diseases caused by our bodies being inadequately adapted to modern environmental conditions like smoking, obesity, and physical inactivity. Although they are commonly classified as 'diseases of aging' because they tend to arise in middle age, they are not caused by aging per se and are rare among elderly hunter-gatherers. This grounds P3 (systematic mismatch) at the epidemiological scale and M10 specifically as one of the three primary mismatch axes.

The Paleolithic nutrition model identifies specific discordances between ancestral and modern diets: higher protein intake, lower carbohydrate (especially refined), much higher fiber, lower sodium, higher potassium, higher calcium from non-dairy sources, and substantially lower sugar consumption. The fat profile differs in kind, not just quantity - ancestral fats were predominantly unsaturated while modern diets are dominated by saturated and trans fats. These specific nutritional parameters define the mismatch that drives metabolic disease.

findings.quote: Farming brought many advantages but also caused many serious problems. Farming enabled humans to have more food, hence more children, but also required new forms of work, transformed diets, and opened a Pandora's box of diseases and social ills.
findings.content: Farming brought many advantages but also caused serious problems. It enabled more food and hence more children, but also required new forms of work, transformed diets, and opened a Pandora's box of diseases and social ills. The agricultural revolution was the first major dysevolution event - the transition from foraging to farming created the first systematic mismatch between human bodies and their environment.

Ancestral work was characteristically small-group, embodied, skill-based, and autonomy-rich. Psychological adaptations for work - cognitive mechanisms for toolmaking, resource acquisition, learning, and cooperative production - evolved in the context of small networks of hunter-gatherers where effort-outcome links were visible and physical.

Digital work exacerbates evolutionary mismatch through multiple simultaneous channels: sedentarism replacing embodied activity, always-on connectivity disrupting circadian boundaries, electronic surveillance replacing autonomy, remote/distributed work weakening face-to-face social bonds, and abstract screen-mediated tasks replacing tangible effort-outcome feedback. These mismatches are predicted to increase chronic work stress and related physical and mental health problems.

Organizational interventions for digital work should be grounded in mismatch logic: restore movement breaks, protect circadian boundaries (right to disconnect), design for team sizes within Dunbar-range cooperation thresholds, increase decision latitude and visible effort-outcome links, and create physical co-presence opportunities for distributed teams.

findings.quote: The data, from over 20,000 participants in 30 countries, confirm that in places where people actually do trust strangers in anonymous experimental settings, they also tend to say, when asked the GTQ, that most people can be trusted.
findings.content: Impersonal trust and cooperation with strangers: in places where people actually trust strangers in anonymous experimental settings, they also report trusting most people in surveys. Impersonal prosociality includes motivations and strategies for punishing those who break impartial norms. This trust-among-strangers is a WEIRD psychological feature that evolved alongside impersonal market institutions.

findings.quote: For example, Hamann et al. (2012) had pairs of three-year-old children work together to bring rewards to the top of a step-like structure. The problem was that for one child the reward, surprisingly, became available midway through. Nevertheless, when this happened, the lucky child delayed consumption of her own reward and persevered until the other got hers (i.e., more than they helped the partner in a similar situation in which they were acting individually, without collaboration). Such commitment to the partner suggests that the children constructed a joint goal at the beginning that "we" get the prizes together, and they made whatever adjustments were necessary to realize that joint goal. Again, great apes do not behave in this same way.
findings.content: 3-year-old children collaborative commitment study (Hamann 2012): pairs of 3yo children worked together to bring rewards to the top of a step structure. One child's reward, surprisingly, became available midway. The 'lucky' child DELAYED consuming her own reward and PERSEVERED until the other got hers - significantly more than in a parallel non-collaborative individual-action condition. This shows commitment to a joint goal: 'we' get the prizes together, and they make adjustments to realize the joint goal. Chimps in parallel experiments show no such commitment. And Hamann 2011: 3yo children (but not chimps) also committed to dividing spoils equally.

findings.quote: other studies have found that young children, but not chimpanzees, learn important new things about the partner's role as they are collaborating. For example, Carpenter et al. (2005) found that after young children played one role in a collaboration, they could quickly switch to the other, whereas chimpanzees could not do this (Tomasello and Carpenter, 2005).
findings.content: Role-switching in collaborative roles: Carpenter 2005 found that young children, after playing one role in a collaboration, could quickly switch to the other role. Chimpanzees could not. This indicates that children attend not just to their own subgoals but to the partner's subgoal AND to the partner attending to them - a specifically recursive level of joint-attention tracking. Fletcher 2012 extended this: 3yo children who had first played role A in collaboration learned role B more easily than children who had only observed - they had learned BOTH roles from their own collaborative experience simultaneously.

Experimental demonstration of altruistic punishment: in repeated public-goods games, participants were willing to pay a personal cost to punish free-riders even when (a) punishment yielded no material benefit to the punisher, (b) interactions were one-shot with no reputational gain, and (c) the punisher would never meet the punished again. Fehr and Gächter's key design innovation was to eliminate all standard self-interest explanations (kin selection, direct reciprocity, reputation) and still observe robust punishment behavior. Across treatments, 84% of participants punished at least once. This falsifies purely selfish models of human cooperation.

Cooperation collapses without altruistic punishment, flourishes with it: in the no-punishment treatment, cooperation decayed from ~65% of endowment contributed in round 1 to ~20% by round 10 - the standard public-goods decay pattern. In the punishment treatment, cooperation rose to ~80-95% of endowment by round 10 and was maintained. The difference was dramatic and persistent. Critically, this held even in 'stranger' designs where group composition was reshuffled each round, eliminating any direct-reciprocity explanation. Cooperation is stable when and only when there exist mechanisms for punishing defectors - even at personal cost to the punisher.

findings.quote: Korean and European American subjects observed pictures of either in- or out-group members in pain. All subjects reported more subjective empathy and showed more activation of Theory of Mind brain regions (i.e., the temporoparietal junction) when observing in-group members, but the bias was significantly greater among Korean subjects.
findings.content: In-group empathy bias is stronger in collectivist than individualist cultures. Korean and European American subjects showed more empathy and Theory of Mind activation for in-group members in pain, but the bias was significantly greater among Korean subjects. Both individualist and collectivist cultures denigrate out-groups, but only individualist cultures inflate assessments of their own group - East Asians do not need to puff up their own group to view others as inferior.

findings.quote: Thus, Warneken et al. (2006, 2007) had infants of this age engage in a joint activity with an adult, such as obtaining a toy by each operating one side of an apparatus. Then, the adult simply stopped playing her role for no reason. The children were not happy about this and did various things to attempt to reengage their partner. (They did not do this if her stopping was for a good reason; e.g., she had to attend to something else [Warneken et al., 2012].) Interesting, when this same situation was arranged for human-raised chimpanzees, they simply ignored the recalcitrant partner and tried to find ways to achieve the goal on their own.
findings.content: Children vs chimps reengagement experiment: Warneken et al. had 14-18 month old human infants engage in joint activity with an adult (operating an apparatus). When the adult stopped playing her role for no reason, children were unhappy and attempted to reengage the partner. When the SAME situation was arranged for human-raised chimpanzees, chimps ignored the partner and tried to complete the goal alone. This dissociation - even at prelinguistic ages, humans expect partners in joint activity to be committed enough to reengage, chimps do not - is a central behavioral marker of joint intentionality.

findings.quote: Importantly, when children of this same age have it in their common ground with a collaborative partner that each is counting on the other to come through (we are interdependent), they both feel obligated to the other (see Gilbert, 1989, 1990). Thus, Gräfenhain et al. (2009) had preschoolers explicitly agree to play a game with one adult, and then another adult attempted to lure them away to a more exciting game. Although two-year-old children mostly just bolted to the new game straightaway, from three years of age children paused before departing and "took leave," either verbally or by handing the adult the tool they had been using together. The children seemed to recognize that joint goals involve joint commitments, the breaking of which requires some kind of acknowledgment or even apology. No study of this type has ever been done with chimpanzees, but there are no published reports of one chimpanzee taking leave from, making excuses to, or apologizing to another for breaking a joint commitment.
findings.content: Taking leave: Gräfenhain 2009 had preschoolers explicitly agree to play a game with one adult; then another adult attempted to lure them to a more exciting game. Two-year-olds mostly bolted to the new game, but from age 3 children paused before departing and 'took leave' - verbally or by handing the adult the shared tool. Children recognized that joint goals involve joint commitments, the breaking of which requires acknowledgment. No published reports of chimpanzees taking leave from, making excuses to, or apologizing to another for breaking a joint commitment exist. This is specific evidence for commitment-as-moral-obligation in joint intentionality.

findings.quote: Human cooperation is an evolutionary puzzle. Unlike other creatures, people frequently cooperate with genetically unrelated strangers, often in large groups, with people they will never meet again, and when reputation gains are small or absent.
findings.content: Altruistic punishment: individuals punish defectors at personal cost with no material gain. Cooperation flourishes when altruistic punishment is possible and breaks down when it is ruled out. Negative emotions toward defectors are the proximate mechanism behind altruistic punishment. Human cooperation with unrelated strangers in large groups cannot be explained by kin selection, signaling theory, or reciprocal altruism alone - altruistic punishment is a key additional mechanism.

findings.quote: The most frequent type of power coalition in egalitarian bands consists of the entire adult community coalescing against a deviant. In addition to the proscription of bullying by upstarts, all foragers are opposed to incest, murder within the group, and undue selfish use of deception.
findings.content: The entire moral community coalesces against deviants. All foragers oppose incest, murder within the group, and undue selfish use of deception. The most frequent type of power coalition in egalitarian bands consists of the entire adult community acting collectively against a deviant. The threat of sanctions (including ostracism and execution) keeps power seekers in their place. When upstartism becomes active, so does the moral community - it unites preemptively and assertively.

findings.quote: those who have things of value but do not give are subject to social control through gossip, ridicule or ostracism.
findings.content: Social control through gossip, ridicule, and ostracism targets free-riders: those who have things of value but do not give are subject to social control. Bullying free-riders are handled by egalitarian sanctioning. Other free-riders take advantage by being lazy, feigning injury, or secretly consuming meat they have killed. Much of the enforcement investment involves gossiping, which brings individual reproductive benefits through rewarding social interaction and exchange of information about subsistence.

findings.quote: Unlike much of the world today, and most people who have ever lived, we WEIRD people are highly individualistic, self-obsessed, control-oriented, nonconformist, and analytical. We focus on ourselves - our attributes, accomplishments, and aspirations - over our relationships and social roles.
findings.content: WEIRD people are psychologically peculiar: highly individualistic, self-obsessed, control-oriented, nonconformist, and analytical. They focus on attributes, accomplishments, and aspirations over relationships and social roles. They see themselves as unique beings, not as nodes in a social network. They prefer a sense of control and making their own choices. They are less willing to conform when this conflicts with their own beliefs. Yet paradoxically, WEIRD people tend to stick to impartial rules and are quite trusting, honest, and cooperative toward strangers.

findings.quote: WEIRD people do conform to others, and this is what surprised Solomon. Only about one-quarter of his participants were never influenced by their peers. WEIRD people, however, conform less than all the other populations that have been studied.
findings.content: WEIRD people conform less than all other studied populations, but they do still conform. Cross-cultural studies show substantial variation in conformity across countries, with WEIRD undergraduate samples at the low end. The reduced conformity in WEIRD populations reflects the dismantling of kin-based social pressure and the institutional promotion of individual autonomy.

findings.quote: Across the three intervals, the mean proportion of repeated campmates was 12.1%.
findings.content: Across 6 years / 4 waves, Hadza camps continuously dissolve and reconstitute: only ~12% of campmates repeat year-over-year (implying ~88% annual turnover), yet cooperative assortment persists.

findings.quote: One lone woman equipped with only the cumulative know-how of her ancestors survived for eighteen years whereas fully provisioned and well-financed teams of experienced explorers struggled in Australia, Texas, and the Arctic.
findings.content: Without culturally transmitted knowledge about how to locate and process plants, fashion tools, and avoid dangers, humans do not last long as hunter-gatherers. European explorers who became separated from their cultural knowledge base routinely perished despite access to the same environments that sustained indigenous populations for millennia. One lone woman equipped with ancestral cumulative know-how survived eighteen years where provisioned, financed exploration teams failed.

findings.quote: In effect, the band keeps a dossier on every individual, noting positive and negative points. Group members exercise the right to take action if a deviant begins to intimidate other group members individually - or threatens the social equilibrium of the group or its very ability to function.
findings.content: Gossip as information processing and social control: the band keeps a dossier on every individual, noting positive and negative points. Types of deviance that all groups watch for include murder, deception, theft, and stinginess. Everyone knows gossiping is constantly taking place and anyone can be a target - this knowledge serves as a deterrent, for most foragers worry about the opinion of their peers and try to exert self-control accordingly.

findings.quote: the various human groups that can be identified in any society seem to cluster rather tightly around a series of values (5, 12, 35, 150, 500, and 2,000) with virtually no overlap in the variance around these characteristic values.
findings.content: Human social groups cluster at characteristic values of approximately 5, 12, 35, 150, 500, and 2,000 with virtually no overlap in variance between layers. These represent stable points in the degrees of familiarity and correspond to support clique, sympathy group, band, clan/village, mega-band, and tribe respectively.

findings.quote: We used measures of effort/reward imbalance in the workplace in our studies in Poland, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Hungary. This study confirmed the importance for poor health of low control at work and generally. In addition, people whose work was characterised by a high degree of imbalance between effort and reward had a 60 per cent greater chance of being in poor health than those with an appropriate balance.
findings.content: People whose work was characterised by a high degree of imbalance between efforts put in and rewards received had higher risk of disease, independently of low control at work. Two distinct psychosocial features - low control and effort/reward imbalance - both contribute to the work-health gradient in Whitehall II.
findings.where: Chapter 7 'Health and Work' p. 190-191, Whitehall II effort/reward analysis, citing Siegrist model

findings.quote: In order to successfully engage in social exchange--cooperation between two or more individuals for mutual benefit--humans must be able to solve a number of complex computational problems, and do so with special efficiency
findings.content: Wason selection task reveals domain-specific reasoning about social exchange. Abstract conditional rules yield 5-30% correct detection of violations. Social contract rules (if you take benefit B, you must meet requirement R) yield 65-80% correct - despite identical logical structure. Cheater detection is operationally defined: agent takes rationed benefit, fails to meet requirement, acts intentionally. The mechanism does not detect all rule violations, only those revealing intentional cheating.

Parametric decomposition of cheater detection: a 2×2×2 design manipulating benefit, intention, and ability shows each factor independently drops performance ~20 percentage points. All three present: 64% correct. Two present: ~46%. One: ~26%. None: ~26%. Effects are additive and independent (ANOVA: Benefit F=7.30 p=0.007; Intention F=10.22 p=0.002; Ability F=4.87 p=0.028). Social exchange activates nonstandard inference rules that diverge sharply from first-order logic.
findings.where: Cognition 31(3):187-276 and extended work in Cosmides, Barrett & Tooby 2010 PNAS

findings.quote: Which raises a third fundamental, alongside individual selection and kin selection: reciprocal altruism. "I'll scratch your back if you scratch mine. I'd rather not actually scratch yours if I can get away with it. And I'm watching you in case you try the same."
findings.content: Reciprocal altruism: cooperation among unrelated organisms where each incurs a fitness cost to enhance the other's fitness with expectation of reciprocation. Trivers (1971) laid out the evolutionary logic. Unrelated animals frequently cooperate - fish school, birds fly in formation, meerkats give alarm calls, vampire bats feed one another's babies, primates groom one another and share meat. Cooperation evolves because many hands lighten the load, but it creates the problem of cheater detection.

findings.quote: The secret of our species' success resides not in the power of our individual minds, but in the collective brains of our communities. Our collective brains arise from the synthesis of our cultural and social natures - from the fact that we readily learn from others (are cultural) and can, with the right norms, live in large and widely interconnected groups (are social).
findings.content: The secret of our species' success resides not in the power of our individual minds, but in the collective brains of our communities. Our collective brains arise from the synthesis of our cultural and social natures - from the fact that we readily learn from others (are cultural) and can, with the right norms, live in large and widely interconnected groups (are social). The striking technologies that characterize our species, from the kayaks and compound bows used by hunter-gatherers to the antibiotics and airplanes of the modern world, emerge not from singular geniuses but from the flow and recombination of ideas, practices, lucky errors, and chance insights among interconnected minds and across generations.

findings.quote: humans not only understand others as intentional agents but also put their heads together with others in acts of shared intentionality
findings.content: The critical difference now seems to be that humans not only understand others as intentional agents but also put their heads together with others in acts of shared intentionality, including everything from concrete acts of collaborative problem solving to complex cultural institutions. The focus now is thus less on culture as a process of transmission and more on culture as a process of social coordination. Modern human cultures were made possible by an earlier evolutionary step in which individuals made a living by coordinating with others in relatively simple acts of collaborative foraging.

findings.quote: There were two key evolutionary steps. The first step, reflecting the focus of social infrastructure theorists such as Mead and Wittgenstein, involved the creation of a novel type of small-scale collaboration in human foraging. Participants in this collaborative foraging created socially shared joint goals and joint attention (common ground), which created the possibility of individual roles and perspectives within that ad hoc shared world or "form of life."
findings.content: Tomasello's two-step evolutionary sequence for uniquely human cognition: (1) Joint intentionality - small-scale ad hoc pair collaboration with 'I'/'you' second-personal engagement, emerging from obligate collaborative foraging ~400,000 years ago; (2) Collective intentionality - group-mindedness with in-group strangers, based on conventions/norms/institutions, emerging as populations grew and competed. This maps to two distinct cognitive-capacity profiles: perspectival/symbolic representations with recursive mind reading (joint) vs agent-neutral thinking with cultural common ground (collective). Both steps were driven by ecological pressure forcing cooperative lifeways.

findings.quote: The situation these early humans faced is perhaps best modeled by the stag hunt scenario from game theory (Skyrms, 2004). Two individuals have easy access to low-payoff "hares" (e.g., low-calorie vegetation), and then there appears on the horizon a high-payoff but difficult-to-obtain "stag" (e.g., large game) that can be acquired only if individuals abandon their hares and collaborate. Their motivations thus align, because it is in both their interests to work together. The dilemma is thus purely cognitive: since collaboration is mandatory and I am risking my hare, I want to go for the stag only if you do, too. But you only want to go for the stag if I do, too.
findings.content: The stag hunt as formal model for early human collaboration: two individuals have easy access to low-payoff hares and see a high-payoff stag that requires joint action. Motivations align but the cognitive problem is coordination - I want to go for the stag only if you do, and vice versa. The leader-follower solution that chimpanzees use is unstable when risk is high. Schelling/Lewis showed that coordination requires mutual knowledge / recursive mind-reading. Tomasello's refinement: humans use 'common ground' with recursive decomposition only when perturbations occur. This is the cognitive architecture that distinguishes human from ape cooperation.

findings.quote: Clark (1996) proposed, as a more realistic account, that humans simply recognize the "common ground" they have with others (e.g., we both know that we both want to go for the stag) and that this is sufficient for making joint decisions toward joint goals. Tomasello (2008) suggested that something like common ground is how people actually operate, but when perturbations occur they often explain them by reasoning that "he thinks that I think he thinks . . ." (typically only a few iterations deep), suggesting an underlying recursive structure.
findings.content: Tomasello's characterization of how humans think about each other recursively: attuned to common ground, and decomposing common ground a few recursive layers deep when perturbations occur ('he thinks that I think he thinks...'). Typically only a few iterations deep - not the infinite regress that Lewis/Schelling formalized. This realistic recursive-mind-reading architecture is what supports joint intentionality in practice: most of the time you just know what the shared situation is, but when things go wrong you can reason explicitly about what the partner thinks about your thinking.

findings.quote: We may characterize the formation of a joint goal (or joint intention) in more detail as follows (see Bratman, 1992). For you and me to form a joint goal (or joint intention) to pursue a stag together, (1) I must have the goal to capture the stag together with you; (2) you must have the goal to capture the stag together with me; and, critically, (3) we must have mutual knowledge, or common ground, that we both know each other's goal.
findings.content: Joint goal formation specification (from Bratman 1992): for you and me to form a joint goal to pursue a stag together, (1) I must have the goal to capture the stag TOGETHER WITH YOU; (2) you must have the goal to capture the stag TOGETHER WITH ME; and critically (3) we must have MUTUAL KNOWLEDGE (common ground) that we both know each other's goal. Each of us wanting separately to capture the stag, even if mutually known, does not count - it would be parallel hunting, not joint hunting. The together-with-the-other structure is essential.

findings.quote: Although humans' great ape ancestors were social beings, they lived mostly individualistic and competitive lives, and so their thinking was geared toward achieving individual goals. But early humans were at some point forced by ecological circumstances into more cooperative lifeways, and so their thinking became more directed toward figuring out ways to coordinate with others to achieve joint goals or even collective group goals. And this changed everything.
findings.content: Tomasello's framing of ape-cognition vs human-cognition: early humans' great ape ancestors were social beings, but they lived mostly individualistic and competitive lives, and so their thinking was geared toward achieving individual goals. Early humans were FORCED by ecological circumstances into more cooperative lifeways, and their thinking became more directed toward coordinating with others to achieve joint goals or collective group goals. This shift - from individual-competitive to joint-cooperative cognition - 'changed everything'. Thinking itself became fundamentally social.

findings.quote: although many animal species can cognitively represent situations and entities at least somewhat abstractly, only humans can conceptualize one and the same situation or entity under differing, even conflicting, social perspectives (leading ultimately to a sense of "objectivity"). Further, although many animals also make simple causal and intentional inferences about external events, only humans make socially recursive and self-reflective inferences about others' or their own intentional states. And, finally, although many animals monitor and evaluate their own actions with respect to instrumental success, only humans self-monitor and evaluate their own thinking with respect to the normative perspectives and standards ("reasons") of others or the group.
findings.content: Objective-reflective-normative thinking: the human-unique cognitive profile. Many animals can cognitively represent situations abstractly, but only humans conceptualize the same situation under differing, even CONFLICTING social perspectives (leading to 'objectivity'). Many animals make simple causal/intentional inferences, but only humans make socially RECURSIVE and self-reflective inferences about others' intentional states. Many animals monitor their actions for instrumental success, but only humans self-monitor with respect to the NORMATIVE perspectives and standards ('reasons') of others or the group. These three social differences - perspectival, recursive, normative - yield an identifiably different type of thinking.

findings.quote: The second step, reflecting the focus of culture theorists such as Vygotsky and Bakhtin, came as human populations began growing in size and competing with one another. This competition meant that group life as a whole became one big collaborative activity, creating a much larger and more permanent shared world, that is to say, a culture. The resulting group-mindedness among all members of the cultural group (including in-group strangers) was based on a new ability to construct common cultural ground via collectively known cultural conventions, norms, and institutions.
findings.content: Collective intentionality (second step): as human populations grew and groups competed, group life as a whole became 'one big collaborative activity' - a culture. The resulting group-mindedness among all members of the cultural group (including in-group strangers) was based on ability to construct common cultural ground via collectively known cultural conventions, norms, and institutions. This shifts from the face-to-face 'I-you' joint-intentionality of the first step to an impersonal 'we-as-group' collective intentionality with conventional communication and cultural institutions. The architectural distinction matters for M11 - humans have BOTH ad hoc joint collaboration AND stable group-mindedness, and these are different cognitive capacities.

findings.quote: Darwin said, 'A tribe including many members who, from possessing in a high degree the spirit of patriotism, fidelity, obedience, courage, and sympathy, were always ready to aid one another, and to sacrifice themselves for the common good, would be victorious over most other tribes.'
findings.content: Darwin's group selection insight: a tribe with many members possessing patriotism, fidelity, obedience, courage, and sympathy who sacrifice for the common good would be victorious over most other tribes. The Nuer-Dinka case demonstrates cultural group selection in practice: cultural differences in norms meant the Nuer could cooperate in larger groups, enabling territorial expansion at the Dinka's expense.

findings.quote: it takes some effort to keep the political tables turned
findings.content: In small local groups that are egalitarian, such as bands, the main political actors - usually adult heads of households - are the individuals who actively participate when the entire group must arrive at important consensual decisions. When the subordinates take charge to firmly suppress competition that leads to domination, it takes some effort to keep the political tables turned. For the most part, the mere threat of sanctions (including ostracism and execution) keeps such power seekers in their place.

findings.quote: How can cheerful, altruistic cooperators, people guided by generous feelings and positive expectations about cooperation, avoid being exploited by lazy slackers and outright cheaters, or by opportunistic bullies who take advantage of situations by force? To whatever degree the cooperating altruists in a group can be successful in circumventing such losses, it becomes far, far easier to explain the natural selection of altruistic traits.
findings.content: How can altruistic cooperators avoid exploitation by lazy slackers, outright cheaters, and opportunistic bullies? To whatever degree cooperating altruists can successfully circumvent such losses, it becomes far easier to explain the natural selection of altruistic traits. Free-rider suppression is the mechanism that makes group selection for cooperation viable - without it, selfish individuals would always outcompete altruists within groups.

findings.quote: we have conducted an experimental research program over the last eight years, exploring the hypothesis that the human mind contains algorithms (specialized mechanisms) designed for reasoning about social exchange. The topic of reasoning about social exchange was selected for several reasons. In the first place, as we will discuss, many aspects of the evolutionary theory of social exchange (also sometimes called cooperation, reciprocal altruism, or reciprocation) are relatively well developed and unambiguous.
findings.content: Cosmides and Tooby's foundational argument for domain-specific reasoning: the human mind contains algorithms specialized for reasoning about social exchange. Social exchange was chosen as the target domain because the evolutionary theory of reciprocal altruism is mathematically well-developed, and because social exchange behavior is universal across human cultures (including hunter-gatherer cultures) AND present in our nearest primate relatives, indicating that cognitive adaptations for social exchange were present in the hominid lineage at least back to the common ancestor with chimpanzees ~5-10 million years ago. This establishes the Pleistocene depth required for a genuine cognitive adaptation rather than a culturally-transmitted pattern.
findings.where: Cosmides & Tooby, 'Cognitive Adaptations for Social Exchange', in Barkow Cosmides Tooby (eds.) The Adapted Mind (1992)

findings.quote: In this dialogue, reasoning has served as the paradigm case of the 'general-purpose' psychological process: It has been viewed as preeminently characteristic of those processes that are purportedly the central engine of the human mind. Even vigorous advocates of modularity have held so-called central processes, such as reasoning, to be general-purpose and content-independent. Consequently, we felt that reasoning about social exchange offered an excellent opportunity to cut to the quick of the controversy. If even human reasoning, the doctrinal 'citadel' of the advocates of content-free, general-purpose processes, turns out to include a large number of content-dependent cognitive adaptations, then the presumption that psychological mechanisms are characteristically domain-general and originally content-free can no longer be accorded privileged status.
findings.content: Cosmides & Tooby's direct challenge to the general-purpose-reasoning citadel: if even human reasoning - traditionally held as the paradigm case of content-free, general-purpose cognition - turns out to include content-dependent cognitive adaptations, then the assumption that psychological mechanisms are characteristically domain-general and originally content-free can no longer be accorded privileged status. This is the specific argumentative move the Wason selection task cheater-detection finding is designed to make: by showing that humans reason about social-exchange problems fundamentally differently than isomorphic abstract problems, it forces the conclusion that reasoning is not a single general-purpose faculty. Load-bearing for P2 Domain-Sensitive Interacting Adaptations.
findings.where: Cosmides & Tooby, Adapted Mind Ch. 3, chapter-opening argument

findings.quote: A model is presented to account for the natural selection of what is termed reciprocally altruistic behavior.
findings.content: Trivers models the natural selection of reciprocally altruistic behavior and shows how selection operates against cheaters. The human psychological system that regulates reciprocal altruism explains friendship, dislike, moralistic aggression, gratitude, sympathy, trust, suspicion, trustworthiness, aspects of guilt, and forms of dishonesty and hypocrisy as adaptations to regulate the altruistic system.

findings.quote: Three instances of altruistic behavior are discussed, the evolution of which the model can explain: (1) behavior involved in cleaning symbioses; (2) warning cries in birds: and (3) human reciprocal altruism.
findings.content: Trivers presents three instances of reciprocal altruism: (1) cleaning symbioses between fish (cleaner wrasse and host grouper), where hosts refrain from eating cleaners despite opportunity; (2) warning cries in birds, reinterpreted as reciprocal altruism rather than kin selection; (3) human reciprocal altruism, the most complex form, regulated by an elaborate psychological system including friendship, moralistic aggression, gratitude, sympathy, trust, suspicion, and aspects of guilt.

findings.quote: Because of the structural complexity of postagricultural societies, I considered only traditional hunter-gatherer and small-scale horticultural societies. Although census data on such societies are limited, those that are available suggest that there is indeed a consistent group size in the region of 150 individuals (Fig. 7).
findings.content: Ethnographic data from hunter-gatherer and horticultural societies validates the ~150 predicted by the primate neocortex regression (95% CI 100-230). The clan/village organizational level consistently clusters at this value, supporting the social brain hypothesis prediction for human-scale groups.

findings.quote: The banning of sororate and levirate marriages were among the first actions taken as the Church began to restructure European families.
findings.content: The Church's Marriage and Family Program (MFP) restructured European families by banning cousin marriage, levirate and sororate marriage, adoption, and polygyny. Starting as early as 315 CE with the Synod of Neocaesarea banning men from marrying a dead brother's wife, these prohibitions systematically dismantled the kin-based institutions that had organized human social life for millennia.

findings.quote: Often, especially in formerly non-state societies, the newly transplanted institutions created a misfit with people's cultural psychology, leading to poorly functioning governments, economies, and civil societies.
findings.content: Impersonal institutions (representative governments, universities, social safety nets) evolved in Europe and have been exported to numerous populations. Often, especially in formerly non-state societies, newly transplanted institutions create a misfit with people's cultural psychology, leading to poorly functioning governments, economies, and civil societies. The institutional-psychological mismatch produces systemic dysfunction.

findings.quote: cultural evolution initiated a process of self-domestication, driving genetic evolution to make us prosocial, docile, rule followers who expect a world governed by social norms monitored and enforced by communities.
findings.content: Cultural evolution initiated a process of self-domestication, driving genetic evolution to make us prosocial, docile, rule followers who expect a world governed by social norms monitored and enforced by communities. Norms influence a vast range of human action, including ancient and fundamentally important domains such as kin relations, mating, food sharing, parenting, and reciprocity. Over our evolutionary history, norm violations such as ignoring a food taboo, botching a ritual, or failing to give one's in-laws their due from one's hunting successes meant reputational damage, gossip, and a consequent loss of marriage opportunities and allies. Repeated norm violations sometimes provoked ostracism or even execution at the hands of one's community.

findings.quote: The key to understanding how humans evolved and why we are so different from other animals is to recognize that we are a cultural species. Probably over a million years ago, members of our evolutionary lineage began learning from each other in such a way that culture became cumulative.
findings.content: Humans are a cultural species. Over a million years ago, members of our evolutionary lineage began learning from each other so that culture became cumulative. Tool-making skills, tracking know-how, and edible-plant knowledge improved and aggregated across generations until the toolkit became so complex that individuals could not figure it out on their own over a lifetime. Culture became the species' primary adaptation.

findings.quote: cultural evolution initiated a process of self-domestication, driving genetic evolution to make us prosocial, docile, rule followers who expect a world governed by social norms monitored and enforced by communities.
findings.content: Cultural evolution initiated a process of self-domestication, driving genetic evolution to make humans prosocial, docile, rule-following organisms who expect a world governed by social norms monitored and enforced by communities. Cultural products like fire, cooking, tools, clothing, and language became the main selective pressures that genetically shaped human minds and bodies - culture-gene coevolution creating a new kind of animal.

findings.quote: Religious rituals that galvanize greater prosociality.
findings.content: Religious rituals galvanize greater prosociality and bind groups through synchronized behavior. Cultural evolution shaped ritual practices that create collective identity, coordinate group action, and suppress free-riding. Rituals are not arbitrary cultural decorations but functional mechanisms for maintaining cooperation at scales beyond face-to-face reciprocity.

findings.quote: The secret of our species' success resides not in the power of our individual minds, but in the collective brains of our communities.
findings.content: The secret of our species' success resides not in the power of individual minds but in the collective brains of communities. Humans became simultaneously the most cooperative and the most warlike of primates - large-scale societies enabling both technological innovation and intergroup conflict. The collective brain hypothesis explains why larger, more interconnected populations innovate faster.

findings.quote: A small group of philosophers of action (e.g., Bratman, 1992; Searle, 1995; Gilbert, 1989; Tuomela, 2007) have investigated how humans put their heads together with others in acts of so-called shared intentionality, or "we" intentionality. When individuals participate with others in collaborative activities, together they form joint goals and joint attention, which then create individual roles and individual perspectives that must be coordinated within them (Moll and Tomasello, 2007).
findings.content: Tomasello's central thesis: what makes human thinking unique is its fundamentally cooperative nature. Humans put their heads together with others in acts of shared intentionality - 'we' intentionality - creating joint goals and joint attention that constitute a plural agent. This capacity enables everything from collaborative hunting to cultural institutions. Great apes, despite knowing much about others as intentional agents, do NOT engage in shared intentionality and do NOT form human-like culture. Shared intentionality is the specific human-unique adaptation.

findings.quote: In the hypothesis of Tomasello et al. (2012), obligate collaborative foraging became an evolutionarily stable strategy for early humans because of two interrelated processes: interdependence and social selection. The first and most basic point is that humans began a lifestyle in which individuals could not procure their daily sustenance alone but instead were interdependent with others in their foraging activities - which meant that individuals needed to develop the skills and motivations to forage collaboratively or else starve. There was thus direct and immediate selective pressure for skills and motivations for joint collaborative activity (joint intentionality). The second point is that as a natural outcome of this interdependence, individuals began to make evaluative judgments about others as potential collaborative partners: they began to be socially selective, since choosing a poor partner meant less food. Cheaters and laggards were thus selected against, and bullies lost their power to bully.
findings.content: Obligate collaborative foraging as evolutionarily stable strategy: interdependence + social selection. Early humans began a lifestyle in which individuals could not procure daily food alone - they were interdependent. This created direct selective pressure for joint-intentionality skills. As a natural outcome, individuals made evaluative judgments about potential collaborative partners - social selection against cheaters and laggards, and against bullies. Critically, individuals had to worry about BOTH evaluating others AND how others were evaluating them (self-image concern) - a uniquely human cognitive preoccupation.

findings.quote: as a specific form of human collaborative activity and shared intentionality, human cooperative communication involves a set of special intentional and inferential processes - first identified by Grice (1957, 1975) and since elaborated and amended by Sperber and Wilson (1996), Clark (1996), Levinson (2000), and Tomasello (2008). Human communicators conceptualize situations and entities via external communicative vehicles for other persons; these other persons then attempt to determine why the communicator thinks that these situations and entities will be relevant for them.
findings.content: Cooperative communication as second-personal process: humans communicators conceptualize situations via external communicative vehicles for other persons; recipients then attempt to determine why the communicator thinks these will be relevant for them. This dialogic process involves not just shared-intentionality motivations but complex recursive inferences about others' intentions toward my intentional states. This form of communication - unique to humans, characteristic even of prelinguistic infant gestures - presupposes a shared conceptual framework (common conceptual ground) AND appreciation of the partner's individual intentions within it. Grounds M11 cooperation AND M3 social bonding through the communication channel.

findings.quote: Moralistic punishment is more effective in supporting large-scale cooperation than reciprocity for two reasons.
findings.content: Moralistic punishment is more effective than reciprocity at supporting large-scale cooperation. Punishment takes forms including reduced status, fewer friends, and fewer mating opportunities. In groups where a norm is common, people who violate it are punished. When newcomers arrive, they rapidly learn local norms and maintain them despite different evolved psychology. Cultural group selection - tribes with cooperation-promoting norms outcompete those without.

findings.quote: The tribal social instincts result from the gene-culture co-evolution of tribal-scale societies by the process described above. Consequently, humans are able to make common cause with a sizable, culturally defined set of distantly related individuals, a form of social organization that is absent in other primates.
findings.content: Tribal social instincts result from gene-culture coevolution of tribal-scale societies. Humans are able to make common cause with a sizable, culturally defined set of distantly related individuals - a form of social organization absent in other primates. These instincts equip humans with the psychological machinery for in-group cooperation, out-group vigilance, and norm-governed behavior in groups of 50-500.

findings.quote: Tribal instincts cause people to use symbolic markers to define the boundaries of in-groups and establish, for example, who is eligible for empathy, who should excite suspicion, and, in some horrible cases, who should be killed.
findings.content: Symbolic markers of group boundaries motivate important behavior. Tribal instincts cause people to use symbolic markers to define who is eligible for empathy, who should excite suspicion, and in some cases who should be killed. Small differences in arrow styles, dress, or dialect become psychologically salient signals of group membership. People essentialist ethnic groups as species-like categories.

findings.quote: In the section that follows, we describe what seem to us to be the main work-around mechanisms, and the conflicts, compromises, and modes of failure that each entails.
findings.content: Complex societies employ institutional work-arounds to simulate tribal-scale relationships: hierarchical command backed by force, segmentary hierarchy, and symbolic in-group marking. Each work-around creates predictable conflicts and failure modes - elite exploitation from hierarchical command, subgroup factionalism from segmentary structure, and fundamentalism from symbolic marking. These are not design flaws but inherent consequences of scaling tribal instincts beyond their natural range.

findings.quote: egalitarianism involves a very special type of hierarchy, a curious type that is based on antihierarchical feelings
findings.content: My thesis is that egalitarianism does not result from the mere absence of hierarchy. Rather, egalitarianism involves a very special type of hierarchy, a curious type that is based on antihierarchical feelings. If a stable egalitarian hierarchy is to be achieved, the basic flow of power in society must be reversed definitively. Our political nature favors the formation of orthodox hierarchies - hierarchies like those of chimpanzees or gorillas, or humans living in chiefdoms or states. It is politically ambitious individuals, those with special learned or innate propensities to dominate, who are likely to become upstarts in egalitarian bands or tribes.
findings.where: Chapter 1, 'The Question of Egalitarian Society,' pp. 8-9

findings.quote: In effect, it is the rank and file who are on top, and the would-be alphas who remain under their thumbs. The fact that the occasional successful intimidator can rise to tyrannize these egalitarians for a time does not negate the characterization, for the group's next move is to dominate the dominator by removing him.
findings.content: Reverse dominance hierarchy: the rank and file are on top, and would-be alphas remain under their thumbs. When an occasional intimidator rises to tyrannize, the group's next move is to dominate the dominator by removing him. This is the fundamental political structure of human forager bands - not the absence of hierarchy but the active suppression of dominance by coalitions of subordinates.

findings.quote: Stigmatized roles such as 'cheater' or 'selfish bully' are labeled (and sanctioned) to make the system work in spite of predictable conflicts. This moralistic approach works reasonably well in curbing individual selfishness or tendencies to dominate, precisely because the group knows how to become aggressive in dealing with those it labels as deviants.
findings.content: Moral enforcement of sharing: the meat-sharing habit of nomadic foragers is transformed by language and morality so that definitive rules exist. Stigmatized roles such as 'cheater' or 'selfish bully' are labeled and sanctioned to make the system work despite predictable conflicts. An armed group can be exceedingly dangerous to any deviant - even the most powerful hunter - and hunters are always armed.

findings.quote: Regarding human reciprocal altruism, it is shown that the details of the psychological system that regulates this altruism can be explained by the model. Specifically, friendship, dislike, moralistic aggression, gratitude, sympathy, trust, suspicion, trustworthiness, aspects of guilt, and some forms of dishonesty and hypocrisy can be explained as important adaptations to regulate the altruistic system.
findings.content: Gratitude, sympathy, trust, suspicion, and guilt are not arbitrary emotions but specific adaptations for regulating reciprocal altruism. Gratitude motivates reciprocation; sympathy motivates initial altruistic acts toward those in need; trust calibrates willingness to cooperate; suspicion monitors potential cheaters; guilt motivates relationship repair after defection. Each emotion functions as a regulatory mechanism within the reciprocal altruism system.
findings.where: Q Rev Biol 46(1):35-57, 1971. DOI: 10.1086/406755. Human reciprocal altruism section.

findings.quote: Species following the model should tend to evolve behaviour such that each organism appears to be attempting to maximize its inclusive fitness.
findings.content: Hamilton's genetical mathematical model allows for interactions between relatives on one another's fitness. Using Wright's Coefficient of Relationship as the measure of replica genes in a relative, Hamilton found inclusive fitness - a quantity incorporating the maximizing property of Darwinian fitness. Species following the model tend to evolve behaviour where each organism appears to maximize its inclusive fitness, implying limited restraint on selfish competitive behaviour and possibility of limited self-sacrifices.

findings.quote: To express the matter more vividly, in the world of our model organisms, whose behaviour is determined strictly by genotype, we expect to find that no one is prepared to sacrifice his life for any single person but that everyone will sacrifice it when he can thereby save more than two brothers, or four half-brothers, or eight first cousins . . .
findings.content: Hamilton's rule, in its modern canonical form, states that a social behaviour is favoured by natural selection when rB > C, where r is the coefficient of relatedness between actor and recipient, B is the fitness benefit to the recipient, and C is the fitness cost to the actor. Hamilton's original 1964 paper introduced this principle using a gain-ratio inequality (his condition for an altruistic action to be favoured was -k > 1/r, with k the ratio of gain and r Wright's coefficient of relationship); the compact "rB > C" algebraic notation is a later popularization. The principle explains when organisms will sacrifice personal fitness to benefit relatives and predicts that the altruism threshold decreases with increasing relatedness - in Hamilton's own example, an organism should sacrifice its life to save "more than two brothers, or four half-brothers, or eight first cousins" (siblings r=0.5, cousins r=0.125).
findings.where: Journal of Theoretical Biology 7(1):1-16 and 7(1):17-52, 1964. PMID: 5875341/5875340

findings.content: Trivers identifies conditions maximizing the chance reciprocal altruism will be selected for: (1) many altruistic situations in the lifetime of the altruists, (2) a given altruist repeatedly interacts with the same small set of individuals, and (3) pairs of altruists are exposed symmetrically to altruistic situations - each able to render roughly equivalent benefits at roughly equivalent costs. He elaborates these into biological parameters: long lifetime, low dispersal rate, mutual dependence, parental care, dominance hierarchy structure (less dominance facilitates reciprocity), and aid in combat. Selection discriminates against cheaters when cheating has later adverse effects that outweigh the benefit of not reciprocating - the altruist curtails future altruistic gestures to the cheater.
findings.where: Q Rev Biol 46(1):35-57, 1971. DOI: 10.1086/406755. Key conditions section.

findings.quote: Throughout most of human history, people grew up enmeshed in dense family networks that knitted together distant cousins and in-laws. In these regulated-relational worlds, people's survival, identity, security, marriages, and success depended on the health and prosperity of kin-based networks, which often formed discrete institutions known as clans, lineages, houses, or tribes.
findings.content: Throughout most of human history, people grew up enmeshed in dense family networks of distant cousins and in-laws. Survival, identity, security, marriages, and success depended on kin-based networks (clans, lineages, houses, tribes). People were endowed with inherited obligations, responsibilities, and privileges in relation to others in a dense social web. This social interdependence bred emotional interdependence, leading people to strongly identify with in-groups and make sharp in-group/out-group distinctions.

findings.quote: group size is only a very gross indicator of social complexity (Dunbar focuses on the greater numbers of social relationships and reputations to be kept track of), and brain size is only a very gross indicator of cognitive capacities, so the social brain hypothesis gives us only a very general indication of the actual processes involved on either side of the correlation.
findings.content: Tomasello discusses the social brain hypothesis as supporting evidence for the evolution of human cooperation. Gowlett et al. (2012) traced brain-group size correlation across human evolution and found an especially big jump at ~400kya (Homo heidelbergensis), coinciding with Tomasello's hypothesized joint intentionality transition. However, Tomasello notes the hypothesis provides only a very general indication: group size is a gross indicator of social complexity and brain size a gross indicator of cognitive capacities.
findings.where: A Natural History of Human Thinking (2014), pp. 133-134 (lines 5168-5185 in text file)

findings.quote: The suggestion that female-female bonding, based on knowledge of the relationships of other individuals, was more important fits much better with views about the structure of nonhuman primate societies where relationships between females are all-important.
findings.content: Language evolved in the context of social bonding between females. Female-female bonding based on knowledge of others' relationships was more important than male-male bonding in driving language evolution. This fits with primate societies where relationships between females are all-important for group cohesion and infant survival.

findings.quote: Kinship provides a surprisingly deep and sometimes unrecognised framework for our social life, not just in traditional small-scale societies, but for us today as well.
findings.content: Kinship provides a deep and often unrecognized framework for social cooperation, not just in traditional small-scale societies but in modern WEIRD contexts as well. Extended family networks function as migration facilitators, employment networks, and mutual-aid systems - illustrating that kin-based cooperation remains active even in supposedly individualistic societies.

findings.quote: In humans, it seems safe to assume that the larger the brain, the greater the degree of political intelligence and the higher the probability that subordinate coalitions could definitively suppress alpha-type behavior. Humans were ready to form moral communities and reverse their dominance hierarchies 100,000 years ago, and probably considerably earlier.
findings.content: The earliest human precursor was likely an African ape that formed political coalitions enabling the rank and file to whittle away at alpha powers. By the Late Paleolithic, humans possessed an egalitarian ethos and political order similar to present-day hunting bands. The larger the brain, the greater the political intelligence and the higher the probability that subordinate coalitions could suppress alpha-type behavior. Humans were ready to form moral communities and reverse their dominance hierarchies 100,000 years ago, probably earlier.

Henrich cites Dunbar 1998 on the social brain hypothesis in the context of arguing that human intelligence is collective rather than individual. Endnote references place Dunbar alongside Byrne and Whiten (1992) and Humphrey (1976) as proponents of the Machiavellian intelligence view that Henrich then challenges: cultural evolution, not individual social cognition, is what makes humans smart. Group size matters for Henrich primarily as a driver of cumulative cultural complexity, not through Dunbar's cognitive constraint mechanism.
findings.where: The Secret of Our Success (2016), endnotes 7 and 19 (lines 12444, 12498), main text ch. 2 and ch. 12

findings.quote: psychologically, these trade-offs are related to the level of trust in a relationship, and that this is itself a function of the time invested in the relationship.
findings.content: Trust is the proximal psychological mechanism mediating social layer structure. Trade-offs at each layer are related to the level of trust in a relationship, and trust is itself a function of time invested. Trust operates as a cognitive heuristic that calibrates relationship investment to expected reciprocity at each layer.

findings.quote: For example, in shame the focus is on the self, while in humiliation the focus is on the harm done by others.
findings.content: Shame, humiliation, and guilt differ as evolved social strategies: shame focuses on the self (submissive appeasement), humiliation focuses on harm done by others (agonistic challenge), guilt focuses on specific actions and consequences for others (relationship repair). These map onto different adaptive responses to different types of social evaluation threat.

findings.quote: Relatedness within camps is low with primary kin comprising, on average, 1.43 and 1.93 of men and women's campmates respectively.
findings.content: Direct relatedness measure: primary kin are a small minority of a camp.

findings.quote: Among the Ache and Hadza, frequent visiting and long lifespans mean that adults typically interact with more than three hundred same-sex adults during their lifetimes. This implies a social universe of about a thousand individuals, when opposite-sex adults and children are included.
findings.content: Among Ache and Hadza foragers, lifetime same-sex interaction exceeds 300 adults, implying a lifetime "social universe" of about a thousand individuals once opposite-sex adults and children are included.

findings.quote: Precontact Northern Ache men, for example, are expected to have hunted with 206 men, conversed with 290 men, and watch tool making by 302 different men in a lifetime (Table S16 in File S1). Eastern Hadza men are expected to converse with 427 other Hadza men, hunt with 303 men, and watch tool making by 395 different men in a lifetime. In contrast, chimpanzees living in typical communities of 11 adult males are expected to interact with a mean of only 21 other adult males in a lifetime
findings.content: Per-activity lifetime interaction counts for Ache/Hadza men (hundreds of partners) vs ~21 for male chimpanzees: lifetime human social universe is an order of magnitude larger.

findings.quote: Additionally, close companions often interact with a somewhat different set of individuals, so that the total number of indirect interactants that each individual hears about repeatedly in detailed stories, and could expect to possibly meet some time during their lifetime is clearly more than 1,000. This is a much higher number of individually known social interactants than reported for any other primate, and possibly more than any other species on earth. It is also much greater than the predicted 150 significant social interactants (known as “Dunbar's number”) that was extrapolated from primate brain by social group size regressions
findings.content: The lifetime pool of individually-known interactants is clearly >1,000 - which Hill et al. explicitly note is far above the ~150 figure (the Dunbar number) that was extrapolated from primate brain / social-group-size regressions.

findings.quote: An "ego" (the naming person) is 44.2 times (95% C.I. 37.6 to 51.4) more likely to name an "alter" (the named person) in the campmate network, and 14.3 times (95% C.I. 12.2 to 16.4) more likely to name an alter in the gift network, if the alter reciprocated the social tie by also naming the ego as a friend
findings.content: Hadza campmate/gift networks show strong dyadic reciprocity even though nominations are private and controlling for kin ties.

findings.quote: in both the campmate and gift networks, social ties are significantly more likely when two people are similar in age, height, weight, body fat, and handgrip strength.
findings.content: Homophily in Hadza social ties runs on age and physical/condition traits (the "shuffle" is similarity-driven, not random).

findings.quote: social distance appears to be as important as genetic relatedness and physical proximity in explaining assortativity in cooperation
findings.content: Cooperative assortment in Hadza networks: similarity in cooperation extends to two degrees, and social distance rivals genetic relatedness in explaining it (kinship is not the sole glue).

findings.quote: first-order relatives make up less than 10% of residential camps
findings.content: Within-camp relatedness is low: most co-residents are not first-order kin.

findings.quote: Our analyses on complementary datasets using different methods yield wildly different numbers. Bayesian and generalized least-squares phylogenetic methods generate approximations of average group sizes between 69-109 and 16-42, respectively. However, enormous 95% confidence intervals (4-520 and 2-336, respectively) imply that specifying any one number is futile. A cognitive limit on human group size cannot be derived in this manner.
findings.content: Redoing the neocortex-ratio-to-group-size regression that produced 'Dunbar's number' with modern phylogenetic comparative methods (Bayesian and generalized least-squares) on complementary primate datasets yields wildly unstable human estimates: point estimates of 69-109 (Bayesian) and 16-42 (GLS), with 95 percent confidence intervals of 4-520 and 2-336 respectively. No single number is statistically supportable; a cognitive limit on human group size cannot be derived this way. CHALLENGE to the precise ~150 figure as a cognitive ceiling, cited to Dunbar 1992's neocortex-ratio extrapolation (ext 483).

findings.quote: This evolving proto-WEIRD psychology gradually laid the groundwork for the rise of impersonal markets, urbanization, constitutional governments, democratic politics, individualistic religions, scientific societies, and relentless innovation.
findings.content: One sect of Christianity drove the spread of social norms that dramatically altered marriage, families, inheritance, and ownership in parts of Europe over centuries. This transformation of family life initiated psychological changes that spurred new forms of urbanization and fueled impersonal commerce. An evolving proto-WEIRD psychology laid the groundwork for impersonal markets, constitutional governments, democratic politics, individualistic religions, scientific societies, and relentless innovation.

findings.quote: Chimpanzees perform best on tests requiring a rudimentary theory of mind when they are in competitive situations.
findings.content: Chimpanzees perform best on tests requiring rudimentary theory of mind when they are in competitive situations.
