In a subsequent investigation, women married to men who shared similar genes in this part of the immune system were also more adulterous. The more of these genes a woman shared with her spouse, the more extra partners she engaged.
findings.where: Chapter 4 'Why Adultery?' The Sweaty T-Shirt Experiment, pp. 94-95, citing Wedekind et al. 1995 and follow-up

findings.quote: By casting wide the web of possible paternity, mothers could increase the prospects of future survival of offspring, since males almost never attack infants carried by females that, in the biblical sense of the word, they have "known." Males use past relations with the mother as a cue to attack or tolerate her infant.
findings.content: Hrdy's elaboration of the infanticide mechanism: males use past relations with the mother as a cue to attack or tolerate her infant. Mothers who cast wide the web of possible paternity increase the prospects of future survival for their offspring, since males almost never attack infants carried by females they have 'known' in the biblical sense. This is the specific behavioral rule that makes paternity confusion adaptive for mothers - it's not promiscuity as failure of pair-bonding but as insurance against infanticide.

findings.quote: This depends, not on a struggle for existence, but on a struggle between the males for possession of the females; the result is not death to the unsuccessful competitor, but few or no offspring. Sexual selection is, therefore, less rigorous than natural selection. Generally, the most vigorous males, those which are best fitted for their places in nature, will leave most progeny.
findings.content: Sexual Selection. This depends, not on a struggle for existence, but on a struggle between the males for possession of the females; the result is not death to the unsuccessful competitor, but few or no offspring. Sexual selection is, therefore, less rigorous than natural selection. Generally, the most vigorous males, those which are best fitted for their places in nature, will leave most progeny.

findings.quote: I have maintained that humankind has evolved three primary brain systems that guide mating and reproduction: the sex drive; romantic love; and the feelings of deep attachment. These three basic neural systems interact with one another (and many other brain systems) in myriad flexible combinations to provide the range of motivations, emotions and behaviors necessary to orchestrate our complex human reproductive strategy. However, these three brain systems are not always well connected. So it is biologically possible to express deep feelings of attachment for a primary partner while one feels intense romantic love for another individual, while one feels the sex drive for even more extra partners.
findings.content: Humans have evolved three primary brain systems that guide mating and reproduction: the sex drive; romantic love; and the feelings of deep attachment. These three basic neural systems interact with one another (and many other brain systems) in myriad flexible combinations to provide the range of motivations, emotions and behaviors necessary to orchestrate our complex human reproductive strategy. However, these three brain systems are not always well connected. So it is biologically possible to express deep feelings of attachment for a primary partner while one feels intense romantic love for another individual, while one feels the sex drive for even more extra partners.
findings.where: Chapter 4 'Why Adultery?' Biology of Adultery section, pp. 94-95

findings.quote: The sex drive motivates us to seek a range of mating partners. Romantic love drives us to focus our mating energy on a single individual at a time. And feelings of deep attachment enable us to remain with this special other at least long enough to rear a single child through infancy together. Each of these basic drives produces different behaviors, feelings, hopes, and dreams. And each is associated primarily with different neurochemical systems. Lust is associated primarily with the hormone testosterone, in both men and women. Romantic love is linked with the natural stimulant, dopamine, and perhaps also with norepinephrine and low activity of serotonin. While feelings of deep attachment are produced principally by the neuropeptides, oxytocin and vasopressin.
findings.content: The sex drive motivates us to seek a range of mating partners. Romantic love drives us to focus our mating energy on a single individual at a time. And feelings of deep attachment enable us to remain with this special other at least long enough to rear a single child through infancy together. Each of these basic drives produces different behaviors, feelings, hopes, and dreams. And each is associated primarily with different neurochemical systems. Lust is associated primarily with the hormone testosterone, in both men and women. Romantic love is linked with the natural stimulant, dopamine, and perhaps also with norepinephrine and low activity of serotonin. While feelings of deep attachment are produced principally by the neuropeptides, oxytocin and vasopressin.
findings.where: Chapter 7 'The Web of Love' section, pp. 179-180

findings.quote: From a Darwinian perspective, it is easy to explain why men are - by nature - interested in sexual variety. If an ancestral man bore children with one woman, he had, genetically speaking, 'reproduced' himself. But if he also engaged in dalliances with another woman and, by chance, sired another child, he doubled his contribution to the next generation. So those men who sought sexual variety throughout deep history also tended to have more children.
findings.content: From a Darwinian perspective, it is easy to explain why men are interested in sexual variety. If an ancestral man bore children with one woman, he had, genetically speaking, reproduced himself. But if he also engaged in dalliances with another woman and sired another child, he doubled his contribution to the next generation. So those men who sought sexual variety throughout deep history also tended to have more children. Women's adultery has separate evolutionary logic: four hypotheses include (1) resource supplementation via gifts/food from lovers, (2) insurance policy against death or desertion of a primary mate, (3) 'upgrade' of genetic quality when the primary mate is deficient, and (4) genetic diversity of offspring against unpredictable environments.

findings.quote: In spite of this common course of love, the three basic brain systems for mating that I have elsewhere proposed - lust, romantic love, and attachment - can actually ignite in any order. Some people have sex first, then fall in love. Some fall madly in love with someone they just met, then have sex several weeks down the road. Some even build a deep attachment to a friend at work or in their social circle, then later fall madly in love and have sex with him or her. Yet, generally, feelings of lust and passionate romantic love are triggered first, followed by feelings of deep attachment - what psychologist Theodor Reik called the warm 'afterglow.'
findings.content: After a while the fire cools and that's how it stays. The three basic brain systems for mating generally transition: feelings of lust and passionate romantic love are triggered first, followed by feelings of deep attachment - what psychologist Theodor Reik called the warm 'afterglow.' But the three systems can also ignite in any order. Some people have sex first, then fall in love. Some fall madly in love with someone they just met, then have sex several weeks down the road. Some build a deep attachment to a friend at work or in their social circle, then later fall madly in love and have sex with him or her.

findings.quote: schizophrenia, Parkinson's disease, and other ailments alter dopamine pathways. In fact, in the last chapter of this book, 'Future Sex,' I will discuss my theory that several serotonin-enhancing antidepressants, such as Prozac, Zoloft, and the newer serotonin boosters, can suppress dopamine pathways, dull the emotions, and potentially kill romantic passion.
findings.content: Several serotonin-enhancing antidepressants, such as Prozac, Zoloft, and the newer serotonin boosters, can suppress dopamine pathways, dull the emotions, and potentially kill romantic passion. The romantic-love component of M14 depends on the dopamine-norepinephrine-low-serotonin neurochemical profile; increasing serotonin chemically disrupts this profile and may interfere with the normal operation of the romantic-love system.
findings.where: Chapter 2 'Love Blindness' pp. 36-37 and Chapter 16 'Future Sex'

findings.quote: So I shall propose that these brain systems for lust, romantic love and attachment began to take their human forms soon after our forebears descended from the fast-disappearing trees of Africa to walk on two feet instead of four and form pair-bonds to rear their helpless young at least through infancy as a team. Lucy loved, some 3.2 million years ago. She felt sexual craving, passionate rapture, and deep feelings of attachment toward her mate - a symphony, sometimes even a cacophony of joyous, exciting, and calming sensations.
findings.content: The three basic brain systems for lust, romantic love and attachment began to take their human forms soon after our forebears descended from the fast-disappearing trees of Africa to walk on two feet and form pair-bonds to rear their helpless young at least through infancy as a team. Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis) loved, some 3.2 million years ago. She felt sexual craving, passionate rapture, and deep feelings of attachment toward her mate - a symphony, sometimes a cacophony of joyous, exciting, and calming sensations.

findings.quote: Users may begin with the intention of seeking platonic companionship but gradually develop romantic or sexual attachments, partly because these systems are designed to deepen emotional engagement over time.
findings.content: Supports the pair-bond / romantic-sexual slice of M14's proxy floor only: Muldoon & Parke treat AI companions as vehicles for romantic and sexual attachment that simulate a partner while structurally foreclosing a genuine reciprocal relationship. PAIR-BOND SLICE ONLY - the paper says nothing about the desire or attraction subsystems, sexual fulfilment, or reproduction, and does not address M14's full three-system (desire / attraction / pair-bonding) scope.

findings.quote: Tennov measured the duration of romantic love from the moment infatuation hit to when a 'feeling of neutrality' for one's love object began. She concluded, 'The most frequent interval, as well as the average, is between approximately 18 months and three years.' But data vary. A study that indicates serotonin activity in the blood suggests that this intoxication lasts twelve to eighteen months. And in our 2012 national Match.com survey of singles, 29% of over 5,000 men and women of every age group, background, and sexual persuasion reported that this passion lasted for two to five years; 8% remained intensely in love for six to ten years, and 18% reported that they remained madly in love for over ten years.
findings.content: The duration of intense romantic love varies but is bounded. Tennov concluded that 'the most frequent interval, as well as the average, is between approximately 18 months and three years.' A study of serotonin activity in blood suggests 12 to 18 months. In the Match.com survey of over 5,000 men and women, 29% reported the passion lasting for two to five years; 8% for six to ten years; and 18% for over ten years. Either the nerve pathways for dopamine and related neurochemicals become habituated to these natural stimulants, or the production and distribution of dopamine decline.

findings.quote: You are engaged in maladaptive behavior right now.
findings.content: Modern middle-class reproductive restraint is a striking maladaptation: professional status-seeking consumes resources (time, money, effort) needed for reproduction. Evolved psychology for status competition in Pleistocene tribal contexts now causes fitness loss in modern economies. People prioritize career advancement, education, and consumption over reproduction - the very success of cultural transmission mechanisms (prestige bias, conformist bias) producing behaviors that reduce genetic fitness.

findings.quote: psychological mechanisms are designed to be predictably biased when the costs of false-positive and false-negative errors were asymmetrical over evolutionary history.
findings.content: Error Management Theory (EMT): psychological mechanisms are designed to be predictably biased when the costs of false-positive and false-negative errors were asymmetrical over evolutionary history. Men's sexual overperception bias (overestimating women's sexual interest) and women's commitment underperception bias (underestimating men's commitment) are adaptive biases shaped by asymmetric error costs. EMT offers a systematic framework for predicting cognitive biases from ancestral cost asymmetries.

findings.quote: Even in normally gentle and herbivorous primates like langurs and gorillas, other members of the same species can be a threat to infant survival every bit as hazardous as lurking predators. This was a new kind of selective pressure on mothers, one not previously dreamed of.
findings.content: Infanticide by males as selective pressure: Even in normally gentle primates like langurs and gorillas, other members of the same species can be a threat to infant survival every bit as hazardous as lurking predators. This creates selective pressure on mothers. Hrdy's specific hypothesis: female langurs' apparently promiscuous mating with invading males (even when pregnant/not ovulating) casts wide the web of possible paternity - males almost never attack infants they might have fathered. Males use past mating relations as a cue to attack or tolerate an infant. This is load-bearing for M14 Reproductive Motivation and for reading female sexuality in light of infanticide risk.

Error Management Theory (EMT): when the costs of false-positive and false-negative errors were asymmetric over evolutionary history, selection favors psychological mechanisms that are predictably biased in the direction that minimizes the more costly error - not mechanisms that minimize total errors or achieve Bayesian optimality. This is a domain-specific alternative to the heuristics-and-biases program: biases are not cognitive flaws but adaptive design features. Haselton and Buss formalize: a mechanism will be biased toward the less costly error type whenever the cost asymmetry persisted recurrently in ancestral environments.

findings.quote: for their pronounced ambivalence toward newborns and their extremely contingent maternal commitment. Infants have adapted, as we will see later, with special traits for attracting the attention of potential caretakers.
findings.content: Humans display pronounced ambivalence toward newborns and extremely contingent maternal commitment. Unlike the steady investment other great ape mothers show, human mothers assess whether conditions support successful rearing before committing fully. Infants have adapted with special traits - cuteness, prolonged eye contact, social smiling - for attracting attention from potential caretakers. Maternal commitment is conditional on perceived alloparental support.

findings.quote: Clearly, for cooperatively breeding mammals, a female's physical capacity to conceive and bear viable young is only a small part of the equation. She must also be able to carry through with the enterprise - rearing offspring to independence.
findings.content: Hrdy on contingent maternal commitment: For cooperatively breeding mammals, a female's physical capacity to conceive and bear viable young is only a small part of the equation. She must also be able to CARRY THROUGH with the enterprise - rearing offspring to independence. This is the foundational argument that maternal investment is context-dependent, not unconditional - mothers evaluate whether circumstances (including alloparent availability, food resources, and infant health) permit successful rearing, and adjust their investment accordingly. Load-bearing for M9 Care/Alloparenting and for reading maternal ambivalence as adaptive rather than pathological.

findings.quote: a woman's maternal emotions (those concerned with producing and nurturing offspring and keeping them alive) continued to be viewed as separate from and even antithetical to the rest of her - her sexuality and, particularly, her ambition. Yet the compartmentalized way we have learned to think about these emotions has nothing to do with how they evolved.
findings.content: Hrdy on the compartmentalization error: maternal emotions (producing/nurturing/keeping offspring alive) have been viewed as separate from and even antithetical to the rest of a woman - her sexuality and her ambition. This compartmentalized framing has nothing to do with how these emotions evolved. In the ancestral environment, the same female was simultaneously pursuing reproductive goals AND maternal goals AND resource goals AND social-position goals, with all of them integrated rather than competing. The modern fragmentation is cultural, not evolutionary.

findings.quote: there is a great deal of neuropeptide specificity in the coding of behavior, and it is esthetically pleasing to note that we often observe a correspondence between the peripheral functions of these neuropeptides and their role within the brain (Table 6.1). For instance, in the periphery, insulin controls metabolic dispersion of nutrients, while in the brain it helps mediate satiety (see Chapter 9). Likewise, in the periphery, the hormone angiotensin promotes water retention in the kidney, while in the brain it promotes thirst. Thus, many neuropeptide languages highlight the tendency of evolution to reutilize existing elements for new tasks that are harmonious with previous functions.
findings.content: Panksepp's observation of evolutionary economy in neuropeptide coding: there is extensive correspondence between the peripheral and central functions of neuropeptides - insulin controls peripheral glucose dispersion AND central satiety; angiotensin controls peripheral water retention AND central thirst; oxytocin controls peripheral birthing and milk letdown AND central maternal acceptance and readiness. Many peptides highlight evolution's tendency to REUTILIZE existing elements for new tasks harmonious with previous functions. This exaptation pattern is load-bearing for the DA8 architectural claim that newer mechanisms (social bonding) are built from older ones (reproductive physiology).

findings.quote: The contemporary psychological investigation of human attachment began with a British psychiatrist, John Bowlby, and an American psychologist, Mary Ainsworth, who proposed that, to promote the survival of their young, primates have evolved an innate attachment system designed to motivate infants to seek comfort and safety from their primary caregiver, generally mother. Since then extensive research has been done on the behaviors, feelings, and biological mechanisms associated with this attachment system in human adults and other creatures. Moreover, researchers have proposed that these attachment circuits remain active throughout the life course - serving as a foundation for emotional commitment between pair-bonded partners for the purpose of raising offspring.
findings.content: The contemporary psychological investigation of human attachment began with Bowlby and Ainsworth, who proposed that, to promote the survival of their young, primates have evolved an innate attachment system designed to motivate infants to seek comfort and safety from their primary caregiver. Extensive research has shown that these attachment circuits remain active throughout the life course - serving as a foundation for emotional commitment between pair-bonded partners for the purpose of raising offspring. The adult pair-bond attachment system is an extension of, not a replacement for, the infant-caregiver attachment system.

findings.quote: It does not pretend to be a complete account of human mental evolution, because it addresses only those psychological adaptations manifest in sexual courtship.
findings.content: Miller's sexual-selection argument is explicitly scope-limited. He says it does NOT explain: adaptations shared with other primates (foraging, predator avoidance, parenting), the nature of consciousness, the dynamics of cultural change, or traits better explained by natural selection, kin selection, or reciprocal altruism. The argument applies to self-ornamentation, display, status, ideology, fashion, and aesthetics - to psychological adaptations manifest in sexual courtship. Miller also flags: minimal sexual dimorphism in human mental traits puzzles the classic "choosy-female, displaying-male" model and requires mutual-choice sexual selection models; sexual selection theory itself remains "very much under development"; empirical support is "patchy"; the theory risks over-emphasizing courtship functions of language and creative intelligence while neglecting their other fitness benefits.

Many distinctively human cognitive and behavioral traits - language fluency, art, music, humor, creativity, generosity, moral judgment - evolved as fitness indicators under sexual selection (mate-choice pressure), not solely as survival adaptations under natural selection. Sexual selection broadens the set of selection pressures shaping the human motivational and cognitive architecture beyond survival to include mate-choice display and discrimination.

findings.quote: Like vasopressin, oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus. Unlike vasopressin, oxytocin is released in all female mammals (including women) during the birthing process. It initiates contractions of the uterus and stimulates the mammary glands to produce milk. But oxytocin also stimulates bonding between a mother and her infant. And more and more data now indicate that oxytocin can also produce feelings of attachment to a preferred mating partner. You have undoubtedly felt the power of these 'cuddle chemicals,' as vasopressin and oxytocin are sometimes called. At orgasm, the activities of oxytocin spike in men and women. These 'satisfaction hormones' undoubtedly contribute to your sense of fusion, closeness, and attachment after sweet sex with a beloved.
findings.content: Like vasopressin, oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus. Unlike vasopressin, oxytocin is released in all female mammals (including women) during the birthing process. It initiates contractions of the uterus and stimulates the mammary glands to produce milk. But oxytocin also stimulates bonding between a mother and her infant. And more and more data now indicate that oxytocin can also produce feelings of attachment to a preferred mating partner. At orgasm, the activities of oxytocin spike in men and women. These satisfaction hormones undoubtedly contribute to your sense of fusion, closeness, and attachment after sweet sex with a beloved.

findings.quote: In addition to the preceding primitive systems that are evident in all mammals soon after birth, we also have more sophisticated special-purpose socioemotional systems that are engaged at appropriate times in the lives of all mammals-for instance, those that mediate sexual LUST (see Chapter 12), maternal CARE (see Chapter 13), and roughhousing PLAY (see Chapter 15). Each of these is built around neural complexities that are only provisionally understood. Sexual urges are mediated by specific brain circuits and chemistries that are quite distinct for males and females but appear to share some components such as the physiological and psychological effects of oxytocin, which also promotes maternal motivation.
findings.content: Panksepp's identification of three additional special-purpose socioemotional systems beyond the 4 primitive ones: sexual LUST (Ch 12), maternal CARE (Ch 13), and roughhousing PLAY (Ch 15). Sexual urges are mediated by distinct brain circuits and chemistries for males and females but share components such as oxytocin, which also promotes maternal motivation. Maternal behavior circuits remain closely intermeshed with sexuality circuits, suggesting how evolution gradually constructed the basic neural substrates for 'the social contract' - the possibilities for love and bonding - in the mammalian brain. This is load-bearing for M14 Reproductive Motivation, M9 Care/Alloparenting, M4 Social Calibration/Play, and the architectural claim that social bonding evolved as an extension of pre-existing reproductive circuits.

findings.quote: People seek help mainly for symptoms, not diseases. Pain, fever, malaise, cough, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are protective responses. So are anxiety, jealousy, anger, and low mood. They are set off when something bad is happening. They are unpleasant but useful.
findings.content: Defensive responses such as pain, fever, cough, nausea, anxiety, jealousy, anger, and low mood are protective responses, not diseases. They are set off when something bad is happening. They are unpleasant but useful.

findings.quote: We now realize that maternal behavior circuits remain closely intermeshed with those that control sexuality, and this suggests how evolution gradually constructed the basic neural substrates for the social contract (i.e., the possibilities for love and bonding) in the mammalian brain.
findings.content: Panksepp's architectural claim about the evolution of social bonding: maternal behavior circuits remain closely intermeshed with those that control sexuality. This suggests how evolution gradually constructed the basic neural substrates for the 'social contract' - 'the possibilities for love and bonding' - in the mammalian brain. Maternal nurturance probably arose gradually from preexisting circuits that initially mediated reproductive behaviors. This is THE foundational architectural claim for why Cor's M3 Social Bonding, M9 Care/Alloparenting, and M14 Reproductive Motivation share substrate - they were built by evolution as extensions and overlays of the same neurochemical machinery, not as independent systems.

Miller frames consumer signaling specifically around the "Central Six" personality dimensions: general intelligence plus the Big Five (openness, conscientiousness, agreeableness, stability, extraversion). These are the traits consumers attempt to display via purchases, and personality research on the Big Five is presented as directly applicable to consumer behavior. This gives a specific mapping: consumer goods = signaling vehicles for Central Six traits = proxies for mate-choice and friend-selection mechanisms that evolved to read these traits in conspecifics.

The two theoretical mechanisms Miller invokes for how courtship traits evolved: (1) Zahavi's handicap principle - costly ornaments reliably signal fitness because low-fitness pretenders cannot afford the costly display, forcing honesty through wastefulness; (2) Fisher's runaway selection - mate preferences become genetically linked to ornaments, creating positive-feedback escalation of trait complexity. Mental traits function as either direct fitness indexes (intelligence correlates intrinsically with fitness) or as handicaps (costly displays revealing hidden quality). Psychological biases including "novelty-seeking and pleasure-seeking" shape ornament design.

findings.quote: Attacks from conspecifics (both infanticide and deaths due to lethal raids by bands of males from neighboring groups) are major sources of mortality.
findings.content: In chimpanzees, attacks from conspecifics - including infanticide and lethal raids by bands of males from neighboring groups - are major sources of mortality.

Consumer goods function substantially as fitness-indicator proxies: signaling intelligence, conscientiousness, openness, stability, and mate value rather than delivering the underlying benefits (mate access, belonging, status-resolution) that the signaling machinery evolved to obtain. Luxury consumption, branded goods, and status markers are industrialized exploitation of mate-choice and status-monitoring mechanisms. Consumers chase proxies that activate these systems without resolving the conditions the systems were selected to track.

findings.quote: the ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven basic affective systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy)
findings.content: The ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven basic affective systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy). These designate specific functional networks of evolutionarily very ancient regions of our brains.
findings.where: Preface, 'Why Psychiatrists, Physicians, and Psychotherapists Should Understand the Seven Basic Affective Systems,' p. xi

findings.quote: Sexual gratification, arising from our capacity for LUST, feels good in a rather different way from the joys of rough-and-tumble PLAY or the tender bliss of caressing, nurturing, and CAREing for one's infant. FEAR is an entirely different kind of emotional 'pain' than frustrated RAGE; both differ from the PANICked misery of social isolation.
findings.content: Sexual gratification from LUST feels good in a different way from the joys of rough-and-tumble PLAY or the tender bliss of caressing and CARing for an infant. FEAR is an entirely different kind of emotional pain than frustrated RAGE; both differ from the panicked misery of social isolation (PANIC/GRIEF). These diverse affects provide guidance for living due to the survival-enhancing advantages each conferred over evolution. Affects are ancestral memories of how effectively we play the game of survival and reproduction.

findings.quote: The underlying circuits are genetically predetermined and designed to respond unconditionally to stimuli arising from major life-challenging circumstances. These circuits organize diverse behaviors by activating or inhibiting motor subroutines and concurrent autonomic-hormonal changes that have proved adaptive in the face of such life-challenging circumstances during the evolutionary history of the species. Emotive circuits change the sensitivities of sensory systems that are relevant for the behavioral sequences that have been aroused. Neural activity of emotive systems outlasts the precipitating circumstances. Emotive circuits can come under the conditional control of emotionally neutral environmental stimuli. Emotive circuits have reciprocal interactions with the brain mechanisms that elaborate higher decision-making processes and consciousness.
findings.content: Panksepp's six methodological criteria for identifying genuine emotional systems in the brain (Figure 3.3): (1) Underlying circuits are genetically predetermined to respond unconditionally to life-challenging stimuli; (2) they organize diverse behaviors by activating/inhibiting motor subroutines and autonomic-hormonal changes; (3) they change sensitivities of sensory systems relevant to the aroused behavioral sequences; (4) their neural activity outlasts precipitating circumstances; (5) they can come under conditional control of emotionally neutral stimuli; (6) they have reciprocal interactions with higher decision-making and consciousness circuits. Plus the seventh psychological criterion: they must generate affective feelings. This is Panksepp's load-bearing methodological framework for distinguishing emotional systems from general-purpose sensorimotor circuits.

ledger_replicated.quote: Unlike much of the world today, and most people who have ever lived, we WEIRD people are highly individualistic, self-obsessed, control-oriented, nonconformist, and analytical. We focus on ourselves - our attributes, accomplishments, and aspirations - over our relationships and social roles.
ledger_replicated.content: WEIRD people are psychologically peculiar: highly individualistic, self-obsessed, control-oriented, nonconformist, and analytical. They focus on attributes, accomplishments, and aspirations over relationships and social roles. They see themselves as unique beings, not as nodes in a social network. They prefer a sense of control and making their own choices. They are less willing to conform when this conflicts with their own beliefs. Yet paradoxically, WEIRD people tend to stick to impartial rules and are quite trusting, honest, and cooperative toward strangers.

ledger_replicated.quote: WEIRD people do conform to others, and this is what surprised Solomon. Only about one-quarter of his participants were never influenced by their peers. WEIRD people, however, conform less than all the other populations that have been studied.
ledger_replicated.content: WEIRD people conform less than all other studied populations, but they do still conform. Cross-cultural studies show substantial variation in conformity across countries, with WEIRD undergraduate samples at the low end. The reduced conformity in WEIRD populations reflects the dismantling of kin-based social pressure and the institutional promotion of individual autonomy.

ledger_replicated.quote: The data, from over 20,000 participants in 30 countries, confirm that in places where people actually do trust strangers in anonymous experimental settings, they also tend to say, when asked the GTQ, that most people can be trusted.
ledger_replicated.content: Impersonal trust and cooperation with strangers: in places where people actually trust strangers in anonymous experimental settings, they also report trusting most people in surveys. Impersonal prosociality includes motivations and strategies for punishing those who break impartial norms. This trust-among-strangers is a WEIRD psychological feature that evolved alongside impersonal market institutions.

ledger_replicated.quote: Degeneracy means "many to one": many combinations of neurons can produce the same outcome. In the quest to map emotion fingerprints in the brain, degeneracy is a humbling reality check.
ledger_replicated.content: The principle of degeneracy in emotion: different combinations of neurons can produce the same emotional outcome (many-to-one). Barrett's lab demonstrated this in brain-imaging studies where men and women reported equivalent feelings of arousal but showed different neural patterns - women's arousal was more strongly linked to the anterior insula, men's to visual cortex. The same subjective experience was associated with different patterns of neural activity.

ledger_replicated.quote: Through prediction, your brain constructs the world you experience. It combines bits and pieces of your past and estimates how likely each bit applies in your current situation.
ledger_replicated.content: The brain constructs the world you experience through prediction. Intrinsic brain activity - millions of nonstop predictions - is the brain's primary mode of operation. Past experience, organized as concepts, generates predictions that are tested against incoming sensory input. Events in the world merely tune these predictions rather than triggering responses. Evolution literally wired the brain for efficient prediction: 90 percent of connections entering primary visual cortex carry predictions from other brain regions, not sensory input from the world.

ledger_replicated.quote: The cortex and limbic system are not separate, as scads of axonal projections course between the two. Crucially, those projections are bidirectional - the limbic system talks to the cortex, rather than merely being reined in by it.
ledger_replicated.content: The frontal cortex is bidirectionally enmeshed with the limbic system. Nauta's landmark discovery showed the frontal cortex is a quasi member of the limbic system, not a hierarchical controller standing above it. In different circumstances the frontal cortex and limbic system stimulate or inhibit each other, collaborate and conflict. The false dichotomy between thought and feeling is a neuroscientific error.

ledger_replicated.quote: while the acute stress response involves enhanced immunity, chronic stress suppresses immunity, increasing vulnerability to some infectious diseases.
ledger_replicated.content: The acute stress response involves enhanced immunity, but chronic stress suppresses immunity, increasing vulnerability to infectious diseases. We get sick not from failing to activate the stress response but from activating it too often, too long, and for purely psychological reasons. The beneficial effects of stress (fight-or-flight for seconds to minutes) become damaging on the sustained timescale of chronic psychological stress.

ledger_replicated.quote: Testosterone was administered to the middle-ranking male in each group (say, rank number 3 out of five), increasing their levels of aggression. Does this mean that these guys, stoked on 'roids, started challenging numbers 1 and 2 in the hierarchy? No. They became aggressive jerks to poor numbers 4 and 5. Testosterone did not create new social patterns of aggression; it exaggerated preexisting ones.
ledger_replicated.content: Testosterone does not create aggression - it amplifies preexisting social patterns. In talapoin monkeys, testosterone given to middle-ranking males did not make them challenge higher-ranking individuals; it made them more aggressive to lower-ranking ones. In humans, testosterone does not raise baseline amygdala activity but boosts amygdala response to angry faces specifically. Testosterone makes subjects more punitive when provoked, enhancing 'vengeful reactive aggression' rather than creating new social patterns.

ledger_replicated.quote: In another study subjects waited an unknown length of time to receive a shock. This lack of predictability and control was so aversive that many chose to receive a stronger shock immediately. And in the others the period of anticipatory dread increasingly activated the amygdala.
ledger_replicated.content: Lack of predictability and control over stressors is so aversive that subjects chose to receive a stronger shock immediately rather than wait an unknown time for a weaker one. The period of anticipatory dread increasingly activated the amygdala.

ledger_replicated.quote: This domain of epigenetics was uncovered in a landmark 2004 study by Meaney and colleagues, one of the most cited papers published in the prestigious journal Nature Neuroscience. They had shown previously that offspring of more "attentive" rat mothers (those that frequently nurse, groom, and lick their pups) become adults with lower glucocorticoid levels, less anxiety, better learning, and delayed brain aging.
ledger_replicated.content: Meaney's landmark 2004 study demonstrated that maternal care style in rats produces epigenetic changes in offspring's stress response genes. Offspring of more attentive mothers (frequent nursing, grooming, licking) become adults with lower glucocorticoid levels, less anxiety, better learning, and delayed brain aging. These changes are epigenetic - mothering style alters gene regulation in pups' brains. Remarkably, such pups as adults become more attentive mothers themselves, passing the trait epigenetically to the next generation.

ledger_replicated.quote: What is social play in the young? Writ large, it's an array of behaviors that train individuals in social competence. Writ medium, it's fragments of the real thing, bits and pieces of fixed action patterns, a chance to safely try out roles and improve motor skills. Writ small and endocrine, it's a demonstration that moderate and transient stress - "stimulation" - is great. Writ small and neurobiological, it's a tool for deciding which excess synapses to prune.
ledger_replicated.content: Social play in the young is an array of behaviors that train individuals in social competence. It consists of fragments of real behavioral patterns - a chance to safely try out roles and improve motor skills. Endocrinologically, play demonstrates that moderate transient stress (stimulation) is beneficial. Neurobiologically, play is a tool for deciding which excess synapses to prune. Play is universal among socially complex species, peaking at puberty. A child deprived of or disinterested in play rarely has a socially fulfilling adult life.

ledger_replicated.quote: Korean and European American subjects observed pictures of either in- or out-group members in pain. All subjects reported more subjective empathy and showed more activation of Theory of Mind brain regions (i.e., the temporoparietal junction) when observing in-group members, but the bias was significantly greater among Korean subjects.
ledger_replicated.content: In-group empathy bias is stronger in collectivist than individualist cultures. Korean and European American subjects showed more empathy and Theory of Mind activation for in-group members in pain, but the bias was significantly greater among Korean subjects. Both individualist and collectivist cultures denigrate out-groups, but only individualist cultures inflate assessments of their own group - East Asians do not need to puff up their own group to view others as inferior.

ledger_replicated.quote: Just as prenatal testosterone exposure generates an adult brain that is more sensitive to environmental triggers of aggression, excessive prenatal glucocorticoid exposure produces an adult brain more sensitive to environmental triggers of depression and anxiety.
ledger_replicated.content: Prenatal glucocorticoid exposure produces organizational effects on fetal brain construction, decreasing growth factors, neurons, and synapses. Just as prenatal testosterone exposure generates an adult brain more sensitive to aggression triggers, excessive prenatal glucocorticoid exposure produces an adult brain more sensitive to environmental triggers of depression and anxiety. Stressed mothers secrete glucocorticoids that enter fetal circulation with the same consequences as postnatal stress.

ledger_replicated.quote: glucocorticoids decrease activation of the (cognitive) medial PFC during processing of emotional faces. Collectively, stress or glucocorticoid administration decreases accuracy when rapidly assessing emotions of faces.
ledger_replicated.content: Chronic stress literally eats away at interoceptive and control networks. It causes the amygdala to expand while the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex atrophy. Glucocorticoids decrease activation of the cognitive medial PFC during emotional processing, decreasing accuracy when rapidly assessing emotions. During sustained stress, the systems that should regulate the stress response are themselves damaged by the stress response - a vicious cycle of worsening misregulation.

ledger_replicated.quote: the worst stress-related health typically occurs in middle management, with its killer combo of high work demands but little autonomy - responsibility without control.
ledger_replicated.content: Subordinate organisms are typically the most stressed and unhealthy. Lab rodents, primates from rhesus monkeys to lemurs, hamsters, guinea pigs, wolves, rabbits, pigs, fish, and sugar gliders all show that subordinate individuals have elevated resting glucocorticoids - chronic activation of the stress response even in the absence of acute stressors. The worst stress-related health in humans occurs in middle management, with its killer combination of high work demands but little autonomy - responsibility without control.

ledger_replicated.quote: The amygdala is particularly sensitive to unsettling circumstances that are social. Stable rankings activated parts of the frontal cortex that we'll soon consider. Instability activated the frontal cortex plus the amygdala. Being unsure of your place is unsettling.
ledger_replicated.content: The amygdala is particularly sensitive to social uncertainty. When a male monkey's social position is threatened by a rival, amygdala activation correlates not with aggression or testosterone but with anxiety (teeth chattering, self-scratching). In humans, unstable social rankings activate both the frontal cortex and amygdala, while stable rankings activate only the frontal cortex. Being unsure of your social place is unsettling - rank uncertainty, not rank itself, drives threat-system activation.

ledger_replicated.quote: Childhood abuse, for example, causes epigenetic changes in hundreds of genes in the human hippocampus. Moreover, Stephen Suomi of the National Institutes of Health and Szyf found that mothering style in monkeys has epigenetic effects on more than a thousand frontocortical genes.
ledger_replicated.content: Childhood abuse causes epigenetic changes in hundreds of genes in the human hippocampus. Mothering style in monkeys has epigenetic effects on more than a thousand frontocortical genes. Hormonal responses to fetal and childhood experiences have epigenetic effects on genes related to BDNF, the vasopressin and oxytocin system, and estrogen sensitivity, with effects pertinent to adult cognition, personality, emotionality, and psychiatric health.

ledger_replicated.quote: Moreover, sustained stress and glucocorticoid exposure enhance LTP and suppress LTD in the amygdala, boosting fear conditioning, and suppress LTP in the frontal cortex. Combining these effects - more excitable synapses in the amygdala, fewer ones in the frontal cortex - helps explain stress-induced impulsivity and poor emotional regulation.
ledger_replicated.content: Sustained stress and glucocorticoid exposure enhance LTP and suppress LTD in the amygdala while suppressing LTP in the frontal cortex. This combination - more excitable synapses in the amygdala, fewer in the frontal cortex - helps explain stress-induced impulsivity and poor emotional regulation.

ledger_replicated.quote: SBT suggests that proximity to social resources decreases the cost of climbing both the literal and figurative hills we face, because the brain construes social resources as bioenergetic resources, much like oxygen or glucose. Indeed, evidence suggests that hills literally appear less steep when standing next to a friend. Moreover, socially isolated individuals consume more sugar, even after adjusting for body mass index, weight related self-image, depression, physical activity, educational level, age and income. To the human brain, social and metabolic resources are treated almost interchangeably.

Evidence suggests that hills literally appear less steep when standing next to a friend. Moreover, socially isolated individuals consume more sugar, even after adjusting for body mass index, weight-related self-image, depression, physical activity, educational level, age, and income.
