ledger_replicated.content: Although the brain is highly responsive to perceived threat, even simple handholding can substantially attenuate threat responses. These effects are potentiated by higher relationship quality, intimacy, and higher perceived mutuality. Critically, the likeliest mechanisms linking social support to diminished threat responding - regulatory circuits within the prefrontal cortex - are not more activated by support provision as originally hypothesized, but less so. During supportive handholding in particular, the threat responsive brain appears to return to a baseline state of relative calm, suggesting the difference is attributable less to the activation of regulatory circuitry and more to a decrease in perceived demand associated with the threat, a decrease proportional to the increase in resources brought to bear by the relational partner.
ledger_replicated.where: Section 'Risk, effort, and the expanded self,' pp. 88-89

ledger_replicated.quote: the brain encodes threats directed at familiar others very similarly to how it encodes threats directed at the self - but no such similarity obtains for strangers. Representing relational partners as extensions or aspects of the self could effectively yield bioenergetic resources by influencing how the brain budgets the resources immediately at its disposal. If the relational partner can be counted on to meet all or part of an environmental demand, one’s own resources can either be conserved or devoted to other problems as if personal bioenergetic resources were literally increased. This could explain how the brain construes resources available to relational partners as resources available to the self. Indeed, it suggests that attachment may reflect a neural (and conceptual) conflation of self and other.
ledger_replicated.content: Social Baseline Theory suggests that the brain encodes what we subjectively experience as the self in ways that literally include close others. The brain encodes threats directed at familiar others very similarly to how it encodes threats directed at the self - but no such similarity obtains for strangers. Representing relational partners as extensions or aspects of the self could effectively yield bioenergetic resources by influencing how the brain budgets the resources immediately at its disposal. If the relational partner can be counted on to meet all or part of an environmental demand, one's own resources can either be conserved or devoted to other problems as if personal bioenergetic resources were literally increased. This suggests that attachment may reflect a neural (and conceptual) conflation of self and other.
ledger_replicated.where: Section 'Risk, effort, and the expanded self,' p. 89

ledger_replicated.quote: Although the brain is highly responsive to perceived threat, even simple handholding can substantially attenuate threat responses.
ledger_replicated.content: SBT describes two mechanisms for social regulation: risk distribution (safety in numbers) and load sharing (distribution of effort toward shared goals). During supportive handholding, the threat-responsive brain returns to a baseline state of relative calm - not through activation of regulatory circuitry but through decreased perceived demand. The brain encodes relational partners as extensions of the self, effectively pooling bioenergetic resources.

ledger_replicated.quote: Thus, Warneken et al. (2006, 2007) had infants of this age engage in a joint activity with an adult, such as obtaining a toy by each operating one side of an apparatus. Then, the adult simply stopped playing her role for no reason. The children were not happy about this and did various things to attempt to reengage their partner. (They did not do this if her stopping was for a good reason; e.g., she had to attend to something else [Warneken et al., 2012].) Interesting, when this same situation was arranged for human-raised chimpanzees, they simply ignored the recalcitrant partner and tried to find ways to achieve the goal on their own.
ledger_replicated.content: Children vs chimps reengagement experiment: Warneken et al. had 14-18 month old human infants engage in joint activity with an adult (operating an apparatus). When the adult stopped playing her role for no reason, children were unhappy and attempted to reengage the partner. When the SAME situation was arranged for human-raised chimpanzees, chimps ignored the partner and tried to complete the goal alone. This dissociation - even at prelinguistic ages, humans expect partners in joint activity to be committed enough to reengage, chimps do not - is a central behavioral marker of joint intentionality.

ledger_replicated.quote: For example, Hamann et al. (2012) had pairs of three-year-old children work together to bring rewards to the top of a step-like structure. The problem was that for one child the reward, surprisingly, became available midway through. Nevertheless, when this happened, the lucky child delayed consumption of her own reward and persevered until the other got hers (i.e., more than they helped the partner in a similar situation in which they were acting individually, without collaboration). Such commitment to the partner suggests that the children constructed a joint goal at the beginning that "we" get the prizes together, and they made whatever adjustments were necessary to realize that joint goal. Again, great apes do not behave in this same way.
ledger_replicated.content: 3-year-old children collaborative commitment study (Hamann 2012): pairs of 3yo children worked together to bring rewards to the top of a step structure. One child's reward, surprisingly, became available midway. The 'lucky' child DELAYED consuming her own reward and PERSEVERED until the other got hers - significantly more than in a parallel non-collaborative individual-action condition. This shows commitment to a joint goal: 'we' get the prizes together, and they make adjustments to realize the joint goal. Chimps in parallel experiments show no such commitment. And Hamann 2011: 3yo children (but not chimps) also committed to dividing spoils equally.

ledger_replicated.quote: Importantly, when children of this same age have it in their common ground with a collaborative partner that each is counting on the other to come through (we are interdependent), they both feel obligated to the other (see Gilbert, 1989, 1990). Thus, Gräfenhain et al. (2009) had preschoolers explicitly agree to play a game with one adult, and then another adult attempted to lure them away to a more exciting game. Although two-year-old children mostly just bolted to the new game straightaway, from three years of age children paused before departing and "took leave," either verbally or by handing the adult the tool they had been using together. The children seemed to recognize that joint goals involve joint commitments, the breaking of which requires some kind of acknowledgment or even apology. No study of this type has ever been done with chimpanzees, but there are no published reports of one chimpanzee taking leave from, making excuses to, or apologizing to another for breaking a joint commitment.
ledger_replicated.content: Taking leave: Gräfenhain 2009 had preschoolers explicitly agree to play a game with one adult; then another adult attempted to lure them to a more exciting game. Two-year-olds mostly bolted to the new game, but from age 3 children paused before departing and 'took leave' - verbally or by handing the adult the shared tool. Children recognized that joint goals involve joint commitments, the breaking of which requires acknowledgment. No published reports of chimpanzees taking leave from, making excuses to, or apologizing to another for breaking a joint commitment exist. This is specific evidence for commitment-as-moral-obligation in joint intentionality.

ledger_replicated.quote: other studies have found that young children, but not chimpanzees, learn important new things about the partner's role as they are collaborating. For example, Carpenter et al. (2005) found that after young children played one role in a collaboration, they could quickly switch to the other, whereas chimpanzees could not do this (Tomasello and Carpenter, 2005).
ledger_replicated.content: Role-switching in collaborative roles: Carpenter 2005 found that young children, after playing one role in a collaboration, could quickly switch to the other role. Chimpanzees could not. This indicates that children attend not just to their own subgoals but to the partner's subgoal AND to the partner attending to them - a specifically recursive level of joint-attention tracking. Fletcher 2012 extended this: 3yo children who had first played role A in collaboration learned role B more easily than children who had only observed - they had learned BOTH roles from their own collaborative experience simultaneously.

ledger_replicated.quote: As to the functional consequences of structural remodeling in hippocampus, repeated stress can impair hippocampal-dependent behaviors in a manner that is reversible, along with dendritic shrinkage in the CA3 region, within days or weeks after the termination of the stressor. This supports the notion that the remodeling is not brain damage but a form of adaptive plasticity that may also protect the hippocampus from permanent excitotoxic damage.
ledger_replicated.content: The brain is the central organ of stress and adaptation to stress because it perceives and determines what is threatening, as well as the behavioral and physiological responses to the stressor. The adult, as well as developing brain, possess a remarkable ability to show reversible structural and functional plasticity in response to stressful and other experiences, including neuronal replacement, dendritic remodeling, and synapse turnover. This is particularly evident in the hippocampus. The amygdala and the prefrontal cortex, brain regions involved in anxiety and fear, mood, cognitive function and behavioral control, also show structural plasticity. Repeated stress can impair hippocampal-dependent behaviors in a manner that is reversible, along with dendritic shrinkage in the CA3 region, within days or weeks after the termination of the stressor. This supports the notion that the remodeling is not brain damage but a form of adaptive plasticity that may also protect the hippocampus from permanent excitotoxic damage.

ledger_replicated.quote: Acute and chronic stress cause an imbalance of neural circuitry subserving cognition, decision making, anxiety and mood that can increase or decrease expression of those behaviors and behavioral states. In the short term, such as for increased fearful vigilance and anxiety in a threatening environment, these changes may be adaptive; but, if the danger passes and the behavioral state persists along with the changes in neural circuitry, such maladaptation may need intervention
ledger_replicated.content: Acute and chronic stress cause an imbalance of neural circuitry subserving cognition, decision making, anxiety and mood that can increase or decrease expression of those behaviors and behavioral states. In the short term, such as for increased fearful vigilance and anxiety in a threatening environment, these changes may be adaptive; but, if the danger passes and the behavioral state persists along with the changes in neural circuitry, such maladaptation may need intervention with a combination of pharmacological and behavioral therapies. Chronic restraint stress causes dendritic shortening in medial prefrontal cortex but produces dendritic growth in neurons of the basolateral amygdala - opposite structural effects in interconnected regions, reflecting different functional roles under sustained stress.
ledger_replicated.where: Introduction and Section 2.4, 'Prefrontal cortex and amygdala,' pp. 3-4

ledger_replicated.quote: the ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven emotional, or affective, systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy). Each of these systems controls distinct but specific types of behaviors associated with many overlapping physiological changes.
ledger_replicated.content: The ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven emotional systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy). Each controls distinct behaviors with overlapping physiological changes and generates distinct types of affective consciousness. When stimulated in humans, people always experience intense emotional feelings. Capitalizations indicate that real physical and distinct networks for these emotions exist in mammalian brains.

ledger_replicated.quote: primal emotional systems are made up of neuroanatomies and neurochemistries that are remarkably similar across all mammalian species. This suggests that these systems evolved a very long time ago and that at a basic emotional and motivational level, all mammals are more similar than they are different.
ledger_replicated.content: Primal emotional systems are made up of neuroanatomies and neurochemistries remarkably similar across all mammalian species. This suggests these systems evolved a very long time ago and that at a basic emotional and motivational level, all mammals are more similar than different. Deep in the ancient affective recesses of our brains, we remain evolutionarily kin. The same neural paths and brain chemicals that arouse each of these seven systems are found within all mammals.

ledger_replicated.quote: The SEEKING, or expectancy, system is characterized by a persistent exploratory inquisitiveness. This system engenders energetic forward locomotion - approach and engagement with the world - as an animal probes into the nooks and crannies of interesting places, objects, and events in ways that are characteristic of its species.
ledger_replicated.content: The SEEKING system is characterized by persistent exploratory inquisitiveness. It engenders energetic forward locomotion - approach and engagement with the world - as animals probe nooks and crannies of interesting places, objects, and events. This system holds a special place among emotional systems because to some extent it plays a dynamic supporting role for all of the other emotions.

ledger_replicated.quote: FEAR is an inborn capacity of the mammalian brain. However, FEAR, just like all other basic emotions, rapidly gets enmeshed with world events as it comes to be regulated by learning and encoded in our conscious minds.
ledger_replicated.content: FEAR is an inborn capacity of the mammalian brain that rapidly gets enmeshed with world events through learning. Most basic emotions need not be expressed immediately after birth. Some - including CARE, LUST, and PLAY - come online long after others such as SEEKING, RAGE, and FEAR. The developmental timing reflects phylogenetic priority: the oldest and most survival-critical systems activate earliest.

Disgust sensitivity is adaptively calibrated to current physiological vulnerability. Women show increased disgust during the first trimester of pregnancy when the immune system is suppressed to tolerate paternal genetic material in the blastocyst. Salivary progesterone correlates positively with disgust sensitivity in normally cycling women - progesterone being the endocrine cue for immune downregulation. Opiate users, whose immune systems are pharmacologically suppressed, make fewer errors identifying disgust faces. Conversely, hunger downregulates disgust for food specifically while maintaining disgust for other pathogen cues - 15 hours of food deprivation reduced facial expressions of disgust to food but not to body wastes.

Females consistently score substantially higher on measures of disgust sensitivity than males across cultures. This sex difference likely reflects women's evolutionary history of responsibility for childcare - women need to be 'disgusted enough for two people' to keep dependent children free of disease. Disgust sensitivity is heritable and shows stable individual trait variation associated with neuroticism. Social learning modulates disgust in both directions: a 15-second verbal and visual display of disgust toward a novel object reduced infants' contact with the object for at least 1 hour in 14-month-olds, while positive attitudes by adults dissipated avoidance behaviors. The 'copy the frequent' heuristic for hygiene behavior can perpetuate either healthy or unhealthy practices.

ledger_replicated.quote: Contact with disgust elicitors, real or imagined, is associated with (i) a characteristic facial expression... (ii) behaviour patterns that include withdrawal, distancing, stopping or dropping the object of disgust... (iii) physiological changes including lowered blood pressure and galvanic skin response.
ledger_replicated.content: Disgust elicitors are universal across cultures: bodily wastes, body contents, sick/deformed/dead/unhygienic people. Contact with disgust elicitors produces a characteristic facial expression, withdrawal/distancing behaviors, and physiological changes including lowered blood pressure and galvanic skin response. Brain imaging reveals a specific neural disgust network including anterior insular cortex, basal ganglia, and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex. All societies demonstrate individual and group-level hygiene behaviors.

ledger_replicated.quote: Monkey grooming is not about removing fleas. Rather, it is about the intimacy of massage. The physical stimulation of the skin triggers the release of endorphins in the brain.
ledger_replicated.content: Primate grooming is not about removing fleas - it is about the intimacy of massage. Physical stimulation of the skin triggers endorphin release in the brain. Low-level pain associated with generalized stresses is dealt with by the endorphin system, creating a sense of wellbeing and relaxed contentedness. Grooming is the mechanism through which primate social bonds are maintained.

ledger_replicated.quote: Laughter - and I mean deep belly laughter, not the polite titters that tinkled among T.S. Eliot's teacups - is an extremely effective releaser of endorphins, probably because the physical effort of laughter's heaving chest is quite hard work for the muscles.
ledger_replicated.content: Laughter - deep belly laughter, not polite titters - is an extremely effective releaser of endorphins, probably because the physical effort is hard work for the muscles. Communal laughter creates a sense of bondedness that goes beyond tension release. Language evolved as a form of grooming at distance - 'I'd rather be here with you than over there with Jennifer.'

ledger_replicated.quote: The innermost group consists of about three to five people.
ledger_replicated.content: Friendship circles nest in a sequence scaling by factors of approximately three: innermost 5 (close confidants who provide emotional and physical support), then 15 (sympathy group, roughly jury size), 50 (typical hunter-gatherer overnight camp), 150 (Dunbar number, clan/tribal size), with additional layers at 500 and 1500. Each layer represents a qualitatively different type of social relationship with different obligations and investment requirements.

ledger_replicated.quote: A quick survey of available ethnography indicates how widespread shared care is among foraging peoples.
ledger_replicated.content: Ethnographic survey of shared care among foraging peoples: !Kung San babies have available the mother's entire social world with intense face-to-face interactions from girls. Trobriand Islanders routinely share infants who are suckled by lactating allomothers. Hadza babies under four are held by mothers 69% of the time and by allomothers the rest. These mothers trust others and allow them to take infants shortly after birth.

ledger_replicated.quote: But primates are unusual. Instead of decamping after they mate, fathers in most species in the order Primates remain year-round in the same social group as the mothers of their offspring.
ledger_replicated.content: Primates are unusual: instead of decamping after mating, fathers in most primate species remain in the same social group year-round. In New World monkeys like titi and night monkeys, fathers are primary attachment figures - infants are more attached to fathers than mothers. This establishes paternal care as an ancestral primate capacity, not a modern cultural invention.

Human application: like subordinate primates, lower-SES humans show elevated basal cortisol, impaired immune function, and accelerated cardiovascular disease. The Whitehall studies of British civil servants show employment grade predicts health outcomes independent of traditional risk factors (smoking, cholesterol, blood pressure account for less than a third of the social gradient in CVD).

ledger_replicated.quote: an epigenomic state of a gene can be established through behavioral programming, and it is potentially reversible.
ledger_replicated.content: Maternal licking/grooming and arched-back nursing in rats alters offspring epigenome at the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) gene promoter in the hippocampus via DNA methylation and histone acetylation changes. Offspring of high-LG mothers have lower glucocorticoid levels, less anxiety, better learning, and delayed brain aging. Methylation differences emerged over the first week of life, were reversed with cross-fostering, and persisted into adulthood. Central infusion of a histone deacetylase inhibitor removed group differences - demonstrating that an epigenomic state established through behavioral programming is potentially reversible.

ledger_replicated.quote: Offspring of mothers that showed high levels of LG and ABN were found to have differences in DNA methylation, as compared to offspring of low-LG-ABN mothers.
ledger_replicated.content: The specific epigenetic mechanism involves altered methylation at the NGFI-A transcription factor binding site in the GR promoter, changing GR expression in the hippocampus. This alters the negative feedback sensitivity of the HPA axis - high-LG offspring have more hippocampal GR, stronger negative feedback, and lower baseline glucocorticoid levels. The effect cascades: lower baseline stress hormones → less anxiety → better learning → delayed brain aging.

ledger_replicated.quote: methylation differences emerged over the first week of life, were reversed with cross-fostering, persisted into adulthood.
ledger_replicated.content: The cross-fostering experiment definitively proved that the epigenetic differences are caused by maternal behavior, not genetic inheritance. Pups born to low-LG mothers but raised by high-LG mothers developed the low-stress phenotype of their foster mothers, and vice versa. The pharmacological reversal via histone deacetylase inhibitor demonstrated that the epigenetic marks are modifiable even in adulthood, establishing that developmental calibration is potentially reversible - a finding with profound therapeutic implications.

Experimental demonstration of altruistic punishment: in repeated public-goods games, participants were willing to pay a personal cost to punish free-riders even when (a) punishment yielded no material benefit to the punisher, (b) interactions were one-shot with no reputational gain, and (c) the punisher would never meet the punished again. Fehr and Gächter's key design innovation was to eliminate all standard self-interest explanations (kin selection, direct reciprocity, reputation) and still observe robust punishment behavior. Across treatments, 84% of participants punished at least once. This falsifies purely selfish models of human cooperation.

Cooperation collapses without altruistic punishment, flourishes with it: in the no-punishment treatment, cooperation decayed from ~65% of endowment contributed in round 1 to ~20% by round 10 - the standard public-goods decay pattern. In the punishment treatment, cooperation rose to ~80-95% of endowment by round 10 and was maintained. The difference was dramatic and persistent. Critically, this held even in 'stranger' designs where group composition was reshuffled each round, eliminating any direct-reciprocity explanation. Cooperation is stable when and only when there exist mechanisms for punishing defectors - even at personal cost to the punisher.

ledger_replicated.quote: Human cooperation is an evolutionary puzzle. Unlike other creatures, people frequently cooperate with genetically unrelated strangers, often in large groups, with people they will never meet again, and when reputation gains are small or absent.
ledger_replicated.content: Altruistic punishment: individuals punish defectors at personal cost with no material gain. Cooperation flourishes when altruistic punishment is possible and breaks down when it is ruled out. Negative emotions toward defectors are the proximate mechanism behind altruistic punishment. Human cooperation with unrelated strangers in large groups cannot be explained by kin selection, signaling theory, or reciprocal altruism alone - altruistic punishment is a key additional mechanism.

Hrdy's identification of infanticide as widespread across primate taxa: infanticide by males is documented across many primate species, establishing it as a recurrent evolutionary pressure shaping female reproductive strategy across primates broadly, not a pathological anomaly of a few species. This cross-taxon distribution is load-bearing for P1 Inclusive Fitness and for M14 Reproductive Motivation's architectural shaping by infanticide risk.

ledger_replicated.quote: The most frequent type of power coalition in egalitarian bands consists of the entire adult community coalescing against a deviant. In addition to the proscription of bullying by upstarts, all foragers are opposed to incest, murder within the group, and undue selfish use of deception.
ledger_replicated.content: The entire moral community coalesces against deviants. All foragers oppose incest, murder within the group, and undue selfish use of deception. The most frequent type of power coalition in egalitarian bands consists of the entire adult community acting collectively against a deviant. The threat of sanctions (including ostracism and execution) keeps power seekers in their place. When upstartism becomes active, so does the moral community - it unites preemptively and assertively.

ledger_replicated.quote: In effect, the band keeps a dossier on every individual, noting positive and negative points. Group members exercise the right to take action if a deviant begins to intimidate other group members individually - or threatens the social equilibrium of the group or its very ability to function.
ledger_replicated.content: Gossip as information processing and social control: the band keeps a dossier on every individual, noting positive and negative points. Types of deviance that all groups watch for include murder, deception, theft, and stinginess. Everyone knows gossiping is constantly taking place and anyone can be a target - this knowledge serves as a deterrent, for most foragers worry about the opinion of their peers and try to exert self-control accordingly.

ledger_replicated.quote: those who have things of value but do not give are subject to social control through gossip, ridicule or ostracism.
ledger_replicated.content: Social control through gossip, ridicule, and ostracism targets free-riders: those who have things of value but do not give are subject to social control. Bullying free-riders are handled by egalitarian sanctioning. Other free-riders take advantage by being lazy, feigning injury, or secretly consuming meat they have killed. Much of the enforcement investment involves gossiping, which brings individual reproductive benefits through rewarding social interaction and exchange of information about subsistence.

Panksepp's textbook Affective Neuroscience establishes the methodology and evidence base for the seven subcortical affective systems. Across cross-species deep brain stimulation, lesion, and pharmacological studies, the same brain regions produce the same functional categories of affective response - SEEKING, FEAR, RAGE, LUST, CARE, PANIC, PLAY - across mammals, providing the empirical foundation for treating these as conserved motivational architecture rather than culturally constructed categories.

Empirical basis for the dissociation (1998 review): Berridge and Robinson review converging evidence that (a) dopamine depletion leaves taste hedonic reactions (orofacial 'liking' responses to sweet tastes) intact, (b) normal new hedonic learning proceeds without intact dopamine neurotransmission, (c) pharmacological hedonic enhancement of palatability is preserved after dopamine depletion, yet (d) dopamine depletion abolishes the motivation to pursue the same rewards. They conclude: dopamine systems are necessary for 'wanting' incentives, but not for 'liking' them or for learning new 'likes' and 'dislikes.'

ledger_replicated.quote: A very important neurochemical in this system is dopamine, especially the dopaminergic mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine circuits, which emanate from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) situated at the very back of the hypothalamus (Figure 3.6). These dopamine circuits tend to energize and coordinate the functions of many higher brain areas that mediate planning and foresight (such as the amygdala, nucleus accumbens, and frontal cortex - see next chapter) and promote states of eagerness and directed purpose in both humans and animals.
ledger_replicated.content: Panksepp's specific neuroanatomical claim for SEEKING: dopamine is the key neurochemical, specifically the mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine circuits emanating from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) at the back of the hypothalamus. These dopamine circuits energize and coordinate higher brain areas mediating planning and foresight - amygdala, nucleus accumbens, frontal cortex - and promote states of eagerness and directed purpose in both humans and animals. Amphetamines and cocaine produce their psychic appeal by temporarily overarousing this emotional system; opiates, nicotine, and alcohol also derive hedonic appeal from interacting with it. This is the specific anatomical substrate that load-bears M2 and DA4 (proxy hijacking by stimulant drugs).

ledger_replicated.quote: The RAGE system (see Chapter 10): Working in opposition to SEEKING is a system that mediates anger. RAGE is aroused by frustration and attempts to curtail an animal's freedom of action. It has long been known that one can enrage both animals and humans by stimulating very specific parts of the brain, which parallel the trajectory of the FEAR system. This system not only helps animals defend themselves by arousing fear in their opponents but also energizes behavior when an animal is irritated or restrained. Human anger may get much of its psychic "energy" from this brain system.
ledger_replicated.content: Panksepp's definition of the RAGE system: working in opposition to SEEKING, it mediates anger. RAGE is aroused by frustration and by attempts to curtail an animal's freedom of action. Electrical stimulation of specific brain regions paralleling the FEAR trajectory produces rage in both animals and humans. The system helps animals defend themselves by arousing fear in opponents, AND energizes behavior when an animal is irritated or restrained. Human anger gets much of its psychic 'energy' from this brain system. Brain tumors irritating the circuit cause pathological rage; damage to the system promotes serenity. This is the canonical primary-source definition for M1 Threat Management (rage component).

ledger_replicated.quote: The FEAR system (see Chapter 1 1): A FEAR circuit was probably designed during evolution to help animals reduce pain and the possibility of destruction. When stimulated intensely, this circuit leads animals to run away as if they are extremely scared. With very weak stimulation, animals exhibit just the opposite motor tendency - a freezing response, common when
ledger_replicated.content: Panksepp's definition of the FEAR system: a circuit designed during evolution to help animals reduce pain and the possibility of destruction. Intense stimulation makes animals run away as if extremely scared; weak stimulation produces the opposite motor tendency - freezing, common when animals are placed in circumstances where they have previously been hurt or frightened. Humans stimulated in these same brain areas report being engulfed by intense anxiety. This is the canonical primary-source evidence that fear is not a derived cognitive state but a hardwired affective circuit with specific neuroanatomy. Load-bearing for M1 Threat Management.

ledger_replicated.quote: especially the endogenous opioid peptides, are already known to modify feeling states in humans and corresponding behavioral changes in animals.
ledger_replicated.content: Panksepp's original discovery linking endogenous opioids to separation distress: brain opioids (especially beta-endorphin and enkephalins) modulate social feelings and separation distress, AND opioids promote social bonding. Oxytocin and opioids work together to inhibit separation distress. This is Panksepp's foundational finding that attachment pain shares neural substrates with physical pain - the 'social pain' hypothesis at the molecular level. Load-bearing for M3 Social Bonding, DA8 Phylogenetic Priority (opioid system is ancient), and for reading depression/grief as dysregulation of an opioid-modulated affective circuit rather than a purely cognitive state.
ledger_replicated.where: Chapter 6 'Neurochemical Maps of the Brain' pp. ~101

ledger_replicated.quote: oxytocin, which mediates various pro-social processes, including maternal behavior and the inhibition of separation distress (Chapters 12 to 14), can yield a tripeptide called PLG (proline-leucine-glycine), which mediates none of the above but has antidepressant effects.
ledger_replicated.content: Panksepp's early summary of oxytocin's pro-social functions: oxytocin mediates various pro-social processes including female sexual response, orgasm, maternal behavior, social memory, and the INHIBITION of separation distress. It is a single neuropeptide that operates across the sexual-maternal-social-bonding domains - exactly the molecular overlap that allows evolution to construct the 'social contract' by repurposing reproductive circuits for broader bonding. ledger_replicated.content: Passivity is the default, not learned. The original learned helplessness theory got it backward. Passivity in response to prolonged aversive events is the unlearned default response, not a learned expectation of uncontrollability. The neural evidence shows that aversive shock per se activates serotonergic (5-HT) neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus regardless of controllability. Both escapable and inescapable shock produce equal excitatory input to the DRN. There is nothing in the brain selectively turned on by lack of control - only something that turns things off when control is present.

Dorsal raphe nucleus 5-HT activation is both necessary and sufficient for passivity/anxiety. Three experimental strategies converge: (1) blocking DRN activation during inescapable shock (via lesion or pharmacological agents) prevents passivity - subjects behave as nonshocked controls; (2) preventing desensitization of 5-HT1A autoreceptors during inescapable shock also eliminates passivity; (3) blocking 5-HT receptors in target regions (amygdala, PAG) during testing eliminates passivity and fear. For sufficiency: directly activating DRN via microinjected GABA antagonist picrotoxin or benzodiazepine antagonist beta-carboline produces the full behavioral syndrome of inescapable shock without any shock at all.

Control is detected via vmPFC-DMS circuit, then vmPFC inhibits dorsal raphe. Two separable prelimbic cortex functions identified: (1) DETECT - a prelimbic-dorsomedial striatum (DMS) circuit detects contingency between response and outcome (the presence of control); (2) ACT - separate prelimbic neurons project to DRN and inhibit 5-HT neurons via GABAergic interneurons. Retrograde tracing confirmed these are distinct neuronal populations - no colocalization. Inactivating the vmPFC-to-DRN pathway during escapable shock makes the animal react as if shock were inescapable despite perfect escape performance. Activating this pathway during inescapable shock makes the animal react as if shock were escapable.

Experience of control produces lasting immunization via plasticity in vmPFC-DRN pathway. Prior escapable shock prevents passivity/anxiety from later inescapable shock even in completely different situations (trans-situational). This 'immunization' requires new protein synthesis in the prelimbic cortex - blocking protein synthesis after escapable shock eliminates immunization but not the immediate protective effect of control. The escapable shock experience induces plasticity proteins (e.g., phosphorylated ERK) in prelimbic neurons projecting to DRN, increasing their excitability. After immunization, even inescapable shock now activates the prelimbic-DRN inhibitory pathway as if the shock were escapable - the circuit now EXPECTs control.

Oxytocin (OT) operates through three distinct but neurobiologically consistent mechanisms to support human affiliative bonds. (a) Parent-infant bonding: maternal OT levels measured in the first trimester predicted postpartum behavior (gaze, positive affect, motherese, affectionate touch); OT was stable within individuals across pregnancy; fathers showed comparable baseline OT to mothers and active paternal care activated the OT system. OT administration to fathers increased their touch behavior AND independently increased infant salivary OT, RSA, social gaze, and toy exploration - demonstrating cross-dyadic transmission. (b) Pair bonding: new romantic partners showed significantly higher plasma OT than singles, even higher than new parents; OT correlated with interactive synchrony (social focus, positive affect, affectionate touch) and was stable over six months. (c) Group affiliation: OT was linked to children's best-friend relationship quality and broader social engagement. Across all bond types, OT levels showed "biological synchrony" between partners - mother-father OT was inter-correlated, parent-infant OT was inter-related, and romantic partners' OT levels were concordant.

In a study of 112 parents and their 4-6 month olds, active parental touch triggered measurable OT responses. Mothers providing high levels of affectionate touch (>66% of interaction time) showed increased salivary OT from pre- to post-interaction, while mothers providing minimal touch (<33%) showed no such increase. Fathers who provided high levels of stimulatory contact (moving child's limbs, throwing infant in air) similarly increased their OT levels, but those engaging in minimal stimulatory touch did not. Risk alleles on the OXTR rs2254298 and CD38 rs3796863 SNPs were associated with both lower plasma OT and reduced parental affectionate touch, paralleling findings of high vs. low licking-and-grooming rat dams.

Cross-generational transmission of the oxytocin system operates through parenting behavior rather than genetics alone. In a study of parents and 6-month-old infants, parent-infant OT levels were inter-related at both baseline and following contact, and the degree of OT increase was correlated between parent and child. Critically, parent-infant behavioral synchrony moderated the intergenerational effect: when synchrony was high, parent-child OT concordance was strong; when synchrony was low, no association emerged. Adults' retrospective accounts of warm parental care in childhood predicted higher current plasma OT. Risk alleles on OXTR and CD38 predicted lower OT, less affectionate touch, and shorter episodes of gaze synchrony. Mothers and fathers who reported more positive care in their own childhood provided more affectionate touch to their infants.

Bio-behavioral synchrony is the mechanism by which organisms become members of a social group. Among mammalian species, dyad-specific maternal-infant bonds are built on repeatedly experienced patterns of sensory, motor, and behavioral cues. Human mothers provide approximately 70% of their social behaviors during the 7% of the time newborns spend in alert-scanning state, creating temporal contingencies between infant state and maternal social behavior from the first post-birth hours. These social contingencies are supported by physiological periodicities maturing in the fetus during the third trimester: the biological clock and cardiac pacemaker. As soon as the human infant is born, it can experience a temporal match between its own state and the response of the social environment. This early temporal concordance is a critical human addition to the physiological provisions embedded in maternal proximity in other mammals.

ledger_replicated.quote: Each layer increases relationship numbers by an approximate multiple of 3 (5-15-50-150) but decreasing levels of intimacy (strong, medium, and weak ties) and frequency of interaction.
ledger_replicated.content: Personal social networks consist of hierarchically inclusive nested layers of approximately 5/15/50/150 individuals, each layer roughly 3x the previous. Support group (~5): individuals from whom one would seek personal advice in severe distress. Sympathy group (~15): people whose sudden death would be greatly upsetting, contacted at least monthly. Affinity group (~50): casual but close friends. Active network (~150): total recognized and annually interacted with.
ledger_replicated.where: British Journal of Psychology 103(2):149-168. DOI: 10.1111/j.2044-8295.2011.02061.x. PMID: 22506741. Abstract-limited.

ledger_replicated.content: Approximately 40% of available social time is devoted to the innermost 5 people (support clique), and another 20% to the next 10 (completing the sympathy group of 15). Two-thirds of total social time goes to just 15 people, despite having ~150 in the active network.
ledger_replicated.where: British Journal of Psychology 103(2):149-168, citing Roberts et al and other empirical sources

ledger_replicated.content: The behavioral immune system's functional flexibility operates at both individual and societal levels. At the individual level, people with chronically higher 'germ aversion' report chronically lower extraversion, and pathogen salience causes reduced extraversion and avoidant motor movements toward pictures of people. At the societal level, countries with higher historical pathogen prevalence show lower population-level extraversion, lower openness to experience, and higher collectivism. The culinary spice usage pattern illustrates this: spices are natural antibiotics, and their use in food preparation is more common under ecological circumstances of high pathogen prevalence, reflecting the cost-benefit calculus of pathogen defense across populations.

At a population level, cross-national data show higher historical pathogen prevalence predicts lower extraversion, lower openness to experience, and higher collectivism (r=0.73 for collectivism-pathogen correlation, Fincher et al. 2008), with correlations surviving controls for latitude, climate, and socioeconomic status. Culinary spice usage illustrates the population-level cost-benefit calculus: spices are natural antibiotics, and their use in food preparation is more common under ecological circumstances of high pathogen prevalence. Women in first trimester of pregnancy show heightened ethnocentrism and xenophobia (Navarrete et al. 2007), consistent with upregulated behavioral immune responses during adaptive immunosuppression.

ledger_replicated.quote: We estimated the proportion of variance for human height explained by 294,831 SNPs genotyped on 3,925 unrelated individuals using a linear model analysis, and validated the estimation method by simulations based upon the observed genotype data. We show that 45% of variance can be explained by considering all SNPs simultaneously. Thus, most of the heritability is not missing but has not previously been detected because the individual effects are too small to pass stringent significance tests.
ledger_replicated.content: The founding GCTA result: estimating genetic variance directly from 294,831 common SNPs genotyped in 3,925 unrelated individuals recovers 45% of the variance in height, with no twin or family structure anywhere in the design. Heritability estimated by twin and family designs is real and hiding in many variants of individually small effect rather than missing. This is the molecular leg of C15, a method family fully independent of the other two; the SNP-heritability approach has since been replicated across traits and cohorts throughout complex-trait genetics.

ledger_replicated.quote: play fighting typically involves the use of behavior patterns from other, functional contexts, is the nape nuzzling of rats derived from serious fighting or from some other form of social behavior? In chapter 2, we will characterize the aggressive and the sexual and non-sexual amicable behavior of rats and place playful nape nuzzling in an appropriate context.
ledger_replicated.content: Pellis & Pellis's 1987 foundational finding: play-fighting in rats differs from serious fighting in both the TARGET of attack (the nape of the neck in play vs other body regions in serious fighting) and the TACTICS of fighting (role reversal between attacker and defender in play vs persistent asymmetry in serious fighting). This is the load-bearing behavioral-marker finding for identifying play as a real behavioral category distinct from aggression - not merely 'low-intensity fighting' but a qualitatively different behavior with its own rules and developmental trajectory.

ledger_replicated.quote: Ablation of the orbital frontal cortex (OFC) produces subordinate rats that fail to make this discrimination; these rats are most likely to use the partial rotation tactic, irrespective of the social status of their partner. What is more, OFC-damaged rats also fail to adjust their responses depending on the identity of their social partners in non-play social interactions. The OFC thus seems critical in modulating social responses in a way that is sensitive to the identity of the partner.
ledger_replicated.content: Pellis lab finding: ablation of the orbital frontal cortex (OFC) in rats produces animals that fail to discriminate social partners - they use the same defensive tactics regardless of whether their partner is a dominant or subordinate male, and they fail to adjust responses by partner identity in non-play social interactions too. This is the specific neuroanatomical evidence that the OFC is load-bearing for social-partner-sensitive behavioral calibration - the exact mechanism M4 Social Calibration/Play depends on.
ledger_replicated.where: Chapter 4 'So, What Does Playing Buy You?' pp. ~90

ledger_replicated.quote: Play deprivation leads to a reduction in the ability of the animal to formulate and engage behavioral options dependent on the executive functions of the prefrontal cortex - the same kinds of problems that animals have when they are reared normally but are subjected to experimental damage of their prefrontal cortex. Complementary to these findings is our demonstration of play fighting experience changing the anatomy of neurons in this area of the cortex.
ledger_replicated.content: Play deprivation leads to a reduction in behavioral options that depend on prefrontal-cortex executive functions - the same kinds of deficits produced by experimental PFC damage in normally-reared rats. Play-deprived rats show cognitive, sexual, and social deficits. This directly parallels the PFC-damage phenotype, giving a functional bridge between play experience and PFC development: play shapes the circuits, and the circuits mediate social competence.
ledger_replicated.where: Chapter 4 'So, What Does Playing Buy You?' pp. ~92

ledger_replicated.quote: In rats, play fighting is not limited to the juvenile period - although it is most frequent at that age - and seems to be used to achieve both delayed and immediate benefits. By engaging in play fighting, both juveniles and adults can regulate their stress response. That is, by playing, the animals can calm themselves following a frightening, but not too frightening, experience. In addition, male adult rats use play fighting as a means of social assessment and manipulation in the context of dominance relationships. Thus, in at least two ways, play fighting provides the rats with immediate benefits.
ledger_replicated.content: Pellis's synthesis: play fighting has BOTH delayed benefits (social competence developing over the juvenile period) AND immediate benefits (stress regulation in both juveniles and adults). By engaging in play, animals can calm themselves following frightening but not too-frightening experiences. Adult male rats also use play fighting as social-assessment and manipulation in dominance relationships. This dual-timescale functionality challenges the common definition of play as 'behavior without immediate purpose' and is load-bearing for M4's cascade structure.

ledger_replicated.quote: Not all the deficits that arise from lack of play fighting experience in the juvenile period require the actual physical contact afforded by play fighting. When deprived of play fighting experience as juveniles, rats show a range of cognitive, sexual, and social deficits. As shown by Dorothy Einon and her colleagues, juveniles reared in social isolation grow into cognitively competent adults if they have but one hour per day of exposure to a peer, with whom the majority of the time is spent in play fighting. In the 1950s, the Forgays showed that if rats that had been reared in social isolation as juveniles were given the opportunity to watch normally raised juveniles engage in peer interactions, they would also grow into adults that were not cognitively challenged. Thus, for rats, merely observing other rats play fighting is enough to protect their developing brains from the ill effects of being raised in isolation. But watching other rats engage in normal interactions seems to be insufficient for these rats to develop normal sexual competency, or the ability to execute socially coordinated actions.
ledger_replicated.content: Critical methodological finding: not all the deficits from play deprivation can be explained by a single mechanism. Rats reared in social isolation but given an hour a day of peer exposure (with most of that time in play fighting) grow into cognitively competent adults. Rats that merely WATCH normally-raised juveniles also recover cognitive function. BUT watching is insufficient for normal sexual competency or socially coordinated action - those require actual play-fighting experience. Guinea pigs show a different pattern (watching sexual play is sufficient for sexual competency). This dissociation demonstrates that play fighting has multiple developmental functions operating through different mechanisms.
ledger_replicated.where: Chapter 4 'So, What Does Playing Buy You?' pp. ~89

ledger_replicated.quote: During the juvenile period, play fighting is organized in such a manner as to maximize the experience of losing and regaining control over one's own body and that of one's play partner. A lack of such experience leads to a reduction in social competence, as does brain damage to specific brain areas. Conversely, this juvenile experience alters the organization of those same areas of the brain. That is, experience in play fighting in the juvenile period
ledger_replicated.content: Pellis synthesis at chapter-summary level: social competence can be compromised by two distinct mechanisms - either by lack of play fighting experience during the juvenile period OR by brain damage to specific prefrontal and amygdala regions. These two mechanisms produce similar phenotypes (failure to discriminate social partners, failed reciprocity, escalation to serious fighting), confirming that play fighting is not incidentally correlated with social-competence development but is causally necessary for it.

ledger_replicated.quote: In our studies, the lonely, both young and old, perceived the hassles and stresses of everyday life to be more severe than did their nonlonely counterparts, even though the objective stressors they encountered were essentially the same. Compounding the problem, the lonely found the small social uplifts of everyday life to be less intense and less gratifying.
ledger_replicated.content: In our studies, the lonely, both young and old, perceived the hassles and stresses of everyday life to be more severe than did their nonlonely counterparts, even though the objective stressors they encountered were essentially the same. The lonely also found the small social uplifts of everyday life to be less intense and less gratifying. The presence of and interaction with other people in their lives did not cause them to rate the severity of everyday stressors any less intensely.

ledger_replicated.quote: recent evidence indicates that dopamine is neither necessary nor sufficient to mediate changes in hedonic 'liking' for sensory pleasures. Dopamine appears necessary for normal 'wanting', and dopamine activation can be sufficient to enhance cue-triggered incentive salience. Drugs of abuse that promote dopamine signals short circuit and sensitize dynamic mesolimbic mechanisms that evolved to attribute incentive salience to rewards.

ledger_replicated.quote: dopamine depletion caused a suppression of subjective ratings of wanting/desire to take more cocaine, but left subjective liking ratings for cocaine pleasure essentially unchanged (Leyton et al. 2005)... In several psychopharmacological studies, Brauer and colleagues (especially deWit) reported that dopamine blockade by neuroleptic antagonists may suppress wanting ratings or behavioral consumption of amphetamine or cigarettes, yet leave subjective liking ratings for the drugs untouched
ledger_replicated.content: In normal human volunteers, temporary dietary manipulation to deplete brain dopamine levels (via ingestion of a deficient amino acid mixture) caused a dopamine-induced dissociation between subjective liking and wanting for intranasally administered cocaine. Dopamine depletion caused a suppression of subjective ratings of wanting/desire to take more cocaine, but left subjective liking ratings for cocaine pleasure essentially unchanged. Several psychopharmacological studies have similarly reported that dopamine blockade by neuroleptic antagonists may suppress wanting ratings or behavioral consumption of amphetamine or cigarettes, yet leave subjective liking ratings for the drugs untouched. Dopamine appears to correspond more closely to ratings of reward wanting than to reward liking.
ledger_replicated.where: Section 'Analysis of hedonia hypothesis,' Leyton et al. 2005 and Brauer/de Wit studies, pp. 397-398

ledger_replicated.quote: Phasic DA transmission is the short-lasting and impulse-dependent release that appears as a consequence of neural burst firing (Gonon, 1988; Suaud-Chagny et al., 1992). Following such bursts, high levels of DA molecules are released into the synaptic cleft at up to mM concentration (Garris et al., 1994), and then rapidly removed via a re-uptake system (Floresco et al. 2003). To the contrary, tonic DA levels are diffused in the extracellular space outside the synaptic clefts, but exist in very small concentrations (in the nM range), and change relatively slowly (Grace, 2000).
ledger_replicated.content: The physiological basis for M2's mixed activation profile: dopamine transmission runs in two modes. Phasic release is short-lasting, impulse-dependent, cue and reward-prediction locked; tonic extracellular dopamine sits at low concentration and changes slowly, carrying a background level of appetitive engagement that varies with state (sleep-wake, arousal). For activation_class this grounds tonic_baseline as M2's primary class with event_triggered phasic spikes as secondary; the phasic incentive-salience side is already carried in C6 by Berridge.
ledger_replicated.where: Section 2.5, Electric activity of DA cells

ledger_replicated.quote: Americans and Australians believed their countries were egalitarian so there would be no social-class difference there. They were wrong. In North America and Australia the differences are as big as, if not bigger, than they are in Britain. Scandinavians said they had no class differences in health, until they looked and found that this phenomenon went deeper and wider than class-ridden Britain. Many continental European countries were slower at picking up on this story, because they did not have the data systems in place. When they looked, they too found a clear social gradient in health. When the doors opened on the former communist countries of Europe, we found big and growing social differences in health within those countries as well as a growing gap in health between them and the flourishing countries of Western Europe. Even in Japan, whose health record is the envy of the world, we find evidence of the status syndrome.
ledger_replicated.content: The social gradient in health is as big as, if not bigger than, it is in Britain in North America and Australia, despite those countries believing themselves to be egalitarian. Even in Japan, whose overall health record is the envy of the world, the status syndrome is found. The findings of a health gradient are remarkably general across developed countries with different health systems, cultures, and political arrangements.

ledger_replicated.quote: The resultant PRC of the midpoint of the melatonin rhythm revealed a characteristic type 1 PRC with a significant peak-to-trough amplitude of 5.02 h. Phase delays occurred when the light stimulus was centred prior to the critical phase at the core body temperature minimum, phase advances occurred when the light stimulus was centred after the critical phase, and no phase shift occurred at the critical phase.
ledger_replicated.content: Definitive characterization of the human phase-response curve (PRC) to single bright-light pulses. Light before the core-body-temperature minimum delays the clock, light after it advances the clock, and there is no phase shift exactly at the critical phase; the melatonin-midpoint PRC has a peak-to-trough amplitude of 5.02 h with no prolonged photic dead zone during the subjective day. Grounds the core M7 claim that light is the entraining signal and that its effect is timing-dependent, so mistimed evening light actively mis-sets the clock.

ledger_replicated.quote: An evolved module for fear elicitation and fear learning with 4 characteristics is proposed.
ledger_replicated.content: Evolved fear module with four characteristics: (a) preferentially activated by phylogenetically relevant stimuli (snakes, spiders, angry faces) in aversive contexts; (b) activation is automatic and pre-attentive; (c) relatively impenetrable to cognitive control (resistant to verbal instruction); (d) originates in dedicated amygdala-centered neural circuitry. Module mediates emotional fear learning dissociable from cognitive learning of stimulus relationships.

ledger_replicated.quote: The fear module is assumed to mediate an emotional level of fear learning that is relatively independent and dissociable from cognitive learning of stimulus relationships.
ledger_replicated.content: Visual search reveals pre-attentive threat detection: snake/spider targets among flower/mushroom distractors detected faster (~615ms) than reverse (~704ms). Fear-relevant detection unaffected by display size (parallel/pop-out processing, slope ~6ms/item). Fear-irrelevant targets show serial search (slope ~15ms/item). Conditioning to fear-relevant stimuli resists verbal instruction to extinguish; backward-masked fear-relevant conditioned stimuli elicit electrodermal responses without conscious awareness.
ledger_replicated.where: Psychological Review 108(3):483-522 and Öhman, Flykt & Esteves 2001 visual search study

ledger_replicated.quote: Contrary to expectations, we found that half of the maximal phase-delaying response achieved in response to a single episode of evening bright light (∼9000 lux (lx)) can be obtained with just over 1 % of this light (dim room light of ∼100 lx). The same held true for the acute suppressive effects of light on plasma melatonin concentrations. This indicates that even small changes in ordinary light exposure during the late evening hours can significantly affect both plasma melatonin concentrations and the entrained phase of the human circadian pacemaker.
ledger_replicated.content: Dose-response study of the human circadian pacemaker to evening light. Half of the maximal phase delay and half of the maximal melatonin suppression produced by bright evening light (about 9000 lux) were obtained with just over 1 percent of that intensity, about 100 lux of dim room light, both following a logistic dose-response curve. Ordinary indoor evening light is therefore enough to suppress melatonin and shift circadian phase, putting M7's indoor (ATTENUATED) and evening-screen (DEFEATED) rungs on direct dose-response evidence.

ledger_replicated.quote: First Law. All human behavioral traits are heritable. Second Law. The effect of being raised in the same family is smaller than the effect of genes. Third Law. A substantial portion of the variation in complex human behavioral traits is not accounted for by the effects of genes or families.
ledger_replicated.content: Turkheimer's canonical compression of five decades of behavior-genetic findings into three laws. For DA10 the first law states the heritable-variation claim across all human behavioral traits; the second and third laws carry the guard rail: shared family environment accounts for less variance than genes, and a substantial residual is accounted for by neither, so heritability describes population variance partitioning, not individual determinism. Later quantitatively confirmed at scale by Polderman et al. 2015.

ledger_replicated.quote: the self-esteem system monitors others' reactions and alerts the individual to the possibility of social exclusion
ledger_replicated.content: Five studies supported the sociometer model: state self-esteem functions as an internal gauge that continuously tracks the individual's perceived relational value (social inclusion versus exclusion) and falls when cues signal potential social devaluation. Self-esteem is the read-out of the monitor rather than an end to be maximized; people act to protect standing. Supplies the measurement axis of M5 - how the organism reads its own position - which the mechanism previously lacked. (Relational value spans both belonging (M3) and rank (M5); tagged to M5 as the standing-monitor per this ingestion pass.)

ledger_replicated.quote: This article explores the possibility that romantic love is an attachment process--a biosocial process by which affectional bonds are formed between adult lovers, just as affectional bonds are formed earlier in life between human infants and their parents.
ledger_replicated.content: Adult romantic love is an attachment process: affectional bonds form between adult lovers just as between infants and parents. Three adult attachment styles parallel Ainsworth's infant categories. Distribution: ~56% secure, ~25% avoidant, ~19% anxious-ambivalent (N=620 in Study 1), closely matching infant distributions (~62/23/15%). Secure adults describe relationships as happy, friendly, trusting. Avoidant adults fear closeness and doubt romantic love exists. Anxious adults experience love as obsessive with constant abandonment worry.

ledger_replicated.quote: attachment style is related in theoretically meaningful ways to mental models of self and social relationships and to relationship experiences with parents.
ledger_replicated.content: Attachment style is related to mental models of self and relationships and to childhood relationship memories. Secure adults recall parents as respectful and accepting. Anxious adults remember intermittently available parents. Avoidant adults recall critical and distant parents. Continuity of style is due in part to Bowlby's internal working models - cognitive representations of self and others formed in early relationships that persist and shape adult relational patterns.

ledger_replicated.quote: Mothers of the securely attached (Group B) babies were, throughout the first year, more sensitively responsive to infant signals than were the mothers of the two anxiously attached groups.
ledger_replicated.content: Feeding does not determine attachment. No evidence that methods of feeding significantly affected infant development. Instead, sensitive maternal responsiveness to infant signals determines attachment security. Securely attached infants develop working models of mother as accessible and responsive - therein lies security. Insecurely attached infants whose signals were disregarded have no basis for believing mother is responsive, consequently they are anxious.
ledger_replicated.where: American Psychologist 34(10):932-937, sensitivity and working models section

ledger_replicated.quote: The distribution’s mean value is systematically different with age, shifting later during adolescence, showing a peak in ‘lateness’ at ~19 years, and shifting earlier thereafter. Men are typically later chronotypes than women before 40, but earlier types after 40.
ledger_replicated.content: First nationally representative estimate of the US chronotype distribution, from 12 years of American Time Use Survey diaries (n=53,689, chronotype = weekend mid-sleep). Chronotype is near-normally distributed and spans almost 10 hours; the mean shifts later through adolescence to a peak in lateness at about 19 years and earlier thereafter, and men are later chronotypes than women before 40 but earlier after. Adolescents are on average the latest chronotypes, which the authors note supports later school start times. Grounds M7's social-jetlag (PARTIAL) rung: fixed social and school schedules collide with a wide, developmentally shifting range of internal circadian phase, and the resolution condition is aligning schedule to internal time.

ledger_replicated.quote: Sleep deprived people are perceived as less attractive, less healthy, and more tired compared with when they are well rested.
ledger_replicated.content: Sleep deprivation is visible in the phenotype: independent judges rate sleep-deprived individuals as less healthy, less attractive, and more fatigued than well-rested individuals from photographs alone. On Cor's reading (not something the study tested, since it measured only perceived health and attractiveness), this makes sleep a phenotypic fitness signal: the physiological state produced by adequate sleep is visible to potential mates and social partners, and sleep loss degrades that signal.
